article_title: Conceptual Frameworks for Intentional Approaches to Improving Economic Security and Child Well-Being
citation: Teresa Eckrich Sommer, P. Lindsay Chase-Lansdale, Emily Sama-Miller, Christine Ross, Scott Baumgartner. (2017). Conceptual Frameworks for Intentional Approaches to Improving Economic Security and Child Well-Being. Washington, DC: Office of Planning, Research and Evaluation, Administration for Children and Families, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. https://www.acf.hhs.gov/opre
title: Design combined parent-child programs around mutually reinforcing outcomes
description: The brief holds that programs combining services for low-income parents and children should be understood in terms of how their services relate to "mutually reinforcing outcomes for parents and children." Designing and studying such programs around the linkage between the two generations' outcomes is presented as central to intentional combined approaches.
requirements: Services for both parents and children within the same program approach
target_learning_goals: economic security for parents
child well-being

article_title: Re-Imagining Accountability in K-12 Education: A Behavioral Science Perspective
citation: Brian P. Gill, Jennifer S. Lerner, Paul Meosky. (2015). Re-Imagining Accountability in K-12 Education: A Behavioral Science Perspective. Working Paper 39, Cambridge, MA: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Design school accountability regimes with multiple forms of accountability, multiple measures, and feedback mechanisms
description: The paper's central design recommendation is that an effective accountability regime for schools should combine several elements rather than rely on test-based sanctions alone. It concludes that effective accountability "will involve (1) multiple forms of accountability, (2) multiple measures of educational practice and educational outcomes, and (3) feedback mechanisms to promote the improvement of practice." This multi-pronged structure is offered as the design implication of the behavioral science literature reviewed in the paper.
requirements: Accountability must extend beyond a single high-stakes testing regime to include varied accountability forms
constraints: Grounded in the behavioral literature as interpreted by the authors; the available text prints no empirical test of the combined design
target_learning_goals: Improving school performance and educational practice through better-designed accountability
examples: The paper's conclusion specifies the three-part structure: multiple forms, multiple measures of practice and outcomes, and feedback mechanisms to improve practice
key_sources: Brian P. Gill, Jennifer S. Lerner, Paul Meosky. (2015). Re-Imagining Accountability in K-12 Education: A Behavioral Science Perspective. Working Paper 39, Cambridge, MA: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/reimagining-accountability-in-k12-education-a-behavioral-science-perspective

article_title: Reimagining Accountability in K-12 Education
citation: Brian P. Gill, Jennifer S. Lerner, Paul Meosky. (2016). Reimagining Accountability in K-12 Education. Behavioral Science and Policy Association, vol. 2, issue 1. https://behavioralsciencepolicy.org
title: Combine multiple, complementary forms of accountability to support continuous improvement
description: The review concludes that policymakers should "use multiple, complementary forms of accountability, creating a complete system that encourages and supports the continuous improvement of educational practice." Rather than relying on a single form such as outcome-based high-stakes testing, the recommendation is to combine forms so their distinct motivational mechanisms complement one another. This follows from the review's analysis of favorable and unfavorable effects of each form.
requirements: State-level discretion over accountability design, as provided by the Every Student Succeeds Act
target_learning_goals: continuous improvement of educational practice
examples: The review's third concluding recommendation is a complete system combining complementary accountability forms.
key_sources: Brian P. Gill, Jennifer S. Lerner, Paul Meosky. (2016). Reimagining Accountability in K-12 Education. Behavioral Science and Policy Association, vol. 2, issue 1. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/reimagining-accountability-in-k12-education

article_title: Using Student Achievement Data to Support Instructional Decision Making
citation: Hamilton, L., Halverson, R., Jackson, S., Mandinach, E., Supovitz, J., & Wayman, J. (2009). Using student achievement data to support instructional decision making (NCEE 2009-4067). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. Retrieved from http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/publications/practiceguides/
title: Use multiple data sources and triangulation because no single assessment suffices
description: The guide recommends gathering annual, interim, and classroom-level data and interpreting them together. "Triangulation" is defined as "the process of using multiple data sources to address a particular question or problem and using evidence from each source to illuminate or temper evidence from the other sources". When multiple sources show similar strengths and weaknesses, teachers can be more confident in their decisions; when tests disagree, teachers should examine items to identify the discrepancy.
requirements: Prepare data in aggregate forms that address teachers' own questions and highlight patterns
Supplement annual state results with beginning-of-year information since students' skills may have changed
constraints: Classroom-level assignments, conditions, and scores are not generally comparable across classrooms
target_learners: K-12 teachers and school data teams
target_learning_goals: Identifying class-wide and individual strengths and weaknesses to allocate instructional time and adapt assignments
examples: A teacher tracking four waves of interim math data by performance quartile on a line graph, ensuring each quartile group contained numerous students so results were not driven by outliers
key_sources: Hamilton, L., Halverson, R., Jackson, S., Mandinach, E., Supovitz, J., & Wayman, J. (2009). Using student achievement data to support instructional decision making (NCEE 2009-4067). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. Retrieved from https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/12

article_title: Supporting Success: Attendance Solutions for Multilingual Students
citation: Gisela Ariza, Attendance Works; Hedy Chang, Attendance Works. (2024). Supporting Success: Attendance Solutions for Multilingual Students. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Multifaceted barrier profile shaping multilingual learners' attendance: communication, health care, trauma, safety fears, curriculum relevance, family responsibilities, and illness clarity
description: The brief enumerates a set of challenges that keep multilingual learners out of school, beyond pandemic-era job loss and limited technology access. Its list includes "ineffective communication from districts and schools," "limited access to health care for students and their families," trauma and anxiety, fears of bullying and lack of school safety among immigrant students, lack of linguistically and culturally relevant curricula, family work responsibilities, social–emotional challenges for newcomers, and family uncertainty about sending ill children to school. It presents this profile as the basis for targeted interventions at every educational stage.
requirements: Schools must recognize that these diverse challenges continue to exist in the postpandemic era to implement targeted interventions supporting English learners at every stage of their educational journeys
constraints: The barrier list is a descriptive synthesis citing external sources rather than a tested finding of this brief
target_learners: English learners / multilingual learners in U.S. K–12 schools, including newcomers and refugees
target_learning_goals: Regular school attendance and engagement
examples: The brief cites sources on pandemic-era job loss, digital divide effects, and immigration enforcement fears as evidence for specific barriers
key_sources: Gisela Ariza, Attendance Works; Hedy Chang, Attendance Works. (2024). Supporting Success: Attendance Solutions for Multilingual Students. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED663795

article_title: Navigating a Sea of Reforms: Sustaining School Health Centers through Statewide Initiatives
citation: Eisenberg, L., Sabalburo, E., & Ford, J. (2025). Navigating a sea of reforms: Sustaining school health centers through statewide initiatives. Alameda County Health, Healthy Schools and Communities. https://WestEd.org
title: Multi-Payer School-Linked Fee Schedule
description: The Fee Schedule is "a new, optional program that reimburses local educational agencies (LEAs) and school-linked designated providers for mental health and substance use disorder services provided to students 25 years of age or younger at or near a school site." It requires commercial and Medi-Cal managed care plans to reimburse school-based and school-linked providers, covering psychoeducation, screening and assessments, therapy, and case management. LEAs enroll in cohorts and may designate contracted or affiliate providers, with claims administered by Carelon.
requirements: Community-based providers such as SHC lead agencies must participate through an LEA enrolled as a Fee Schedule provider
LEAs must enroll as providers and designate other providers as contracted or affiliate members of their network
constraints: Outcomes of participation are still largely unknown; as of December 2024 only a small number of LEAs statewide had successfully submitted a claim
The program is not intended to replace existing service delivery covered by Medi-Cal specialty and nonspecialty mental health systems
target_learners: Students age 25 or younger receiving services at or near school sites
target_learning_goals: Access to mental health and substance use disorder services regardless of insurance type
examples: Six Alameda County districts with SHCs enrolled in Cohorts 1 and 2 (January and July 2024); five SHCs' potential revenue was estimated in Table 1
key_sources: Eisenberg, L., Sabalburo, E., & Ford, J. (2025). Navigating a sea of reforms: Sustaining school health centers through statewide initiatives. Alameda County Health, Healthy Schools and Communities. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673564

article_title: Codesigning Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education with Families and Communities
citation: Jahneille Cunningham, Rebecca Colina Neri, and Carlos Sandoval. (2024). Codesigning Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education With Families and Communities. WestEd brief. https://education.uw.edu/sites/default/files/programs/epsc/Users%20Guide%20Road%20Map%20Survey.pdf
title: Treat learning as multidirectional: school leaders and teachers should provide ample space to learn from and with families and communities
description: This principle holds that educators must not prioritize school-based knowledge in ways that devalue learning outside school. The brief urges that school leaders and teachers "provide ample space to learn from and with families, caregivers, and other respected leaders in the community," because "learning should be multidirectional." It is one of four recommendations for codesigning CRSE in mathematics.
requirements: A shift in educator mindsets and practices, and sustained, meaningful school–family partnerships, to welcome alternative ways of knowing and doing mathematics
constraints: The brief warns that prioritizing school-based knowledge can unintentionally undermine or devalue learning that takes place outside of the school context
target_learners: K-12 mathematics students and their families and communities
target_learning_goals: Mathematics learning that bridges students' home and school lives
examples: The brief instructs that educators' interactions with families and community members incorporate their feedback into meaningful decision-making processes
key_sources: Jahneille Cunningham, Rebecca Colina Neri, and Carlos Sandoval. (2024). Codesigning Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education With Families and Communities. WestEd brief. https://education.uw.edu/sites/default/files/programs/epsc/Users%20Guide%20Road%20Map%20Survey.pdf

article_title: Codesigning Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education with Families and Communities
citation: Jahneille Cunningham, Rebecca Colina Neri, and Carlos Sandoval. (2024). Codesigning Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education With Families and Communities. WestEd brief. https://education.uw.edu/sites/default/files/programs/epsc/Users%20Guide%20Road%20Map%20Survey.pdf
title: Engage families and communities through activities that are mutually beneficial and extend beyond the school setting
description: The brief frames family and community engagement as part of a mutually beneficial relationship, asking what role schools can play in improving outcomes for the broader community and how mathematics can make a difference locally. It states that "broadening engagement to encompass activities beyond the school setting shows an investment in families and communities," citing financial literacy campaigns and community garden planning as examples.
requirements: Activities should center the community's own needs and desires
target_learners: Mathematics students, their families, and the broader community
target_learning_goals: Mathematical learning applied to real-world community problems
examples: Financial literacy campaigns and community garden planning engage the broader community in mathematical learning; STEM fairs and community health assessments let students share mathematical learning with the community

article_title: Academy Breaks the Isolation of Special Education Directors
citation: Academy Breaks the Isolation of Special Education Directors. (2014). WestEd R&D Alert, Vol. 14, No. 3. https://www.wested.org
title: Multi-phase professional learning structure: summer institute, school-year follow-ups, annual reunions, and pre-program needs assessment
description: The Academy's design runs "for three and a half days in August, followed by three additional full-day follow-up sessions later in the school year, plus annual two-day follow-up seminars ("reunions") for prior Academy participants." Sessions are highly interactive and customized: prior to the Academy, participants are asked what their biggest issues are and what they want addressed, informing coverage of current topics such as transition planning.
requirements: Pre-program collection of participant issues to customize content
Ongoing sponsorship to fund follow-up sessions and reunions across years
constraints: Designed for a small cohort; annual attendance averages between 15 and 20 participants
target_learning_goals: Updating legal and leadership knowledge
Sustaining peer support networks over time
examples: Evening sessions let participants share successful project details and effective materials they have developed.

article_title: Creating New Futures for Newcomers: Lessons from Five Schools That Serve K-12 Immigrants, Refugees, and Asylees
citation: MAEC, Inc. (2019). Creating New Futures for Newcomers: Lessons from Five Schools that Serve K-12 Immigrants, Refugees, and Asylees. Bethesda, MD.
title: Multi-approach English language and content instruction: SIOP, native-language leveraging, and scaffolding
description: The report's fourth promising practice is instruction guided by shared beliefs: it should be culturally responsive, meet students at their levels while providing high-challenge, high-support opportunities, give continuous practice in reading, writing, speaking, and listening, incorporate multiple learning modalities, use data to guide decisions, and be collaboratively planned. "Across the grades, teachers are trained in and routinely implement SIOP," with content and language objectives posted and reviewed each lesson. Schools also leverage students' native languages and differentiate and scaffold instruction toward more independent performance.
requirements: Teachers trained in SIOP
collaborative planning between ESL and content-area teachers
evidence-based conceptual frameworks and materials vetted for English Learners
constraints: None of the bright spot schools are bilingual programs because their student populations are linguistically diverse; native-language use varies by school
target_learners: K-12 newcomers with limited or no English proficiency, including SLIFE
target_learning_goals: English language proficiency in tandem with content learning
grade-level content standards mastery
college and career preparation
examples: Winooski integrates the multisensory Fundations program with SIOP for phonics and spelling; Manhattan International requires seniors to produce a graduation portfolio including work in their native language
key_sources: MAEC, Inc. (2019). Creating New Futures for Newcomers: Lessons from Five Schools that Serve K-12 Immigrants, Refugees, and Asylees. Bethesda, MD. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED627813

article_title: Encouraging Social and Emotional Learning in the Context of New Accountability
citation: Melnick, H., Cook-Harvey, C. M., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2017). Encouraging social and emotional learning in the context of new accountability. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. http://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/sel-new-accountability
title: Multitiered accountability framework with four tiers of indicators under ESSA
description: The report conceptualizes accountability as a multilayered system rather than only federally mandated indicators. It distinguishes federal indicators used to identify schools for intervention, state-reported indicators for public information and improvement, state-supported indicators (tools districts may choose), and locally selected indicators. Different indicators belong in different tiers "depending on the nature of the data, who will be using it, and for what purpose." California's proposed ESSA system is presented as an example, and indicators may be shown on a dashboard as status or growth.
requirements: Federal indicators must be valid, reliable, comparable statewide, meaningfully differentiate schools, and be disaggregated by ESSA student subgroups
constraints: State-supported and locally selected indicators are not required and would largely inform ongoing improvement; some measures could fit in multiple tiers depending on state context
target_learners: K-12 students in state accountability systems
target_learning_goals: school quality and student success measurement, including SEL and school climate
examples: California's proposed multitiered ESSA system places chronic absenteeism and suspension rates among federal indicators and school climate surveys among locally selected indicators
key_sources: Melnick, H., Cook-Harvey, C. M., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2017). Encouraging social and emotional learning in the context of new accountability. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. http://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/sel-new-accountability

article_title: Adversarial Stress Testing of Role-Playing Language Agents using Multi-Agent Evaluation
citation: Saqib Shouqi, Abdullah Nazly, Januki Wanniarachchi, Ravisha De Alwis. (2026). Adversarial Stress Testing of Role-Playing Language Agents using Multi-Agent Evaluation. ADScAI Conference, University of Moratuwa, Sri Lanka. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03166
title: Multi-agent adversarial evaluation framework coordinating Interrogator, Target, and Judging agents
description: The article proposes a modular multi-agent framework in which "a strategy-driven Interrogator Agent that applies six progressive adversarial strategies" probes a Target Agent representing the RPLA under evaluation, while "an automated Judging Agent that scores behavior across role fidelity, drift, ethical deviation, and consistency dimensions" evaluates the full transcript afterward. The Judging Agent does not participate in dialogue generation, ensuring evaluation does not alter the behavior measured. The framework treats the Target Agent as a black box and supports multiple LLM providers through a unified abstraction layer.
requirements: A persistent database storing experiment metadata, conversation transcripts, and evaluation results to enable replay, comparison, and auditing
A unified LLM provider abstraction layer so the same experimental setup runs across models without changing evaluation logic
constraints: The Target Agent is treated as a black box, reflecting deployment conditions where internal model parameters are not accessible
The framework focuses on prompt-based adversarial attacks and does not consider vulnerabilities arising from training, fine-tuning, or reinforcement learning processes
target_learners: Developers and researchers evaluating role-playing language agents for education, healthcare assistance, and customer support
target_learning_goals: Assessing robustness, reliability, and alignment of role-playing language agents under sustained adversarial conditions
examples: Experiments ran 10-turn interactions per experiment across three personas (Healthcare Assistant, Customer Support Agent, Financial Advisor) with three random seeds per condition
key_sources: Saqib Shouqi, Abdullah Nazly, Januki Wanniarachchi, Ravisha De Alwis. (2026). Adversarial Stress Testing of Role-Playing Language Agents using Multi-Agent Evaluation. ADScAI Conference, University of Moratuwa, Sri Lanka. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03166

article_title: Taking the Long View: State Efforts to Solve Teacher Shortages by Strengthening the Profession
citation: Espinoza, D., Saunders, R., Kini, T., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2018). Taking the long view: State efforts to solve teacher shortages by strengthening the profession. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/long-view
title: Address teacher shortages with a set of mutually reinforcing policies rather than any single policy in isolation
description: The report argues no single policy solves teacher shortages if enacted alone: research on hard-to-staff schools indicates it is important "both to raise salaries and to provide for more collegial, supportive, well-resourced environments," and induction works best alongside school-level collaboration and mentorship policies. It recommends that policymakers consider how to ensure a set of mutually reinforcing strategies spanning recruitment, preparation, induction, leadership, compensation, and retention. Washington State's comprehensive approach, profiled in the report, illustrates this combined strategy.
requirements: Coordination across multiple policy areas (scholarships, pathways, induction, leadership, compensation, recruitment)
constraints: Effectiveness hinges on the size, scope, and comprehensiveness of the policy, quality of implementation, and responsiveness to state, local, and labor market context
target_learners: State policymakers designing teacher workforce systems
Prospective and practicing teachers in shortage fields
target_learning_goals: Recruiting, developing, and retaining a strong, stable, diverse teacher workforce
examples: Washington State combined service scholarships, high school pathways and Grow Your Own programs, mentoring and induction, school leadership investment, competitive compensation, and recruitment policies in a single comprehensive approach
The report concludes states should continually evaluate implementation and outcomes to strengthen the effectiveness of their actions
key_sources: Espinoza, D., Saunders, R., Kini, T., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2018). Taking the long view: State efforts to solve teacher shortages by strengthening the profession. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/long-view

article_title: An AI-supported E-mentoring model to develop EFL pre-service teachers' self-efficacy and emotional intelligence
citation: Ismael I, Luo X and Li S (2026). An AI-supported E-mentoring model to develop EFL pre-service teachers' self-efficacy and emotional intelligence. Front. Psychol. 17:1853510. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1853510
title: Multi-platform e-mentoring environment (Google Classroom, Nearpod, Facebook, Padlet) with distinct pedagogical functions
description: The intervention combined four digital platforms, each with a distinct function: 'Google Classroom functioned as the main organizational platform through which participants accessed weekly tasks, instructional videos, and learning resources'. Nearpod delivered interactive presentations and lesson-design demonstrations, Facebook served as a collaborative mentoring space for sharing teaching videos and peer feedback, and Padlet supported anonymous reflection and scenario-based analysis. The article states the multi-platform use 'was intended to create an integrated mentoring environment and avoid repetitive interaction through a single tool'.
requirements: Participants need access to all platforms so each pedagogical function is served
constraints: Platform roles were defined for this practicum context; the article does not claim the same configuration generalizes elsewhere
target_learning_goals: collaborative reflection
peer feedback
lesson planning
examples: Reflections were shared in a Facebook group for discussion, peer feedback, and collaborative problem-solving during the practicum
key_sources: Ismael I, Luo X and Li S (2026). An AI-supported E-mentoring model to develop EFL pre-service teachers' self-efficacy and emotional intelligence. Front. Psychol. 17:1853510. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1853510

article_title: Ensuring Academic Integrity through Automated Online Exam Proctoring: A Decade-Long Systematic Review
citation: Malhotra, M., & Chhabra, I. (2026). Ensuring academic integrity through automated online exam proctoring a decade long systematic review. Discover Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s44217-026-01224-3
title: Conceptual multi-layered framework integrating biometric verification, visual/audio analysis, and environmental monitoring
description: The review proposes a conceptual multi-layered framework for automated proctoring that combines biometric verification, visual and audio analysis, and environmental monitoring to improve academic integrity. It is offered as an integrative synthesis of the reviewed ML, DL, IoT, and hybrid techniques, addressing the review's finding that "a clear, unified framework that balances detection accuracy, privacy preservation, and context-aware -ness remains lacking." The framework is a design proposal, not an evaluated system.
requirements: Integration of multimodal behavioral inputs such as keystroke dynamics, gaze tracking, and environmental monitoring in a cost-effective and scalable way, as the review states is currently insufficient
constraints: The review states many existing models are limited by dataset biases, generalization issues across diverse environments, and ethical concerns around intrusive surveillance
target_learners: higher education students in online examinations
target_learning_goals: uphold academic integrity and fair assessment in online examinations
examples: The review's contribution list states it "Proposes a conceptual multi-layered framework integrating biometric verification, visual/audio analysis, and environmental monitoring to improve academic integrity."
key_sources: Malhotra, M., & Chhabra, I. (2026). Ensuring academic integrity through automated online exam proctoring a decade long systematic review. Discover Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s44217-026-01224-3

article_title: AICoFe: Implementation and Deployment of an AI-Based Collaborative Feedback System for Higher Education
citation: Alvaro Becerra, Alejandra Palma and Ruth Cobos. (2026). AICoFe: Implementation and Deployment of an AI-Based Collaborative Feedback System for Higher Education. LASI Spain 26: Learning Analytics Summer Institute Spain 2026. https://orcid.org/0009-0003-7793-2682
title: Multi-LLM feedback generation pipeline combining three independently fine-tuned models
description: AICoFe's Feedback Generation Module extends prior single-model work to a multi-model setting in which "three independent feedback instances are generated, one per LLM" (GPT-4.1-mini, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Llama 3.1). Each model receives the same structured prompt built from average rubric scores, validated qualitative observations, rubric level descriptions, and instructional materials. Using three distinct models is argued to enrich feedback with diverse perspectives while reducing the risk of single-model biases or systematic errors reaching students. Each instance follows a three-paragraph structure: strengths, areas for improvement, and an action plan.
requirements: All models are fine-tuned on teacher-validated feedback instances from the SOPHIAS dataset, and a post-processing validation stage enforces teacher-defined constraints such as length, coherence, and exclusion of restricted terms
constraints: All data sent to the generative models are anonymised prior to transmission to commercial LLM providers
target_learners: higher education students receiving personalized feedback
target_learning_goals: actionable personalized feedback on assessed skills
examples: GPT-4.1-mini fine-tuned via the OpenAI API for 3 epochs; Gemini 2.5 Flash via Vertex AI for 40 cycles; Llama 3.1 locally via LoRA with 4-bit NF4 quantisation
key_sources: Alvaro Becerra, Alejandra Palma and Ruth Cobos. (2026). AICoFe: Implementation and Deployment of an AI-Based Collaborative Feedback System for Higher Education. LASI Spain 26: Learning Analytics Summer Institute Spain 2026. https://orcid.org/0009-0003-7793-2682

article_title: AI-Powered Math Tutoring: Platform for Personalized and Adaptive Education
citation: Jarosław A. Chudziak and Adam Kostka. (2025). AI-Powered Math Tutoring: Platform for Personalized and Adaptive Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.12484
title: Multi-agent AI tutoring architecture with an orchestrating Tutor Agent and specialist agents
description: The article proposes a multi-agent architecture implemented on LangGraph in which a central Tutor Agent (GPT-4o) interprets student input and orchestrates other components via a ReAct-style framework. A Memory Dispatcher oversees conversations and controls memory modules, while a pipeline of agents (Research, Planning, Step Handling, Coding) builds courses, and auxiliary tools include a Symbolic Solver, Function Plotter, and Course Graph Drawer. The design prioritizes "deep understanding and independent problem-solving over direct answers" through guided, tool-assisted learning.
requirements: Underlying LLM capabilities: the article states system performance remains fundamentally dependent on underlying LLM capabilities and possible biases
constraints: Personalization currently operates on a basic set of attributes
Pedagogical effectiveness of generated courses is yet to be evaluated empirically
target_learners: students learning mathematics, including exam-preparation students
target_learning_goals: deep conceptual understanding of mathematics topics
independent problem-solving
exam revision and targeted practice
examples: The Tutor Agent uses Socratic questioning instead of solving an equation immediately, dynamically adjusting support based on progress tracked in memory
key_sources: Jarosław A. Chudziak and Adam Kostka. (2025). AI-Powered Math Tutoring: Platform for Personalized and Adaptive Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.12484

article_title: Educating minds with generative AI
citation: Laura Desiree Di Paolo, Andy Clark & Thomas Wachter. (2026). Educating minds with generative AI. Communications Psychology 4:128. https://doi.org/10.1038/s44271-026-00522-8
title: Education as a multitechnological cognitive ecology in which AI is one deliberately combined component among many
description: The article's concluding proposal is to conceive of education as a multitechnological cognitive ecology in which 'no single technology dominates: low-tech, embodied, and collaborative tools are combined with digital and AI-based resources according to pedagogical aims rather than market logic'. GenAI is framed not as a ready-made solution but as a diagnostic catalyst and stress test that exposes tensions between efficiency-oriented schooling and broader developmental aims, compelling a redesign guided by embodied, situated, collaborative and materially grounded learning. A principle of deliberate use calls for combining tools by pedagogical affordances and treating AI as one component among many.
requirements: A prepared conceptual and practical vocabulary for transformation; the article states the vision already exists but has lacked institutional will, technological ecology and resources
constraints: AI systems are among the most resource-intensive technologies deployed in education, with substantial energy, water and infrastructural costs, which the article says must be accounted for
target_learning_goals: the full range of human learning and development, including agency, critical judgment, collaboration and meaningful participation
examples: The article cites initiatives such as Learn Your Way, which transforms traditional textbooks into multimedia learning materials including audio lessons, narrated slides, and mind maps tailored to learners' preferences, as pointing toward this ecology.
key_sources: Laura Desiree Di Paolo, Andy Clark & Thomas Wachter. (2026). Educating minds with generative AI. Communications Psychology 4:128. https://doi.org/10.1038/s44271-026-00522-8

article_title: Effectiveness of GenAI in Enhancing Writing Performance: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Mark Feng Teng. (2026). Effectiveness of GenAI in enhancing writing performance: a meta-analysis. Asian-Pacific Journal of Second and Foreign Language Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40862-026-00444-2
title: Multilevel conceptualization of moderators in GenAI-mediated writing research (technological, learner, and contextual factors)
description: The article proposes a multilevel framework for understanding variability in GenAI-mediated writing outcomes. It states that "Technological factors (e.g., tool type) determine the nature and depth of available feedback; learner factors (e.g., proficiency, education level) shape the capacity to interpret and internalize that feedback; and contextual factors (e.g., instructional model, sociocultural environment) influence how GenAI is integrated into learning practices." The framework holds that these moderators interact dynamically rather than operating independently, providing a principled basis for synthesizing cross-contextual studies and interpreting empirical variability.
requirements: Moderators must be coded at technological, learner, and contextual levels to interpret cross-study variability in GenAI writing effects
constraints: The article notes the moderators interact dynamically, so single-factor explanations of outcome variability are incomplete
target_learners: L2/EFL writing learners across secondary, university, and adult education settings
target_learning_goals: L2/EFL writing performance, including linguistic accuracy, lexical sophistication, and text quality
examples: The meta-analysis operationalized the framework by coding intervention duration, education level, instructional model, and sample size as moderators in subgroup and meta-regression analyses
key_sources: Mark Feng Teng. (2026). Effectiveness of GenAI in enhancing writing performance: a meta-analysis. Asian-Pacific Journal of Second and Foreign Language Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40862-026-00444-2

article_title: A Multi-Agent Approach to Validate and Refine LLM-Generated Personalized Math Problems
citation: Fareya Ikram, Nischal Ashok Kumar, Junyang Lu, Hunter McNichols, Candace Walkington, Neil Heffernan, and Andrew S. Lan. (2026). A Multi-Agent Approach to Validate and Refine LLM-Generated Personalized Math Problems. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.05160
title: Multi-agent generate–validate–revise framework with four specialized validator agents for math problem personalization
description: The framework formalizes context personalization of math problems as an iterative generate–validate–revise loop. A conversion agent generates an initial topic-aligned candidate problem, and "four independentvalidator agentsthat return a binary decision (pass/fail) and brief diagnostic feedback" check the candidate against solvability, realism, readability, and authenticity criteria; one or more refinement agents then revise the candidate using validator feedback until all validators pass or a maximum iteration count is reached. The framework is evaluated on 600 ASSISTments problems personalized to 20 student interest topics.
requirements: A target topic reflecting a learner's interest, a target grade reading level computed with the Flesch–Kincaid metric, and validator feedback to drive refinement
constraints: Refinement iterates for at most k iterations (set to k=3 in the evaluation) and stops early only if the candidate passes all validator agent checks
target_learning_goals: math word problem solving with personally interesting contexts
examples: The article's Table 1 example converts a pizza-slice circle problem to a basketball court context, where the realism validator fails a 7-inch center circle and the refinement agent revises it to 7 ft
key_sources: Fareya Ikram, Nischal Ashok Kumar, Junyang Lu, Hunter McNichols, Candace Walkington, Neil Heffernan, and Andrew S. Lan. (2026). A Multi-Agent Approach to Validate and Refine LLM-Generated Personalized Math Problems. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.05160

article_title: Kutti AI: A Voice-First, Offline-Capable Learning Companion with Real-Time Struggle Detection for Visually-Impaired Children
citation: Kadharmoideen Fadurudeen. (2026). Kutti AI: A Voice-First, Offline-Capable Learning Companion with Real-Time Struggle Detection for Visually-Impaired Children. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22377
title: Multi-signal struggle detection fusing latency, wrong-attempt, and hesitation-keyword signals
description: Kutti AI's adaptivity rests on a struggle-detection engine that "fuses three independent signals and acts the moment any of them indicates difficulty": response latency beyond a threshold, wrong-attempt counts, and hesitation keywords in the transcript. Any single signal can fire, so the system reacts to silence, error, and verbalized uncertainty using lightweight on-device computation, triggering hints, simplified questions, or encouragement in real time.
requirements: Simplified question variants must be authored in advance as part of lesson content
Thresholds (e.g., a 2.5-second pause threshold) must be set to balance responsiveness against thinking time
constraints: Fixed parameters (2.5-second pause threshold, two-attempt limit, 0.6 similarity threshold) should become adaptive and personalized per the authors
target_learning_goals: sustained engagement and persistence when a child struggles
examples: In the prototype, a pause beyond 2.5 seconds triggers a spoken hint; after two incorrect attempts a pre-authored simplified question is presented; hesitation cues such as "don't know" trigger encouragement
key_sources: Kadharmoideen Fadurudeen. (2026). Kutti AI: A Voice-First, Offline-Capable Learning Companion with Real-Time Struggle Detection for Visually-Impaired Children. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22377

article_title: IKS-Instruct: A 24,000-Example Multilingual Dataset for Teaching Language Models Indian Knowledge Systems
citation: Shwetha Singaravelu, Gayathri Muruganantham, Lakshmi Rajendran, Santhosh Sivasubramani. (2026). IKS-Instruct: A 24,000-Example Multilingual Dataset for Teaching Language Models Indian Knowledge Systems. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23322
title: Multi-judge quality assessment framework
description: A quality-evaluation framework in which independent language-model judges score instruction responses across multiple dimensions, with per-model quality reported as the median of per-judge overall scores. The paper states that "Quality is assessed through a multi-judge evaluation framework in which independent language models score responses on 12 dimensions" grouped into IKS Fidelity, Pedagogy, Content, and Adaptation categories. A stratified sample of 1,201 items is scored by a uniform five-judge external panel, with Nemotron-family judges excluded to avoid self-preference circularity.
requirements: Multiple independent judges applied identically to every model; stratified sampling by language and technique category
constraints: Language-model judges exhibit systematic biases (favoring longer, formal responses); residual Llama-lineage circularity remains; scores are comparative under a fixed panel, not calibrated ratings
target_learners: Researchers and builders of educational AI systems
target_learning_goals: Assessing pedagogical quality, technique fidelity, and cultural depth of AI-generated instructional content
examples: The uniform five-judge panel (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.3-70B, Dracarys-70B, GPT-4o-mini) scored 1,201 stratified items with median aggregation
key_sources: Shwetha Singaravelu, Gayathri Muruganantham, Lakshmi Rajendran, Santhosh Sivasubramani. (2026). IKS-Instruct: A 24,000-Example Multilingual Dataset for Teaching Language Models Indian Knowledge Systems. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23322

article_title: Aligning LLM-Simulated and Human Examinees for Psychometric Calibration: A Cognitive Diagnostic Profiling Approach
citation: Wenjie Zhou, Yunting Liu, Renjiao Tang, & Mark Wilson. (2026). Aligning LLM-Simulated and Human Examinees for Psychometric Calibration: A Cognitive Diagnostic Profiling Approach. https://osf.io/p6fam/
title: Evaluate LLM-simulated examinees at multiple levels — distribution, profile, and item — because no single indicator captures all misalignment
description: The article's three-tier evaluation framework (distribution, profile, item) revealed discrepancies that no single indicator would have captured: a configuration can match the overall distribution while misaligning at the profile level, or rank items correctly while producing parameter values far from the human scale. The authors "suggest that future studies evaluating LLM-based simulation adopt multi-level assessment". Profile-level analysis in particular offers an actionable diagnostic pinpointing which mastery patterns the model handles well and where fidelity breaks down.
requirements: A human-examinee reference dataset and a cognitive model fit (such as a CDM) to define profile-level expectations
constraints: Demonstrated on a single 15-item, five-attribute instrument with 536 examinees; the informative prior was in-sample, marking an upper bound
target_learners: Researchers and testing programs evaluating LLM-based examinee simulation
target_learning_goals: Validating simulated examinee data for psychometric calibration before operational use
examples: The study evaluated alignment via overlapping coefficients at the distribution level, prevalence-weighted profile correlations, and Spearman/Pearson correlations with bias and RMSE at the item level
key_sources: Wenjie Zhou, Yunting Liu, Renjiao Tang, & Mark Wilson. (2026). Aligning LLM-Simulated and Human Examinees for Psychometric Calibration: A Cognitive Diagnostic Profiling Approach. https://osf.io/p6fam/

article_title: Multimodal Item Parameter Estimation using Simulated Response Probabilities
citation: Christopher Ormerod and YoungKoung Kim. (2026). Multimodal Item Parameter Estimation using Simulated Response Probabilities. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10154v1
title: Multimodal mathematics item-response corpus: 970 item models, 4,848 items, 13.88 million responses
description: The study's dataset consists of multiple-choice mathematics items, each with a stimulus and four options where stimulus and options may include image components combined into one image, generated from item models specifying structure, content and variable features. The article reports "There were a total of 970 item models and a total of 4,848 items" and "There are 13.88 million responses", split into train, development and test sets by item model to avoid conflation, with approximately 2860 responses per item on average.
requirements: Responses tied to independently derived ability levels from a larger calibrated dataset of items
constraints: Items were split by item model rather than at random, to avoid conflation between related generated items
target_learners: students responding to large-scale mathematics assessment items
target_learning_goals: item parameter estimation and difficulty calibration for assessment development
examples: Table 1 splits items into 727 item models / 3633 items for training, 97 / 485 for development, and 146 / 730 for test
key_sources: Christopher Ormerod and YoungKoung Kim. (2026). Multimodal Item Parameter Estimation using Simulated Response Probabilities. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10154

article_title: Multimodal Examination Answer Data with Expert-Designed Outcome-Based Education Rubrics for Criterion-Level Assessment
citation: Jahangir Alam SM, Md Khalid Syfullaha, Saad Ahmed, Munira Akter Mou, A K Z Rasel Rahman, A.K.M. Masudur Rahman, Mohammed Sowket Ali. (2026). Multimodal examination answer data with expert-designed Outcome-Based Education rubrics for criterion-level assessment. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.22346
title: Multimodal OBE examination-answer dataset of 485 scanned submissions with criterion-level rubric marks
description: A research dataset pairing scanned examination answer PDFs with answer-level JSON metadata containing subject, question, model answer, criterion definitions, criterion marks, and total marks. The collection "contains 485 answer submissions from 415 consenting students at four academic institutions", with eight faculty contributors supplying materials across nine subjects and 12 question templates. Scans retain handwriting, equations, tables, code, figures, and diagrams, with variation from CamScanner, Adobe Scan, and conventional scanners.
requirements: Student consent obtained for preparation and research use of the scripts
Restricted research-only access due to residual identifiers in some scans
constraints: Not intended to determine official student grades
Covers nine subjects and only 12 question templates with uneven subject distribution
target_learners: higher education students in computer science and related subjects
target_learning_goals: criterion-level assessment of examination answers
outcome-based education assessment research
examples: Eight faculty contributors supplied scanned scripts and examiner-prepared assessment spreadsheets covering Machine Learning, Digital Image Processing, Database Systems, Computer Networks, Data Mining, Algorithms, Fisheries, Object Oriented Programming, and E-commerce
key_sources: Jahangir Alam SM, Md Khalid Syfullaha, Saad Ahmed, Munira Akter Mou, A K Z Rasel Rahman, A.K.M. Masudur Rahman, Mohammed Sowket Ali. (2026). Multimodal examination answer data with expert-designed Outcome-Based Education rubrics for criterion-level assessment. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.22346

article_title: Mind the Student: Behavioral and Contextual Cues for Automated Engagement Prediction in Online Learning
citation: Alperen Kantarcı, Visvanathan Ramesh, and Gemma Roig. 2026. Mind the Student: Behavioral and Contextual Cues for Automated Engagement Prediction in Online Learning. ICMI '26, Napoli, Italy. https://doi.org/10.1145/3776574.3832485
title: Multimodal engagement-prediction framework with Perceiver IO fusion, hierarchical Bayesian participant context, and uncertainty-aware heads
description: A computational framework that jointly predicts a continuous engagement score in [1,5] and a binary label from tutoring-video clips. It fuses pretrained encoders (V-JEPA 2 for student and instructor video, CLIP for screen content, AudioMAE for audio) with five explicit behavioral streams — "head pose, CWT head dynamics, facial action units, gaze/head angles, and emotion prediction probabilities" — through a Perceiver IO latent bottleneck. Student and instructor personalities are modeled as variational posteriors over learnable embeddings with partial pooling toward a shared prior, and evidential NIG regression and SNGP classification heads output predictions with explicit epistemic uncertainty.
requirements: Pretrained encoders for video, screen, and audio modalities; personality metadata are optional and masked at test time
A student-independent evaluation split so that training and testing sets contain different students
constraints: The authors state the population prior in the Bayesian context layer is too weakly constrained to prevent the model from fitting student appearance rather than engagement dynamics
Perceiver IO mean-pooling over 64 frames suppresses within-clip fluctuations because each clip receives a single label
target_learning_goals: automated prediction of student engagement level from behavioral and contextual cues
examples: The framework was entered in the CASED challenge, where it achieved competitive regression performance (RMSE 0.68, matching the best methods) while producing calibrated epistemic uncertainty estimates at inference time
key_sources: Alperen Kantarcı, Visvanathan Ramesh, and Gemma Roig. 2026. Mind the Student: Behavioral and Contextual Cues for Automated Engagement Prediction in Online Learning. ICMI '26, Napoli, Italy. https://doi.org/10.1145/3776574.3832485

article_title: LoRA Fine-Tuned Models for Control Systems Course Q&A: A Multidimensional Evaluation of Model Scale and Rank Effects
citation: Shaowen Lu, Chengxu Liu, Ping Zhou and Tao Yang. (2026). LoRA Fine-Tuned Models for Control Systems Course Q&A: A Multidimensional Evaluation of Model Scale and Rank Effects. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13918
title: Multidimensional evaluation framework separating reference-answer similarity, structured-output stability, and domain-specific correctness
description: The article proposes an evaluation framework for educational question-answering models that combines automatic text metrics with structured-output features and bootstrap confidence intervals. ROUGE-1/2/L measure lexical overlap, BERTScore-F1 measures semantic proximity, and has_solution/has_method/has_teaching_points coverage rates measure conformity to the pedagogical template. The framework's central boundary condition is that "ROUGE and BERTScore primarily capture lexical and semantic proximity, while the structured-output metrics measure template stability" — none can certify formula accuracy, derivational rigor, or instructional usefulness, which require expert assessment or task-specific rubrics.
requirements: A held-out test set of course questions with structured reference answers
Expert assessment or task-specific rubrics for evaluating domain-specific correctness
constraints: Metrics do not directly establish improvements in domain-specific reasoning or mathematical correctness
No bootstrap confidence interval was calculated for BERTScore-F1 because per-sample values were not retained
target_learners: upper-level undergraduate automation and electrical engineering students
target_learning_goals: evaluating course-specific question-answering models for instructional use
examples: The framework used paired bootstrap resampling with B=10,000 iterations to compute 95% confidence intervals for ROUGE and structured-output gains
key_sources: Shaowen Lu, Chengxu Liu, Ping Zhou and Tao Yang. (2026). LoRA Fine-Tuned Models for Control Systems Course Q&A: A Multidimensional Evaluation of Model Scale and Rank Effects. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13918

article_title: MUSE: Benchmarking Large Vision-Language Models on Multi-Modal Understanding in Situated Education
citation: Luyao Zhu, Xun Wei Yee, Wei Li, Mun Thye Mak, Wee Siong Ng. (2026). MUSE: Benchmarking Large Vision-Language Models on Multi-modal Understanding in Situated Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19088
title: MUSE: a 12-task benchmark of artistic image understanding for situated education
description: MUSE is a benchmark for evaluating large vision-language models on artistic image understanding in image-based language learning and educational interaction. It contains "2,400 questions over 1,174 images" at 1920×1080 resolution, spanning 12 tasks across five capability dimensions: visual perception, semantic understanding, affective interpretation, compositional reasoning, and cultural understanding. Images were commissioned from artists and curated to center Singaporean and Southeast Asian multicultural contexts alongside Western art traditions, with annotation by 127 trained annotators under consensus review.
requirements: Each artwork is annotated once with a reusable structured representation of its visual and semantic content before task-specific questions are generated
constraints: Tasks use multiple-choice, numerical, and open-ended response formats; open-ended tasks are scored by semantic similarity rather than exact match
target_learners: learners in image-based language learning and educational interaction with AI tutors
target_learning_goals: multi-modal understanding of artistic imagery: perception, semantics, affect, composition, and culture
examples: Evaluation of 30 open-source and proprietary VLMs on the 12 tasks, with models run at temperature 0 and scored by accuracy or semantic similarity
key_sources: Luyao Zhu, Xun Wei Yee, Wei Li, Mun Thye Mak, Wee Siong Ng. (2026). MUSE: Benchmarking Large Vision-Language Models on Multi-modal Understanding in Situated Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19088

article_title: Human-Centered Design of LLM-Powered Educational Chatbots: A Study with Secondary Teachers
citation: Reichert, H., Briceno, D., Tabarsi, B., Barnes, T. (2026). Human-Centered Design of LLM-Powered Educational Chatbots: A Study with Secondary Teachers. In: Degen, H., Ntoa, S. (eds) Artificial Intelligence in HCI. HCII 2026. LNCS vol 16746. Springer, Cham. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-31048-4_32
title: Multi-layered safety architecture for teacher-supervised educational chatbots
description: Teachers in the study articulated a safety architecture for LLM-powered chatbots composed of four component types: "content scoping, presentation strategies, oversight mechanisms, and adaptation frameworks". This architecture gives teachers a reusable lesson/unit-level design that keeps chatbot behavior within professionally supervised bounds. It operationalizes the bounded authority model by layering protective mechanisms rather than relying on any single safeguard.
requirements: Human oversight mechanisms must be retained in the design
constraints: Articulated by secondary teachers for LLM-powered chatbots in educational settings
target_learning_goals: safe, scope-limited interaction with AI chatbots during learning
examples: Study participants prototyped chatbots with content scoping and oversight mechanisms during paper-prototype design sessions
key_sources: Reichert, H., Briceno, D., Tabarsi, B., Barnes, T. (2026). Human-Centered Design of LLM-Powered Educational Chatbots: A Study with Secondary Teachers. In: Degen, H., Ntoa, S. (eds) Artificial Intelligence in HCI. HCII 2026. LNCS vol 16746. Springer, Cham. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-31048-4_32

article_title: TeachLM: Post-Training LLMs for Education Using Authentic Learning Data
citation: Janos Perczel, Jin Chow, and Dorottya Demszky. (2025). TeachLM: Post-Training LLMs for Education Using Authentic Learning Data. https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.05087
title: Multi-turn evaluation protocol combining a fine-tuned student model with single-shot LLM judging
description: A novel evaluation protocol in which a fine-tuned student model and a candidate tutor model generate synthetic multi-turn dialogues that are scored by conversational statistics and a reasoning LLM judge, with results aggregated. The article introduces "a novel multi-turn evaluation protocol that combines a fine-tuned student model and a fine-tuned tutor model to generate a large number of synthetic dialogues." Each evaluation point corresponds to 100 simulated conversations (10 repetitions across 10 student models) to limit variability and ensure reproducibility.
requirements: A fine-tuned student model whose conversational statistics align with human-to-AI dialogues
A dedicated LLM judge (Gemini 2.5 Flash) to detect conversation end and a turn limit to prevent indefinite conversations
constraints: The article notes the six benchmarks are intentionally simple proxies; optimizing solely for them does not guarantee high-quality teaching
target_learners: LLM tutor models being evaluated for educational use
target_learning_goals: Measuring conversational and pedagogical quality of AI tutors across multi-turn dialogue
examples: The protocol was used to benchmark models from OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, Meta, and XAI against human tutors on six metrics
key_sources: Janos Perczel, Jin Chow, and Dorottya Demszky. (2025). TeachLM: Post-Training LLMs for Education Using Authentic Learning Data. https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.05087

article_title: MuTSE: A Human-in-the-Loop Multi-use Text Simplification Evaluator
citation: Rares-Alexandru Roșcan, Gabriel Petre, Adrian-Marius Dumitran, Angela-Liliana Dumitran. (2026). MuTSE: A Human-in-the-Loop Multi-use Text Simplification Evaluator. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.08947
title: MuTSE: an interactive human-in-the-loop web application for evaluating LLM-generated text simplifications
description: MuTSE is a web application that supports concurrent execution of P×M prompt-model permutations for text simplification, generating a comparison matrix in real time. It integrates a tiered semantic alignment engine with a linearity bias heuristic (λ), readability metrics (e.g., Flesch-Kincaid), and a customizable manual annotation system. The article states it is "designed to streamline the evaluation of LLM-generated text simplifications across arbitrary CEFR proficiency targets," serving educators selecting texts and NLP researchers building annotated datasets.
requirements: Cloud-based serverless LLM access (e.g., Together AI) or local models, plus a Python/FastAPI backend and Vue.js 3 frontend
constraints: Relies on a local JSON-based persistence layer that does not scale for concurrent multi-user deployments in large laboratory settings
Users face initial deployment friction regarding environment configuration (e.g., Python, Node.js dependencies)
target_learners: Language learners at CEFR proficiency targets such as A2 and B1
target_learning_goals: Matching text complexity to learner proficiency through text simplification
examples: The platform is pre-loaded with a curated set of 5 pre-defined prompts for standard language proficiency objectives (e.g., A2, B1)
Users can dynamically add new models by inputting the model's official string identifier without altering the codebase
key_sources: Rares-Alexandru Roșcan, Gabriel Petre, Adrian-Marius Dumitran, Angela-Liliana Dumitran. (2026). MuTSE: A Human-in-the-Loop Multi-use Text Simplification Evaluator. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.08947

article_title: Mathematics Teachers’ Interactions with a Multi-Agent System for Personalized Problem Generation
citation: Walkington, C., Beauchamp, T., Ikram, F., Koçyiğit Gürbüz, M., Xia, F., Lee, M., Lan, A. (2025). Mathematics Teachers’ Interactions with a Multi-Agent System for Personalized Problem Generation.
title: Multi-agent teacher-in-the-loop architecture for context personalization
description: The article introduces a multi-agent, teacher-in-the-loop architecture for context personalization in which a teacher enters a base problem and desired topic, an LLM generates the problem, and then four AI agents evaluate it using criteria each specializes in: mathematical accuracy, authenticity, readability, and realism. Each agent has a specified role and prompt and returns a binary pass/fail decision. Failed cases trigger a refinement agent that revises the problem, iterating until all evaluations pass or a maximum of five refinement steps is reached. After refinement, teachers can further author the problem before submitting it.
requirements: A teacher provides a base problem and a topic, and can choose whether to retain or modify the original numerical values
constraints: The process iterates until all agent evaluations pass or a maximum number of refinement steps is reached (five in this study)
target_learning_goals: Personalized mathematics word problems aligned to student interests
examples: Eight middle school mathematics teachers created 212 problems in ASSISTments using the system and assigned these problems to their students
key_sources: Walkington, C., Beauchamp, T., Ikram, F., Koçyiğit Gürbüz, M., Xia, F., Lee, M., Lan, A. (2025). Mathematics Teachers’ Interactions with a Multi-Agent System for Personalized Problem Generation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.12066

article_title: Adaptive teaching assistance model combining generative AI and big data analytics
citation: Zhu Z, Luo C and Li L (2026) Adaptive teaching assistance model combining generative AI and big data analytics. Front. Psychol. 17:1844703. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1844703
title: Multidimensional performance evaluation and reward-mapping module using DTW, GMM and weighted Euclidean distance
description: The big data analysis module quantifies learner performance along three dimensions: rhythm stability via Dynamic Time Warping (±15 ms threshold, weight 0.35), pitch accuracy via Gaussian Mixture Model fitting (±10 cents, weight 0.40), and dynamic control via velocity mapping (±8 levels, weight 0.25). Dimensions are min-max normalized and aggregated with a weighted Euclidean distance into a comprehensive evaluation score D, which is mapped into real-time reward signals Rt and capability defect matrices Mt used as constraints for the PPO framework. Thresholds were derived from expert consensus among three senior instructors rating 50 pilot recordings, with weights assigned via the Analytic Hierarchy Process.
requirements: Expert-derived error thresholds and AHP-assigned weights fixed across experiments to maintain a consistent evaluation standard
Relaxed thresholds (±20 ms, ±15 cents) for absolute beginners during the first 2 weeks of intervention to prevent over-correction
constraints: Thresholds were held constant across instruments and proficiency levels on the stated rationale that perceptual criteria for rhythmic stability and pitch accuracy are instrument-independent
target_learning_goals: objective diagnosis of skill gaps in rhythm, pitch and dynamics
examples: Inter-annotator agreement for expert annotation of the 4,320 recordings was κ = 0.87 for pitch accuracy, rhythmic stability and dynamic control
key_sources: Zhu Z, Luo C and Li L (2026) Adaptive teaching assistance model combining generative AI and big data analytics. Front. Psychol. 17:1844703. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1844703

article_title: The Effects of Agent Type and Feedback Style on Self-Directed Learning: A Mixed-Methods Study
citation: Han Xue, Cao Jing, Wang Zi, Luo Heng. (2026). The Effects of Agent Type and Feedback Style on Self-Directed Learning: A Mixed-Methods Study. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16071069
title: Multidimensional framework for examining AI-generated feedback in self-directed learning
description: The article proposes a structured analytical framework of "four interrelated dimensions: feedback quality, self-regulatory behaviors, learning experiences, and learning outcomes" for examining AI-supported feedback use in self-directed learning. Feedback quality covers accuracy, specificity, and task alignment; self-regulatory behaviors cover monitoring, evaluation, and revision; learning experiences cover technology acceptance, engagement, critical thinking disposition, and cognitive load; outcomes are operationalized as short-term task-specific improvement via gain scores. The framework connects feedback design features to learners' interpretive and regulatory processes.
requirements: Multiple data sources: coded interaction logs, experience questionnaires, and gain-scored drafts
Operational definitions and coding anchors for each dimension
constraints: The authors state the dimensions "should not be understood as an exhaustive model of self-directed learning itself"
Outcomes reflect immediate task performance improvement rather than long-term learning, transfer, or general SDL development
target_learning_goals: Self-directed learning skills
Instructional design quality
Self-regulated feedback use
examples: The 2×2 mixed factorial study measured all four dimensions for each of 51 participants across two instructional design tasks
key_sources: Han Xue, Cao Jing, Wang Zi, Luo Heng. (2026). The Effects of Agent Type and Feedback Style on Self-Directed Learning: A Mixed-Methods Study. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16071069

article_title: What differentiates educational literature? A multimodal fusion approach of transformers and computational linguistics
citation: Jordan J. Bird. (2024). What Differentiates Educational Literature? A Multimodal Fusion Approach of Transformers and Computational Linguistics. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.17593
title: Multimodal fusion framework combining transformer text classification with computational-linguistic feature analysis for readability assessment
description: The article proposes a framework in which fine-tuned transformer encoders (frozen, output layer removed) are fused with a neural network trained on numerical linguistic features (lexical diversity, readability formulae, part-of-speech counts, sentiment, named entities) through a unified output layer. The authors state the aim "to increase classification performance while maintaining model complexity, selecting pareto-optimal models in the trade-off between capability and real-world accessibility", motivated by traditional readability formulae lacking semantic depth and large language models being too computationally complex for school hardware.
requirements: Fixed-length linguistic feature vectors; text segmented to transformer maximum input length of 512 tokens to the nearest complete sentence
constraints: Validated only on UK Key Stage 2–5 classification of public-domain English texts; the authors note internationalisation as future work
target_learners: UK Key Stage 2–5 English learners, via educator-facing tooling
target_learning_goals: Rapid assessment of text complexity, reading difficulty and curriculum alignment for English literature
examples: ELECTRA transformer fused with a one-hidden-layer ANN via late fusion achieved the framework's best result
key_sources: Jordan J. Bird. (2024). What Differentiates Educational Literature? A Multimodal Fusion Approach of Transformers and Computational Linguistics. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.17593

article_title: Assessing Learning When AI Can Produce the Product: An Integrated Framework for Cognitive Ownership
citation: William J. Rothwell. (2026). Assessing Learning When AI Can Produce the Product: An Integrated Framework for Cognitive Ownership and Mutual Evaluation. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-4503-1957
title: Mutual evaluation: independent learner and instructor judgments compared with evidence-based, documented responses to disagreement
description: Mutual evaluation is a structured process in which learner and instructor independently evaluate the same work against shared criteria, compare their reasons, examine discrepancies, and document a warranted response. The instructor retains responsibility for standards and the final decision; reconciliation means accounting for differences, not forcing consensus or averaging ratings. The author stresses that "agreement is neither necessary nor sufficient evidence of ownership; reasoned judgment and corroborated performance provide the relevant support."
requirements: Criteria, permitted assistance, and evidence types are disclosed before submission; students practice applying criteria before evaluative performance carries substantial grading consequences
The learner records an evaluation before receiving the instructor's comments, and the instructor evaluates independently before seeing the student's ratings whenever feasible
constraints: Students may imitate rubric language, generate an insightful self-critique with AI, or agree to avoid conflict; instructors may misread disagreement as resistance, so assessors should score the disciplinary adequacy of reasons
target_learners: higher education students and their instructors
target_learning_goals: evaluative judgment about quality of work
evidence-based reasoning about discrepancies between self- and instructor evaluation
examples: In the worked example, a student rates a readiness matrix highly; the instructor questions whether the case supports the readiness judgments, and the student must identify which entries derive from case evidence and which are provisional assumptions
key_sources: William J. Rothwell. (2026). Assessing Learning When AI Can Produce the Product: An Integrated Framework for Cognitive Ownership and Mutual Evaluation. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-4503-1957

article_title: Assisting self-explanation prompts are more effective than open prompts when learning with multiple representations
citation: Berthold, K., Eysink, T.H.S. & Renkl, A. (2009). Assisting self-explanation prompts are more effective than open prompts when learning with multiple representations. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9051-z
title: Multi-representational worked-out examples on probability theory with self-explanation prompts
description: A learning environment of multi-representational worked-out examples teaching probability theory, used in an experiment with N = 62 participants. Learners studied the examples under one of three conditions: open self-explanation prompts, assisting self-explanation prompts in an "assistance-giving-assistance-withholding procedure", or no prompts as control. The environment's tasks were jointly constructed within the Dutch-German LEMMA cooperation project.
requirements: Worked-out examples presenting the content in multiple representations that learners must integrate
Self-explanation prompts embedded to elicit integration-focused explanations
constraints: Evaluated for probability theory learning in the reported experiment
target_learners: Learners of probability theory (experiment participants, N = 62)
target_learning_goals: Procedural knowledge
Conceptual knowledge of domain principles and their rationale
examples: The experiment assigned participants to open prompts, assisting prompts, or a no-prompt control group while learning probability theory
key_sources: Berthold, K., Eysink, T.H.S. & Renkl, A. (2009). Assisting self-explanation prompts are more effective than open prompts when learning with multiple representations. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9051-z

article_title: Contributions of Motivation, Early Numeracy Skills, and Executive Functioning to Mathematical Performance. A Longitudinal Study
citation: Mercader J, Miranda A, Presentación MJ, Siegenthaler R and Rosel JF (2018) Contributions of Motivation, Early Numeracy Skills, and Executive Functioning to Mathematical Performance. A Longitudinal Study. Front. Psychol. 8:2375. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.02375
title: Multifactorial longitudinal model of mathematical performance with motivation as distal and executive functioning and early numeracy as proximal predictors
description: The article proposes and tests a structural equation model in which mathematical performance in second grade is a function of three kindergarten latent variables: motivation (competence-motivation, attention-persistence, positive internality), executive functioning (inhibition and working memory), and early numeracy skills (procedural counting, conceptual counting, logical operations, symbolic comparison). The model hypothesizes a cascade in which "The latent variable Executive Functioning is inﬂuenced by the latent variable Motivation" and early numeracy skills depend on both, with performance assessed at T2. It is framed by the Opportunity-Propensity model, in which propensity factors such as motivational disposition and prior cognitive skills condition benefit from learning opportunities.
requirements: Assessment of motivational, executive functioning, and early numeracy indicators in early childhood education prior to the mathematical outcome measure
Structural equation modeling to reduce error variance relative to single observable variables
constraints: The model excludes planning/monitoring EF components, linguistic precursors such as phonological awareness, family variables such as socio-economic status, and instructional factors such as type and amount of teaching
target_learners: children in kindergarten (5–6 years) transitioning to early primary education
target_learning_goals: early mathematical performance and identification of its cognitive and motivational precursors
examples: The model was tested with 180 children assessed at two time points using TEDI-MATH, Stroop and tapping inhibition tasks, working memory tasks, the PLBS, and the CASI, with TEMA-3 at T2
key_sources: Mercader J, Miranda A, Presentación MJ, Siegenthaler R and Rosel JF (2018) Contributions of Motivation, Early Numeracy Skills, and Executive Functioning to Mathematical Performance. A Longitudinal Study. Front. Psychol. 8:2375. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.02375

article_title: Intervention Provided to Linguistically Diverse Middle School Students with Severe Reading Difficulties
citation: Denton, C. A., Wexler, J., Vaughn, S., & Bryan, D. (2008). Intervention Provided to Linguistically Diverse Middle School Students with Severe Reading Difficulties. Learning Disabilities Research & Practice, 23(2), 79–89. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-5826.2008.00264.x
title: Multicomponent middle school reading intervention: modified phonics program with ESL practices, vocabulary, fluency, and comprehension strategy instruction on a 2-day decoding/encoding cycle
description: A research intervention delivered in small groups of two to four students in daily 40-minute sessions over about 13 weeks. It was "a signiﬁcantly modiﬁed version of a phonics-based remedial program" (adapted from the Wilson reading system) augmented with ESL practices, vocabulary instruction, fluency practice, and comprehension strategies. Lessons alternated on a 2-day cycle between decoding days (letter-sound review, decoding rules, word and sentence reading, text reading) and encoding days (dictation, spelling practice, text reading), with heavy emphasis on phonics, word recognition, spelling, and fluency and integrated vocabulary and comprehension strategy instruction.
requirements: Teachers trained at least 10 hours with ongoing coaching and supervision
Small instructional groups of two to four students
Decodable text for applying decoding skills and motivating novels plus expository text for fluency and comprehension practice
constraints: Minimal emphasis on phonological awareness instruction
The majority of lesson time was spent on word-level instruction rather than vocabulary and comprehension, which the authors later hypothesized may have been a mismatch for these students' needs
target_learners: Middle school students (grades 6–8) with severe deficits in word reading, fluency, and comprehension
Spanish-speaking English language learners with identified disabilities
target_learning_goals: Decoding and encoding (spelling)
Word recognition and fluency
Vocabulary development
Comprehension strategy use
examples: Treatment students attended an average of 43 sessions (SD = 9), receiving an average of 29 hours of instruction (SD = 6; range 15–35), with fidelity ratings between 91% and 98% for both interventionists
key_sources: Denton, C. A., Wexler, J., Vaughn, S., & Bryan, D. (2008). Intervention Provided to Linguistically Diverse Middle School Students with Severe Reading Difficulties. Learning Disabilities Research & Practice, 23(2), 79–89. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-5826.2008.00266.x

article_title: Empirically-Based Guidelines for the Design of Interactive Multimedia
citation: Innwoo Park and Michael J. Hannafin. (1993). Empirically-Based Guidelines for the Design of Interactive Multimedia. Educational Technology Research and Development, Vol. 41, No. 3, pp. 63-85. http://www.jstor.org/stable/30218388
title: Support multiple perspectives and cross-referencing to build cognitive flexibility with ill-structured knowledge
description: For ill-structured knowledge, instruction that oversimplifies complex concepts produces rigid cognitive structures that interfere with transfer. The article notes that "Spiro and Feltovich (1991) applied cognitive flexibility theory to the design of hypertext," enabling learners to represent knowledge from different perspectives and understand when and how knowledge applies. Interactive multimedia should provide design overlays that allow the same resources to be used differently according to pedagogical and psychological requirements.
requirements: Design overlays must supply a coherent learning system despite resources that differ in form and reflect different psychological and pedagogical perspectives
constraints: The issue is not technological connectivity but the human rationale for making connections
target_learning_goals: cognitive flexibility and transfer of complex knowledge
examples: Overlays might create chronological sequences of events, support student-centered research toward solving a problem, or link conceptual or temporal associations
key_sources: Innwoo Park and Michael J. Hannafin. (1993). Empirically-Based Guidelines for the Design of Interactive Multimedia. Educational Technology Research and Development, Vol. 41, No. 3, pp. 63-85. http://www.jstor.org/stable/30218388

article_title: Mutualistic Coupling Between Vocabulary and Reasoning Supports Cognitive Development During Late Adolescence and Early Adulthood
citation: Kievit, R. A., Lindenberger, U., Goodyer, I. M., Jones, P. B., Fonagy, P., Bullmore, E. T., the Neuroscience in Psychiatry Network, & Dolan, R. J. (2017). Mutualistic Coupling Between Vocabulary and Reasoning Supports Cognitive Development During Late Adolescence and Early Adulthood. Psychological Science. https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797617710785
title: Mutualism model of cognitive development
description: The mutualism model, associated with van der Maas et al. (2006), proposes that "causal interactions between multiple basic cognitive abilities across developmental time" exist, "such that cognitive abilities mutually facilitate longitudinal growth." Under this assumption, developmental change yields a positive manifold even from initially uncorrelated abilities.
