In this article it was instantiated as a bivariate latent change score model with bidirectional coupling parameters between vocabulary and matrix reasoning, which outperformed g-factor and investment alternatives.
requirements: Longitudinal data with repeated measurement of multiple cognitive domains to estimate coupling parameters
constraints: Evidence here comes from adolescents and young adults (14–25) measured on two occasions with two subtests; the authors note generalizability is limited to this developmental period
target_learning_goals: development of fluid reasoning and vocabulary (crystallized knowledge)
examples: Fitted as a bivariate LCS model with coupling parameters conceptually similar to the M matrix in van der Maas et al.'s mutualism model
key_sources: Kievit, R. A., Lindenberger, U., Goodyer, I. M., Jones, P. B., Fonagy, P., Bullmore, E. T., the Neuroscience in Psychiatry Network, & Dolan, R. J. (2017). Mutualistic Coupling Between Vocabulary and Reasoning Supports Cognitive Development During Late Adolescence and Early Adulthood. Psychological Science. https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797617710785

article_title: Language, literacy, attentional behaviors, and instructional quality predictors of written composition for first graders
citation: Kim, Y.-S., Al Otaiba, S., Sidler Folsom, J., & Gruelich, L. (2013). Language, literacy, attentional behaviors, and instructional quality predictors of written composition for first graders. Early Childhood Research Quarterly, 28(3), 461–469. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecresq.2013.01.001
title: Attend to multiple component skills — oral language, literacy, and attentiveness — alongside transcription when supporting beginning writing development
description: This principle holds that written composition in early grades draws on multiple component skills beyond transcription: oral language (especially grammatical knowledge), reading comprehension, letter writing automaticity, spelling, and attentiveness. The article states that 'attention needs to be paid to multiple components beyond transcription skills such as children's oral language (e.g., sentence level grammatical knowledge) and attentiveness.' Different component skills relate differentially to substantive quality versus writing conventions dimensions of writing.
requirements: Assessment and instruction should address grammatical knowledge, reading comprehension, letter writing automaticity, spelling, and attentiveness rather than transcription alone
constraints: Findings are correlational from first-grade classrooms in a northern Florida community; causal directionality is not established
target_learners: First-grade students in early elementary classrooms
target_learning_goals: Written composition — substantive quality and writing conventions
examples: The study assessed 527 first graders on expressive vocabulary, grammatical knowledge, reading comprehension, spelling, letter writing automaticity, and teacher-rated attentiveness, then modeled their unique relations to two written composition dimensions
key_sources: Kim, Y.-S., Al Otaiba, S., Sidler Folsom, J., & Gruelich, L. (2013). Language, literacy, attentional behaviors, and instructional quality predictors of written composition for first graders. Early Childhood Research Quarterly, 28(3), 461–469. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecresq.2013.01.001

article_title: Integrating performance assessments across a PK-20 continuum: A locally developed collaboration
citation: McCurdy, K., Reagan, E. M., Schram, T., & Rogers, A. (2018). Integrating performance assessments across a PK-20 continuum: A locally developed collaboration. Education Policy Analysis Archives, 26(14). http://dx.doi.org/10.14507/epaa.26.3437
title: Multilayered system of assessment practices influenced by actors at all levels
description: The commentary adopts Stosich et al.'s (2018) framing of a "multilayered system of assessment practices" that is "influenced by actors at all levels of the educational system," including decision-makers at the school, district or network, state, and federal level. The article uses this framework to argue that a higher education voice should be added to the ecosystem, operating through a PK-20 rather than PK-12 lens. It also notes the framework's claim that creating such a multilayered system can provide more coherent or fragmented support for performance assessments.
requirements: Multiple stakeholders operating with a shared and co-created vision, characterized by open dialogue that enhances trust across all stakeholders
constraints: The framework is attributed to Stosich et al. (2018) and is developed from their review of PK-12 state-level policies; the commentary extends it to teacher preparation
target_learning_goals: meaningful student learning supported by coherent assessment systems
examples: The commentary applies the framework to New Hampshire, where PACE and the NH TCAP are locally developed performance assessments reflecting a state culture valuing local influence
key_sources: McCurdy, K., Reagan, E. M., Schram, T., & Rogers, A. (2018). Integrating performance assessments across a PK-20 continuum: A locally developed collaboration. Education Policy Analysis Archives, 26(14). http://dx.doi.org/10.14507/epaa.26.3437

article_title: Longitudinal stability of pre‐reading skill profiles of kindergarten children: implications for early screening and theories of reading
citation: Ozernov-Palchik, O., Norton, E. S., Sideridis, G., Beach, S. D., Wolf, M., Gabrieli, J. D. E., & Gaab, N. (2017). Longitudinal stability of pre-reading skill profiles of kindergarten children: Implications for early screening and theories of reading. Developmental Science. https://doi.org/10.1111/desc.12471
title: Multi-deficit data-driven conceptualization of dyslexia risk profiles
description: The article advances a multi-deficit, person-centered framework in which dyslexia risk is characterized by homogeneous profiles of performance on multiple pre-reading constructs rather than a single core deficit or pre-set cutoffs. The authors note that "a multi-deficit conceptualization of dyslexia is becoming increasingly accepted", and operationalize it via latent profile analysis, which is "a person-centered approach that groups individuals by the probability of their response patterns". The framework yields distinct PA, RAN, and double-deficit risk profiles with different longitudinal reading outcomes.
requirements: Requires a battery of pre-reading measures (PA, RAN, letter knowledge, verbal short-term memory) administered before or at the start of reading instruction
Requires large samples for stable latent profile model estimation
constraints: The authors note the theoretical interpretation could be affected by measure selection; other measures could have yielded profiles aligned with other theories of dyslexia
target_learning_goals: early identification of dyslexia risk
differentiated early literacy intervention
examples: The study fit 1–7 profile models to 1,215 children and selected a 6-class solution, then validated the classes longitudinally against 1st-grade reading measures
key_sources: Ozernov-Palchik, O., Norton, E. S., Sideridis, G., Beach, S. D., Wolf, M., Gabrieli, J. D. E., & Gaab, N. (2017). Longitudinal stability of pre-reading skill profiles of kindergarten children: Implications for early screening and theories of reading. Developmental Science. https://doi.org/10.1111/desc.12471

article_title: The Effects of Age, Control Beliefs, and Feedback on Self-Regulation of Reading and Problem Solving
citation: Soederberg Miller, L. M., & West, R. L. (2010). The Effects of Age, Control Beliefs, and Feedback on Self-Regulation of Reading and Problem Solving. Experimental Aging Research, 36(1), 40-63. https://doi.org/10.1080/03610730903418380
title: Use both subjective and objective measures, including online assessments, to capture the complexity of self-regulation
description: The article's differential findings across outcome measures show that age, control beliefs, and feedback type had different effects on task-specific beliefs, attention, and problem solving accuracy. The authors recommend that "a wide range of measures is needed to fully capture the complexity of self-regulation." They suggest combining subjective measures (beliefs and perceptions) with objective measures (strategy use, time spent, attention), and pairing online real-time assessments with offline measures. This principle guides researchers and designers to avoid relying on a single self-report or performance indicator when evaluating self-regulatory processes.
requirements: Studies of self-regulation should include measures sensitive to different components (beliefs, attention, performance) to detect differential patterns
constraints: The article notes that noncentral memory questions had unacceptable internal consistency (alpha = .05) and were excluded, illustrating measurement challenges in multi-measure designs
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning
reading comprehension
problem solving
examples: In this study, self-efficacy and expectations showed additive feedback effects while attention showed a three-way interaction with age and control beliefs, demonstrating that different measures reveal different self-regulatory responses
key_sources: Soederberg Miller, L. M., & West, R. L. (2010). The Effects of Age, Control Beliefs, and Feedback on Self-Regulation of Reading and Problem Solving. Experimental Aging Research, 36(1), 40-63. https://doi.org/10.1080/03610730903418380

article_title: Creative Thinking in Adolescents with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)
citation: Abraham, Anna; Windmann, Sabine; Siefen, Rainer; Daum, Irene; Güntürkün, Onur. (2006). Creative thinking in adolescents with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Child Neuropsychology, 12(2), 111-123. https://doi.org/10.1080/09297040500320691
title: Multi-measure creativity assessment battery spanning example-constraint and imagery invention tasks
description: The study assessed creativity using several measures rather than a single test, including a task measuring the ability to overcome the constraining influence of examples and an imagery task requiring generation of a functional invention. This multi-measure approach is what allowed the ADHD group's profile to appear selective, with advantages on some measures and disadvantages on others, rather than uniformly better or worse than the comparison groups.
requirements: Multiple distinct creativity measures are needed to reveal selective, task-dependent cognitive profiles.
target_learning_goals: assessment of creative thinking
examples: Performance across several creativity measures was compared in adolescents with ADHD, those with conduct disorder, and a healthy control sample.
key_sources: Abraham, Anna; Windmann, Sabine; Siefen, Rainer; Daum, Irene; Güntürkün, Onur. (2006). Creative thinking in adolescents with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Child Neuropsychology, 12(2), 111-123. https://doi.org/10.1080/09297040500320691

article_title: Adults with dyslexia exhibit large effects of crowding, increased dependence on cues, and detrimental effects of distractors in visual search tasks
citation: Moores, E., Cassim, R. and Talcott, J.B. (2011). Adults with dyslexia exhibit large effects of crowding, increased dependence on cues, and detrimental effects of distractors in visual search tasks. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2011.00285
title: Visual attention deficits in dyslexia require multi-factor accounts combining crowding, cue dependence and distractor exclusion
description: The article proposes that visual attention in dyslexia must be understood through the combined influences of crowding, attention orientation and focussing of attention/distractor exclusion, rather than any single mechanism. It reports that "AwD do not use cues less, but they do use cues less successfully" and that "It is not clear how any single theory on its own can fully account for the entirety of findings presented here." The account holds that crowding effects operate independently from, and in parallel with, the allocation of visual attention, and that pre-cueing eliminated effects of crowding for AwD.
requirements: Simultaneous investigation of crowding, orientation and distractor exclusion factors rather than isolated paradigms
constraints: The article states further research should aim to confirm that greater set size effects occur independently of task difficulty and in other paradigms
target_learning_goals: understanding visual attention contributions to literacy difficulties in dyslexia
examples: Calibrated discrimination accuracy across conditions for each individual, then compared relative performance across display types, cue types and difficulties
key_sources: Moores, E., Cassim, R. and Talcott, J.B. (2011). Adults with dyslexia exhibit large effects of crowding, increased dependence on cues, and detrimental effects of distractors in visual search tasks. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2011.00285

article_title: Automaticity of word recognition is a unique predictor of reading fluency in middle-school students.
citation: Roembke Tanja C., Hazeltine Eliot, Reed Deborah K., McMurray Bob. (2019). Automaticity of Word Recognition is a Unique Predictor of Reading Fluency in Middle-School Students. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000279
title: Multi-pathway framework of automatic word recognition (O→S and O→P→S routes)
description: The article describes a connectionist multi-pathway framework in which readers access meaning either directly from spelling (orthography to semantics, O→S) or indirectly via decoding (O→P→S). It states that "Both the O→S and O→P→S pathways are implemented over learnable networks of connections, which transmit activation more or less efficiently depending on how well these connections are organized." Automaticity could reflect pathway dominance or be achievable in both pathways to varying degrees, including for nonwords. The study's tasks were designed to shift reliance toward one pathway or the other.
requirements: Tasks must be designed to change the degree to which OS or OP pathways contribute, since pathways cannot be truly isolated
constraints: The article notes pathways cannot be truly isolated, as readers likely use a combination to solve most tasks
target_learners: middle-school students with average to below-average reading comprehension
target_learning_goals: word recognition automaticity
reading fluency
decoding
examples: Find the Picture emphasized OS processing; Find the Rhyme and Verify nonword trials emphasized OP processing
key_sources: Roembke Tanja C., Hazeltine Eliot, Reed Deborah K., McMurray Bob. (2019). Automaticity of Word Recognition is a Unique Predictor of Reading Fluency in Middle-School Students. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000279

article_title: Examining reciprocal influences among family climate, school attachment, and academic self-regulation: Implications for school success.
citation: Xia, M., Fosco, G. M., & Feinberg, M. E. (2016). Examining Reciprocal Influences Among Family Climate, School Attachment, and Academic Self-Regulation: Implications for School Success. Journal of Family Psychology, 30(4), 442-452. https://doi.org/10.1037/fam0000141
title: Multi-contextual family-systems and ecological framework of adolescent school success
description: Guided by family systems and ecological theories, the study proposes that adolescent school success emerges from the interplay of three domains: family climate, school attachment, and academic self-regulation. Rather than studying these "in relative isolation", the framework models reciprocal, transactional influences among contexts over time, with family climate and school attachment mutually reinforcing each other and each unidirectionally feeding ASR, which in turn drives achievement and adjustment. Figure 1 depicts the hypothesized model.
requirements: Testing the framework requires longitudinal data with repeated measures across the middle school years
constraints: The study measured family climate, school attachment, and ASR with youth-report mono-informant assessments, a limitation the authors state
target_learning_goals: academic self-regulation
school adjustment
academic achievement
examples: The study applied a four-wave cross-lag structural equation model to longitudinal data from 979 6th grade students followed through 9th grade
key_sources: Xia, M., Fosco, G. M., & Feinberg, M. E. (2016). Examining Reciprocal Influences Among Family Climate, School Attachment, and Academic Self-Regulation: Implications for School Success. Journal of Family Psychology, 30(4), 442-452. https://doi.org/10.1037/fam0000141

article_title: Neural correlates of oral word reading, silent reading comprehension, and cognitive subcomponents
citation: Xia Zhichao, Zhang Linjun, Hoeft Fumiko, Gu Bin, Gong Gaolang, Shu Hua. (2018). Neural Correlates of Oral Word Reading, Silent Reading Comprehension, and Cognitive Subcomponents. International Journal of Behavioral Development. https://doi.org/10.1177/0165025417727872
title: Multi-componential view of reading with neuroanatomical subdivisions
description: The article frames reading as "multi-componential in nature, i.e., the entire process consists of many subcomponents", with oral word reading and comprehension drawing on partly different subcomponents. It proposes that this hierarchical structure is mirrored at the neuroanatomical level, such that specific brain regions' cortical thickness maps onto specific subcomponents (e.g., LSMG to phonological awareness, LITG to orthography-phonology mapping, LPHP to morphological awareness). The study's findings are presented as "neuroanatomical evidence in support of the multi-componential view of reading" in typically developing Chinese children.
requirements: Requires measuring reading at multiple levels (word reading efficiency and sentence comprehension) alongside tasks tapping distinct cognitive subcomponents
constraints: Evidence here comes from typically developing Chinese children aged 10-12; the authors note the findings need replication with larger sample sizes and cover a limited number of central subcomponents of reading
target_learners: Typically developing children in upper elementary grades (grades 5-6) learning Chinese
target_learning_goals: Oral word reading fluency and silent sentence reading comprehension, and their underlying phonological, orthographic and morphological subcomponents
examples: The study measured word list reading, sentence reading fluency, tone identification and detection, morphological production, and six Chain Test subtests, then regressed subcomponent scores on cortical thickness of reading-defined ROIs.
key_sources: Xia Zhichao, Zhang Linjun, Hoeft Fumiko, Gu Bin, Gong Gaolang, Shu Hua. (2018). Neural Correlates of Oral Word Reading, Silent Reading Comprehension, and Cognitive Subcomponents. International Journal of Behavioral Development. https://doi.org/10.1177/0165025417727872

article_title: Fostering Critical Thinking Skills in Preschool Education: Designing, Implementing and Assessing a Multiliteracies-Oriented Program Based on Intercultural Tales
citation: Papadopoulos, I., & Bisiri, E. (2020). Fostering Critical Thinking Skills in Preschool Education: Designing, Implementing and Assessing a Multiliteracies-Oriented Program Based on Intercultural Tales. Multilingual Academic Journal of Education and Social Sciences, 8(1), 87–105. https://doi.org/10.46886/MAJESS/v8-i1/7263
title: Multiliteracies pedagogy organized around four knowledge processes: experiencing, conceptualizing, analyzing, applying
description: The article applies the pedagogy of multiliteracies, in which literacy is treated as active meaning-making across multiple modes rather than sentence-bound rules of spelling and grammar. It states that "The pedagogy of Multiliteracies suggests transformative ways of knowing, the four ‘knowledge processes’: ‘experiencing, conceptualizing, analyzing and applying’", and these processes serve as an outline for educators' pedagogical actions. Each folk-tale thematic unit in the program was designed around these four processes, with tasks such as experiencing the known/new, conceptualizing by naming and with theory, analysing functionally and critically, and applying appropriately and creatively.
requirements: Implementation depends on the active roles of both teachers and learners as instruments of design in a multimodal environment, with teachers facilitating and creating motivating learning conditions
constraints: The article frames the framework for early-childhood literacy instruction in multicultural preschool settings; assessment of multiliterate skills requires alternative methods such as portfolios rather than discrete-point testing
target_learning_goals: critical thinking skills
multiliteracies and multimodal meaning-making
multicultural sensitivity
examples: Each of the seven folk-tales formed a thematic unit lasting 2 to 3 weeks, with tasks A–L mapped onto the four knowledge processes
key_sources: Papadopoulos, I., & Bisiri, E. (2020). Fostering Critical Thinking Skills in Preschool Education: Designing, Implementing and Assessing a Multiliteracies-Oriented Program Based on Intercultural Tales. Multilingual Academic Journal of Education and Social Sciences, 8(1), 87–105. https://doi.org/10.46886/MAJESS/v8-i1/7263

article_title: Academic Race Stereotypes, Academic Self-Concept, and Racial Centrality in African American Youth
citation: Okeke, N. A., Howard, L. C., Kurtz-Costes, B., & Rowley, S. J. (2009). Academic race stereotypes, academic self-concept, and racial centrality in African American youth. Journal of Black Psychology, 35(3), 366–387. https://doi.org/10.1177/0095798409333615
title: Multidimensional model of African American racial identity with four dimensions
description: The article adopts Sellers et al.'s conceptualization of racial identity in African Americans as "a multidimensional construct including four dimensions". Racial salience is how important race is at a particular time and context; racial ideology is beliefs about how African Americans should act; racial regard is evaluative judgment of one's race, with private and public aspects; and racial centrality is "the extent to which race is a central aspect of an individual's self-definition". The study uses the centrality subscale of the MIBI as its moderator variable.
requirements: Measured with the Multidimensional Inventory of Black Identity centrality subscale (6 items, α = .74 in both studies)
constraints: The article examines centrality only; salience, ideology, and regard are not tested as moderators
target_learning_goals: Academic self-concept and achievement motivation
examples: Both studies measured centrality with six MIBI items rated on a 5-point Likert-type scale, e.g., "Being Black is an important part of my self-image"
key_sources: Okeke, N. A., Howard, L. C., Kurtz-Costes, B., & Rowley, S. J. (2009). Academic race stereotypes, academic self-concept, and racial centrality in African American youth. Journal of Black Psychology, 35(3), 366–387. https://doi.org/10.1177/0095798409333615

article_title: Multisensory Integration as a Window into Orderly and Disrupted Cognition and Communication
citation: Wallace, M. T., Woynaroski, T. G., & Stevenson, R. A. (2020). Multisensory Integration as a Window into Orderly and Disrupted Cognition and Communication. Annual Review of Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-psych-010419-051112
title: Multisensory maturation scaffolds the development of higher-order cognitive and communicative skills
description: The review advances a developmental framework in which sensory and multisensory systems, which mature before higher-level cognitive and communicative processes, provide "a key developmental scaffold upon which higher-order representations are formed and refined". Early multisensory development relies heavily on low-level statistical stimulus features, and disruptions in foundational sensory function early in life are proposed to produce cascading effects across developmental domains. The framework is compatible with embodied cognition, the extended mind thesis, and enactivism.
requirements: Sensory and multisensory systems must develop ahead of, and provide foundational input to, higher-order cognitive and linguistic systems
constraints: The review notes that associations between multisensory function and cognition have largely been concurrent and correlational, so causality cannot yet be concluded
target_learners: infants and children in typical and atypical development
target_learning_goals: language acquisition
cognitive development
perceptual representation formation
examples: Quail embryos prenatally exposed to synchronous multisensory stimulation showed enhanced learning and memory for the mother's call relative to asynchronous or unisensory exposure
key_sources: Wallace, M. T., Woynaroski, T. G., & Stevenson, R. A. (2020). Multisensory Integration as a Window into Orderly and Disrupted Cognition and Communication. Annual Review of Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-psych-010419-051112

article_title: Geopolitical Configuration of Identities and Learning: Othering through the Institutionalized Categorization of “English Language Learners”
citation: Takeuchi, M.A. (2020). Geopolitical configuration of identities and learning: Othering through the institutionalized categorization of “English language learners. Cognition and Instruction. Advance online publication https://doi.org/10.1080/07370008.2020.1825438
title: Multi-layered identities framework: figurative, positional, and geopolitical layers interact and thicken through repeated practices
description: The article extends Holland et al.'s distinction between figurative identities (“the stories, acts, and characters that make the world a cultural world”) and positional identities (day-to-day relations of power and entitlement) by adding a layer of geopolitical configuration of identities. This added layer captures how colonial and geopolitical histories shape who becomes the Other, deprived of discursive space to speak and represent. Layers can be “thickened or laminated through repeated practices,” framing how interactions unfold and shaping learners' becoming.
requirements: Analysis attends to interactions across micro, meso, and macro timescales of history, since layers are inextricably woven together
constraints: The article states the macro-level geopolitical configuration and colonial matrix of identity had not been fully considered in prior scholarship on identities and mathematics learning
target_learners: elementary students institutionally classified as English language learners
immigrant and refugee students in linguistically diverse schools
target_learning_goals: understanding how identity layers shape access to agentive learning opportunities in mathematics classrooms
examples: The framework was applied to four focal students in a Grade 4 transforming recess mathematics unit, contrasting cases of Cathy and Iris with Daniel and Karim
key_sources: Takeuchi, M.A. (2020). Geopolitical configuration of identities and learning: Othering through the institutionalized categorization of “English language learners. Cognition and Instruction. Advance online publication https://doi.org/10.1080/07370008.2020.1825438

article_title: The multi-layered nature of small-group learning: Productive interactions in object-oriented collaboration
citation: Damşa, C. I. (2014). The multi-layered nature of small-group learning: Productive interactions in object-oriented collaboration. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. (2014) 9:247–281. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-014-9193-8
title: Multi-layer analytic framework linking productive interaction, knowledge objects, and shared epistemic agency over time
description: The article constructs an integrative analytic framework in which learning is analyzed as knowledge co-construction across three interwoven layers: productive interactions, knowledge objects, and shared epistemic agency, unfolding in time via interaction trajectories. Knowledge objects are "an externalization of knowledge, 'freezing' knowledge at certain moments in time", accessible to the whole group and usable to produce new knowledge. The unit of analysis is the joint action directed at co-construction of knowledge objects — mediated interaction — rather than the individual or the group. A temporal perspective captures how moment-to-moment episodes build into continuity and how interaction generates actions that affect developing objects.
requirements: Analysis requires identifying theme-based episodes, coding verbal actions within episodes, and pairing key events in interaction with object versions within a maximum of one week
constraints: Productivity is defined in epistemic terms by each case and context rather than universal criteria
The framework was developed and applied in higher-education collaborative research projects
target_learning_goals: collaborative knowledge co-construction
conducting and reporting empirical research
examples: The analysis combined discourse-analysis coding of episodes, document analysis of report iterations (11 to 29 per group), and qualification of agentic action sequences
key_sources: Damşa, C. I. (2014). The multi-layered nature of small-group learning: Productive interactions in object-oriented collaboration. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. (2014) 9:247–281. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-014-9193-8

article_title: The symmetry of partner modelling
citation: Dillenbourg, P., Lemaignan, S., Sangin, M., Nova, N., & Molinari, G. (2016). The symmetry of partner modelling. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-016-9235-5
title: Mutual modelling in collaboration: each partner needs some model of what the other partners know, want and intend
description: The article frames collaborative tasks as requiring "some level of mutual modelling", i.e. a representation each partner holds of what the others know, want and intend at a given time. The deliberate term "some model" stresses that such representations are "not necessarily detailed or complete". The framework is used to pose the article's research question: whether partner-model quality depends on the modeler's representational ability, the modelée's clarity, or the quality of their interactions. It links partner modelling to the psycholinguistic machinery of common ground in collaborative learning.
requirements: Collaborative tasks that require partners to build representations of each other's knowledge, wants and intentions
constraints: The model is explicitly partial: "not necessarily detailed or complete"
target_learners: collaborating peers in dyads or small teams
target_learning_goals: building shared understanding during collaborative problem solving and collaborative learning
examples: The five experiments varied in terms of tasks (how important it is to build an accurate model) and settings (how difficult it is to build an accurate model).
key_sources: Dillenbourg, P., Lemaignan, S., Sangin, M., Nova, N., & Molinari, G. (2016). The symmetry of partner modelling. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-016-9235-5

article_title: The symmetry of partner modelling
citation: Dillenbourg, P., Lemaignan, S., Sangin, M., Nova, N., & Molinari, G. (2016). The symmetry of partner modelling. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-016-9235-5
title: Open online dataset and statistical analyses of the mutual-modelling emotions study
description: The authors state that "The data and statistical analyses of this study are available online" at the repository https://github.com/chili-epfl/mutual-modelling-emotions-study. This artifact accompanies the five experiments on collaborative problem solving and collaborative learning and provides the underlying data and analysis code for the symmetry-of-partner-modelling findings, supporting reanalysis of the mutual model accuracy results.
requirements: Access to the GitHub repository hosting the study's data and statistical analyses
target_learners: researchers studying collaborative learning and mutual modelling
target_learning_goals: transparent secondary analysis of partner-modelling accuracy data
examples: The study's five experiments on collaborative problem solving or collaborative learning are the source of the released data and analyses.
key_sources: Dillenbourg, P., Lemaignan, S., Sangin, M., Nova, N., & Molinari, G. (2016). The symmetry of partner modelling. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-016-9235-5

article_title: From Cognitive Load Theory to Collaborative Cognitive Load Theory
citation: Kirschner, P. A., Sweller, J., Kirschner, F., & Zambrano R., J. (2018). From Cognitive Load Theory to Collaborative Cognitive Load Theory. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9277-y
title: Mutual cognitive interdependence principle
description: A sub-principle of the borrowing and reorganising principle added to cognitive load theory to account for collaboration. The article states it 'acts as a subsidiary of the borrowing and re-organising principle by detailing how cognitive systems (i.e., inter-cognitive processes) acquire information between them', presupposing relative openness between cognitive systems and attending to intrinsic transactive processes. It holds that individuals depend on the instructor's guidance, appropriate peer interactions, and appropriate instructional environments of collaboration, without reducing them to the components of an individual system.
requirements: Relative openness between cognitive systems and transactive processes that allow cognitive exchange between them
constraints: The relation between systems and their environment must not be reduced to the cognitive components of an individual system
target_learners: collaborators in face-to-face or computer-supported groups
target_learning_goals: inter-cognitive exchange and shared knowledge construction
examples: The article says incorporating this principle into cognitive load theory's architecture 'provides the basis for the collective working memory effect'
key_sources: Kirschner, P. A., Sweller, J., Kirschner, F., & Zambrano R., J. (2018). From Cognitive Load Theory to Collaborative Cognitive Load Theory. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9277-y

article_title: Students’ multimodal knowledge practices in a makerspace learning environment
citation: Anu Kajamaa & Kristiina Kumpulainen. (2020). Students' multimodal knowledge practices in a makerspace learning environment. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (2020) 15:411–444. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-020-09337-z
title: Four intertwined multimodal knowledge practices in makerspace learning: orienting, interpreting, concretizing, and expanding knowledge
description: The article identifies a taxonomy of four multimodal knowledge practices that mediated students' collaborative maker work: "orienting, interpreting, concretizing, and expanding knowledge". Orienting involves selecting challenges, materials and spaces via cumulative talk; interpreting involves verbally reflecting on instructions and ideating; concretizing involves externalizing knowledge into epistemic objects and tangible artifacts; expanding involves critically revising objects and plans when difficulties arise. The practices are realized through discourse, materials, embodied actions and spatial arrangements and guided the creation of shared epistemic objects and artifacts.
requirements: Identification requires analysis of discursive, material, embodied and spatial dimensions of interaction, as coded in the article's three-phase sociocultural discourse and multimodal interaction analysis
constraints: The practices were identified from video data of two student groups in one school's FUSE Studio makerspace, and the authors acknowledge results might have looked different with newly formed groups
target_learners: Elementary students aged 9–12 carrying out STEAM design challenges in small groups
target_learning_goals: Collaborative knowledge creation in STEAM design and making activities
examples: Each practice was illustrated with episodes, such as two boys relocating to the corridor to build a Laser Defender security system, moving through all four practices to a completed artifact.
key_sources: Anu Kajamaa & Kristiina Kumpulainen. (2020). Students' multimodal knowledge practices in a makerspace learning environment. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (2020) 15:411–444. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-020-09337-z

article_title: Many are the ways to learn identifying multi-modal behavioral profiles of collaborative learning in constructivist activities
citation: Jauwairia Nasir, Aditi Kothiyal, Barbara Bruno, Pierre Dillenbourg. (2021). Many are the ways to learn identifying multi-modal behavioral profiles of collaborative learning in constructivist activities. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn (2021) 16:485–523. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09358-2
title: Two-approach multi-modal learning analytics technique linking behavioral clusters to learning outcomes (Approach A backward, Approach B forward)
description: This technique builds behavioral profiles of dyads by clustering teams on multi-modal behaviors (log, video, audio features) and then relating behavioral clusters to learning and performance outcomes. Approach A connects "the learning outcomes back to the behaviors observed during the learning process", while Approach B is "a forward approach as it helps to move from multi-modal behaviors to learning outcomes". Approach B was designed to detect multiple behavioral profiles for the same learning profile, which Approach A's one-cluster-one-profile assumption cannot do; it succeeded where Approach A found no significantly discriminating behavior between its cluster pairs.
requirements: Behavioral clusters from Approach B must show significant differences in learning gains (requirement 1) and a comprehensible one-to-many or many-to-many mapping to learning/performance clusters (requirement 2) before their labels are used as classifier ground truth for the final classifier.
constraints: The dataset treats all behaviors as cross-sectional averages over the entire task duration, not time series data, and behaviors were normalized across teams to values between 0 and 1.
target_learners: Children aged 9 to 12 years working in dyads on open-ended collaborative problems
target_learning_goals: Conceptual understanding of minimum-spanning-tree problems in a problem-based learning activity
examples: The technique applied to the JUSThink dataset produced three behavioral clusters (Expressive Explorers, Calm Tinkerers, Silent Wanderers) with excellent classification results, reported previously in Nasir, Bruno, and Dillenbourg (2020a).
key_sources: Jauwairia Nasir, Aditi Kothiyal, Barbara Bruno, Pierre Dillenbourg. (2021). Many are the ways to learn identifying multi-modal behavioral profiles of collaborative learning in constructivist activities. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn (2021) 16:485–523. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09358-2

article_title: Relations Matter – CSCL Research Informing and Developing CL Competencies
citation: Sanna Järvelä, Carolyn P. Rosé. (2022). Relations Matter – CSCL Research Informing and Developing CL Competencies. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn (2022) 17:185–189. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-022-09373-x
title: Multilayered relations as a lens for designing collaboration scripts, self-regulation and group awareness
description: This lens, attributed by the editors to Crook's (2022) discussion paper, treats 'relations' — between students, actions, and digital artifacts — as multilayered and as consequential for CSCL outcomes. The editorial writes that Crook pointed to "a concept of multilayered 'relations' as a lens for understanding how increasing knowledge of the synergy between collaboration scripts, self-regulation, and group awareness can help guide us as we design joint activity." Relations are enacted through processes studied via multiple data streams.
requirements: Collection and analysis of multiple data streams to reveal interactions at social and cognitive levels
constraints: The editorial presents the lens as attributed to Crook (2022), not as its own tested model
target_learning_goals: collaborative knowledge building
key_sources: Sanna Järvelä, Carolyn P. Rosé. (2022). Relations Matter – CSCL Research Informing and Developing CL Competencies. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn (2022) 17:185–189. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-022-09373-x

article_title: Learning within fiber-crafted algorithms: Posthumanist perspectives for capturing human-material collaboration
citation: Anna Keune. (2024). Learning within fiber-crafted algorithms: Posthumanist perspectives for capturing human-material collaboration. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09412-1
title: Multi-angle video capture disrupting human visual centrality to allow human-material analysis
description: This capture pattern combines eye-level, bird's-eye-view, and close-up turntable videos so that material movements are analytically visible. The study collected approximately 13.5 hours each of eye-level and bird's-eye views plus 435 close-up videos, because data centered predominantly on human actions limits theorizing materially driven phenomena. Viewing angles simultaneously afforded verification of what had been seen from another angle through visual evidence.
requirements: Synchronized timestamps across camera angles, a 360-degree camera rig above the craft table, directional and wireless microphones, and turntable close-ups of projects
constraints: The camera remains "a necessary but distorting component in video-based educational research," so angle and frame choices always include or exclude analytical aspects
target_learners: middle school youth in org small-group making settings
target_learning_goals: capturing collaborative learning processes that involve tangible and computational materials
examples: Eye-level video was the primary source for weaving's z-axis movements; bird's-eye video was primary for fabric manipulation's folded layers; close-ups reverse-engineered production processes
key_sources: Anna Keune. (2024). Learning within fiber-crafted algorithms: Posthumanist perspectives for capturing human-material collaboration. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09412-1

article_title: Capturing temporal pathways of collaborative roles: A multilayered analytical approach using community of inquiry
citation: Ramy Elmoazen, Mohammed Saqr, Laura Hirsto, Matti Tedre. (2025). Capturing temporal pathways of collaborative roles: A multilayered analytical approach using community of inquiry. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09431-6
title: Multilayered temporal analysis pattern for collaborative learning: roles as states, sequences, and trajectories
description: This analytical pattern combines several learning-analytics methods into layers to capture role dynamics over time: latent class analysis converts CoI-coded discourse into role states, epistemic network analysis maps code co-occurrence within roles, sequence mining orders roles across weeks, and Markov process mining estimates transition probabilities within trajectories. The authors motivate the layering with Reimann et al.'s warning that "relying on a single sequential approach can hide in details due to the ontological flatness of educational data", so that "such a combination yields a much better understanding of the temporal aspects of students' roles".
requirements: Timestamped interaction logs with author identifiers, discourse coded against a theoretical framework in ordered time frames (weekly stanzas), and R tooling (glca, ENA Webkit, TramineR, seqHMM)
constraints: The Markov model was chosen partly because it avoids the data-trimming other process-mining methods require; transitions below 5% probability are thinned for readability
target_learners: students in online discussion-based cross-course collaborative programs
target_learning_goals: understanding and monitoring students' evolving collaboration roles and dispositions
examples: Applied to 13 weeks of PBL discussion across four dental-science courses, the pipeline identified three roles, three trajectories, and their Markov transition structures.
key_sources: Ramy Elmoazen, Mohammed Saqr, Laura Hirsto, Matti Tedre. (2025). Capturing temporal pathways of collaborative roles: A multilayered analytical approach using community of inquiry. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09431-6
grain_size: course-level analytic pattern spanning multiple consecutive courses

article_title: Exploring interconnections between communicative activities, situational stress reactions and cognitive engagement in undergraduate mathematics lesson
citation: Lehesvuori, S., Järvinen, M., Lämsä, J., Heilala, V., Hämäläinen, R. (2026). Exploring interconnections between communicative activities, situational stress reactions and cognitive engagement in undergraduate mathematics lesson. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09786-3
title: Macro–meso–micro multimodal analysis framework combining classroom interaction coding with second-by-second cardiac stress measurement
description: The article develops a three-level analytical framework: macro-level overviews of communicative activities, meso-level visualisation of situational stress across the lesson, and micro-level second-by-second analysis of critical incidents combining discourse analysis with stress data. The authors state that "the methodological contribution of this research lies in the combination of both physiological (i.e., cardiac data) and multimodal interactional data (i.e., eye tracking, video, audio)." Stress is operationalised via the ASV derived from HRV, applying an approach from psychotherapist settings to an authentic learning environment.
requirements: Cardiac sensor data from consenting students, synchronised video/audio classroom recording, and a communicative-activity coding scheme applied in 20-second intervals
constraints: Exploratory use of second-by-second ASV beyond validated five-minute intervals; no baseline normalisation or interindividual comparison of HRV; three consenting students only
target_learners: first-year engineering students in undergraduate mathematics
target_learning_goals: understanding how communicative activities relate to situational stress and cognitive engagement during mathematical problem-solving and presentation
examples: The framework was applied to one demonstration session in which three sensor-wearing students presented solutions, with coding reliability of Cohen's kappa 0.70 (teacher) and 0.77 (student)
key_sources: Lehesvuori, S., Järvinen, M., Lämsä, J., Heilala, V., Hämäläinen, R. (2026). Exploring interconnections between communicative activities, situational stress reactions and cognitive engagement in undergraduate mathematics lesson. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09786-3

article_title: Students’ voices—the dynamic interactions between learning preferences, gender, learning disabilities, and achievements in science studies
citation: Oshra Aloni, Michal Zion, Ornit Spektor-Levy. (2024). Students' voices—the dynamic interactions between learning preferences, gender, learning disabilities, and achievements in science studies. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09666-8
title: Implement multi-faceted instructional strategies and an ongoing metacognitive dialogue with students about learning preferences to address student diversity in science classrooms
description: The article argues that because students favored all four learning modalities and expected variety, science instruction should be multi-faceted. The authors state that "the study results show the importance of implementing multi-faceted instructional strategies to address students' diversity and learning preferences", and that offering equal opportunities should be reflected in "an ongoing, metacognitive dialogue between the teachers and the students" about outcomes, achievements, and learning processes. Without such explicit discussion, they warn, providing learning choices may leave students confused and underachieving.
requirements: Explicit discussions with students about their learning preferences, so that offering learning choices does not end in confusion and unmet potential
constraints: The study addressed only a binary gender system and did not consider students who do not identify as male or female
Effect sizes for gender differences were low-moderate and the authors call for further examination
target_learners: Middle school (ninth-grade) science students in heterogeneous, inclusive classrooms, including students with and without learning disabilities
target_learning_goals: Scientific knowledge and skills in ninth-grade science (nutrition and the digestive system, scientific inquiry, graph reading)
examples: The study asked 305 ninth-grade students about their science learning preferences via a validated Learning Preferences Questionnaire based on Fleming's VARK model and the Multi-Faceted Holistic Approach, and found all four modalities preferred above the mid-point with visual and sensorimotor highest
key_sources: Oshra Aloni, Michal Zion, Ornit Spektor-Levy. (2024). Students' voices—the dynamic interactions between learning preferences, gender, learning disabilities, and achievements in science studies. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09666-8

article_title: Semiempty collaborative concept mapping in history education: students’ engagement in historical reasoning and coconstruction
citation: Lucero, M., Montanero, M., & van Boxtel, C. (2024). Semiempty collaborative concept mapping in history education: students' engagement in historical reasoning and coconstruction. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09659-7
title: MUPEMURE model: negotiation and knowledge building are shaped by the type of external knowledge representation tool
description: The MUPEMURE (MUltiple PErspectives on MUltiple REpresentations) model of Weinberger et al. holds that "these negotiation and knowledge building processes are strongly influenced by the type of external knowledge representation tool used". It predicts a reciprocal effect between representation type and collaboration: how learners interact depends on the type and quality of the external representation. The study's finding that semiempty concept maps elicited more transactive, convergence-oriented interaction than summary writing is presented as consistent with this model.
requirements: Learners must use a shared external knowledge representation tool during collaboration
target_learning_goals: collaborative knowledge convergence
historical reasoning
examples: The authors state their analysis of interaction in both conditions confirmed the hypothesis, finding the result consistent with what is predicted by the MUPEMURE model
key_sources: Lucero, M., Montanero, M., & van Boxtel, C. (2024). Semiempty collaborative concept mapping in history education: students' engagement in historical reasoning and coconstruction. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09659-7

article_title: Learning from animation enabled by collaboration
citation: Rebetez, C., Betrancourt, M., Sangin, M., & Dillenbourg, P. (2010). Learning from animation enabled by collaboration. Instructional Science, 38(5), 471–485. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-009-9117-6
title: Multimedia comprehension framework with working-memory load as the explanation for weak animation effects
description: The article frames animation effects within the multimedia comprehension framework, in which multimedia processing is constrained by human cognitive capacity. It offers a cognitive-load explanation for why intuitive expectations about animation fail: multimedia, including animated graphics, "challenges human processing capacities, and in particular imposes a substantial working memory load". The study's results are discussed within this framework "in order to propose the conditions under which animation can benefit to learning".
requirements: The account presumes that instruction design must be evaluated against learners' working-memory processing capacities, per the article's cognitive-load framing.
target_learners: Learners studying multimedia instruction explaining how natural or artificial dynamic systems work
target_learning_goals: Comprehension of dynamic systems, including retention and transfer of how such systems work
examples: The three-factor experiment crossed static versus animated graphics, snapshots versus no snapshots, and individual versus collaborative settings to test conditions for animation benefits.
key_sources: Rebetez, C., Betrancourt, M., Sangin, M., & Dillenbourg, P. (2010). Learning from animation enabled by collaboration. Instructional Science, 38(5), 471–485. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-009-9117-6

article_title: Seeking a science of instruction
citation: Richard E. Mayer. (2010). Seeking a science of instruction. Instr Sci 38:143–145. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-009-9113-x
title: Use both lab-based and school-based studies to build a complete science of instruction
description: Responding to concerns about the external validity of laboratory studies with short lessons, Mayer argues that "educational research is strengthened by multiple research methods", so both lab-based and school-based studies are useful. Each approach has its own strengths and weaknesses, and together they build a more complete science of instruction. He notes some of Sweller's cited work involved trainees in industrial training programs, and that researchers have investigated the modality principle in real school settings.
requirements: Research programs should include both lab and school venues rather than relying on one method
constraints: Lab-based work with short lessons has limited external validity, a concern Mayer says his own research reports have repeatedly recognized
target_learning_goals: building externally valid, research-based instructional theory
examples: Mayer points to Harskamp et al. (2007) investigating the modality principle in real school settings
key_sources: Richard E. Mayer. (2010). Seeking a science of instruction. Instr Sci 38:143–145. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-009-9113-x

article_title: External and internal smartphone distractions: Effects on phone use and learning performance in college classrooms
citation: Liao, H.-H., Liu, T.-C., & Lin, Y.-C. (2026). External and internal smartphone distractions: Effects on phone use and learning performance in college classrooms. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09794-3
title: Multistage smartphone-distraction process linking cues, vigilance, phone-use patterns, and mental effort to learning outcomes
description: The article proposes that classroom smartphone distraction unfolds as a multistage process: external notification cues and internal smartphone vigilance shape distinct phone-use patterns (checking frequency versus session duration), which raise phone-use mental effort and thereby lower learning performance. The authors state that "smartphone distraction is best conceptualized as a multistage process linking cues, vigilance, phone-use patterns, and mental effort to learning outcomes, as summarized in Fig. 6." The framework distinguishes exogenous (notification-driven) from endogenous (vigilance-driven) distraction and shows that hiding notifications changes the form of use rather than eliminating its cost.
requirements: Smartphones remain accessible to students during learning, so vigilance can translate into observable use
Measurement of both frequency and duration of phone use, since the two patterns respond differently to notification settings
constraints: The authors note that merely hiding notifications may be insufficient to prevent distractions in classrooms where smartphones remain accessible
Group-level path coefficients were weaker than the base model and should be interpreted with caution
target_learners: college and university students in device-permitted classrooms
target_learning_goals: sustaining attention and learning performance during video-based or lecture instruction despite smartphone access
examples: In the experiment, NR students checked phones frequently (many checks of one to three seconds) while NH students who did use phones engaged in longer sessions, yet both groups performed equally on the quiz
key_sources: Liao, H.-H., Liu, T.-C., & Lin, Y.-C. (2026). External and internal smartphone distractions: Effects on phone use and learning performance in college classrooms. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09794-3

article_title: Online teaching in networked learning communities: A multi-method approach to studying the role of the teacher
citation: de Laat, M., Lally, V., Lipponen, L. & Simons, R.-J. (2007). Online teaching in networked learning communities: A multi-method approach to studying the role of the teacher. Instructional Science, vol. 35, no. 3, pp. 257-286. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-006-9007-0
title: Multi-method research framework combining SNA, content analysis and contextual analysis for studying networked learning
description: The article develops a framework in which three methods answer complementary questions about networked learning: social network analysis to find out "who is talking to whom", content analysis of coded learning and tutoring activities to find out "what they are talking about", and contextual analysis (including critical event recall) to find out "why they are talking as they do". The methods triangulate and contextualise findings, using the outcomes of one method to understand the results of the next. Timeline analysis across beginning, middle and end phases adds the dimension of time, which the authors say has been largely ignored in NL research.
requirements: Methods must capture processes and outcomes of learning as well as experienced effects and individual interpretations of participation, as Hakkinen et al. suggest
constraints: Applied here to two NLCs within one workshop of an online Master's programme, with 10-day message samples per phase
target_learners: mid-career professional students in an online Master's programme in e-learning
target_learning_goals: understanding collaborative learning and tutoring processes in networked learning communities
examples: Density and centrality measures from WebCT log-files, NVivo-coded learning/tutoring activities, and CER interviews with both teachers
key_sources: de Laat, M., Lally, V., Lipponen, L. & Simons, R.-J. (2007). Online teaching in networked learning communities: A multi-method approach to studying the role of the teacher. Instructional Science, vol. 35, no. 3, pp. 257-286. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-006-9007-0

article_title: Exploring multiuser virtual teaching simulation as an alternative learning environment for student instructors
citation: Ke, F., Dai, Z., Pachman, M. et al. (2021). Exploring multiuser virtual teaching simulation as an alternative learning environment for student instructors. Instr Sci, 49, 831–854. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09555-4
title: Multiuser VR-supported teaching simulation for participatory training of student instructors
description: A multiuser, virtual reality supported teaching simulation investigated as an environment for the participatory training of teaching and development of teaching knowledge among student instructors. In the study, 40 university teaching assistants were randomly assigned to this VR simulation or a live classroom simulation during a 4-h training session. The VR condition featured domain-specific challenges and authentic environmental prompting.
requirements: Multiuser support so that participants can engage in role-playing of teaching within the virtual environment.
constraints: VR participants lacked mutual engagement in collaborative role-playing.
target_learning_goals: development of teaching knowledge
teaching self-efficacy
examples: The VR condition was compared against a live classroom teaching simulation in a randomized 4-h training session.
key_sources: Ke, F., Dai, Z., Pachman, M. et al. (2021). Exploring multiuser virtual teaching simulation as an alternative learning environment for student instructors. Instr Sci, 49, 831–854. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09555-4

article_title: Analyzing multimodal data to understand medical trainees' regulation strategies and physiological responses in high- fidelity medical simulation scenarios
citation: Moreno, M., Patino Melo, L., Grewal, K., Matin, N., Azher, S., & Harley, J.M. (2024). Analyzing Multimodal Data to Understand Medical Trainees' Regulation Strategies and Physiological Responses in High-Fidelity Medical Simulation Scenarios. Metacognition and Learning, 19, 1161–1213. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09403-z
title: Multimodal medical-simulation coding scheme combining behavioral, SRL and SSRL codes
description: A composite coding scheme used to code leaders' behaviors and regulation strategies in recorded CRM simulations. As the article describes it, "Our coding scheme included codes for: 1) behaviors (posture and gestures, facial expression, and vocalics) and 2) regulation strategies, including SRL and SSRL which were then modified to fit a medically based research context." It nests subordinate codes under superordinate codes with definitions and medical-context examples, borrows established SRL and SSRL codes, and was refined with input from researchers, simulation educators and medical doctors. Three trained raters reached Cohen's Kappas of 0.71 to 0.82 before deliberation and perfect agreement after deliberation.
requirements: Trained raters and negotiated coding, with medical-doctor and simulation-educator input to clarify clinical interactions
constraints: Codes were modified for a medical context and applied to leaders' and teams' observable behavior in recorded simulations only
target_learners: Medical residents participating in team-based CRM simulations
target_learning_goals: Describing observable regulation strategies (SRL and SSRL) and team behaviors during simulated patient care
examples: Ten simulations were coded with segmentation into 'Beginning', 'Escalation' and 'Peak', with frequencies and percentages reported per segment
key_sources: Moreno, M., Patino Melo, L., Grewal, K., Matin, N., Azher, S., & Harley, J.M. (2024). Analyzing Multimodal Data to Understand Medical Trainees' Regulation Strategies and Physiological Responses in High-Fidelity Medical Simulation Scenarios. Metacognition and Learning, 19, 1161–1213. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09403-z

article_title: Metacognitive writing strategies, critical thinking skills, and academic writing performance: A structural equation modeling approach
citation: Mark Feng Teng, Mei Yue. (2022). Metacognitive writing strategies, critical thinking skills, and academic writing performance: A structural equation modeling approach. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09328-5
title: Multi-faceted framework of metacognition: monitoring and control across knowledge, experiences, and skills
description: Drawing on Flavell, Efklides, Nelson, and Teng et al. (2022b), the article presents metacognition as a multifaceted construct spanning metacognitive knowledge, metacognitive experiences, and metacognitive skills/strategies. Learners are "consciously aware of the monitoring and control of cognition"; the monitoring function covers knowledge and experiences while control of cognition comprises skills/strategies, depicted as metacognitive regulation (planning, monitoring, evaluating) with reflection as an essential component. Metacognitive knowledge divides into declarative, procedural, and conditional types; regulation adds debugging and information management strategies. The framework frames metacognition as formed through dynamics between monitoring and control, with the three facets interacting.
requirements: Distinguishing the meta-level and object-level of cognitive processes, with acquisition, retention, and retrieval as stages between the two levels
constraints: The article notes there is not sufficient evidence showing that metacognitive deficits are solely responsible for writing performance
target_learners: EFL student writers in higher education
target_learning_goals: Self-regulated academic writing through metacognitive knowledge and regulation
examples: Operationalized in this study via the MAWSQ's eight strategy factors, all of which loaded significantly (parameter values larger than 0.50) in the SEM models
key_sources: Mark Feng Teng, Mei Yue. (2022). Metacognitive writing strategies, critical thinking skills, and academic writing performance: A structural equation modeling approach. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09328-5

article_title: The pivotal role of monitoring for collaborative problem solving seen in interaction, performance, and interpersonal physiology
citation: Haataja, E., Malmberg, J., Dindar, M., & Järvelä, S. (2021). The pivotal role of monitoring for collaborative problem solving seen in interaction, performance, and interpersonal physiology. Metacognition and Learning, 17, 241–268. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09279-3
title: Multilevel framework of regulation in collaborative learning across physiological, psychological, and interpersonal levels
description: The article frames regulation in collaborative learning as a multifaceted phenomenon that unfolds across multiple systemic levels. Monitoring challenges "can be seen as adjustments on different systemic levels (physiological, psychological, and interpersonal) of a collaborative group." This framework motivates simultaneously measuring interactional indicators (video-coded monitoring) and physiological indicators (EDA arousal and synchrony) to capture how regulation manifests across levels during collaboration.
requirements: Capturing the multilevel nature of regulation requires multimodal data combining video interaction coding with physiological recordings such as electrodermal activity.
constraints: The article notes that relations between interpersonal physiology and monitoring have not held true for all tasks and all groups.
target_learning_goals: collaborative problem solving
socially shared regulation of learning
key_sources: Haataja, E., Malmberg, J., Dindar, M., & Järvelä, S. (2021). The pivotal role of monitoring for collaborative problem solving seen in interaction, performance, and interpersonal physiology. Metacognition and Learning, 17, 241–268. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09279-3

article_title: Measuring strategy use with self-report instruments: theoretical and empirical considerations
citation: Gonny Schellings & Bernadette Van Hout-Wolters. (2011). Measuring strategy use with self-report instruments: theoretical and empirical considerations. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9081-9
title: Combine multiple measuring methods (triangulation) to assess learning strategies, since neither self-report surveys nor think-aloud studies alone suffice
description: Because self-report instruments have both strong and flawed points, the article reports that many researchers recommend combining measuring methods. In multi-method designs the same instruments are given to the same participants in the same learning situation, so the strengths and weaknesses of each method can be examined. The combination is said to yield a broad picture and deep insight into learners' learning strategies.
requirements: Instruments administered to the same participants in the same learning situation
Comparison should go beyond total scores and correlations, measuring the same specific strategies in a similar learning situation
constraints: Different methods may lead to a variety of results, raising the question of how to judge and combine them
Multi-method designs and interpreting combined data can be labor-intensive and cost-consuming
target_learners: school and higher-education learners studied in strategy research
target_learning_goals: cognitive and metacognitive learning strategies
examples: The article cites Dinsmore et al.'s (2008) review of 255 studies concluding that some combination of quantitative and qualitative approaches may be required to reveal self-regulated learning strategies
key_sources: Gonny Schellings & Bernadette Van Hout-Wolters. (2011). Measuring strategy use with self-report instruments: theoretical and empirical considerations. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9081-9

article_title: Measuring strategy use with self-report instruments: theoretical and empirical considerations
citation: Gonny Schellings & Bernadette Van Hout-Wolters. (2011). Measuring strategy use with self-report instruments: theoretical and empirical considerations. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9081-9
title: Multiple-choice strategy use measure requiring readers to enact strategies while retaining group administration and simple scoring
description: Cromley and Azevedo developed a domain-general and domain-specific multiple-choice strategy use measure as an alternative to self-report questionnaires. The method requires readers to enact a strategy and measures whether they perform it accurately by posing multiple-choice questions. It preserves the practical advantages of questionnaires, namely group administration and simple scoring, and was examined with three samples within a series of studies testing a model of reading comprehension.
requirements: Multiple-choice items that require enacting the strategy
Correlation with standard reading comprehension and component measures such as vocabulary, word reading, inference and background knowledge
constraints: Convergent validity among the different instruments was still being searched for; commonality analysis examined the degree to which strategy use contributes to single-text comprehension
target_learners: readers assessed across three samples in reading comprehension studies
target_learning_goals: accurate enactment of reading comprehension strategies
examples: In the three studies the instrument was correlated with standard reading comprehension and component measures, and commonality analysis examined strategy use's contribution to single-text comprehension
key_sources: Gonny Schellings & Bernadette Van Hout-Wolters. (2011). Measuring strategy use with self-report instruments: theoretical and empirical considerations. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9081-9

article_title: Individual differences in local and global metacognitive judgments
citation: Marion Händel & Anique B. H. de Bruin & Markus Dresel (2020). Individual differences in local and global metacognitive judgments. Metacognition and Learning (2020) 15:51–75. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09220-0
title: Measure metacognitive judgment accuracy with more than one score, including sensitivity and specificity
description: The article argues that a single accuracy score gives an incomplete picture of metacognitive monitoring. Absolute accuracy (bias) captures over- or underconfidence, while relative measures such as sensitivity (accurately detected correct answers) and specificity (accurately detected incorrect answers) capture discrimination of correct versus incorrect items. The article states "Overall, it is suggested to measure accuracy by more than only one score" and calculated sensitivity and specificity in addition to bias in both studies.
requirements: Dichotomous local judgments and item-level performance data to build the 2 × 2 contingency table for sensitivity and specificity
constraints: Sensitivity and specificity depend on item performance and, as composite scores, their reliability is challenging to calculate and interpret; accuracy scores are statistically dependent on performance, so performance must be excluded as a predictor in accuracy analyses
target_learning_goals: accurate self-assessment of test performance
examples: Both studies calculated bias, sensitivity, and specificity, revealing patterns (e.g., higher self-concept with higher sensitivity but lower specificity) that a bias score alone would not show
key_sources: Marion Händel & Anique B. H. de Bruin & Markus Dresel (2020). Individual differences in local and global metacognitive judgments. Metacognition and Learning (2020) 15:51–75. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09220-0

article_title: The many facets of metacognition: comparing multiple measures of metacognition in healthy individuals
citation: Terneusen, A., Quaedflieg, C., van Heugten, C., Ponds, R., & Winkens, I. (2024). The many facets of metacognition: comparing multiple measures of metacognition in healthy individuals. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09350-1
title: Multi-measure metacognition assessment paradigm combining MAI, confidence judgments, and trial-by-trial AUROC2
description: An online assessment paradigm in which participants complete the Metacognitive Awareness Inventory, give prospective and retrospective confidence judgments (0-10 scales) about a word-pair memory task, and make trial-by-trial confidence ratings during a two-alternative forced-choice recognition test. The article states "The memory task was a word pair learning task consisting of two phases: an encoding phase and a recognition phase". These measures yield metacognitive knowledge, discrepancy scores, and metacognitive sensitivity (AUROC2), allowing within-person comparison of metacognitive elements.
requirements: A task with enough correct and incorrect trials for confidence judgments to be meaningful; the authors suggest an adaptive task as a solution
constraints: AUROC2 may not be meaningful under floor or ceiling effects in performance accuracy; the abstract reasoning task was disregarded because performance was at chance level
target_learners: healthy young adults (19-24 years) in the reported study
target_learning_goals: measuring metacognitive sensitivity, monitoring, and metacognitive knowledge
examples: 128 participants completed the session from home in about an hour using Qualtrics, with validity questions used to exclude inattentive responders
key_sources: Terneusen, A., Quaedflieg, C., van Heugten, C., Ponds, R., & Winkens, I. (2024). The many facets of metacognition: comparing multiple measures of metacognition in healthy individuals. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09350-1

article_title: Measuring strategic processing when students read multiple texts
citation: Ivar Bråten & Helge I. Strømsø. (2011). Measuring strategic processing when students read multiple texts. Metacognition Learning 6:111–130. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9075-7
title: Multiple-Text Strategy Inventory (MTSI)
description: The MTSI is a 15-item task-specific self-report questionnaire measuring strategic processing during multiple-text reading, with five accumulation items and ten cross-text elaboration items rated on a 10-point Likert-type scale. The authors state: "We designed the Multiple-Text Strategy Inventory (MTSI) for this purpose. This 15-item questionnaire was based on prior empirical research on students' reading of multiple texts reviewed above." Each item referred to the recently completed reading task, with verbs in the past tense. It is intended for individual assessment and large-scale investigations.
requirements: Administered immediately after completion of a specific administered text task, with items referring to that task in past tense
constraints: The two identified dimensions were limited by the inventory content; sourcing and contextualization items were not included
target_learning_goals: multiple-text comprehension strategies
reading comprehension
examples: 216 Norwegian education undergraduates completed the MTSI immediately after reading seven climate change texts
key_sources: Ivar Bråten & Helge I. Strømsø. (2011). Measuring strategic processing when students read multiple texts. Metacognition Learning 6:111–130. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9075-7

article_title: Transfer of metacognitive skills in self-regulated learning: effects on strategy application and content knowledge acquisition
citation: Stebner, F., Schuster, C., Weber, X.-L., Greiff, S., Leutner, D., & Wirth, J. (2022). Transfer of metacognitive skills in self-regulated learning: effects on strategy application and content knowledge acquisition. Metacognition and Learning, 17, 715-744. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09322-x
title: Multi-Strategy Test (MST) scenario-based vignette measure with a new seven-category quality-focused coding manual
description: The Multi-Strategy Test (MST; Stebner et al., 2015) presents fictitious learning scenarios in which students describe their intended approach in open-response format, coded for metacognitive skills. The new coding manual covers "Goal setting, planning, monitoring (observing), monitoring (assessing), reacting, reflecting, and evaluating," awarding zero to two points per category (maximum 14). Three versions were used: MST_E (experimenting), MST_T (text highlighting), and MST_P (preparing for a class exam), serving as near- or far-transfer tasks depending on group.
requirements: Trained raters applying the category system; inter-rater reliability was checked with 25 doubly coded answers
constraints: MST_P was not practiced in the training but represented a familiar everyday scenario; the measure captures intended, not actual, strategy application
target_learning_goals: assessment of spontaneous recall and intended application of metacognitive skills across transfer distances
examples: Two raters coded 25 answers with average Cohen's κ = 0.98 (0.89 ≤ κ ≤ 1.0; n = 25) before answers were randomly assigned to one rater
key_sources: Stebner, F., Schuster, C., Weber, X.-L., Greiff, S., Leutner, D., & Wirth, J. (2022). Transfer of metacognitive skills in self-regulated learning: effects on strategy application and content knowledge acquisition. Metacognition and Learning, 17, 715-744. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09322-x

article_title: Cognitive Profiles of Children with Isolated and Comorbid Learning Difficulties in Reading and Math: a Meta-analysis
citation: Nurit Viesel-Nordmeyer, Julia Reuber, Jörg-Tobias Kuhn, Kristina Moll, Heinz Holling, Christian Dobel. (2023). Cognitive Profiles of Children with Isolated and Comorbid Learning Difficulties in Reading and Math: a Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09735-3
