title: Multi-deficit model versus three independent disorders model of comorbid reading and math difficulties
description: The article frames two competing explanatory models for comorbid RDMD. Under the "multi-deficit model", the RDMD profile is "characterized by the sum of domain-specific core deficits of RD and MD (additivity)" plus shared domain-general risk factors producing less severe EF deficits than expected (under-additivity). The "three independent disorders model" instead treats RDMD as a distinct disorder with "distinct and/or more severe deficits, compared to the sum of RD's and MD's profiles (over-additivity)". The meta-analysis was designed to adjudicate between them.
requirements: Studies must include groups of children with isolated RD, isolated MD, and comorbid RDMD plus a control group, so that the linear additivity hypothesis g1 + g2 − g3 can be tested
constraints: The article limits the age span to 6–12 years, the age span where LD mostly become visible
Detecting a small interaction effect would require screening around 10,000 children, which the authors note requires large multicenter studies
target_learners: children aged 6–12 with isolated or comorbid reading and math learning difficulties
target_learning_goals: reading skills
math skills
executive function skills
examples: The meta-analysis translated additivity into the linear hypothesis gAdd = g1 + g2 − g3 = 0 and tested it across math, reading, and EF outcomes in 74 studies
key_sources: Nurit Viesel-Nordmeyer, Julia Reuber, Jörg-Tobias Kuhn, Kristina Moll, Heinz Holling, Christian Dobel. (2023). Cognitive Profiles of Children with Isolated and Comorbid Learning Difficulties in Reading and Math: a Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09735-3

article_title: A Systematic Meta-analysis of the Reliability and Validity of Subjective Cognitive Load Questionnaires in Experimental Multimedia Learning Research
citation: Felix Krieglstein, Maik Beege, Günter Daniel Rey, Paul Ginns, Moritz Krell, Sascha Schneider. (2022). A Systematic Meta-analysis of the Reliability and Validity of Subjective Cognitive Load Questionnaires in Experimental Multimedia Learning Research. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09683-4
title: Four frequently used multidimensional subjective cognitive load questionnaires (Eysink 2009; Leppink 2013; Leppink 2014; Klepsch 2017)
description: The meta-analysis examines four subjective cognitive load questionnaires that measure the cognitive load types separately with multiple items: the Eysink et al. (2009) six-item instrument (which also includes one item on perceived overall load), the Leppink et al. (2013) ten-item scale (three ICL, three ECL, four GCL items), the revised Leppink et al. (2014) version with added mental-effort items, and the Klepsch et al. (2017) instrument with ICL (two items), ECL (three items), and GCL (three items), which "is not specific to the learning topic and can therefore be easily adapted to the material used in a specific study." Across the meta-analysis sample, the Leppink (2013) questionnaire was used in 33 experiments, Leppink (2014) in seven, Klepsch (2017) in 20, and Eysink (2009) in 10.
requirements: Multiple items per load type so internal consistency can be calculated
For the Klepsch naïve rating, the authors recommend conducting a reliability test
constraints: The Klepsch GCL items "should be used with caution because of varying levels of under standings on the part of respondents"; the Leppink (2014) added mental effort items increased reliability of intrinsic and extraneous load factors, but not for germane load
target_learners: participants in experimental multimedia learning studies (mean age 20.4 years, 63.5% women)
target_learning_goals: measuring intrinsic, extraneous, and germane cognitive load during multimedia learning
examples: Klepsch et al. validated their instrument with an informed rating (students trained on CLT) and a naïve rating; the naïve rating is frequently used in experimental studies
key_sources: Felix Krieglstein, Maik Beege, Günter Daniel Rey, Paul Ginns, Moritz Krell, Sascha Schneider. (2022). A Systematic Meta-analysis of the Reliability and Validity of Subjective Cognitive Load Questionnaires in Experimental Multimedia Learning Research. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09683-4

article_title: A Systematic Meta-analysis of the Reliability and Validity of Subjective Cognitive Load Questionnaires in Experimental Multimedia Learning Research
citation: Felix Krieglstein, Maik Beege, Günter Daniel Rey, Paul Ginns, Moritz Krell, Sascha Schneider. (2022). A Systematic Meta-analysis of the Reliability and Validity of Subjective Cognitive Load Questionnaires in Experimental Multimedia Learning Research. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09683-4
title: Use multi-item multidimensional cognitive load scales rather than single-item measures to enable reliability estimation and differentiation of load types
description: The article argues that measuring cognitive load with a single item, as in the popular Paas (1992) nine-point mental-effort scale, is psychometrically questionable because "a measuring instrument consisting of only one item makes it impossible to calculate internal consistency, an important indicator for an instrument's reliability." It further reports that measuring cognitive load without differentiating between the individual cognitive load types "seems to be insufficient when evaluating the effectiveness of multimedia learning environments or interventions." The principle therefore recommends multi-item scales targeting the load types separately.
requirements: Scales must include multiple items per cognitive load type so internal consistency can be calculated
constraints: Test-retest reliability is only valid for constructs stable over time, and cognitive load is dynamic in nature
target_learners: researchers and instructional designers evaluating multimedia learning environments
target_learning_goals: reliable and valid measurement of cognitive load types in experimental research
examples: The meta-analysis restricted inclusion to studies using the four multi-item questionnaires measuring all cognitive load types with multiple items
key_sources: Felix Krieglstein, Maik Beege, Günter Daniel Rey, Paul Ginns, Moritz Krell, Sascha Schneider. (2022). A Systematic Meta-analysis of the Reliability and Validity of Subjective Cognitive Load Questionnaires in Experimental Multimedia Learning Research. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09683-4

article_title: Editor’s Note
citation: Daniel Robinson. (2009). Editor's Note. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-009-9103-1
title: Replication studies in educational psychology should use a multi-experiment structure that first replicates the original method and then extends it to identify boundary conditions of the effect
description: The editorial sets out the journal's expectation for replication manuscripts: a successful replication article requires at least three experiments, the first reproducing the original study's method with only participants changed, later ones extending the method. The stated aim is that 'we can begin to identify the boundary conditions of the effect'.
requirements: The first experiment must follow the method used in the original study, with participants as the only difference
Extensions must change one aspect of the method besides participants, such as materials, exposure, or delay between acquisition and testing
constraints: Applies to replication manuscripts submitted to Educational Psychology Review, which does not publish primary empirical reports but does publish replications
target_learning_goals: establishing the generality and boundary conditions of empirical learning effects
examples: A failed replication should be followed by a second replication attempt, and if results still cannot be replicated, a third experiment containing an extension the authors believe would allow replication of the original results
key_sources: Daniel Robinson. (2009). Editor's Note. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-009-9103-1

article_title: Leveraging What Students Know to Make Sense of Texts: What the Research Says About Prior Knowledge Activation
citation: Courtney Hattan, Patricia A. Alexander, and Sarah M. Lupo. (2023). Leveraging What Students Know to Make Sense of Texts: What the Research Says About Prior Knowledge Activation. Review of Educational Research. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Leveraging+What+Students+Know+to+Make+Sense+of+Texts+Prior+Knowledge+Activation
title: Multidimensional Knowledge in Text Comprehension framework
description: Introduced by McCarthy and McNamara (2021) and used by the review as a lens on definitional adequacy, this framework "posits that researchers should consider the amount, accuracy, specificity, and coherence of readers' academic knowledge, including topic and domain knowledge, before reading." The review uses it to judge whether researchers' definitions captured the multidimensionality of knowledge, finding only a few articles' implicit conceptual definitions encompassed it. The review also discusses extending activation beyond academic knowledge to personal knowledge and funds of knowledge drawn from students' life experiences and sociocultural resources.
requirements: Researchers should characterize readers' knowledge on amount, accuracy, specificity, and coherence before judging activation effectiveness
constraints: The framework addresses academic knowledge before reading; the review notes some researchers contend activating only academic knowledge undervalues other forms of background knowledge
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension grounded in relevant prior knowledge
examples: The review illustrates with a middle school teacher preparing students to read a book on the Great Migration, where students could activate social studies content, expository text structure knowledge, or personal and sociocultural knowledge
key_sources: Courtney Hattan, Patricia A. Alexander, and Sarah M. Lupo. (2023). Leveraging What Students Know to Make Sense of Texts: What the Research Says About Prior Knowledge Activation. Review of Educational Research. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Leveraging+What+Students+Know+to+Make+Sense+of+Texts+Prior+Knowledge+Activation

article_title: A Systematic Review of the Impact of the Multilevel Digital Divide in Technology-Integrated Family–School Partnerships
citation: Badiuzzaman, Md; Lee, Jung-Sook; Cumming, Terry. (2025). A Systematic Review of the Impact of the Multilevel Digital Divide in Technology-Integrated Family–School Partnerships. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543251400771
title: Multilevel digital divide framework applied to technology-integrated family–school partnerships
description: The review organizes its analysis around a multilevel digital divide framework, in which barriers to technology-integrated family–school partnerships occur at different levels. Its most emphasized level is "the second-level digital divide, which relates to skills and usage gaps," beyond first-level access barriers such as having technology at all. The framework explains why access alone does not ensure that parents benefit from technology-integrated partnership practices, and it grounds the review's recommendation that schools address parental socioeconomic differences, information provision, and training.
requirements: Schools must account for multiple divide levels, including skills and usage gaps, not only physical access to technology.
constraints: The framework is applied here to parents in technology-integrated family–school partnerships, based on 10 included studies.
target_learning_goals: effective participation in technology-integrated family–school partnership practices
examples: The review analyzed 10 high-quality studies of technology-integrated family–school partnership practices through this multilevel lens.
key_sources: Badiuzzaman, Md; Lee, Jung-Sook; Cumming, Terry. (2025). A Systematic Review of the Impact of the Multilevel Digital Divide in Technology-Integrated Family–School Partnerships. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543251400771

article_title: Educational Responses Toward Community Violence: A Critical Analysis of Perspectives on Causes and Solutions
citation: van Dijk, A, de Haan, M & de Winter, M 2026, 'Educational Responses Toward Community Violence : A Critical Analysis of Perspectives on Causes and Solutions', Review of Educational Research, vol. 96, no. 3, pp. 829-869. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543251324491
title: Multidisciplinary taxonomy of educational approaches to counter community violence
description: The review establishes a multidisciplinary taxonomy that organizes the broad range of educational interventions to counter community violence into distinguishable approaches. It was built, in the authors' words, by a "critical analysis of distinctions in perspectives, objectives, and strategies", so approaches are differentiated by what they take the causes of violence to be, what objectives they pursue, and what strategies they deploy. The taxonomy serves as the organizing framework for the paper's coherent overview of current educational responses and for identifying which kinds of approaches are underrepresented.
requirements: Requires critical analysis of distinctions in perspectives, objectives, and strategies across theory and research on educational interventions
constraints: The review reports that strategies for transformation of social systems are underrepresented among the approaches captured by the taxonomy
target_learning_goals: violence prevention
conflict resolution
promotion of peace
examples: The review uses the taxonomy to show that most interventions focus on either individual behavior or group interaction while systems-transformation strategies are underrepresented
key_sources: van Dijk, A, de Haan, M & de Winter, M 2026, 'Educational Responses Toward Community Violence : A Critical Analysis of Perspectives on Causes and Solutions', Review of Educational Research, vol. 96, no. 3, pp. 829-869. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543251324491

article_title: Fostering creativity in formal schooling: A systematic review of explicit and implicit interventions for young learners
citation: Gu, X., Ritter, S. M., Frossard, F., van den Boom, L., Delfmann, L. R. & Barajas, M. (2026). Fostering creativity in formal schooling: A systematic review of explicit and implicit interventions for young learners. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2026.100784
title: Multidimensional developmental frameworks of creativity (4-C model and 4Ps model) grounding the review
description: The review grounds its synthesis in two frameworks. Kaufman and Beghetto's 4-C model 'categorizes creativity into four levels: mini-c (personal insights), little-c (everyday problem-solving), pro-C (professional-level creativity), and big-C (eminent, historically recognized creativity)', treating creativity as a developmental continuum. Rhodes' 4Ps model—Person, Process, Press (environment), and Product—provides a taxonomy underscoring that creativity is shaped by individual traits, cognitive and affective processes, environmental influences, and creative outcomes. Together these frameworks motivate the review's contextualized, multidimensional approach to intervention design.
requirements: Interventions must address cognitive, motivational, and environmental factors together rather than treating creativity as a fixed trait
constraints: Frameworks are theoretical background the review adopts; the review applies them to K-12 formal schooling contexts
target_learning_goals: Understanding creativity as multidimensional and developmental to guide intervention design
examples: The review uses the mini-c to big-C continuum to argue educators must support developmental pathways from early creative dispositions toward more complex forms
key_sources: Gu, X., Ritter, S. M., Frossard, F., van den Boom, L., Delfmann, L. R. & Barajas, M. (2026). Fostering creativity in formal schooling: A systematic review of explicit and implicit interventions for young learners. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2026.100784

article_title: Learning Foreign Language Vocabulary with Gestures and Pictures Enhances Vocabulary Memory for Several Months Post-Learning in Eight-Year-Old School Children
citation: Andrä, C., Mathias, B., Schwager, A., Macedonia, M., & von Kriegstein, K. (2020). Learning Foreign Language Vocabulary with Gestures and Pictures Enhances Vocabulary Memory for Several Months Post-Learning in Eight-Year-Old School Children. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09527-z
title: Enrich auditorily presented L2 vocabulary with self-performed gestures or pictures to boost children's vocabulary memory over months
description: The article supports enriching foreign-language vocabulary instruction with semantically congruent gestures performed by the children themselves, or with pictures, rather than audio-only learning. In three classroom experiments, both enrichment types "enhanced children 's test performance compared with non-enriched learning," with benefits persisting up to 6 months. Training involved 5 consecutive days of short blocks in ordinary primary school classrooms.
requirements: Auditory presentation of L2 words paired with their L1 translations
Gestures must be semantically congruent (iconic) with word meanings and performed by the children
Repeated training over multiple consecutive days with counterbalanced conditions
constraints: Benefits were demonstrated in 8-year-old German third-graders learning English nouns in a movement-oriented school
Gesture enrichment did not outperform picture enrichment in children, unlike in adults
Overall test accuracy was low relative to the number of stimuli in Experiment 1
target_learners: Primary school children (grade three, around 8 years old)
target_learning_goals: Foreign language (L2) vocabulary acquisition and long-term retention
examples: Children heard English words, their German translations, and repetitions while viewing gesture videos or pictures, then performed gestures or recited words with their teacher over 5 days
Tests were free recall, German-English, and English-German translation administered orally at 3 days, 2 months, and 6 months post-learning
key_sources: Andrä, C., Mathias, B., Schwager, A., Macedonia, M., & von Kriegstein, K. (2020). Learning Foreign Language Vocabulary with Gestures and Pictures Enhances Vocabulary Memory for Several Months Post-Learning in Eight-Year-Old School Children. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09527-z

article_title: How Learners Use Their Hands for Learning: an Eye-Tracking Study
citation: Babette Park · Andreas Korbach · Paul Ginns · Roland Brünken. (2023). How Learners Use Their Hands for Learning: an Eye-Tracking Study. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09833-2
title: Multimodal memory model explanation of the tracing effect
description: The article introduces the multimodal memory model (Engelkamp & Zimmer, 1994) as a novel system-oriented explanation for tracing effects. It posits a non-verbal output system for action besides output-lexica, such that "The execution of action should make motor information on the cognitive level available, which becomes part of memory traces that can affect the later recall in a positive way." The model grew out of subject-performed task effect research, and its limits suggest tracing effects should appear in comprehension of complex systems with visuospatial information rather than pure recall of single terms. This yielded hypotheses H2a–H2b, predicting only the tracing group would outperform the other two groups.
requirements: Learning tasks involving kinesthetic experience during the learning phase, e.g., finger tracing against a surface, so motor information enters memory traces
constraints: The subject-performed task effect was not found for recall of associated word pairs or serial recall, implying episodic-relational information limits, though some self-performed task effects do support relational processing (Kormi-Nouri & Nilsson, 2001)
target_learners: School students learning from multimedia lessons
target_learning_goals: Comprehension of complex systems involving visuospatial information
examples: H2a predicted the tracing group would outperform pointing and no-touch groups only on comprehension; the experiment instead found pointing superior, contradicting this hypothesis
key_sources: Babette Park · Andreas Korbach · Paul Ginns · Roland Brünken. (2023). How Learners Use Their Hands for Learning: an Eye-Tracking Study. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09833-2

article_title: The Multicomponent Working Memory Model, Attention, and Long-term Memory in Multimedia Learning: A Comment on Schweppe and Rummer (2014)
citation: Soemer, A. (2015). The Multicomponent Working Memory Model, Attention, and Long-term Memory in Multimedia Learning: A Comment on Schweppe and Rummer (2014). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-015-9303-9
title: Baddeley's multicomponent model is a functional, not structural, working memory model compatible with activated long-term memory representations forming part of working memory
description: The multicomponent model of working memory (Baddeley and Hitch 1974; Baddeley 2000) separates working memory from long-term memory functionally, not structurally, in order to account for functionality beyond mere activation of long-term memory traces, such as learning new information. The commentary quotes Baddeley and Logie (1999) that working memory and LTM "comprise two functionally separable cognitive systems", and notes the model's subcomponents have direct connections to long-term memory that do not involve the episodic buffer. This reading contradicts the characterization in multimedia learning theories that the model posits structural separation.
requirements: Interpreting the model requires distinguishing functional from structural separation, as the commentary argues structural separation "is nowhere asserted in Baddeley (2000)"
constraints: The commentary notes multimedia learning theories deviate from the multicomponent model by assuming visual and auditory, rather than visuospatial and verbal, components
target_learning_goals: theoretical foundations for explaining learning from multimedia materials
examples: The commentary cites work on the phonological loop's heavy involvement in verbal learning (Baddeley et al. 1998) as establishing long-term memory contributions to subcomponent processing within the framework.
key_sources: Soemer, A. (2015). The Multicomponent Working Memory Model, Attention, and Long-term Memory in Multimedia Learning: A Comment on Schweppe and Rummer (2014). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-015-9303-9

article_title: The AIR and Apt-AIR Frameworks of Epistemic Performance and Growth: Reflections on Educational Theory Development
citation: Sarit Barzilai & Clark A. Chinn. (2024). The AIR and Apt-AIR Frameworks of Epistemic Performance and Growth: Reflections on Educational Theory Development. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09927-5
title: The Multifaceted Framework of Epistemic Thinking defines cognitive and metacognitive aspects of epistemic thinking aligned with central models of metacognition
description: The Multifaceted Framework of Epistemic Thinking, developed by Barzilai and Zohar, defined the cognitive and metacognitive aspects of epistemic thinking in ways aligned with central models of metacognition. Following Flavell, the cognitive aspects were defined as those used to make cognitive progress, including thinking about the epistemic status and properties of specific information, knowledge claims, and sources. The metacognitive aspects were defined as knowledge, skills, and experiences related to the nature of knowledge and knowing, such as knowledge about criteria and strategies for evaluating claims or sources. The article states this framework "has informed research on self-regulated learning and was, along with the AIR framework, central to the development of the Apt-AIR framework."
requirements: Researchers using this framework must situate epistemic thinking within existing theoretical models of the meta/cognitive system rather than treating it as disconnected
constraints: The framework was developed to increase coherence between epistemic thinking research and metacognition research, which had mostly developed in distinct niches
target_learners: researchers and educators studying or supporting epistemic thinking across educational levels
target_learning_goals: understanding the cognitive and metacognitive dimensions of epistemic thinking including evaluating claims and sources
examples: The framework informed research on self-regulated learning and was central to developing the Apt-AIR framework's cognitive and metacognitive engagement aspects
key_sources: Sarit Barzilai & Clark A. Chinn. (2024). The AIR and Apt-AIR Frameworks of Epistemic Performance and Growth: Reflections on Educational Theory Development. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09927-5

article_title: How Representation Matters: Conceptualizing Systemic Racism to Develop Diversity Research Agendas for Undergraduate STEM Education
citation: Sedlacek, Q., Villa, A. M., III, Friend, M., Pérez, G., Dozier, S., Haeger, H., Lomelí, K., & Mejia, J. A. (2025). How Representation Matters: Conceptualizing Systemic Racism to Develop Diversity Research Agendas for Undergraduate STEM Education. Educational Psychology Review, 37:49. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10021-7
title: Multi-path model of hypothesized mediators of instructor diversity benefits in STEM
description: The review proposes a path model in which exposure to racially marginalized STEM instructors relates to positive outcomes for racially marginalized students through multiple hypothesized mediators: instructors' use of inclusive pedagogy (Arrow B), changes in peer interaction patterns at the classroom level (Arrow C), and students' belonging (Arrow D) and group-as-target stereotype threat (Arrow E). The authors state, "We present such a model in Fig. 2, and will expand on this model throughout the paper," elaborating it with additional mediators such as instructors' experiences of marginalization and racial ideology.
requirements: Future empirical tests of the hypothesized mediation paths, which the review generates as predictions
constraints: The model is hypothesized, not tested; the review notes few studies provide direct causal evidence identifying the specific mechanisms
target_learning_goals: explaining how and under what circumstances instructor racial/ethnic diversity benefits racially marginalized students
examples: Arrow A depicts exposure to racially marginalized instructors increasing grades and/or persistence, potentially mediated by inclusive pedagogy (Arrow B) or classroom interaction patterns (Arrow C)
key_sources: Sedlacek, Q., Villa, A. M., III, Friend, M., Pérez, G., Dozier, S., Haeger, H., Lomelí, K., & Mejia, J. A. (2025). How Representation Matters: Conceptualizing Systemic Racism to Develop Diversity Research Agendas for Undergraduate STEM Education. Educational Psychology Review, 37:49. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10021-7

article_title: How Many Classes and Students Should Ideally be Sampled When Assessing the Role of Classroom Climate via Student Ratings on a Limited Budget? An Optimal Design Perspective
citation: Steffen Zitzmann, Wolfgang Wagner, Martin Hecht, Christoph Helm, Christian Fischer, Lisa Bardach, Richard Göllner. (2021). How Many Classes and Students Should Ideally be Sampled When Assessing the Role of Classroom Climate via Student Ratings on a Limited Budget? An Optimal Design Perspective. Educational Psychology Review (2022) 34:511–536. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09635-4
title: The multilevel latent covariate model as the method of choice for unbiased estimation of class-level climate-outcome relations from student ratings
description: The article recaps Lüdtke et al.'s (2008) multilevel latent covariate model, in which students' ratings of classroom climate are latently aggregated to a latent class mean that is regressed on an outcome at the class level. The model is presented as "the method of choice because it allows researchers to obtain unbiased estimates of the relations between classroom climate and outcome variables even when the ICC(2) values are not very high." It applies to reflective group-level constructs such as student-rated classroom management or teacher support.
requirements: Student ratings of a classroom climate characteristic are aggregated latently on the class level, and the outcome is regressed on the latent class mean at the class level
constraints: The model is most appropriate for reflective class-level constructs, not formative group-level constructs such as the percentage of girls in a class
The procedures in the article target the between slope; they might not provide optimal solutions for other parameters such as the within slope
target_learners: Students in classrooms participating in classroom climate research
target_learning_goals: Estimating relations between classroom climate constructs (e.g., teaching quality, classroom management) and student outcomes such as achievement and motivation
examples: The article illustrates the model with research on classroom management, where students rate whether their teacher does not have to wait a long time for students to quiet down, and with Arens and Morin's (2016) study of teacher support and reading achievement in the German PIRLS 2006 sample
key_sources: Steffen Zitzmann, Wolfgang Wagner, Martin Hecht, Christoph Helm, Christian Fischer, Lisa Bardach, Richard Göllner. (2021). How Many Classes and Students Should Ideally be Sampled When Assessing the Role of Classroom Climate via Student Ratings on a Limited Budget? An Optimal Design Perspective. Educational Psychology Review (2022) 34:511–536. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09635-4

article_title: Does Spelling Still Matter—and If So, How Should It Be Taught? Perspectives from Contemporary and Historical Research
citation: Steven C. Pan, Timothy C. Rickard, Robert A. Bjork. (2021). Does Spelling Still Matter— and If So, How Should It Be Taught? Perspectives from Contemporary and Historical Research. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09611-y
title: Contemporary multi-component definition of spelling skills
description: The review describes a contemporary, expanded definition of spelling skills that goes beyond correct spelling to include component knowledge domains: "phonological knowledge (i.e., phonemics and phonics), morphological knowledge (e.g., prefixes and suffixes), orthographic knowledge (e.g., phoneme-grapheme relationships), etymological knowledge (i.e., word origins), and visual knowledge", many of which may develop in stages. It also includes functional skills such as dictionary use, spellcheck use, and spelling or learning unfamiliar words. This framework underpins the review's argument that modern explicit instruction should target these components rather than word-by-word memorization.
requirements: Instruction targeting the components requires learners to develop phonological, morphological, orthographic, etymological, and visual knowledge, which may develop in stages
constraints: The review focuses its evidence base on normally developing learners, excluding much of the literature on students with learning disabilities
target_learning_goals: spelling proficiency
literacy skills including reading and writing
key_sources: Steven C. Pan, Timothy C. Rickard, Robert A. Bjork. (2021). Does Spelling Still Matter— and If So, How Should It Be Taught? Perspectives from Contemporary and Historical Research. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09611-y

article_title: The Case for Multifaceted, Integrative Motivation Interventions Embedded in Classrooms
citation: Linnenbrink-Garcia, L., Wigfield, A., Cabrera, L., Mouzaoir, S., McKinney, D., Liu, P. P., Marchand, G., Schmidt, J. A., Harris, C. J., & Guthrie, J. (2026). The Case for Multifaceted, Integrative Motivation Interventions Embedded in Classrooms. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10177-w
title: Design motivation interventions that are multifaceted, theoretically integrated, and embedded in classrooms, creating sustained supports — a "fertile soil" for motivation
description: The paper's central recommendation is a paradigm shift: develop interventions that integrate across motivation theories, address multiple forms of motivation, and are embedded in classroom curricula and instruction with teachers as partners, so that "students will have sustained supports for their motivation that creates a "fertile soil" for motivation to develop further". Multifaceted interventions can meet the motivational challenges of more students in a single classroom than single-construct targeted interventions, and changing the educational context can shift the attractor state landscape toward more adaptive motivation.
requirements: Work with classroom instructors and embed supports in curriculum and instructional practice rather than delivering stand-alone add-on modules
Integrate multiple motivation theories deliberately, following the paper's integration guidelines
constraints: Multicomponent interventions may cost more researcher time and resources, take more teacher implementation time, and make it harder to isolate which components drive effectiveness (per Rosenzweig et al., 2022, as cited in the paper)
target_learning_goals: students' motivation, engagement, and learning across reading and science domains
examples: CORI embedded motivational practices in a 12-week science-reading program; M-PLANS used CDS as its underlying framework for teacher professional learning
key_sources: Linnenbrink-Garcia, L., Wigfield, A., Cabrera, L., Mouzaoir, S., McKinney, D., Liu, P. P., Marchand, G., Schmidt, J. A., Harris, C. J., & Guthrie, J. (2026). The Case for Multifaceted, Integrative Motivation Interventions Embedded in Classrooms. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10177-w

article_title: Effects and Characteristics of Mathematics Interventions for Students with Co-Occurring Difficulties in Mathematics and Reading: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis
citation: Ellinor Waaland, Vibeke Rønneberg, Dieuwer ten Braak. (2026). Effects and Characteristics of Mathematics Interventions for Students with Co-Occurring Difficulties in Mathematics and Reading: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10184-x
title: Multiple cognitive deficit model as the framework for understanding co-occurring mathematics and reading difficulties
description: The review adopts the multiple cognitive deficit model as "the most plausible framework for understanding learning difficulties as well as their co-occurrence." The model posits that learning difficulties are multifactorial and arise from interacting risk factors that partly overlap across disorder pairs. Within this framework, the review identifies executive function, language, and rapid naming as shared risk factors for co-occurring mathematics and reading difficulties, with students showing greater challenges in these processes than students with isolated difficulties. Phonological processing is linked more specifically to reading, and numerical/magnitude processing to mathematics.
requirements: Explains co-occurrence as arising from partly overlapping multifactorial risk factors rather than a single cause or a fully distinct disorder
constraints: The review notes the evidence for domain-general skills accounting for shared variance "remains somewhat inconclusive"
target_learners: Early elementary students (grades 1-3) with co-occurring mathematics and reading difficulties
target_learning_goals: Mathematics achievement
Understanding responsiveness to mathematics interventions
examples: The review cites Viesel-Nordmeyer et al. (2023) finding an additive pattern for mathematics and reading skills but an under-additive pattern in executive function among students with co-occurring difficulties, suggesting executive function is a shared risk factor.
key_sources: Ellinor Waaland, Vibeke Rønneberg, Dieuwer ten Braak. (2026). Effects and Characteristics of Mathematics Interventions for Students with Co-Occurring Difficulties in Mathematics and Reading: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10184-x

article_title: The Relation Between Teacher-Student Eye Contact and Teachers’ Interpersonal Behavior During Group Work: a Multiple-Person Gaze-Tracking Case Study in Secondary Mathematics Education
citation: Haataja, E., Salonen, V., Laine, A., Toivanen, M., & Hannula, M. S. (2021). The Relation Between Teacher-Student Eye Contact and Teachers' Interpersonal Behavior During Group Work: a Multiple-Person Gaze-Tracking Case Study in Secondary Mathematics Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09538-w
title: Multiple-person mobile gaze-tracking combined with continuous interpersonal coding for studying classroom eye contact
description: The article introduces a methodological approach described as "A novel approach in educational science, multiple-person mobile gaze-tracking", which "allows us to gather data on these momentary processes of nonverbal interaction". Teachers and target students wore mobile gaze-tracking glasses (accuracy 1.5 degrees of visual angle) while stationary cameras recorded the classroom; gaze dwells were coded in ELAN by target and duration, and teachers' interpersonal behavior was continuously coded with Sadler's computer-joystick method. The two codings were synchronized in half-second intervals to relate gaze types and durations to momentary communion and agency.
requirements: Gaze and joystick codings must be synchronized (here by dividing gazes into half-second intervals), and coding validity must be confirmed, e.g., by double coding with inter-rater reliability checks.
constraints: Despite high device accuracy, the authors cannot be sure that all face-directed gazes were targeted at the eyes of the other person; they interpreted mutual gazing at faces as essentially eye contact.
target_learners: Secondary school students in authentic classroom lessons
target_learning_goals: Studying momentary teacher-student nonverbal interaction and eye contact in natural classroom settings
examples: In the study, three teachers and 47 students participated; target students wore the glasses in groups of three to four during collaborative problem-solving phases of 16-18 minutes.
key_sources: Haataja, E., Salonen, V., Laine, A., Toivanen, M., & Hannula, M. S. (2021). The Relation Between Teacher-Student Eye Contact and Teachers' Interpersonal Behavior During Group Work: a Multiple-Person Gaze-Tracking Case Study in Secondary Mathematics Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09538-w

article_title: Culture and school belonging: Towards a global research agenda
citation: Ronnel B. King, Faming Wang. (2026). Culture and school belonging: Towards a global research agenda. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10213-9
title: Multilevel cultural framework for school belonging: individual, classroom, school/institutional, national, and global culture
description: Transposing Erez and Gati's (2004) hierarchical model of culture into educational psychology, the commentary proposes that cultural influence on belonging operates at nested levels: "individual, classroom, school/institutional, national, and global culture". Each level offers a distinct unit of analysis, from students' values and self-construals, through peer mindset cultures and school climates, to national value orientations and global narratives such as meritocracy and neoliberalism. The model also emphasizes top-down and bottom-up dynamic processes across levels.
requirements: Researchers must specify which level of culture they are theorizing, how they are measuring it, and how processes across levels interact over time
constraints: The framework was originally developed for organizational contexts and is transposed by the authors into educational psychology
target_learners: Students at individual, classroom, school, national, and global levels of analysis
target_learning_goals: Multilevel theorizing of how culture shapes school belonging
examples: The commentary maps topical-collection constructs onto levels: Browman's goal fit (individual), Seo et al.'s peer mindset culture (classroom), Byrd et al.'s racial climate (school), Hofstede-style value comparisons (national), and global brilliance/meritocracy narratives
key_sources: Ronnel B. King, Faming Wang. (2026). Culture and school belonging: Towards a global research agenda. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10213-9

article_title: Stimming as Thinking: a Critical Reevaluation of Self-Stimulatory Behavior as an Epistemic Resource for Inclusive Education
citation: Sofia Tancredi, Dor Abrahamson. (2024). Stimming as Thinking: a Critical Reevaluation of Self-Stimulatory Behavior as an Epistemic Resource for Inclusive Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09904-y
title: A multi-E (post-cognitivist) model of stimming as integral to cognitive-affective dynamics
description: The article proposes a model of stimming grounded in 4E (and beyond) embodied cognition, treating stimming as an intrinsic part of the cognitive system rather than peripheral noise. It advances five precepts: stimming as embodied (impacting thought and cognitive load), enactive (a substrate for complex actions and concepts), embedded and emotional (reflecting and regulating cognitive-affective system dynamics), ecological (responding to environmental properties), and extended (functioning as socially communicative). The authors state that "post-cognitivist theory offers an alternative conceptualization of stimming as part of the cognitive system's dynamic interactions, through the body, with the physical and social environment." The model reinterprets constructs from psychiatry, psychology, HCI, occupational therapy, and communication studies under the unifying term stimming.
requirements: Recognizes neurodivergent testimony of sensory experiences and practices, and models self-regulative, communicative, and cognitive functions of stimming
constraints: The authors acknowledge contention among post-cognitivist theorists, who endorse the Es to different extents and disagree on topics such as mental representations
target_learners: the full spectrum of the general population
target_learning_goals: curricular content learning through sensorimotor engagement
self-regulation supporting attention and affect during learning
examples: The article reinterprets fidgeting, stereotypies, sensation seeking, embodied self-regulation, adapters, and stimming semiosis as overlapping constructs along axes of focal population, scope (overt vs. covert), and consciousness
key_sources: Sofia Tancredi, Dor Abrahamson. (2024). Stimming as Thinking: a Critical Reevaluation of Self-Stimulatory Behavior as an Epistemic Resource for Inclusive Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09904-y

article_title: Twelve- and Fourteen-Year-Old School Children Differentially Benefit from Sensorimotor- and Multisensory-Enriched Vocabulary Training
citation: Brian Mathias, Christian Andrä, Anika Schwager, Manuela Macedonia, Katharina von Kriegstein. (2022). Twelve- and Fourteen-Year-Old School Children Differentially Benefit from Sensorimotor- and Multisensory-Enriched Vocabulary Training. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09648-z
title: Multisensory learning theory: enrichment benefits are driven by modality-specific sensory and motor representations
description: The article describes multisensory learning theory as the notion that "brain regions that support the processing of enrichment also drive enrichment-based learning benefits". At a neural level, the same sensory and motor regions that process visuo-motor enrichment information during learning are causally relevant for subsequent auditory L2 recognition. This implies benefits arise from specific motor and sensory representations formed under the learning conditions, rather than from general mechanisms such as enhanced attention or arousal. The theory sits alongside embodied, dual coding, mental imagery, and predictive coding accounts, which share the premise that novel information can be mentally represented in terms of its perceptual and motor features.
requirements: Learning must present congruent information in the enrichment modality alongside the primary auditory stimulus
constraints: Benefits may be partially limited by the high dependence of semantics on linguistic context
target_learners: foreign language learners across age groups
target_learning_goals: L2 vocabulary learning and retention
key_sources: Brian Mathias, Christian Andrä, Anika Schwager, Manuela Macedonia, Katharina von Kriegstein. (2022). Twelve- and Fourteen-Year-Old School Children Differentially Benefit from Sensorimotor- and Multisensory-Enriched Vocabulary Training. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09648-z

article_title: Motivation and Personality: Current Integrative Perspectives and the Way Ahead
citation: Lisa Bardach, Luise von Keyserlingk, Jacque S. Eccles. (2026). Motivation and Personality: Current Integrative Perspectives and the Way Ahead. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10147-2
title: Mutualism theory applied to motivation–personality co-development
description: Mutualism theory (van der Maas et al., 2006), originally an alternative account of the positive manifold in cognitive abilities, proposes that positive correlations may be "a by-product of increasingly beneficial interactions that develop over time between initially undeveloped and uncorrelated cognitive processes". The article transfers this principle to motivation and personality, foregrounding mutually reinforcing developmental interactions between motivational and personality processes rather than isolated examples. The theory also accounts for differentiation and specialization: some mutualistic interactions strengthen during development while others weaken or shift toward competitive relationships, for instance conscientiousness supporting interest early in skill acquisition but becoming a barrier with ill-structured problems.
requirements: Developmental interactions between motivation and personality processes must be modeled as mutually reinforcing rather than as isolated effects
constraints: Mutualistic couplings can be interrupted: highly conscientious individuals may lose the link with task-specific interests when tasks require creativity, and highly agreeable individuals may inhibit engagement in competitive evaluation contexts
target_learners: students across educational levels and developmental transitions
target_learning_goals: co-development of motivation, personality, and learning-related outcomes
examples: The article cites the meta-analysis by Mammadov (2022) finding the link between agreeableness and academic achievement was stronger in earlier educational levels (elementary/middle school) than in later ones, aligning with mutualism-inspired reasoning
key_sources: Lisa Bardach, Luise von Keyserlingk, Jacque S. Eccles. (2026). Motivation and Personality: Current Integrative Perspectives and the Way Ahead. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10147-2

article_title: A consideration of racial/ethnic diversity conceptualization and measurement: Clarifying ambiguities and advancing scholarship
citation: Chan, M.-k., & Benner, A. D. (2023). A Consideration of Racial/Ethnic Diversity Conceptualization and Measurement: Clarifying Ambiguities and Advancing Scholarship. Educational Psychologist (accepted manuscript). https://orcid.org/0000-0001-6451-2417
title: A multidimensional conceptual model of diversity: attributes, three evaluative frameworks (normic, dual-concept, representative), and static versus dynamic social spaces
description: The article proposes a conceptual model, built on Steel et al.'s (2018) framework plus dynamic diversity (Graham, 2018; Garces & Jayakumar, 2014), in which diversity conceptualization varies along three axes. "Figure 1 is a conceptual model detailing the multidimensional nature of diversity conceptualization." Attributes are the categorization used (e.g., race/ethnicity); evaluative frameworks define what counts as diverse — normic (divergence from a "norm"), dual-concept (variety plus even concentration), and representative (similarity to a reference population); social spaces distinguish static context-level from person-specific dynamic diversity. The model is used to map and critique existing measures.
requirements: Researchers must specify the attribute, its categorization, the norm or reference population, and the social space when defining diversity for a study
constraints: The authors state these frameworks are not the only available approaches, though they encompass the major conceptualizations actively studied in the literature
target_learning_goals: characterizing school racial/ethnic composition to study its impact on student adjustment, academic performance, intergroup interactions, and school climate
examples: A San Francisco school (38% White, 40% Asian, 16% Hispanic, 3% Black, 3% other) is judged diverse or not depending on which of the three evaluative frameworks is applied
key_sources: Chan, M.-k., & Benner, A. D. (2023). A Consideration of Racial/Ethnic Diversity Conceptualization and Measurement: Clarifying Ambiguities and Advancing Scholarship. Educational Psychologist (accepted manuscript). https://orcid.org/0000-0001-6451-2417

article_title: Little and often: Causal inference machine learning demonstrates the benefits of homework for improving achievement in mathematics and science
citation: Nathan McJames, Andrew Parnell, and Ann O'Shea. (2023). Little and Often: Causal Inference Machine Learning Demonstrates the Benefits of Homework for Improving Achievement in Mathematics and Science. https://timssandpirls.bc.edu/timss2019/international-results
title: Multivariate Bayesian Causal Forests for estimating homework treatment effects on multiple outcomes
description: This study adopts a multivariate extension of Bayesian Causal Forests (BCF), a non-parametric causal inference machine learning model built on Bayesian Additive Regression Trees. The article states it "adopts a multivariate extension of BCF developed by McJames et al. (2023), which allows BCF to be applied to multiple outcome variables such as mathematics and science achievement simultaneously". The model estimates baseline achievement (mu) and treatment effects (tau) for four treatment groups covering higher frequencies and longer durations, with a classroom random intercept, capturing interactions and non-linear relationships without assuming linearity.
requirements: Observational data with a rich set of confounding covariates that can be controlled for, since the model assumes all confounding can be accounted for
Sufficiently large samples; the authors chose the Irish sample of 4118 students because it is large enough for the model to detect relationships and interactions
constraints: The model assumes all possible sources of confounding are accounted for; unmeasured confounders not collected in TIMSS could bias results
Imputed missing values (6% of data) carry uncertainty not reflected in the reported credible intervals
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement
science achievement
examples: The model was fit with 50 trees in the mu part and 20 trees in each tau part, 5000 MCMC iterations with the first 3000 discarded as burn-in, applied to five plausible values per student
key_sources: Nathan McJames, Andrew Parnell, and Ann O'Shea. (2023). Little and Often: Causal Inference Machine Learning Demonstrates the Benefits of Homework for Improving Achievement in Mathematics and Science. https://timssandpirls.bc.edu/timss2019/international-results

article_title: The effects of achievement goal instructions in game-based learning on students’ achievement goals, performance, and achievement emotions
citation: Hu, Y., Wouters, P., van der Schaaf, M., & Kester, L. (2024). The effects of achievement goal instructions in game-based learning on students' achievement goals, performance, and achievement emotions. Learning and Instruction, 93, 101943. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2024.101943
title: Multiple goal perspective mechanisms and match/mismatch hypotheses for achievement goal instructions
description: The article organizes its predictions through the multiple goal perspective (Barron & Harackiewicz, 2001), which proposes four mechanisms by which combined mastery-approach and performance-approach goals may produce optimal outcomes: the "specialized mechanism", "additive mechanism", "selective mechanism", and "interactive mechanism". It pairs these with the match hypothesis (instructions work best when they match prior achievement goals) and mismatch hypothesis (mismatched instructions may be vibrated, migrated, or exacerbated) from Murayama & Elliot. The study tested the specialized, additive, and interactive mechanisms and the moderation hypotheses in chemistry game-based learning.
requirements: Achievement goal instructions that assign learners' goals beforehand, and measurement of prior achievement goals before the intervention
constraints: The study tested only state-based approach goals, excluding avoidance goals because they may not be as prevalent among secondary school students as theory expected
target_learners: secondary school students in chemistry game-based learning
target_learning_goals: chemistry content learning (separation techniques) in game-based learning
examples: The 2×2 experiment assigned 450 students to mastery-approach, performance-approach, multiple goal, or no goal instructions conditions before playing CosmiClean
key_sources: Hu, Y., Wouters, P., van der Schaaf, M., & Kester, L. (2024). The effects of achievement goal instructions in game-based learning on students' achievement goals, performance, and achievement emotions. Learning and Instruction, 93, 101943. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2024.101943

article_title: Teacher self-efficacy and self-reported cognitive activation and classroom management: A multilevel perspective on the role of school characteristics
citation: Holzberger, D., & Prestele, E. (2021). Teacher Self-Efficacy and Self-Reported Instructional Quality: A Multilevel Perspective on the Role of School Characteristics. Learning and Instruction, 76, 101513. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2021.101513
title: Multilevel motivation-to-performance framework: teacher self-efficacy modeled at both individual and school level with context effects and cross-level interactions
description: The article transfers a work-team motivation framework (Chen & Kanfer) to teaching, modeling teacher self-efficacy simultaneously as an individual variable and as a composite school variable (collective efficacy), and distinguishing Level 2 associations, unique context effects, and cross-level interactions. It defines a context effect in terms of "equally motivated teachers reporting more or less instructional quality in a more or less efficacious school". The framework organizes the study's three research questions and its multilevel modeling strategy.
requirements: Multiple teachers per school and school-level aggregates of individual efficacy ratings to separate within- from between-school associations
constraints: Applied to self-reported instructional quality in a cross-sectional secondary dataset, so causal direction cannot be established
target_learning_goals: instructional quality (cognitive activation and classroom management) as an outcome of teacher motivation
examples: Austrian TALIS 2018 data from 4,255 teachers at 246 schools analyzed with grand-mean and school-mean centering to separate Level 1 and Level 2 associations
key_sources: Holzberger, D., & Prestele, E. (2021). Teacher Self-Efficacy and Self-Reported Instructional Quality: A Multilevel Perspective on the Role of School Characteristics. Learning and Instruction, 76, 101513. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2021.101513

article_title: A Bayesian approach to students’ perceptions of teachers’ autonomy support
citation: Flunger, B., Verdonschot, A., Zitzmann, S., Hornstra, L., & van Gog, T. (2024). A Bayesian approach to students' perceptions of teachers' autonomy support. Learning and Instruction, 91, 101873. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2023.101873
title: Multilevel conceptualization of autonomy support: climate, contextual, and perceived-difference constructs
description: The article conceptualizes teachers' autonomy support as a multilevel construct with distinct operationalizations: class-directed support measured with class-referent items forms an L2 climate construct reflecting the "overall classroom-specific autonomy-supportive climate"; individual support is an L1 construct whose class aggregate forms a contextual construct indicating how similarly teachers support students; and perceived differences (including relative lack of support) capture within-classroom inequality. The overall autonomy-supportive atmosphere is a shared perception combining class-aggregated individual and class-directed support. This framework motivated the study's doubly latent multilevel modeling of student perceptions.
requirements: Measures must make the referent explicit ("me/I" vs "us/class" items) so individual and class-directed support can be distinguished
constraints: Uniform ratings of a class-level construct by students are unlikely because within-cluster differences in subjective perceptions are expected
target_learners: primary school students in mathematics classrooms
target_learning_goals: students' intrinsic motivation, extrinsic regulation, effort, and persistence
examples: The study measured four autonomy-supportive strategies (choice provision, rationale provision, interest stimulation, frustration acknowledgment) with parallel individual and class-directed items, plus newly developed perceived-difference items
key_sources: Flunger, B., Verdonschot, A., Zitzmann, S., Hornstra, L., & van Gog, T. (2024). A Bayesian approach to students' perceptions of teachers' autonomy support. Learning and Instruction, 91, 101873. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2023.101873

article_title: Applying multilevel modelling to content analysis data: Methodological issues in the study of role assignment in asynchronous discussion groups
citation: De Wever, B., Van Keer, H., Schellens, T., & Valcke, M. (2007). Applying multilevel modelling to content analysis data: Methodological issues in the study of role assignment in asynchronous discussion groups. Learning and Instruction, 17, 436-447. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2007.04.001
title: Multilevel modelling as the appropriate statistical framework for analysing content analysis data from CSCL environments
description: The article presents multilevel modelling as a statistical approach for hierarchically clustered data in collaborative learning research, in which messages are nested within students (and measurement occasions) within groups. It argues that traditional unilevel techniques violate the independence assumption, that "conventional modelling can result in underestimation of standard errors", and that multilevel modelling handles "the hierarchical nesting, the interdependency, and the unit of analysis problem in a natural way". The article demonstrates the framework through three-level and four-level random intercept models with roles, themes, and ASIMeC dimensions as predictors.
requirements: Data collected at different levels with a clustered hierarchical structure (messages within students within groups)
Decomposition of variance via a random intercept null model before adding explanatory variables
constraints: The article states a demonstration of the full power of multilevel modelling was beyond the scope of the article
target_learners: Researchers analysing content analysis data from CSCL environments
target_learning_goals: Methodologically sound analysis of collaborative learning processes in asynchronous discussion groups
examples: Three-level model testing role effects and four-level model with measurement occasions nested within subjects, estimated with RIGLS in MLwiN 2.01
key_sources: De Wever, B., Van Keer, H., Schellens, T., & Valcke, M. (2007). Applying multilevel modelling to content analysis data: Methodological issues in the study of role assignment in asynchronous discussion groups. Learning and Instruction, 17, 436-447. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2007.04.001

article_title: Methodological issues in developing a multi-dimensional coding procedure for small-group chat communication
citation: Jan Willem Strijbos, Gerry Stahl. (2007). Methodological issues in developing a multi-dimensional coding procedure for small group chat communication. Learning and Instruction. https://hal.science/hal-00703042
title: Multi-dimensional coding procedure for small group chat communication
description: A multi-dimensional coding procedure for analyzing small group chat communication in CSCL research, developed by the authors to address three methodological issues: "the unit of analysis and unit fragmentation", "the reconstruction of the response structure" and "determining reliability without overestimation". The procedure treats analysis units and the connections between them — threading — as central, since threading "proved essential to handle unit fragmentation, to reconstruct the response structure and for reliability of coding". It extends chat analysis beyond the dyadic settings that have dominated CSCL research.
requirements: Analysis units must be defined for chat communication, with threading (connections between analysis units) incorporated to handle fragmentation and reconstruct the response structure.
Reliability must be determined in a way that avoids overestimation.
constraints: The procedure was developed for small group chat communication; the article notes CSCL chat research has primarily studied dyadic settings, so extension to small groups is its distinguishing scope.
target_learners: small groups of learners collaborating through chat in CSCL settings
target_learning_goals: analysis and understanding of collaborative learning processes in chat communication
examples: The article reports the procedure's development for small group chat communication in Learning and Instruction, illustrating unit fragmentation, response-structure reconstruction, and a reliability overestimation risk.
key_sources: Jan Willem Strijbos, Gerry Stahl. (2007). Methodological issues in developing a multi-dimensional coding procedure for small group chat communication. Learning and Instruction. https://hal.science/hal-00703042

article_title: Putting excellence first: How rubric performance level order and feedback type influence students’ reading patterns and task performance
citation: Panadero, E., Delgado, P., Zamorano, D., Pinedo, L., Fernández-Ortube, A., & Barrenetxea-Mínguez, L. (2025). Putting excellence first: How rubric performance level order and feedback type influence students' reading patterns and task performance. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102168
title: Multimodal process-tracing approach to rubric use: triangulating eye-tracking and think-aloud protocols
description: The article adopts a methodological framework combining eye-tracking with think-aloud protocols to capture students' real-time engagement with rubrics during academic tasks. Eye-tracking supplies fixation times, number of visits, and gaze transitions between rubric and task stimuli, while think-aloud protocols capture verbalized reasoning and strategies. The authors state that "The integration of these two data sources follows a logic of triangulation common in mixed-methods research", allowing them to identify convergences (prioritization of PL4) and divergences (visual behavior predicting performance while verbal references did not). No prior study had combined both methods to examine how students read and use rubrics.
requirements: Concurrent collection of eye-tracking and think-aloud data during task performance; tasks of moderate cognitive demand so participants can verbalize without being overwhelmed
constraints: Triangulation operates at the level of interpretive patterns rather than fine-grained synchronized episode-level coding; think-aloud independence assumptions were not always met when participants contributed multiple protocols
target_learning_goals: understanding how students read and use rubrics formatively during complex academic tasks
examples: The study combined eye-tracking (fixation times, visits, gaze transitions) with coded think-aloud protocols across five task phases, using the two streams in parallel to identify converging and diverging patterns.
key_sources: Panadero, E., Delgado, P., Zamorano, D., Pinedo, L., Fernández-Ortube, A., & Barrenetxea-Mínguez, L. (2025). Putting excellence first: How rubric performance level order and feedback type influence students' reading patterns and task performance. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102168

article_title: Contrasting orthographically similar words facilitates adult second language vocabulary learning
citation: Baxter, P.A.; Bekkering, H.; Dijkstra, A.F.J.; Droop, W.; Hurk, M.M. van den; Léoné, F.T.M. (2022). Contrasting orthographically similar words facilitates adult second language vocabulary learning. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2022.101582
title: Multiple-choice contrasting task with sorted/shuffled word-list shuffling system
description: A multiple-choice vocabulary learning task in which learners select the correct translation among three options and receive feedback. A shuffling system creates a sorted condition, where triplets contain similar answer options inducing contrasting, and a shuffled condition with dissimilar options. Crucially, "we used a shuffling system that enabled the words to be learned to be identical across conditions, eliminating list effects as an explanation during group comparison." The task includes repeated retrieval (a testing effect) and can test learning in both productive and receptive directions.
requirements: Triplets must be constructed so sorted and shuffled conditions contain exactly the same words, avoiding word or list confounds
constraints: Participants were instructed to avoid their own learning strategies, and a response time limit limited conscious association strategies
target_learning_goals: L2 vocabulary form-meaning acquisition in productive and receptive directions
examples: Experiment 1 used 75 words in orthographically similar, semantically similar, and fully dissimilar conditions, six blocks of 75 trials with feedback highlighting correct translations in green
key_sources: Baxter, P.A.; Bekkering, H.; Dijkstra, A.F.J.; Droop, W.; Hurk, M.M. van den; Léoné, F.T.M. (2022). Contrasting orthographically similar words facilitates adult second language vocabulary learning. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2022.101582

article_title: The contributions of domain-general and numerical factors to third-grade arithmetic skills and mathematical learning disability.
citation: Cowan, R., & Powell, D. (2014). The Contributions of Domain-General and Numerical Factors to Third-Grade Arithmetic Skills and Mathematical Learning Disability. Journal of Educational Psychology, 106(1), 214-229. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0034097
title: Multiple deficits framework for mathematical learning disability
description: The article evaluates and supports a multiple deficits view of number difficulties, in which arithmetical difficulties arise from combinations of deficits in domain-general factors (working memory, reasoning, processing speed, oral language) and numerical factors (single digit processing, multidigit skills). The authors state that "Most children with number difficulties exhibit deficits in both domain-general and numerical factors." This contrasts with accounts attributing difficulties solely to single-digit processing deficits. The framework was tested by examining deficit incidence in MLD, LA, and TA groups.
requirements: Assessment of both domain-general and numerical factors to identify deficit combinations
constraints: Findings are from a single cohort of children assessed in one grade over one year; the article notes findings might vary with year of schooling
target_learners: Third-grade children with mathematical learning difficulties
target_learning_goals: Arithmetic skills including calculation fluency, written computation, and word problems
examples: Children categorized as having deficits if their score on one or more constituent factors was more than 1SD below the mean, examined across MLD, LA, and TA groups
key_sources: Cowan, R., & Powell, D. (2014). The Contributions of Domain-General and Numerical Factors to Third-Grade Arithmetic Skills and Mathematical Learning Disability. Journal of Educational Psychology, 106(1), 214-229. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0034097

article_title: The social class test gap: A worldwide investigation of the role of academic anxiety and income inequality in standardized test score disparities.
citation: Nele Claes, Annique Smeding, Arnaud Carré, Nicolas Sommet. (2024). The social class test gap: A worldwide investigation of the role of academic anxiety and income inequality in standardized test score disparities. Journal of Educational Psychology, 116(6), 871-888. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000881
title: Multidimensional conceptualization of family social class: economic capital and cultural capital as related yet distinct resources
description: The article defines family social class by unequal access to resources and distinguishes two critical forms. It states that "economic capital refers to access to economic resources and is typically measured using household income and material possessions", while "cultural capital refers to access to cultural resources and is typically measured using parental education and cultural possessions". The two are "related yet conceptually distinct", associated with different psychological processes and school experiences. The article argues that prior studies often combined them, making it difficult to disentangle their contributions, and uses fine-grained indicators separating the two across its PISA studies.
requirements: Operationalizing social class requires separate indicators for economic capital (household income, material possessions) and cultural capital (parental education, cultural possessions) to disentangle their effects.
constraints: Many extant studies operationalized social class as a combination of economic and cultural capital, which the article says makes it difficult to disentangle their relative contributions.
target_learning_goals: Standardized test performance in mathematics, reading, and science
examples: Studies 2a-2b measured parental education and cultural possessions as culturally based indicators and a twelve-item wealth measure as the economically based indicator, in separate model series.
key_sources: Nele Claes, Annique Smeding, Arnaud Carré, Nicolas Sommet. (2024). The social class test gap: A worldwide investigation of the role of academic anxiety and income inequality in standardized test score disparities. Journal of Educational Psychology, 116(6), 871-888. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000881

article_title: Multimedia effects in initial instruction and feedback on problem solving.
citation: Gök, S., Zhang, T., Goldstone, R. L., & Fyfe, E. R. (2025). Multimedia Effects in Initial Instruction and Feedback on Problem Solving. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000943
title: Provide multimedia materials in feedback to improve problem-solving performance, and in initial instruction when the aim is spontaneous diagram generation
description: The article recommends placing multimedia materials (text plus diagrams) selectively depending on the instructional goal. It states: "It may be important for practitioners to provide multimedia materials in feedback to improve problem-solving performance, whereas they may include them in initial instruction if the aim is for students to spontaneously generate diagrams in their own solutions." The recommendation follows directly from the experiment's dissociated effects: feedback modality drove posttest accuracy, instruction modality drove perceptions and drawings.
requirements: Feedback or instruction materials must combine text with content-based diagrams (icon arrays and tables in this study) aligned with multimedia learning design principles of contiguity and coherence.
constraints: Effects were demonstrated only for conditional probability problems with undergraduate students; the study's design and analysis were not pre-registered.
target_learning_goals: problem-solving accuracy on conditional probability problems
spontaneous diagram generation during problem solving
examples: In the experiment, 129 undergraduates were randomly assigned across four conditions crossing text-only vs multimedia initial instruction with text-only vs multimedia feedback on conditional probability problems.
key_sources: Gök, S., Zhang, T., Goldstone, R. L., & Fyfe, E. R. (2025). Multimedia Effects in Initial Instruction and Feedback on Problem Solving. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000943

article_title: The interplay of mastery and performance goals in social comparison: A multiple-goal perspective.
citation: Darnon, C., Dompnier, B., Gilliéron, O., & Butera, F. (2010). The Interplay of Mastery and Performance Goals in Social Comparison: A Multiple-Goal Perspective. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0018161
title: Multiple-goal perspective: achievement goals are pursued simultaneously and interact rather than operate in isolation
description: The multiple-goal perspective holds that learners pursue several achievement goals at once — mastery goals (the desire to acquire knowledge), performance-approach goals (the desire to outperform others), and performance-avoidance goals (not to be outperformed by others) — and that these goals interact in shaping outcomes. The article uses this perspective to motivate testing the interaction between mastery and performance-approach goals in predicting social comparison. Its results are discussed "in terms of the importance of multiple-goal pursuit in academic settings."
requirements: Educational settings must be considered as containing multiple co-occurring goals, since settings are rarely free from performance-approach goals even when mastery goals are promoted
target_learning_goals: understanding how achievement goal pursuit shapes learners' social comparison behavior
examples: Study 1 measured self-set mastery, performance-approach, and performance-avoidance goals together; Study 2 manipulated goal conditions to test their joint effect on social comparison interest.
key_sources: Darnon, C., Dompnier, B., Gilliéron, O., & Butera, F. (2010). The Interplay of Mastery and Performance Goals in Social Comparison: A Multiple-Goal Perspective. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0018161

article_title: Supplemental Material for Important Text Characteristics for Early-Grades Text Complexity
citation: J. Fitzgerald et al. (2014). Important Text Characteristics for Early-Grades Text Complexity. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0037289
title: Multiple-perspective measurement of early-grades text complexity at the intersection of texts, readers, and tasks
description: The article defines text complexity not as an intrinsic text property but relationally: "Because text complexity was defined at the intersection of printed texts with students reading them for particular purposes and doing particular tasks, a multiple-perspective measure of text complexity was created using student responses during a reading task and teachers’ ordering of texts according to complexity." Two Rasch logit scales (student maze responses, teacher comparative judgments) are linked by linear equating and transformed to a 0–100 developmental scale. This framework grounds the study's outcome measure for identifying important text characteristics.
requirements: Both student response data from a reading task and teacher complexity orderings of the same texts are needed before equating onto a single scale
constraints: The resulting 0–100 scale was developed for first- and second-grade readers and early-grades texts, with scores ranging from 0 to 100
target_learning_goals: Reading development and matching text difficulty to early readers
examples: 1,258 students completed maze tasks on 89 texts while 90 teachers compared digitized text pairs side by side; the two logit scales were equated and linearly transformed to a 0–100 scale
key_sources: J. Fitzgerald et al. (2014). Important Text Characteristics for Early-Grades Text Complexity. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0037289

article_title: From individual word recognition to word list and text reading fluency.
citation: Altani, A., Protopapas, A., Katopodi, K., & Georgiou, G. K. (2019). From Individual Word Recognition to Word List and Text Reading Fluency. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000359
title: Multi-item sequence processing account of reading fluency development
description: The article advances and tests the account that fluent reading of multiple words is co-determined, after basic word recognition is mastered, by an additional ability to process multi-item sequences, indexed by serial naming tasks. Readers process one stimulus while articulating the previous one and previewing upcoming items, buffering information about "items that have already been viewed but not yet pronounced." This endogenously controlled sequential processing is proposed as the mechanism underlying the transition from word-by-word reading to efficient processing of word sequences, potentially underpinning prosody via syntactic and semantic planning.
requirements: Basic accuracy and speed in individual word recognition must first be achieved (around Grade 3 for high-frequency short words) before the sequence-processing component contributes unique fluency variance
