constraints: The aspect of multiword processing addressed is word-level multi-item processing, not supralexical processing involving syntactic, semantic, and discourse structures of text
target_learners: Elementary school children in Grades 1, 3, and 5 learning to read in alphabetic orthographies
target_learning_goals: Reading fluency development, including word-list reading fluency and text reading fluency
examples: A two-predictor regression model with discrete word reading and serial digit naming was tested across grades and languages; serial digit naming uniquely predicted fluency in Grades 3 and 5 in both Greek and English
key_sources: Altani, A., Protopapas, A., Katopodi, K., & Georgiou, G. K. (2019). From Individual Word Recognition to Word List and Text Reading Fluency. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000359

article_title: Mediational effects of reading-related intermediate phenotypes from polygenic scores to reading skills
citation: Remon, A., Mascheretti, S., Voronin, I., Feng, B., Ouellet-Morin, I., Brendgen, M., Vitaro, F., Robaey, P., Andlauer, T. F. M., Boivin, M. & Dionne, G. (2025). Mediational effects of reading-related intermediate phenotypes from polygenic scores to reading skills. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00346-x
title: Multimodal sensory-to-phonological sequence account of genetic influences on reading acquisition
description: The article advances an etiological account in which genetic susceptibility for reading is phenotypically expressed through a sequence from basic multimodal sensory processing to phonological skills to reading behavior. It states that "the genetic variation represents the first step in a multiple-layered liability that ultimately leads to behavioral phenotypes," consistent with the multiple deficits model, and that training programs targeting attentional control have improved reading. The serial mediation results are presented as supporting "one of the most robust theoretical hypothesis underlying reading acquisitions."
requirements: Longitudinal or genetically informed designs with sensitive measures of sensory processing and phonological skills to trace the sequence
constraints: The cross-sectional design cannot determine causal influences among measures over time; only a first formal test of the sequential association
target_learning_goals: Reading decoding
Reading comprehension
examples: Sequential SEM models tested RBTP enabling PA, PA underpinning decoding, and decoding supporting comprehension
key_sources: Remon, A., Mascheretti, S., Voronin, I., Feng, B., Ouellet-Morin, I., Brendgen, M., Vitaro, F., Robaey, P., Andlauer, T. F. M., Boivin, M. & Dionne, G. (2025). Mediational effects of reading-related intermediate phenotypes from polygenic scores to reading skills. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00346-x

article_title: Enhancing children’s numeracy and executive functions via their explicit integration
citation: Scerif, G., Sučević, J., Andrews, H., Blakey, E., Gattas, S. U., Godfrey, A., et al. (2025). Enhancing children's numeracy and executive functions via their explicit integration: the ONE programme cluster randomised controlled trial. npj Science of Learning 10, 8. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00302-9
title: Mutualistic / interactive-specialisation framework of EF-mathematics co-development
description: The article grounds the ONE programme in frameworks of neurocognitive development, such as interactive specialisation and mutualistic/transactional views, in which the dynamic interplay of domain-general control functions (EFs) and domain-specific skills (numerical cognition) promotes their change. Large-scale longitudinal data are cited to show that EF does not act as a unidirectional influence on mathematics; instead, components of EF and mathematics predict change in each other across the primary school years. The mechanism hypothesis is that "practising EF challenge in the context of mathematical content provides opportunities for deeper processing and learning, thereby enhancing the co-development of EF and mathematics." The ONE programme was designed to test this integrated-intervention mechanism directly.
requirements: Interventions must embed executive challenge within mathematical content rather than training EF in isolation, so that co-developing skills are practised together
constraints: The article notes the empirical evidence for integrated interventions in very young children was limited and mixed prior to this trial
No neural or long-term longitudinal data were collected in this study
target_learners: preschool children aged 3-4 years, especially those growing up in economic disadvantage
target_learning_goals: early numeracy and executive functions (working memory, inhibitory control, cognitive flexibility) developing together
examples: The ONE programme operationalised the framework by training educators to deliver 25 activities combining EF challenge with mathematics content in preschool routines
key_sources: Scerif, G., Sučević, J., Andrews, H., Blakey, E., Gattas, S. U., Godfrey, A., et al. (2025). Enhancing children's numeracy and executive functions via their explicit integration: the ONE programme cluster randomised controlled trial. npj Science of Learning 10, 8. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00302-9

article_title: A population-wide gene-environment interaction study on how genes, schools, and residential areas shape achievement
citation: Rosa Cheesman, Nicolai T. Borgen, Torkild H. Lyngstad, Espen M. Eilertsen, Ziada Ayorech, Fartein A. Torvik, Ole A. Andreassen, Henrik D. Zachrisson and Eivind Ystrom. (2022). A population-wide gene-environment interaction study on how genes, schools, and residential areas shape achievement. npj Science of Learning 7:29. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00145-8
title: Agnostic multilevel gene-environment interaction framework for testing latent environmental moderation
description: The article advances a social-genetic research strategy that estimates total interactions between polygenic indices and environmental levels (schools, neighbourhoods, districts, municipalities) using multilevel random-slope models, "thus remaining agnostic to specific features of environments". Controlling parental EA-PGI exploits random genetic segregation to disentangle within-family genetic effects from environments selected by parents. The authors present it as a framework within which to test the interactive roles of specific school characteristics.
requirements: Requires genotype data on parent-child trios so parental PGI can be adjusted, plus linked environmental membership identifiers and standardised outcome data
constraints: Latent interactions do not identify which specific environmental features drive moderation; measured-environment approaches alone could miss the interaction
PGI based on between-family GWAS weights may leave some bias and do not capture the full genetic component
target_learning_goals: standardised academic achievement in maths, reading and English
examples: Applied to 23,471 Norwegian MoBa trios across 2578 schools and 7700 neighbourhoods, comparing 11 nested multilevel models by AIC
key_sources: Rosa Cheesman, Nicolai T. Borgen, Torkild H. Lyngstad, Espen M. Eilertsen, Ziada Ayorech, Fartein A. Torvik, Ole A. Andreassen, Henrik D. Zachrisson and Eivind Ystrom. (2022). A population-wide gene-environment interaction study on how genes, schools, and residential areas shape achievement. npj Science of Learning 7:29. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00145-8

article_title: The impact of premature birth on auditory-visual processes in very preterm schoolchildren
citation: Marion Décaillet, Solange Denervaud, Cléo Huguenin-Virchaux, Laureline Besuchet, Céline J. Fischer Fumeaux, Micah M. Murray & Juliane Schneider. (2024). The impact of premature birth on auditory-visual processes in very preterm schoolchildren. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00257-3
title: Multisensory stimulus contexts may serve as an access point for remediating highly variable behaviour in children
description: The article proposes that presenting multisensory (simultaneous audio-visual) stimuli can reduce behavioural variability, because performance variability was significantly decreased under multisensory stimulus conditions in both full-term and preterm schoolchildren alike. As the authors put it, "Multisensory stimulus contexts ma y thus provide an access point for remediating situations where highly variable behavior may be a contributor to poorer performance and cognition". This recommendation extends the observed IQR reduction under multisensory conditions to potential remediation contexts.
requirements: Highly variable behaviour must be a contributor to the poorer performance being targeted, as the article frames the remedy
Multisensory stimulus presentation must be feasible in the setting, as in the simple detection task with simultaneous audio-visual stimuli
constraints: The recommendation is grounded in reduced interquartile ranges under multisensory conditions in schoolchildren, not in a tested intervention
The article cites variability's contribution to poorer performance in children with ADHD as an example, not a tested population here
target_learners: Schoolchildren, including very preterm children and children with highly variable behaviour
target_learning_goals: Reducing behavioural performance variability that contributes to poorer performance and cognition
examples: In the simple detection task, interquartile ranges of RTs were significantly smaller under multisensory than unisensory conditions in both VPT and FT children, despite generally slower and more variable RTs in VPT children
key_sources: Marion Décaillet, Solange Denervaud, Cléo Huguenin-Virchaux, Laureline Besuchet, Céline J. Fischer Fumeaux, Micah M. Murray & Juliane Schneider. (2024). The impact of premature birth on auditory-visual processes in very preterm schoolchildren. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00257-3

article_title: Individual differences in the learning potential of human beings
citation: Elsbeth Stern (2017). Individual differences in the learning potential of human beings. npj Science of Learning 2:2. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-016-0003-0
title: Multi-store model of human information processing with working memory as gatekeeper to a self-organizing long-term memory network
description: The article presents a model of human information processing (developed together with Dr. Lennart Schalk, Fig. 1) in which sensory memory feeds a limited working memory, which "is responsible for temporarily maintaining and manipulating information during cognitive activity" and acts as gatekeeper to long-term memory. Long-term memory is described as "a self-organizing network, in which verbal terms, images, or procedures are represented as interlinked nodes with varying associative strength". Working memory selects incoming information, aligns it with retrieved knowledge, inhibits irrelevant input, and updates knowledge by adding nodes and altering associative strengths; procedural knowledge automates with practice and frees working-memory resources.
requirements: Appropriate learning opportunities that connect core knowledge and working memory to symbol systems
Instructional support for restructuring declarative knowledge, such as self-explanations, contrasting cases, and metacognitive questions
constraints: Working memory capacity is limited, so only a fractional amount of incoming sensory information passes into it
The full potential of working memory is not in place at birth but matures during childhood and changes until puberty
target_learning_goals: Acquisition of procedural and conceptual knowledge in academic subjects
Efficient use of working memory resources through chunking and automatization
examples: The article illustrates chunking with the digit series 91119893101990, which becomes reproducible when stored as two historical dates, freeing working memory resources
Conceptual change is illustrated by children who equate weight with being heavy and deny that a single grain of rice has weight
key_sources: Elsbeth Stern (2017). Individual differences in the learning potential of human beings. npj Science of Learning 2:2. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-016-0003-0

article_title: How to capture developmental brain dynamics: gaps and solutions
citation: van Atteveldt, N., Vandermosten, M., Weeda, W. & Bonte, M. (2021). How to capture developmental brain dynamics: gaps and solutions. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00088-6
title: Example framework unifying developmental change across levels, functions, and time
description: The article proposes an example framework unifying developmental changes across three dimensions: levels of change (genes, brain function and structure, behavior, cognition, and social environment), interactively emerging functions (reading, math, executive function), and time. As the figure caption states, "During development (TIME dimension), there is continuous interaction across levels of change (LEVELS: gray bars) as well as across emerging functions (FUNCTIONS: presented as interactive networks)." Neural and cognitive correlates of functions first appear as wide, overlapping networks that gradually specialize to more focused networks with learning and maturation.
requirements: Must encompass multiple levels and functional networks and their dynamic interactions across time
Used across studies and disciplines to allow communication between experts at each level
constraints: The article presents it as an example framework, a suggestion for how such a framework could look
target_learning_goals: Reading, math, executive function development
examples: Table 1 maps each workshop speaker's research onto the framework's levels and functions
key_sources: van Atteveldt, N., Vandermosten, M., Weeda, W. & Bonte, M. (2021). How to capture developmental brain dynamics: gaps and solutions. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00088-6

article_title: Impaired audio-visual associations in dyslexia: evidence beyond linguistic processing
citation: Pasqualotto, A., Cochrane, A., Venuti, P. et al. (2025). Impaired audio-visual associations in dyslexia: evidence beyond linguistic processing. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00382-7
title: Mutualistic developmental account of audio-visual associative learning and reading
description: The article proposes that AV associative learning and reading develop mutually: children with stronger reading skills tended to reach higher asymptotic accuracy, and the mechanisms supporting AV learning develop alongside reading expertise. The authors state this "could align with a mutualistic model of cognitive development, wherein advances in the acquisition of one ability, such as reading, may support and interact with other learning processes". They further propose a developmental transition: in pre-readers AV learning relates to phonological awareness, while in proficient readers it is associated with domain-general skills, particularly working memory capacity.
requirements: Capturing short-term learning trajectories across multiple stages, as in the dynamic framework of reading acquisition, to characterize the learning process rather than a single outcome point
constraints: The correlational findings offer insights but should be interpreted with caution given small sample sizes and multiple uncorrected associations; further research with larger samples is needed to validate these patterns
target_learners: Children across reading-development stages, from pre-readers to proficient readers, including children with dyslexia
target_learning_goals: Reading acquisition
Formation and consolidation of cross-modal (audio-visual) associations
examples: Reading-matched controls (younger children) still outperformed children with DD despite being younger, suggesting AV learning difficulties in DD are not simply a byproduct of reading skill
key_sources: Pasqualotto, A., Cochrane, A., Venuti, P. et al. (2025). Impaired audio-visual associations in dyslexia: evidence beyond linguistic processing. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00382-7

article_title: Helping children with reading difficulties: some things we have learned so far
citation: Genevieve McArthur and Anne Castles. (2017). Helping children with reading difficulties: some things we have learned so far. npj Science of Learning (2017) 2:7. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0008-3
title: Multi-component cognitive models of reading as a roadmap of proximal causes
description: The article draws on several theoretical and computational models of reading which, despite varying in some respects, all include cognitive components representing letter and word recognition, recognition and production of speech sounds and spoken words, access to stored word meanings, and links between these components. Impairment in any component or link directly impairs reading behaviour. The article uses these models as "a useful roadmap, providing an explicit account of the key processes directly underpinning successful reading behaviour" when assessing poor readers.
requirements: Standardized tests of potential proximal causes, such as vocabulary and letter-sound knowledge tests, are needed to apply the roadmap in assessment.
constraints: The models vary in some respects, as the article notes, so the component list is a common core rather than a single settled architecture.
target_learning_goals: reading accuracy and comprehension
examples: The article cites the dual route cascaded model, the simple view of reading, the CDP+ model, and connectionist models as examples of this model family.
key_sources: Genevieve McArthur and Anne Castles. (2017). Helping children with reading difficulties: some things we have learned so far. npj Science of Learning (2017) 2:7. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0008-3

article_title: Training the Body: The Potential of AIED to Support Personalized Motor Skills Learning
citation: Olga C. Santos. (2016). Training the Body: The Potential of AIED to Support Personalized Motor Skills Learning. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:730–755. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0103-2
title: Build accurate-movement models from recordings of several experts, since no one performs a movement identically each time
description: When modelling expert movements for comparison, the article recommends building the model from several recordings — repeated movements by the same expert and by other experts — and extrapolating the "accurate" movement in terms of relevant parameters. Because "it is not possible for any person to perform a given movement in the same exact way each time", a single recording would misrepresent the target. This supports diagnosing the mismatch between learner and expert movements.
requirements: Movements for which support is provided must be identified and isolable; accurate movements are recorded from experts with physical capabilities similar to the learner.
constraints: Whether movements are domain-defined or must be extracted from domain experts depends on the kind of activity.
target_learners: Learners practising specific motor skills against expert reference models
target_learning_goals: Correcting and refining movement technique toward expert performance
examples: Comparison is usually done against the movement carried out by an expert, with a threshold triggering feedback when overcome.
key_sources: Olga C. Santos. (2016). Training the Body: The Potential of AIED to Support Personalized Motor Skills Learning. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:730–755. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0103-2

article_title: Can Multi-Label Classifiers Help Identify Subjectivity? A Deep Learning Approach to Classifying Cognitive Presence in MOOCs
citation: Yuanyuan Hu. (2023). Can Multi-Label Classifiers Help Identify Subjectivity? A Deep Learning Approach to Classifying Cognitive Presence in MOOCs. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00310-6
title: Multi-label, fine-tuned BERT classifier architecture of five binary BERT classifiers with sigmoid outputs
description: The article builds a multi-label classifier by revising "the standard BERT model from a class-independent model to five binary BERT classifiers for each category", one per cognitive presence category. Messages are pre-processed (emojis and URLs replaced, abbreviations expanded, stop words removed), tokenised with BertTokenizer, and passed through a bert-base-uncased model with 12 transformer layers and 768 dimensions, followed by a linear classification layer and a sigmoid function outputting five probability scores between 0 and 1. Because the sigmoid layer "can allow more than one phase to reach a score of over 0.5", multiple labels may attach to one message; predictions above a 0.33 threshold, chosen because a human coder's weight over three coders' decisions was equivalent to around 0.33, become labels. Training used tenfold cross-validation with data augmentation and over-sampling performed after the dataset splits, Binary Cross-Entropy loss, batch size 8, 10 epochs, and a learning rate of 2 × 10−5.
requirements: Requires pre-trained BERT weights (bert-base-uncased) fine-tuned on manually labelled discussion messages where expert coders agreed without confusion
Requires data augmentation and over-sampling of minority categories applied after the training-test split to avoid over-optimistic results
constraints: Trained and tested on discussion messages from one introductory Philosophy MOOC on the FutureLearn platform
The data augmentation method might deepen the confusion between Exploration and Integration, where most coder disagreements occurred
target_learners: MOOC learners in an introductory Philosophy course on FutureLearn
target_learning_goals: Automatic identification of phases of cognitive presence (critical discourse and knowledge construction) in learners' online discussion messages
examples: Applied to 1,917 discussion messages sampled from 16 tasks of the Logical and Critical Thinking MOOC, with the AgreementSet used for training and the DisagreementSet for validation
key_sources: Yuanyuan Hu. (2023). Can Multi-Label Classifiers Help Identify Subjectivity? A Deep Learning Approach to Classifying Cognitive Presence in MOOCs. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00310-5

article_title: Keep Me in the Loop: Real-Time Feedback with Multimodal Data
citation: Di Mitri, D., Schneider, J., & Drachsler, H. (2022). KeepMeInTheLoop: Real-Time Feedback with Multimodal Data. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education (2022) 32:1093–1118. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00281-z
title: Multimodal Pipeline: a five-step framework for collection, storing, annotation, processing and exploitation of multimodal data
description: The Multimodal Pipeline is a framework proposed by Di Mitri et al. for handling data from multiple modalities in learning systems. The CPR Tutor architecture implements its five steps — collection, storing, annotation, processing and exploitation — organised into a Presentation Layer interfacing with the user, an Application Layer implementing the tutor logic, and a Data Layer. The article presents it as the basis for closing the feedback loop with real-time multimodal feedback.
requirements: sensor applications assigning Recording Objects with timestamps for synchronised data collection
annotation tooling (Visual Inspection Tool) to label time intervals
constraints: The article states this was the first complete implementation of the pipeline, in the CPR Tutor context
target_learning_goals: real-time feedback for psychomotor skill acquisition
examples: The CPR Tutor realised the five steps with Kinect and Myo recording, MLT-JSON session storage, VIT annotation, SharpFlow processing, and real-time audio feedback

article_title: A Multi-Temporal Context-aware System for Competences Management
citation: João H. Rosa, Jorge L. V. Barbosa, Marcos Kich, Lucas Brito. (2015). A Multi-Temporal Context-aware System for Competences Management. Int J Artif Intell Educ 25:455–492. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0047-y
title: Multi-temporal context awareness: joint use of workers' present and past contexts to assist competence development
description: The article names and defines multi-temporal context awareness as an organizing concept for competence-management systems. It observes that context-aware applications 'usually use data only from the users' current situations (i.e. the present) and do not consider the previous contexts observed during a period (i.e. the past)'. The framework holds that combining the present dimension (current location, events, people, resources) with the past dimension (contexts histories or trails) gives applications 'an additional and more complete information source' for decisions, enabling automatic detection of competence advances and personalized services.
requirements: Storage of observed contexts over time (contexts history/trail mechanism) in addition to sensing the current context
constraints: The past dimension is defined as contexts as per Dey et al.'s definition, which includes location data; the article states Trail Management is considered only as this use of the past dimension
target_learners: knowledge workers in organizations developing professional competences
target_learning_goals: development and advancement of professional competences
examples: MultCComp operationalizes the framework: the present dimension suggests nearby events, resources and experienced people; the past dimension records development activities in trails and detects competence improvements automatically
key_sources: João H. Rosa, Jorge L. V. Barbosa, Marcos Kich, Lucas Brito. (2015). A Multi-Temporal Context-aware System for Competences Management. Int J Artif Intell Educ 25:455–492. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0047-y

article_title: A Multi-Temporal Context-aware System for Competences Management
citation: João H. Rosa, Jorge L. V. Barbosa, Marcos Kich, Lucas Brito. (2015). A Multi-Temporal Context-aware System for Competences Management. Int J Artif Intell Educ 25:455–492. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0047-y
title: MultCComp: a multi-temporal context-aware system for competences management
description: MultCComp is a context-aware system that applies proficiency levels to competences and uses present and past context information to help workers develop competences. Its present-dimension architecture has 'seven components': three modules (Profile, Competence, Context), three agents (Personal Assistant, Relationship Agent, Competences Agent) and an Administrative Website. The Competences Agent makes recommendations about people, events and resources triggered by context changes, and the past dimension uses the UbiTrail model to record development activities and automatically detect users' advances in their competences.
requirements: Users authorize their location; workers inform the system about activities they performed to develop their competences; a mapped set of location contexts and an organization-wide competence map
constraints: Design decisions were based on consulting in an ERP vendor in Southern Brazil; the system tolerates loss of wireless connectivity only through a local buffer with limited functionalities
target_learners: workers in organizations undertaking competence management
target_learning_goals: identifying and closing competence gaps; advancing proficiency levels
examples: The prototype was evaluated in two experiments in an evaluation environment: a functionality demonstration with two evaluation scenarios followed by two users, and an acceptance scenario followed by 21 users
key_sources: João H. Rosa, Jorge L. V. Barbosa, Marcos Kich, Lucas Brito. (2015). A Multi-Temporal Context-aware System for Competences Management. Int J Artif Intell Educ 25:455–492. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0047-y

article_title: Crosslingual Content Scoring in Five Languages Using Machine-Translation and Multilingual Transformer Models
citation: Andrea Horbach, Joey Pehlke, Ronja Laarmann-Quante, Yuning Ding. (2024). Crosslingual Content Scoring in Five Languages Using Machine-Translation and Multilingual Transformer Models. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00370-1
title: Multilingual ASAP content scoring datasets in five languages with three newly collected variants, publicly released
description: The article presents language variants of the ASAP short-answer content scoring dataset covering Chinese, English, French, German and Spanish for three science-related prompts. Three variants were newly collected via crowdsourcing (ASAPen, ASAPes, ASAPfr, about 300 usable answers per prompt), alongside ASAPde and a Chinese dataset from high school students. Each was double-annotated by native speakers using the original scoring guidelines, with inter-annotator agreement in QWK reported per prompt (e.g. .83-.69 for ASAPen). The article states the data "is publicly available under https://github.com/andreahorbach/CrosslingualScoring/".
requirements: Answers double-annotated by native speakers trained on the original English ASAP scoring guidelines
constraints: Crowdsourced datasets show higher amounts of low-scoring answers and lower inter-annotator agreement than the original ASAP data
target_learners: high school students (Chinese and original ASAP data)
target_learning_goals: automated scoring of conceptual correctness of short written answers to science prompts
examples: The French data was collected via platforms including Facebook and Amazon Mechanical Turk, yielding 1,070 answers of which 672 were usable
key_sources: Andrea Horbach, Joey Pehlke, Ronja Laarmann-Quante, Yuning Ding. (2024). Crosslingual Content Scoring in Five Languages Using Machine-Translation and Multilingual Transformer Models. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00370-1

article_title: Preface-Emerging Technologies and Landmark Systems for Learning Mathematics and Science: Dedicated to the Memory of Erica Melis-Part 2
citation: Sergey Sosnovsky & Bruce M. McLaren & Vincent Aleven. (2014). Preface-Emerging Technologies and Landmark Systems for Learning Mathematics and Science: Dedicated to the Memory of Erica Melis-Part 2. Int J Artif Intell Educ 24. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0025-9
title: Build ITS for math and science to be cognitively, metacognitively and motivationally aware
description: The preface argues that math and science classes require teachers to promote general problem-solving skills, self-regulation strategies, and coping with negative affective traits like boredom, frustration and anxiety. Therefore, "to be maximally effective in these domains, Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS) and other AIED technologies need to address a wide range of student characteristics and adapt to various categories of students by being cognitively, metacognitively, and motivationally aware." The three landmark systems showcased in the issue exemplify this versatile adaptivity, with Wayang Outpost explicitly tracking cognitive, metacognitive and affective learner states.
requirements: Tracking of multiple learner dimensions (cognitive, metacognitive, affective) to drive adaptation
target_learners: students in mathematics and science classes
target_learning_goals: problem solving skills
self-regulation strategies
coping with negative affect such as boredom, frustration and anxiety
examples: Wayang Outpost keeps track of cognitive, metacognitive and affective dimensions of individual learners and uses them to make adaptive pedagogical decisions.

article_title: SMILI☺: a Framework for Interfaces to Learning Data in Open Learner Models, Learning Analytics and Related Fields
citation: Susan Bull & Judy Kay. (2016). SMILI☺: a Framework for Interfaces to Learning Data in Open Learner Models, Learning Analytics and Related Fields. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0090-8
title: Offering a choice of learner model visualisations to suit purpose, competency-set size and user preference
description: The Next-TELL OLM offers five visualisations of the same underlying learner model — skill meters, table, treemap, competency network and word clouds — that can be selected according to the user's preferred way of accessing the data. The treemap is "particularly useful for displaying large, hierarchically structured learner models", while the network visualisation gives a clearer overview in a smaller space but "can sometimes be hard to read". The word cloud provides "a clear and quick overview of the extremes (strengths and weaknesses)", useful for teachers' on-the-spot classroom decision-making.
requirements: The system must support multiple visualisations of the same underlying learner model so that users can select the one best suited to their purpose and preference.
constraints: The table and skill meters require scrolling if the competencies do not all fit onto the screen, so are less usable in large learner models; the treemap makes it harder to compare competencies from different parts of the tree.
target_learning_goals: understanding one's own competency profile
classroom orchestration and on-the-spot decision-making
examples: In the Next-TELL OLM, some participants at the AIED 2013 conference performed self and peer assessments of areas of expertise to familiarise themselves with the OLM.
key_sources: Susan Bull & Judy Kay. (2016). SMILI☺: a Framework for Interfaces to Learning Data in Open Learner Models, Learning Analytics and Related Fields. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0090-8

article_title: An Interview Reflection on “Intelligent Tutoring Goes to School in the Big City”
citation: Kenneth R. Koedinger & Vincent Aleven. (2016). An Interview Reflection on “Intelligent Tutoring Goes to School in the Big City”. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 26, 13–24. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0082-8
title: Use multiple kinds of assessment — both standardized tests and curriculum-aligned open-ended items — when evaluating learning interventions
description: Following Ann Brown's suggestion, the 1997 study measured outcomes with both standardized test items and items designed to reflect curriculum goals of practical, general algebra understanding. The authors argue the debate over standardized versus open-ended assessment is best answered by “to include both kinds of assessments,” because a single standardized measure may lack validity and “is likely to miss (or underestimate) all of the learning that may be resulting from an intervention.” They express frustration that this practice, and multiple-assessment designs in randomized field trials generally, has not caught on.
requirements: Assessments must include both standardized items and items designed to reflect the intervention's curriculum goals
constraints: The idea has not caught on in practice; the What Works Clearinghouse stuck to single standardized tests as its only outcome measure
target_learners: K-12 and higher-education students in evaluated learning interventions
target_learning_goals: valid measurement of intervention learning outcomes, including complex problem solving and use of representations
examples: The 1997 study used standardized test items plus items measuring complex problem solving and use of representations

article_title: LECTOR: Summarizing E-book Reading Content for Personalized Student Support
citation: Erwin Daniel López Zapata, Cheng Tang, Valdemar Švábenský, Fumiya Okubo, Atsushi Shimada. (2025). LECTOR: Summarizing E-book Reading Content for Personalized Student Support. Int J Artif Intell Educ 35. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00478-6
title: Multimodal integration of reading activity and content data via matrix M
description: The article formalizes the integration of reading activity data and reading content data as a matrix multiplication between traditional reading logs and a matrix M encoding topic distributions across pages of the reading material. The article interprets "this multimodal integration ... as a matrix multiplication between traditional reading logs and a matrix M that encodes topic distributions across pages of the reading material". This reframes non-contextualized reading logs as an optimization problem of accurately estimating topic distributions across educational materials, enabling topic-based reading characteristics such as student topic preference vectors derived from l1-normalized reading time.
requirements: An accurate estimate of the matrix M of Slide-Topic relationships, since the integration's value depends on the quality of that estimate
constraints: The article states this multimodal integration had not been formally defined prior to this work; prior exploratory studies used simplified models (binary scores, co-occurrence graphs) without validating technical NLP performance
target_learners: university students using e-book reading systems
target_learning_goals: interpreting student reading behavior at the topic level to inform at-risk prediction and personalized interventions
examples: LECTOR's output M was multiplied with slide-wise reading logs to derive vectors of topic preferences used in Experiment 2
key_sources: Erwin Daniel López Zapata, Cheng Tang, Valdemar Švábenský, Fumiya Okubo, Atsushi Shimada. (2025). LECTOR: Summarizing E-book Reading Content for Personalized Student Support. Int J Artif Intell Educ 35. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00478-6

article_title: Patterns of Adults with Low Literacy Skills Interacting with an Intelligent Tutoring System
citation: Fang, Y., Lippert, A., Cai, Z., Chen, S., Frijters, J. C., Greenberg, D., & Graesser, A. C. (2021). Patterns of Adults with Low Literacy Skills Interacting with an Intelligent Tutoring System. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00266-y
title: Graesser and McNamara's multilevel theoretical framework of reading comprehension
description: The article organizes AutoTutor lessons around a multilevel framework identifying "Six levels of comprehension": word, syntax, the explicit textbase, the referential situation model, the genre/rhetorical structure, and the pragmatic communication level. Word and syntax represent basic reading components; textbase, situation model, and rhetorical structure cover higher-level semantic and discourse components. The pragmatic communication level was not directly implemented in AutoTutor because it is highly constrained by contexts difficult to stage reliably in a computer environment.
requirements: Lessons and questions must be categorizable by theoretical level (via a Q-matrix with primary, secondary, tertiary, or no relevance codes)
constraints: The pragmatic communication level was not directly implemented because it is highly constrained by contexts difficult to stage reliably in the computer environment
target_learners: adults with low literacy skills reading between 3rd and 8th grade levels
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension across word, textbase, situation model, and rhetorical structure levels
examples: AutoTutor's 29 lessons were coded by primary theoretical level (word, textbase, situation model, or rhetorical structure) using an expert-assigned Q-matrix
key_sources: Fang, Y., Lippert, A., Cai, Z., Chen, S., Frijters, J. C., Greenberg, D., & Graesser, A. C. (2021). article_title: The SIETTE Automatic Assessment Environment
citation: Conejo, R., Guzmán, E., & Trella, M. (2016). The SIETTE Automatic Assessment Environment. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26, 270–292. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0078-4
title: Multi-unidimensional approach to bridging psychometric and ITS learner models
description: Siette addresses the mismatch between the fine-grained multidimensional learner models of ITSs and the single-latent-trait focus of CTT and IRT through a multi-unidimensional approach. Rather than using true multidimensional IRT models, the system "developed a mechanism that assumes that multiple independent traits are assessed simultaneously." This allows a CAT component to produce separate knowledge estimates for each domain topic in a hierarchical learner model, supporting adaptive question selection across multiple nodes. The domain model uses part-of relationships with topics and subtopics, and items can be attached to one or more sibling nodes.
requirements: A hierarchical domain model that can be overlaid with an ITS domain model
Item pools calibrated per trait under the assumption of independent traits
constraints: Currently does not support true multidimensional items
Classic multidimensional IRT models are complex and more than two or three dimensions are rarely used
target_learning_goals: fine-grained diagnosis of knowledge per domain topic
adaptive question selection
examples: Adaptive question-selection algorithm selects the next question according to which domain nodes require higher precision

article_title: A Framework System for Intelligent Support in Open Distributed Learning Environments—a Look Back from 16 Years Later
citation: H. Ulrich Hoppe. (2015). A Framework System for Intelligent Support in Open Distributed Learning Environments—a Look Back from 16 Years Later. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26, 504–511. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0058-8
title: Multiple student modelling to configure and inform group learning situations
description: Multiple student modelling is an approach to configuring and informing group learning situations based on individually assessed learner models. As characterized by Greer et al. in this commentary, Hoppe's COSOFT was "the first ambitious project to address several issues related to the use of student modelling in order to parameterize human-human collaboration," including group composition, peer-helper selection, problem identification and task selection. The 1998 paper took this up and Mühlenbrock et al. pursued it further.
requirements: Individually assessed learner models for the students in the known set
constraints: Precise learner modelling on an individual level is not possible when the system is not in full control of task specification and credit assignment
target_learners: students in collaborative group learning settings
target_learning_goals: forming learning groups and selecting tasks and peer helpers suited to group learning
examples: The idea was taken up in the Intelligent IntraNet Peer Help-Desk (later I-Help) at the University of Saskatchewan
key_sources: H. Ulrich Hoppe. (2015). A Framework System for Intelligent Support in Open Distributed Learning Environments—a Look Back from 16 Years Later. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26, 504–511. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0058-8

article_title: Role of Working Memory and Strategy-Use in Feedback Effects on children’s Progression in Analogy Solving:an Explanatory Item Response Theory Account
citation: Stevenson, C. E. (2017). Role of Working Memory and Strategy-Use in Feedback Effects on children's Progression in Analogy Solving: an Explanatory Item Response Theory Account. Int J Artif Intell Educ 27:393–418. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0129-5
title: Multilevel explanatory IRT based on Embretson's Multidimensional Rasch Model for Learning and Change
description: The article applies an item response theory approach based on Embretson's Multidimensional Rasch Model for Learning and Change, extended with multilevel and explanatory components, to model children's pretest-to-posttest change in analogy solving. Ability is built up in a summation term over testing occasions, with an initial ability factor and modifiabilities representing change. Person covariates such as age and working memory are entered with regression parameters on the latent scale, and nested models are compared with likelihood ratio tests. The authors state this "allowed for reliable estimates of learning from feedback" where classical gain scores are unreliable.
requirements: Repeated testing occasions (pretest and posttest) with items that can be linked or equated across age-group test versions using IRT procedures
constraints: The article notes results are likely similar to those using classical test theory sum scores with standard linear regression; the advantages are reliable change scores, equating across datasets, and accounting for random school and experiment differences
target_learners: primary school children (kindergarten through fourth grade)
target_learning_goals: figural analogical reasoning
examples: Models M0–M3 were estimated successively with lme4 in R, adding item difficulty, age, session, condition, working memory, and strategy-use effects, each tested with likelihood ratio tests
key_sources: Stevenson, C. E. (2017). Role of Working Memory and Strategy-Use in Feedback Effects on children's Progression in Analogy Solving: an Explanatory Item Response Theory Account. Int J Artif Intell Educ 27:393–418. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0129-5

article_title: A multimodal representation framework for collaborative knowledge-building in an immersive astronomy simulation: using transmodal ordered network analysis
citation: Zhou, Y., Kang, J., Wang, Y., & Ashiq, M. (2025). A multimodal representation framework for collaborative knowledge-building in an immersive astronomy simulation: using transmodal ordered network analysis. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10510-0
title: A multimodal framework for knowledge representation across virtual, conceptual, and physical spaces in AR-enhanced CSCL.
description: The article proposes a multimodal framework that examines knowledge representations across three interconnected spaces in immersive environments: virtual, conceptual, and physical spaces. Virtual Space refers to the digital environment (the simulation platform), Conceptual Space includes abstract thought and internal knowledge representation, and Physical Space refers to the tangible environment where gestures and hands-on activities help learners ground abstract concepts. The framework synthesizes collaborative knowledge-building, distributed cognition, and multiple representations in science education. It provides a structured way to analyze multimodal knowledge construction in immersive environments and is "adaptable to various technology-rich CSCL contexts."
requirements: Requires an environment with multiple forms of representation across digital, verbal, and embodied modes.
constraints: The application of the framework may be limited in environments that rely predominantly on verbal or non-digital interactions.
target_learners: College students in introductory science courses
target_learning_goals: Collaborative knowledge construction of complex scientific concepts
key_sources: Zhou, Y., Kang, J., Wang, Y., & Ashiq, M. (2025). A multimodal representation framework for collaborative knowledge-building in an immersive astronomy simulation: using transmodal ordered network analysis. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10510-0

article_title: A meta-analysis of technology-delivered literacy instruction for elementary students
citation: Dahl-Leonard, K., Hall, C., & Peacott, D. (2024). A meta-analysis of technology-delivered literacy instruction for elementary students. Education Tech Research Dev (2024) 72:1507–1538. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10354-0
title: Multicomponent technology-delivered literacy instruction
description: The dominant design pattern in this corpus of technology-delivered elementary literacy programs is multicomponent instruction: almost all programs (90%) addressed multiple literacy skills, averaging four of the seven coded domains (phonological awareness, phonics/decoding/word reading, encoding/spelling, text reading/fluency, vocabulary, comprehension, writing). The article states this finding "is in alignment with recommendations from prior systematic reviews of reading research, such as the NRP (2000) report and the WWC practice guide on effective early reading instruction." Typical dosage averaged 36 minutes a day, 4 days per week, for 18 weeks (about 37 total hours).
requirements: Instruction delivered primarily on a technological device in English
Coverage of multiple literacy domains within one program
constraints: The pattern describes the corpus; the moderator analysis found no statistically significant effect difference associated with any single literacy domain
target_learners: Elementary students in Grades K-5, primarily K-2
target_learning_goals: Reading and writing-related literacy skills including phonics, fluency, phonological awareness, and comprehension
examples: Programs such as ABRACADABRA, Lexia, and Fast ForWord addressed an average of four literacy domains per treatment condition
key_sources: Dahl-Leonard, K., Hall, C., & Peacott, D. (2024). A meta-analysis of technology-delivered literacy instruction for elementary students. Education Tech Research Dev (2024) 72:1507–1538. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10354-0

article_title: Exploring groups’ affective states during collaborative learning: what triggers activating affect on a group level?
citation: Törmänen, T., Järvenoja, H., & Mänty, K. (2021). Exploring groups’ affective states during collaborative learning: what triggers activating affect on a group level? Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-10037-0
title: Group-level affective states can be captured by combining video observation of emotional expressions with EDA measures of physiological activation
description: The article presents a multimodal approach in which group affective valence is coded from video-observed emotional expressions and physiological activation is measured with electrodermal activity, segmented into commensurable 30-s units. The authors argue that "by combining different process data modalities revealing the different components of affect, it might be possible to track emotionally meaningful situations that shape the course of the collaborative learning process." The approach treats valence and activation as complementary dimensions of group-level affect.
requirements: Synchronized video and EDA data segmented into common time units (30-s segments in this study)
Manual video coding of group valence with interrater reliability checking
constraints: Generalizable conclusions cannot be made from the results due to the small sample size
Poor quality EDA data from some students limited the sample; one individual's data loss excluded the whole group
target_learning_goals: understanding affective processes in collaborative learning
key_sources: Törmänen, T., Järvenoja, H., & Mänty, K. (2021). Exploring groups’ affective states during collaborative learning: what triggers activating affect on a group level? Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-10037-0

article_title: Designing for robot-mediated interaction among culturally and linguistically diverse children
citation: Yanghee Kim, Sherry Marx, Hung Viet Pham, Tung Nguyen. (2021). Designing for robot-mediated interaction among culturally and linguistically diverse children. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-10051-2
title: Multidisciplinary conceptual framework of child development, intercultural communication, and culturally sustaining pedagogy for robot-mediated interaction
description: The article synthesizes child development, intercultural communication theory, and culturally sustaining pedagogy into a framework for designing robot-mediated collaborative interaction. CSP is described as an approach that "respects, maintains, and builds on children's diverse languages, cultures, and identities," and intercultural communication theory highlights newcomers' gradual adaptation through prolonged exposure in nonjudgmental, supportive climates. The framework guided both the design of loosely structured fantasy play, personalized invitations, familiar contexts, and bilingual communication, and the interpretation of the qualitative data.
requirements: Small-group settings of two children with one robot, which the authors describe as the most effective way of using technology with children
constraints: Natural dialogue was not possible because natural language processing and automatic speech recognition for children is still developing
target_learners: culturally and linguistically diverse kindergarten children
target_learning_goals: positive collaborative peer interaction
cultural and social integration
key_sources: Yanghee Kim, Sherry Marx, Hung Viet Pham, Tung Nguyen. (2021). Designing for robot-mediated interaction among culturally and linguistically diverse children. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-10051-2

article_title: Can videos affect learning outcomes? Evidence from an actual learning environment
citation: Tani, M., Manuguerra, M., & Khan, S. (2022). Can videos affect learning outcomes? Evidence from an actual learning environment. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10147-3
title: Design multimedia presentations following established multimedia learning principles
description: The article's innovation followed seven principles for multimedia learning, including that "Students learn better from words and pictures than from words alone" (multimedia principle), spatial and temporal contiguity, coherence, modality, redundancy, and individual differences principles. The presentation used images and words rather than full sentences, linked images and words simultaneously, and used narration with storytelling linking abstract concepts to historical contexts.
requirements: Presentations should avoid extraneous sounds beyond narration and should not introduce new information beyond face-to-face lectures.
constraints: Design effects are stronger for low-knowledge learners than for high-knowledge learners (individual differences principle).
target_learning_goals: Procedural and evaluative knowledge in economics
examples: Two 30-minute presentations on GDP and CPI used images, unfolding symbols, and worked examples narrated by a native English speaker.
key_sources: Tani, M., Manuguerra, M., & Khan, S. (2022). Can videos affect learning outcomes? Evidence from an actual learning environment. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10147-3

article_title: Role-playing monument exploration: an online educational game with a role-playing mechanism and multi-dimensional scaffolding for monument tours
citation: Shu-Wei Liu, Hung-Yu Chan, & Huei-Tse Hou. (2025). Role-playing monument exploration: an online educational game with a role-playing mechanism and multi-dimensional scaffolding for monument tours. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10480-3
title: Multi-dimensional scaffolding framework for game-based monument education
description: The article proposes a framework in which game-based monument education provides learners with simultaneous support from five scaffold types: cognitive, procedural, emotional, and strategic scaffolds embedded in the game, plus peer scaffolding among learners. The authors write that learners "can obtain complete and immediate learning support through the cognitive, procedural, emotional, and strategic scaffolds within the game, as well as peer scaffolds among learners", with the aims of enhancing interactivity, maintaining flow, and generating motivation. Guides role-playing historical characters act as dynamic scaffolds that observe learners and give immediate, situation-dependent assistance, while static scaffolds (buildings, observation spots, whiteboard tips) provide fixed knowledge and task structure.
requirements: Guides available to observe learner performance and provide immediate dynamic scaffolding
Game-embedded static scaffolds (buildings, observation spots, game space, whiteboard tips)
Group collaboration among learners for peer scaffolding
constraints: The authors note the challenge of whether instructors can provide the same level of scaffolding at different times and the guiding-manpower cost issue
target_learners: adult learners in online monument guide activities
target_learning_goals: monument history knowledge
strategic planning and problem solving
sustained flow and motivation
examples: Table 1 details each scaffold type: cognitive scaffolding via buildings, observation spots and game space; procedural scaffolding via whiteboard tips; emotional scaffolding via guides' in-character tone and costume; strategic scaffolding via the whiteboard and commander feedback
key_sources: Shu-Wei Liu, Hung-Yu Chan, & Huei-Tse Hou. (2025). Role-playing monument exploration: an online educational game with a role-playing mechanism and multi-dimensional scaffolding for monument tours. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10480-3

article_title: Exploring the structure of digital literacy competence assessed using authentic software applications
citation: Frank Reichert, Nancy W. Y. Law, Gary K. W. Wong, Jimmy de la Torre. (2020). Exploring the structure of digital literacy competence assessed with authentic software applications. Education Tech Research Dev, 68, 2991–3013. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09825-x
title: Use multiple digital tools in learning and assessment, and avoid relying on a single tool when assessing DL, because tool-specific performance may not correlate highly
description: The article recommends that educators treat DL as comprehensive across tools while using several applications for learning and assessment, since the study found tool-specific performance dimensions. It states that "reliance on only one specific tool is particularly likely to provide biased results of students' DL and should be avoided unless the assessment of a tool-specific competence is the explicit goal". Teachers and assessment developers should consider tool dependencies when analyzing and interpreting results.
requirements: Assessment or learning designs must incorporate multiple software applications rather than a single tool
constraints: Reliance on one tool is acceptable when assessing a tool-specific competence is the explicit goal
target_learning_goals: digital literacy competence
examples: The ILPA technical DL module required students to search the Internet, edit a Word document, create a PowerPoint presentation, and discuss in an online forum, spanning multiple applications
key_sources: Frank Reichert, Nancy W. Y. Law, Gary K. W. Wong, Jimmy de la Torre. (2020). Exploring the structure of digital literacy competence assessed with authentic software applications. Education Tech Research Dev, 68, 2991–3013. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09825-x

article_title: Shifting to digital: informing the rapid development, deployment, and future of teaching and learning
citation: Lin Lin, Tristan Johnson. (2021). Shifting to digital: informing the rapid development, deployment, and future of teaching and learning. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09960-z
title: Seek multiple, diverse perspectives when informing rapid shifts to digital teaching and learning
description: The editors made it 'a top priority to seek multiple response essays to each of the 17 selected publications, with each essay focusing on a primary perspective'. They deliberately sought authors with varying professional experiences and diverse nationalities, writing from perspectives including Adoption & Diffusion, Critical Pedagogy, Culture & Equity, Design, Ethics, Evaluation, Inclusion, Pedagogy, Policy, Practice, Research, Theory, and International Perspective, spanning K12, non-profit, profit, and higher education settings.
requirements: Multiple response essays per anchor publication, each focused on a primary perspective
Authors from different sectors, backgrounds, cultures, and nationalities
constraints: Only one first-authored or single-authored paper from each scholar was included in the special issue
target_learners: K12, non-profit, profit, and higher education settings
target_learning_goals: providing contextual differences while informing practices for shifting to digital
examples: Guest editors each oversaw one or two of the 17 selected papers and provided summaries of the accepted essays responding to the publications they oversaw
key_sources: Lin Lin, Tristan Johnson. (2021). Shifting to digital: informing the rapid development, deployment, and future of teaching and learning. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09960-z

article_title: Forum posts, communication patterns, and relational structures: A multi-level view of discussions in online courses
citation: Poquet, O., Trenholm, S., & Santolini, M. (2024). Forum posts, communication patterns, and relational structures: A multi-level view of discussions in online courses. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10262-9
title: Multi-level framework separating posting activity, communication structures, and emergent relational structures in online discussions
description: The framework holds that analysis of digital learner interactions should differentiate three overlapping processes: posting activity at the individual level, communication structures as learner-to-learner projections, and emergent relational structures as filtered backbones of communication networks. The article proposes that "posting activity gives rise to communication patterns and emergent relational structures," operationalizing the levels as interdependent so that statistical modeling of lower levels affords inference about higher ones. It supplies level-specific units of analysis, comparison methods, and example research questions (Table 1), demonstrated on twenty courses.
requirements: The analyst must specify a generative (conceptual) model of the fundamental principles for how participation and communication emerge
constraints: The example includes no self-report or learning-gain data to triangulate inferences about outcome nature and quality
The framework presents the three processes as static, not dynamically interacting over a course
The example null model is limited; further work is needed to integrate temporal aspects and discourse properties
target_learners: university students in online and blended courses
target_learning_goals: participation in discussion forums
communication and relationship formation among learners
examples: Applied to twenty Moodle courses using PCA grouping, null-model simulation of posting networks, edge-weight filtering, and ERGM analysis
key_sources: Poquet, O., Trenholm, S., & Santolini, M. (2024). Forum posts, communication patterns, and relational structures: A multi-level view of discussions in online courses. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10262-9

article_title: Touch Arithmetic: A process-based Computer-Aided Assessment approach for capture of problem solving steps in the context of elementary mathematics
citation: Adesina, A., Stone, R., Batmaz, F., & Jones, I. (2014). Touch Arithmetic: A process‐based Computer‐Aided Assessment approach for capture of problem solving steps in the context of elementary mathematics.
title: MuTAT: a multi-touch arithmetic assessment tool capturing solution steps via trace links
description: MuTAT (Multi-Touch Arithmetic Tool) is a tablet-based prototype for process-based computer-aided assessment in elementary mathematics. Its interface has a problem pane with draggable numeric values and a solution pane; a touch-and-hold gesture activates arithmetic operators, and interactions are recorded with timestamps and coordinates so that "visual representations of the process data is constructed" from traces of problem-solving actions.
requirements: An interactive interface that provides problem-solvers opportunities to explicitly enter their solutions, with integrated problem text and solution workspace so trace links can be created between solution items and their origins
constraints: The tool presents stepwise information horizontally, which may disadvantage students who prefer vertical sums especially with carry-over digits
The 9.7-inch tablet screen may affect problems that require three or more stages
target_learning_goals: multi-digit addition in arithmetic word problems
arithmetic strategy use and number bonds understanding
examples: In the observational study, 39 children answered 390 questions on MuTAT and 156 on paper, producing a log file of 8,221 records
key_sources: Adesina, A., Stone, R., Batmaz, F., & Jones, I. (2014). Touch Arithmetic: A process‐based Computer‐Aided Assessment approach for capture of problem solving steps in the context of elementary mathematics. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2014.06.015

article_title: A framework to analyze argumentative knowledge construction in computer-supported collaborative learning
citation: Armin Weinberger, Frank Fischer. (2006). A Framework to Analyze Argumentative Knowledge Construction in Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. Computers and Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2005.04.003
title: Multi-dimensional analysis approach for CSCL discourse corpora
description: The article proposes a multi-dimensional approach to analyzing argumentative knowledge construction in CSCL. It proceeds in stages, covering "sampling and segmentation of the discourse corpora" before applying the analysis of the four process dimensions (participation, epistemic, argumentative, social mode). The approach serves researchers who need to evaluate the effects of instructional supports such as collaboration scripts on discourse processes.
requirements: Discourse corpora must be sampled and segmented before the process-dimension analyses can be applied.
target_learners: researchers and designers evaluating CSCL environments
target_learning_goals: assessment of argumentative knowledge construction processes
key_sources: Armin Weinberger, Frank Fischer. (2006). A Framework to Analyze Argumentative Knowledge Construction in Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. Computers and Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2005.04.003

article_title: The effectiveness of brain-compatible blended learning material in the teaching of programming logic
citation: van Niekerk, J.F. (2015). The effectiveness of brain-compatible blended learning material in the teaching of programming logic. Nelson Mandela Metropolitan University.
title: Use rich, multi-sensory and multifaceted learning experiences that engage emotion and multiple memory pathways
description: The dissertation argues that learning involves both focused attention and peripheral perception, and that "Experiences that provide rich sensory input well beyond the capacity of a book or a worksheet have the greatest chance of sparking dendritic growth and increased synaptic connections" (McGeehan, 2001). Emotions are crucial because they focus attention and drive learning and memory; Materna is cited recommending engaging multiple memory pathways through multi-sensory formats combining discussion, visuals and hands-on activities.
requirements: Designers should engage both visual and verbal faculties and consider the entire context in which teaching occurs
constraints: Motivation for the e-learning material depends on students finding it meaningful and engaging
target_learners: higher education students with varied learning styles and preferences
target_learning_goals: long-term retention and meaningful engagement with subject content
examples: Theme 5 of the qualitative instrument asked whether the e-learning material was "rich" enough (multimedia), with responses reported in Table 4.8
key_sources: van Niekerk, J.F. (2015). The effectiveness of brain-compatible blended learning material in the teaching of programming logic. Nelson Mandela Metropolitan University. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2016.09.008

article_title: Virtual vs. traditional learning in higher education: A systematic review of comparative studies
citation: Santilli T.; Ceccacci S.; Mengoni M.; Giaconi C. (2025). Virtual vs. traditional learning in higher education: A systematic review of comparative studies. COMPUTERS & EDUCATION. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105214
title: Multidimensional framework for analysing comparative VR-vs-traditional studies in higher education
description: The review proposes an organizing framework for systematically analysing studies that compare VR-based and traditional teaching in higher education. It states: "The analysis focuses on a set of dimensions including the adopted research design, participants' characteristics, disciplinary field of application, VR technological features (i.e., immersivity, interactivity, operability, commercial availability, and presence of VR training), adopted teaching methodologies, assessed VR impact on learning outcomes and presence of studies involving students with disabilities or Specific Learning Disorders (SpLDs)." The framework structures the review's coding of 71 studies and offers a multidimensional perspective for educators, researchers and policymakers.
requirements: Systematic identification of comparative VR-vs-traditional studies in higher education contexts to which the dimension set can be applied
constraints: The framework is stated for comparative studies in higher education contexts, not for other levels of education or non-comparative VR studies
target_learning_goals: Evaluating the effectiveness of VR-based teaching on learning outcomes
examples: The framework was applied to code a corpus of 71 VR-in-higher-education studies across research design, participants, discipline, technology features, methodology and outcomes
key_sources: Santilli T.; Ceccacci S.; Mengoni M.; Giaconi C. (2025). Virtual vs. traditional learning in higher education: A systematic review of comparative studies. COMPUTERS & EDUCATION. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105214

article_title: An interactive multimedia learning environment for VLSI built with COSMOS
citation: Angelides, M. C. & Agius, H. W. (2001). An interactive multimedia learning environment for VLSI built with COSMOS. https://www.brunel.ac.uk/~cssthwa/
title: Use multimedia to demonstrate products and processes in action
description: The article argues that multimedia offers significant benefits for VLSI education because it enables products and processes to be demonstrated 'in action', affording better understanding than text alone. Photographic images can demonstrate applications and video segments can demonstrate fabrication processes, providing a pragmatic alternative for real-life observation.
requirements: media that exemplifies the domain knowledge being taught
constraints: text alone often adds little value over textbooks
target_learning_goals: understanding of products and processes
key_sources: Angelides, M. C. & Agius, H. W. (2001). An interactive multimedia learning environment for VLSI built with COSMOS. https://www.brunel.ac.uk/~cssthwa/

article_title: Look at me and pay attention! A study on the relation between visibility and attention in weblectures
citation: Korving, H., Hernández, M. & De Groot, E. (2016). Look at me and pay attention! A study on the relation between visibility and attention in weblectures. Computers and Education, vol. 94, pp. 151-161. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2015.11.011
title: Multiple resource model of attention as an explanation for visibility effects in weblectures
description: The article draws on the theory of cross-modalities for multiple attentional resources to explain why a visible lecturer might aid attention. The human information-processing system is thought to have two main input-channels, an auditory/verbal channel and a visual/pictorial channel. Dividing input over these two modalities minimises the risk of overloading one channel. The article states: "A lecturer's face changes constantly and will keep attracting visual attention", unlike static slide content, which may explain why a visible lecturer supports attention.
requirements: The explanation assumes that dividing input across auditory and visual channels reduces cognitive load on either channel alone.
constraints: The article notes this is a theoretical explanation; the moderator analysis found no effect of lecturer appeal, and the visibility effect was found only for the second weblecture.
target_learning_goals: maintaining attention during weblectures
key_sources: Korving, H., Hernández, M. & De Groot, E. (2016). Look at me and pay attention! A study on the relation between visibility and attention in weblectures. Computers and Education, vol. 94, pp. 151-161. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2015.11.011

article_title: Using multi-platform learning analytics to compare regional and global MOOC learning in the Arab world
citation: Ruipérez-Valiente, José A; Halawa, Sherif; Slama, Rachel; Reich, Justin. (2020). Using multi-platform learning analytics to compare regional and global MOOC learning in the Arab world. Computers and Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/J.COMPEDU.2019.103776
title: Multi-platform learning analytics procedure with common data format and script
description: The article documents a "multi-platform learning analytics procedure, where we establish a common data format and script that enables an 'apples-to-apples' comparison without exchanging data". The procedure allows comparing learner behavior across MOOC platforms while avoiding data exchange, which the authors identify as "a common privacy and data security concern".
requirements: Access to platform data from each provider to map into the common data format
constraints: Designed so that raw data need not be exchanged between platforms, addressing privacy and data security concerns
target_learning_goals: Understanding learner behavior and preferences across MOOC platforms
examples: Applied to compare edX and Edraak learner demographics and behavior
key_sources: Ruipérez-Valiente, José A; Halawa, Sherif; Slama, Rachel; Reich, Justin. (2020). Using multi-platform learning analytics to compare regional and global MOOC learning in the Arab world. Computers and Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/J.COMPEDU.2019.103776

article_title: A multilevel analysis of what matters in the training of pre-service teacher's ICT competencies
citation: Tondeur, Jo; Aesaert, Koen; Prestridge, Sarah; Consuegra, Els. (2018). A multilevel analysis of what matters in the training of pre-service teacher's ICT competencies. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.03.002
title: A multilevel model integrating background characteristics, ICT profile and institutional strategies to explain pre-service teachers' perceived ICT competencies
description: The article proposes and tests a model to explain pre-service teachers' perceived ICT competencies that integrates three levels: background characteristics (age and gender), their ICT profile (e.g., attitudes towards ICT), and the multiple strategies experienced in the teacher training institution. The model was tested with multilevel analyses on a survey of 931 final-year pre-service teachers in Flanders (Belgium), motivated by the observation that prior research is "generally limited to the impact of one single strategy".
requirements: Survey data capturing perceived strategy occurrences, ICT profile and perceived ICT competencies from pre-service teachers
constraints: Tested with final-year pre-service teachers in Flanders (Belgium); outcomes are perceived ICT competencies
target_learning_goals: ICT competencies for learning processes and instructional practice
key_sources: Tondeur, Jo; Aesaert, Koen; Prestridge, Sarah; Consuegra, Els. (2018). A multilevel analysis of what matters in the training of pre-service teacher's ICT competencies. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.03.002

article_title: The Effect of Multiple Intelligences Theory-Based Education on Academic Achievement: A Meta-Analytic Review
citation: Baş, G. (2016). The effect of multiple intelligences theory-based education on academic achievement: A meta-analytic review. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice, 16, 1833–1864. https://doi.org/10.12738/estp.2016.6.0015
title: Multiple Intelligences Theory (MIT) as a pluralistic account of intelligence and a method of instruction
description: Gardner's theory of multiple intelligences defines intelligence as "a psychobiological information processing capacity to solve problems or fashion products that are valued in at least one community and culture", rejecting a single IQ-measured general intelligence. It posits at least eight modalities of intelligence — verbal-linguistic, logical-mathematical, visual-spatial, bodily-kinesthetic, musical-rhythmic, social-individual, personal-intrapersonal, and natural-naturalist — processed autonomously and localized in different brain areas. The article treats MIT not just as an intelligence theory but "as a method of instruction", providing a template for valuing individual differences in curriculum and teaching.
requirements: Teachers shift continuously between intelligence modalities in MIT-based classrooms and expand their repertoire of techniques beyond typical linguistic and logical ones
constraints: The article records criticisms that the eight potentials may not form abilities or mental domains, that MIT has not been subjected to strong experimental tests, and that it may be too broad for curriculum planning and present a static view of student competence
target_learners: students at elementary, high school, and university levels in Turkey
target_learning_goals: academic achievement across course types through instruction matched to multiple intelligence modalities
examples: In 2005 MIT was implemented into Turkey's elementary curriculum, after which the number of studies based on it increased significantly
key_sources: Baş, G. (2016). The effect of multiple intelligences theory-based education on academic achievement: A meta-analytic review. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice, 16, 1833–1864. https://doi.org/10.12738/estp.2016.6.0015

article_title: Music-mediated Pedagogy to Boost Efl Students' Listening Engagement and Fluency in Emi Contexts: A Scoping Review (2015-2025).
citation: Nguyen Phuong Bao Tran, Tran Ngoc Bao Chau, Nguyen Minh Tan. (2025). Music-mediated Pedagogy to Boost Efl Students' Listening Engagement and Fluency in Emi Contexts: A Scoping Review (2015–2025). F1000Research. https://doi.org/10.12688/f1000research.170296.1
title: Theoretical mechanisms linking music and language processing
