description: The review organizes its synthesis around four theoretical accounts for why music may enhance listening engagement and fluency: the Shared Neural Resources Hypothesis, under which "Music and language processing draw on overlapping brain networks, particularly in the temporal and frontal lobes"; the Affective Filter Hypothesis, whereby low-stress song activities reduce anxiety and increase receptivity to input; Prosodic Bootstrapping, in which music's rhythmic and melodic patterns aid acquisition of L2 prosody; and Dual Coding Theory, applied to music-video tasks providing auditory and visual encoding channels. These mechanisms ground the review's interpretation of its four thematic clusters.
requirements: The accounts are used interpretively; the review treats them as explanatory frames rather than tested within its own data
constraints: Evidence for the mechanisms is drawn from cited EFL literature, not directly tested in the reviewed EMI studies
target_learners: EFL learners in EMI higher education contexts
target_learning_goals: listening engagement
oral fluency
L2 prosody
examples: The review interprets song-based affective gains via the Affective Filter Hypothesis and rhythm-training fluency gains via the Shared Neural Resources Hypothesis
key_sources: Nguyen Phuong Bao Tran, Tran Ngoc Bao Chau, Nguyen Minh Tan. (2025). Music-mediated Pedagogy to Boost Efl Students' Listening Engagement and Fluency in Emi Contexts: A Scoping Review (2015–2025). F1000Research. https://doi.org/10.12688/f1000research.170296.1

article_title: Nurses' Knowledge and Attitudes Toward Pressure Injury Prevention: A Systematic Review.
citation: Saleh Zyad T., Rababa Majdi, Al‐Za'areer Majed S., Elshatarat Rami A., Shahin Mahmoud Abdel Hameed, Hamithi Manal Ali, Abdelkader Raghad, Alnawafleh Khaldoon Aied, Alharbi Amal Ali, Alasmari Amal Ali, Al‐Sayaghi Anas Khaled, Al‐Sayaghi Khaled M. (2026). Nurses' Knowledge and Attitudes Toward Pressure Injury Prevention: A Systematic Review. International Wound Journal. https://doi.org/10.1111/iwj.70855
title: Structured education programmes, simulation-based training, and strengthened organisational support are needed to improve pressure injury prevention.
description: The review concludes that educational initiatives alone are unlikely to yield sustained improvements unless accompanied by enabling organisational conditions such as adequate staffing, access to pressure-relieving equipment, and embedding prevention protocols into routine workflows. It recommends combining "structured education programmes, simulation‐based training, and strengthened organisational support" to enhance adherence to evidence-based prevention strategies.
requirements: Educational initiatives must be accompanied by enabling organisational conditions such as adequate staffing and access to pressure-relieving equipment.
constraints: Impact of simulation-based learning and workshops will be limited if nurses lack the time, resources, or authority to implement preventive measures.
target_learners: Registered nurses in hospital and long-term care settings
target_learning_goals: Pressure injury prevention knowledge, attitudes, and practices
key_sources: Saleh Zyad T., Rababa Majdi, Al‐Za'areer Majed S., Elshatarat Rami A., Shahin Mahmoud Abdel Hameed, Hamithi Manal Ali, Abdelkader Raghad, Alnawafleh Khaldoon Aied, Alharbi Amal Ali, Alasmari Amal Ali, Al‐Sayaghi Anas Khaled, Al‐Sayaghi Khaled M. (2026). Nurses' Knowledge and Attitudes Toward Pressure Injury Prevention: A Systematic Review. International Wound Journal. https://doi.org/10.1111/iwj.70855

article_title: Effectiveness of education and training programmes to help clinicians assess and classify perineal tears: a systematic review.
citation: Simpson G, Philip M, Richards A, Eggleston AJ, Vogel JP, Wilson AN, Homer C. (2025). Effectiveness of education and training programmes to help clinicians assess and classify perineal tears: a systematic review. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2024-095961
title: Use multimodal approaches with multidisciplinary facilitators targeting all personnel involved in the birthing process.
description: The review recommends that perineal tear educational and training programmes should use multimodal approaches with multidisciplinary facilitators, and target all personnel involved in the birthing process including students, midwives, junior doctors and obstetricians. A multidisciplinary team was used to facilitate programmes in seven studies with promising results.
requirements: Programmes should include multidisciplinary training with facilitators and participants from various levels of experience.
target_learning_goals: Perineal tear assessment and classification
Interdisciplinary communication and teamwork
key_sources: Simpson G, Philip M, Richards A, Eggleston AJ, Vogel JP, Wilson AN, Homer C. (2025). Effectiveness of education and training programmes to help clinicians assess and classify perineal tears: a systematic review. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2024-095961

article_title: Self-directed learning assessment practices in undergraduate health professions education: a systematic review.
citation: Taylor, T.A.H., Kemp, K., Mi, M., & Lerchenfeldt, S. (2023). Self-directed learning assessment practices in undergraduate health professions education: a systematic review. Medical Education Online, 28(1). https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2023.2189553
title: Assess self-directed learning with multiple assessments combining direct and indirect measures
description: The review recommends that evidence-based best practices for assessing SDL in undergraduate health professions education include multiple assessments with both direct and indirect measures, because each assessment type has distinct strengths and shortcomings. Direct measures such as objective exams provide "direct evidence of student learning", while indirect measures such as reflections, surveys, and focus groups provide information about students' perceptions and the learning process itself. The authors found less than half of reviewed studies (48.9%) used more than one assessment method, and multiple assessments were associated with higher study quality.
requirements: Use of more than one assessment method, blending direct measures (exams, presentations, papers) and indirect measures (reflections, surveys, focus groups)
constraints: The association between multiple assessments and quality is correlational; the review also notes internal knowledge exams were often administered shortly after the activity and did not test long-term retention
target_learning_goals: self-directed learning outcomes and lifelong learning skills
examples: The review found 69 studies used one assessment, 59 used two, and 13 used three; studies with one assessment had a mean MERSQI of 9.49 versus 11.25 and 11.27 for two and three assessments
key_sources: Taylor, T.A.H., Kemp, K., Mi, M., & Lerchenfeldt, S. (2023). Self-directed learning assessment practices in undergraduate health professions education: a systematic review. Medical Education Online, 28(1). https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2023.2189553

article_title: A meta-analytic perspective on the valid use of subjective human judgement to make medical school admission decisions.
citation: Kreiter Clare, O'Shea Marie, Bruen Catherine, Murphy Paul, Pawlikowska Teresa. (2018). A meta-analytic perspective on the valid use of subjective human judgement to make medical school admission decisions. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2018.1522225
title: Format traditional interviews to yield a reliable score, e.g., by engaging each applicant in multiple independent interviews
description: The review concludes that the traditional interview's low reliability significantly limits its validity, but that its reliable variance is moderately predictive of relevant outcomes. It therefore recommends reformatting the interview so it produces a reliable score: 'if traditional subjective interviews can be formatted to yield a reliable score (e.g., by engaging an applicant in multiple independent interviews), it might significantly enhance its value as a subjective assessment'. This preserves the subjective component while addressing the measurement weakness the meta-analysis identified.
requirements: The interview must be reformatted so the score reflects comprehensive error sources, allowing an inference about maximum attainable validity
constraints: The recommendation is conditional ('might significantly enhance'), derived from reliability and validity coefficients rather than a direct test of the reformatted format
target_learning_goals: valid and reliable selection of applicants with potential to succeed as medical students and physicians
examples: The review's Table 1 aggregates G-study and repeat-interview alpha estimates showing reliabilities from r = .23 to r = .46 across medical education and employment studies
key_sources: Kreiter Clare, O'Shea Marie, Bruen Catherine, Murphy Paul, Pawlikowska Teresa. (2018). A meta-analytic perspective on the valid use of subjective human judgement to make medical school admission decisions. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2018.1522225

article_title: Tools used to assess medical students competence in procedural skills at the end of a primary medical degree: a systematic review.
citation: Morris Marie C., Gallagher Tom K., Ridgway Paul F. (2012). Tools used to assess medical students competence in procedural skills at the end of a primary medical degree: a systematic review. Medical Education Online. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3427596/
title: Assess procedural competence with many methods by many people at regular intervals across the curriculum
description: The review concludes that single method, single testing of procedural skills is limited in ensuring clinical competence. It recommends that "Assessment needs to include many methods by many people at regular intervals across the primary training curriculum". This programmatic approach would allow students to receive feedback on their level of competence, be it novice, intermediate, advanced intermediate or expert, and whether they are meeting expected levels for their training stage.
requirements: Provided construct validity of a global assessment tool is assured in the undergraduate setting
constraints: The review notes the assertion of competence in a simulated setting does not guarantee transferability of the skill to the workplace
target_learners: medical students from first to final year of training
target_learning_goals: procedural skills competence development and feedback across the curriculum
examples: The review suggests a global assessment tool could be used incrementally on a yearly basis from first to final year, allowing feedback on competence level relative to peers
key_sources: Morris Marie C., Gallagher Tom K., Ridgway Paul F. (2012). Tools used to assess medical students competence in procedural skills at the end of a primary medical degree: a systematic review. Medical Education Online. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3427596/

article_title: The role of feedback in improving the effectiveness of workplace based assessments: a systematic review.
citation: Saedon H, Salleh S, Balakrishnan A, Imray CHE, Saedon M. (2012). The role of feedback in improving the effectiveness of workplace based assessments: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education, 12, 25. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3432628/
title: Multisource feedback (MSF) as a workplace based assessment method
description: Multisource feedback (MSF) is a workplace based assessment method in which feedback and scoring are provided by multiple assessors and compiled and fed back to educational supervisors. Tools include the Sheffield Peer Review Assessment Tool (SPRAT) and team assessment of behaviour (TAB). MSF "has the sole purpose of providing feedback of doctors' practice and behaviours", and the review found most evidence supporting feedback from WBAs comes from MSF studies, with 7 of 15 included studies focusing on MSF.
requirements: Multiple assessors including patients, co-workers and medical colleagues
Free-text comment capacity to transmit actionable information
constraints: Unregulated self-selection of assessors introduces leniency bias, as reported in the review
target_learners: postgraduate doctors in training across specialties including general practice, general medicine, general surgery, dermatology, paediatrics and anaesthetics
target_learning_goals: formative assessment of professional behaviour and clinical skills
examples: Archer et al's analysis of SPRAT data from 4770 paediatric trainees in the UK, and Violato et al's 5-year longitudinal study of 250 general practice doctors in Canada
key_sources: Saedon H, Salleh S, Balakrishnan A, Imray CHE, Saedon M. (2012). The role of feedback in improving the effectiveness of workplace based assessments: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education, 12, 25. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3432628/

article_title: Educational strategies for teaching evidence-based practice to undergraduate health students: systematic review.
citation: Kyriakoulis Konstantinos, Patelarou Athina, Laliotis Aggelos, Wan Andrew C, Matalliotakis Michail, Tsiou Chrysoula, Patelarou Evridiki. (2016). Educational strategies for teaching evidence-based practice to undergraduate health students: systematic review. Journal of Educational Evaluation for Health Professions. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5066070/
title: Use a multifaceted approach when teaching EBP to undergraduate health students
description: The review concludes that a multifaceted approach may be best suited when teaching EBM to health students. Multifaceted interventions combine methods such as lectures, computer sessions, small group discussions, journal clubs, and assignments, and were "more likely to improve knowledge, skills, and attitude compared to SI or no interventions". The principle directs curriculum designers to combine multiple instructional formats rather than relying on a single delivery method.
requirements: Combination of multiple teaching strategies (e.g., lectures, computer sessions, small group discussions, journal clubs, and assignments) rather than a single format
constraints: The review notes this is based on existing evidence that MI were "more likely to improve" outcomes, not a meta-analytic pooled estimate; heterogeneity prevented meta-analysis
target_learners: Undergraduate health students (medical, nursing, pharmacy, physiotherapy, dentistry)
target_learning_goals: EBP competence including knowledge, skills, and attitudes
examples: Included multifaceted interventions combined lectures, practicals, group discussions, teamwork, and students' presentations (Spain nursing study); lectures, seminars, online search, and answering worksheets (Jordan medical study); and didactic, small-group sessions and EBP assignments (US medical study)
key_sources: Kyriakoulis Konstantinos, Patelarou Athina, Laliotis Aggelos, Wan Andrew C, Matalliotakis Michail, Tsiou Chrysoula, Patelarou Evridiki. (2016). Educational strategies for teaching evidence-based practice to undergraduate health students: systematic review. Journal of Educational Evaluation for Health Professions. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5066070/

article_title: Preparing Students for Class: A Clinical Trial Testing the Efficacy between Multimedia Pre-Lectures and Textbooks in an Economics Course
citation: Jose J. Vazquez & Eric P. Chiang. (2016). Preparing Students For Class: A Clinical Trial Testing The Efficacy Between Multimedia Pre-lectures And Textbooks in an Economics Course. Journal of College Teaching & Learning, 13(2). https://clutejournals.com
title: Four multimedia pre-lecture modules for principles of microeconomics topics
description: The authors developed four multimedia learning modules, one each for production possibilities frontier, the benefits of trade, price elasticity of demand, and other elasticities. Each pre-lecture covered one lecture's worth of content in approximately eight scenes, implemented as videos with "dynamic animations synchronized with an audio narration that was controlled by the student (pause, play, and rewind)". Embedded formative questions in two or three scenes had to be answered correctly before proceeding. Average narration time was 12 minutes; students averaged 17 minutes to complete a pre-lecture.
requirements: Embedded questions must be answered correctly before the student can proceed to the next scene
constraints: The pre-lectures "were not designed to replicate an entire lecture, but instead to provide a visual introduction to the key concepts"
target_learners: novice students in an introductory principles of microeconomics course
target_learning_goals: first-time comprehension of key economics concepts prior to class
examples: In the clinical trial, the study group watched these modules while the control group read selected pdf pages from Mankiw's Principles of Microeconomics 6th edition
key_sources: Jose J. Vazquez & Eric P. Chiang. (2016). Preparing Students For Class: A Clinical Trial Testing The Efficacy Between Multimedia Pre-lectures And Textbooks in an Economics Course. Journal of College Teaching & Learning, 13(2). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1095763

article_title: The Effect of Teaching Strategy Based on Multiple Intelligences on Students' Academic Achievement in Science Course
citation: Ali abdi, Soosan Laei, Hamze Ahmadyan. (2013). The Effect of Teaching Strategy Based on Multiple Intelligences on Students’ Academic Achievement in Science Course. Universal Journal of Educational Research 1(4): 281-284. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2013.010401
title: Gardner's theory of multiple intelligences outlining eight intelligences
description: The article presents multiple intelligences theory as the framework underlying the experimental teaching strategy. It states that "The current Multiple Intelligences Theory outlines eight intelligences": verbal/linguistic, logical/mathematical, visual/spatial, bodily/kinaesthetic, musical, interpersonal, intrapersonal, and naturalist, each defined as an ability to use language, numbers, spatial ideas, the body, rhythm, understanding of others, self-knowledge, or classification of living things. The theory holds that humans possess distinct intelligences applied to solve problems and create things valued by a community.
requirements: Teachers need knowledge and application of the multiple intelligences to provide enough variety in activities so pupils' learning potential can be tapped
constraints: The article notes Gardner continues to explore additional possibilities beyond the eight listed intelligences
target_learning_goals: science achievement
scientific literacy
examples: The experimental group's lesson plans and activities were prepared in the light of the eight multiple intelligence types over 8 weeks
key_sources: Ali abdi, Soosan Laei, Hamze Ahmadyan. (2013). The Effect of Teaching Strategy Based on Multiple Intelligences on Students’ Academic Achievement in Science Course. Universal Journal of Educational Research 1(4): 281-284. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2013.010401

article_title: Music Activities as a Meaningful Context for Teaching Elementary Students Mathematics: A Quasi-Experiment Time Series Design with Random Assigned Control Group
citation: Song A. An, and Daniel A. Tillman. (2015). Music activities as a meaningful context for teaching elementary students mathematics: a quasi-experiment time series design with random assigned control group. European Journal of Science and Mathematics Education, 3(1), 45-60. https://ejsme.com
title: Sequence of 14 music-mathematics integrated lessons using composition, performance, and instruments as mathematical manipulatives
description: The intervention was a series of 14 classroom lessons integrating mathematics content with music activities, delivered weekly at "one or two 45-minute music-mathematics integrated lessons". Students used graphic notation (music color cards) and instruments such as handbells, drums, music sticks, and keyboards as physical manipulatives, and mathematics problems were individualized based on students' own music compositions and instrument designs. The lessons were developed from An and Capraro's (2011) textbook and piloted over two semesters before the study.
requirements: Teacher professional development in music-mathematics integrated instruction prior to implementation
constraints: The control group received standard mathematics lessons only; the intervention was tested in a single school with two classes
target_learning_goals: number operations, algebra, geometry, measurement, data analysis, and mathematical reasoning
examples: In lessons 3, 5, 8 and 9 students made algebraic charts and statistical tables based on music works; in lessons 5, 7, 9, 13 and 14 students solved real-world related mathematics problems
key_sources: Song A. An, and Daniel A. Tillman. (2015). Music activities as a meaningful context for teaching elementary students mathematics: a quasi-experiment time series design with random assigned control group. European Journal of Science and Mathematics Education, 3(1), 45-60. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1107839

article_title: Music Activities as a Meaningful Context for Teaching Elementary Students Mathematics: A Quasi-Experiment Time Series Design with Random Assigned Control Group
citation: Song A. An, and Daniel A. Tillman. (2015). Music activities as a meaningful context for teaching elementary students mathematics: a quasi-experiment time series design with random assigned control group. European Journal of Science and Mathematics Education, 3(1), 45-60. https://ejsme.com
title: Use music activities as an authentic, engaging context for teaching elementary mathematics
description: The article recommends that teachers integrate music activities such as composition and instrument design into mathematics lessons as an authentic context, because doing mathematics in the context of music allowed students to analyze, interpret, and understand mathematics through different disciplinary perspectives. The authors conclude that "teachers should take advantage of the opportunities that music offers as an authentic and engaging context to help students learn mathematics".
requirements: Teachers require interdisciplinary pedagogy training; the music group teacher received intensive training and ongoing mentoring from the authors
constraints: The authors state the positive results might be partially attributable to the Hawthorne effect, small sample size, unique demographic structures, unequal teacher professional development, and unbalanced musical dispositions between groups
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement and mathematics process ability
examples: The intervention used music composition and performance as the two primary music activities, with students posing their own mathematics problems based on their music works in all lessons
key_sources: Song A. An, and Daniel A. Tillman. (2015). Music activities as a meaningful context for teaching elementary students mathematics: a quasi-experiment time series design with random assigned control group. European Journal of Science and Mathematics Education, 3(1), 45-60. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1107839

article_title: Development and Implementation of an Instructional Design for Effective Teaching of Ecosystem, Biodiversity, and Environmental Issues
citation: Elif Ozata Yucel, Muhlis Ozkan. (2015). Development and Implementation of an Instructional Design for Effective Teaching of Ecosystem, Biodiversity, and Environmental Issues. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice. https://doi.org/10.12738/estp.2015.4.2579
title: Select teaching materials addressing all of the students' senses
description: The design adopted an approach addressing all of the students' senses when selecting and developing teaching materials. Written, visual, auditory, and technology-supported materials were combined so learning would be easy and permanent. The article states that "An approach addressing all of the students' senses was adopted in selecting and developing teaching materials".
requirements: Combining written materials such as books, posters, and worksheets
Visual materials such as photos, figures, charts, and maps
Auditory materials such as sound recordings
Technology-supported materials such as videos, slide-shows, and animations
target_learning_goals: Learning ecosystem, biodiversity, and environmental issues effectively and permanently
examples: Teachers reported that pictures, slides, and videos selected from daily life were attention-grabbing and made learning easy and permanent
key_sources: Elif Ozata Yucel, Muhlis Ozkan. (2015). Development and Implementation of an Instructional Design for Effective Teaching of Ecosystem, Biodiversity, and Environmental Issues. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice. https://doi.org/10.12738/estp.2015.4.2579

article_title: Extensions beyond Program Impacts: Conceptual and Methodological Considerations in Studying the Implementation of a Preschool Social Emotional Learning Program
citation: Choles JR, Roeser RW and Mashburn AJ (2022) Extensions beyond program impacts: Conceptual and methodological considerations in studying the implementation of a preschool social emotional learning program. Front. Educ. 7:1035730. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2022.1035730
title: Build FOI measure sets that are comprehensive and multi-informant, triangulating observer, teacher, and implementor reports
description: The article recommends that implementation measure sets within impact studies be comprehensive and triangulated. The authors set two explicit goals: first, at least one measure for each FOI component for each program element within each program level; second, "when feasible, we believe there should be more than one measure for an FOI element, and that these multiple measures should be from different reporters or sources (i.e., multi-informant)." In their study, third-party observers rated training and community of practice sessions, teachers self-reported responsiveness and quality, and the implementation director reported on coaching sessions.
requirements: Measures from different reporters or sources (observer, teacher, implementor) for the same FOI element when feasible
Development through piloting and revision before use in the impact study
constraints: It was not developmentally appropriate for preschoolers to report on their curriculum experiences, though older students can be included as informants when applicable
Third-party observers did not rate one-on-one coaching sessions
target_learning_goals: fidelity of implementation of a mindfulness-based SEL curriculum
examples: Teachers filled out a weekly implementation log for curriculum activities and the brain break, and researchers rated all FOI components on two classroom observation occasions
key_sources: Choles JR, Roeser RW and Mashburn AJ (2022) Extensions beyond program impacts: Conceptual and methodological considerations in studying the implementation of a preschool social emotional learning program. Front. Educ. 7:1035730. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2022.1035730

article_title: Developing a Theory of Treatment Effect Heterogeneity through Better Design: Where Do Behavioral Science Interventions Work Best?
citation: Tipton, E., Yeager, D., & Iachan, R. (2016). Developing a theory of treatment effect heterogeneity through better design: Where do behavioral science interventions work best? SREE Spring 2016 Conference Abstract. https://www.sree.org
title: Multipurpose design framework for answering three generalization questions in behavioral science experiments
description: The paper develops a 'multipurpose' study design that fuses survey sampling and experimental design results so that a single study can answer three generalization questions: the average effect, its variability, and treatment effect moderation. The article states the design 'requires researchers to develop hypotheses about treatment effect heterogeneity at the outset of the study, to develop methods to measure these moderators, and to use a stratified selection procedure, with strata based on potential moderators.' Power for all three estimands involves trade-offs.
requirements: Researchers must identify possible moderators at the outset, based on previous research, the theory of change, and policy-relevant context questions
Moderators may require dimension reduction methods such as k-means cluster analysis or a latent-variable approach
Power must be considered for the multipurpose design as a whole, not for each parameter separately
constraints: The design that is most powerful for estimating the average treatment effect results in less power for estimation of moderator effects, and vice versa
target_learners: 9th grade students in U.S. public high schools
target_learning_goals: Estimating population average treatment effects, variability in impacts, and treatment effect moderation in behavioral science intervention studies
examples: The NGMI study applies the framework: schools are randomly selected from a population frame of regular U.S. public high schools and students within schools are randomly assigned to the intervention
key_sources: Tipton, E., Yeager, D., & Iachan, R. (2016). Developing a theory of treatment effect heterogeneity through better design: Where do behavioral science interventions work best? SREE Spring 2016 Conference Abstract. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED567217

article_title: Multimedia Approach and Its Effect in Teaching Mathematics for the Prospective Teachers
citation: D.R. Robert Joan and S.P. Denisia. (2012). Multimedia Approach and its Effect in Teaching Mathematics for the Prospective Teachers. li-manager's Journal on School Educational Technology. https://www.eric.ed.gov
title: Multimedia Learning Package for Mathematics for prospective teachers
description: The instructional tool used with the experimental group: a slide-based multimedia package developed by the authors in 2012 for teaching Mathematics to prospective teachers. As printed, "The Multimedia package was prepared as 4 units. It consists of 76 slides with animations, pictures, video and audio." It was the treatment contrasted against Active Learning Methodology in the experiment.
requirements: Requires learners to work through the slide package in an instructional situation where the learner may review material at his or her own pace
constraints: Developed specifically for Mathematics content for prospective teachers in a college of education in Kanyakumari District
target_learning_goals: achievement in Mathematics content
examples: Used as the experimental treatment: the experimental group was taught Mathematics using this package while the control group was taught using Active Learning Methodology
key_sources: D.R. Robert Joan and S.P. Denisia. (2012). Multimedia Approach and its Effect in Teaching Mathematics for the Prospective Teachers. li-manager's Journal on School Educational Technology. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1101646

article_title: Develop and Evaluate the Effects of Multimodal Presentation System on Elementary ESL Students
citation: Kuo, F.-O., Yu, P.-T., & Hsiao, W.-H. (2013). Develop and evaluate the effects of multimodal presentation system on elementary ESL students. The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 12(4). https://www.tojet.net/
title: Multimodal Presentation System (MPS): presentation software integrated with an interactive whiteboard
description: The MPS is a multimodal presentation software integrated with an interactive whiteboard, developed by the authors to present verbal and visual instructional materials and manage interactive classroom activities in elementary ESL lessons. It "consists of four primary components, which are Office Card Component, Media Card Component, Annotation Card Component, and Manager Card Component", supporting document control, media playback, screen capture, handwriting annotation, focusing, and multi-monitor container management. It was designed to bring students to the IWB and directly involve them in the lesson.
requirements: An interactive whiteboard in the classroom to display the multimodal materials
constraints: The authors state the MPS "cannot compensate for the teacher's lack of subject matter content knowledge, capability to produce instructional materials, instructional competency, and classroom management skills"
target_learners: elementary school students learning English as a second language
target_learning_goals: English vocabulary learning through storytelling
examples: Used across a two-month ESL unit (mid-March to mid-May 2011) in a warm-up phase with video storytelling, an implementation phase with recorded vocabulary teaching, and an application phase where students practiced and reviewed materials on the IWB
key_sources: Kuo, F.-O., Yu, P.-T., & Hsiao, W.-H. (2013). Develop and evaluate the effects of multimodal presentation system on elementary ESL students. The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 12(4). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1018039

article_title: Utilizing Authentic Materials on Students' Listening Comprehension: Does It Have Any Influence?
citation: Resti Citra Dewi. (2018). Utilizing Authentic Materials on Students' Listening Comprehension: Does it have Any Influence? Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 9(1). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.9n.1p.70
title: 20-item multiple-choice listening comprehension test
description: The study's instrument was a multiple-choice test used to collect listening-comprehension data. The article states "The test consisted of 20 items, each item of the test consisted of 3 options, namely a,b, and c." Validity was examined with the product-moment correlation with 38 second-grade respondents, and reliability was addressed as the consistency of the measure across retests. The same instrument served as pre-test and post-test for both groups.
requirements: Validity and reliability of the test were established before use, per the article
target_learners: second-year junior high school EFL students
target_learning_goals: listening comprehension achievement
examples: The test was administered as a pre-test before treatment and a post-test after treatment in both the experimental and control groups.
key_sources: Resti Citra Dewi. (2018). Utilizing Authentic Materials on Students' Listening Comprehension: Does it have Any Influence? Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 9(1). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.9n.1p.70

article_title: The Effects of Different Pre-Writing Strategies on Iranian EFL Writing Achievement
citation: Lily Mahnam; Dariush Nejadansari. (2012). The Effects of Different Pre-Writing Strategies on Iranian EFL Writing Achievement. International Education Studies, 5(1). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v5n1p154
title: Multiple-intelligence-informed strategy teaching as an explanation for pre-writing strategy effects
description: In the discussion, the authors offer Gardner's theory of multiple intelligences as "the best explanation for this result", arguing it gives teachers a guide for classroom activities addressing "multiple ways of learning and knowing". Such teaching transfers some control from teachers to learners by giving students choices in how they learn, and encourages learners to build on existing strengths and knowledge.
requirements: Teaching strategies informed by the theory that offer learners choices in how they learn and demonstrate learning
constraints: The article presents this as an interpretation of its findings, not as a tested component of the treatment
target_learning_goals: improved writing through strategy use and learner control
key_sources: Lily Mahnam; Dariush Nejadansari. (2012). The Effects of Different Pre-Writing Strategies on Iranian EFL Writing Achievement. International Education Studies, 5(1). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v5n1p154

article_title: Effectiveness of a Program Based on a Multi-Sensory Strategy in Developing Visual Perception of Primary School Learners with Learning Disabilities: A Contextual Study of Arabic Learners
citation: Alenizi, M.A. (2019). Effectiveness of a Program Based on A Multi-Sensory Strategy in Developing Visual Perception of Primary School Learners with Learning Disabilities: A Contextual Study of Arabic Learners. International Journal of Educational Psychology, 8(1), 72-104. https://doi.org/10.17583/ijep.2019.3346
title: Multi-sensory visual perception training program of three parts delivered in six 40-minute sessions
description: A training program used with Saudi primary-school learners with learning disabilities to develop visual perception through multiple senses. "The program included three major parts: the first one focused on paper flyer, the second one focused on the articles from day-to-day life and the third one focused on articles identification. Each part was further distributed into two sessions (each one was of 40 mins)." Learners inferred factual information from texts, identified everyday articles using multiple senses, and described shape, size, color and materials of visual stimuli, with rest periods maintained so the program was not too tiring.
requirements: Researchers were required to make use of the materials and be available with the learners during practice sessions and to exchange dialogue with the learners, with stability and flexibility maintained so amendments could be made
constraints: The study applied the program with primary-school learners with learning disabilities in Saudi Arabia in 2017/2018
target_learners: primary school learners with learning disabilities (third and fourth graders)
target_learning_goals: visual perception skills, including recognizing visually stimulating texts and connecting sensorimotor experience to reading materials
examples: Sessions included a paper-flyer activity in which a child and father gather thread, paper and glue to make a paper flyer, presented with visual-perception training activities
key_sources: Alenizi, M.A. (2019). Effectiveness of a Program Based on A Multi-Sensory Strategy in Developing Visual Perception of Primary School Learners with Learning Disabilities: A Contextual Study of Arabic Learners. International Journal of Educational Psychology, 8(1), 72-104. https://doi.org/10.17583/ijep.2019.3346

article_title: The Effect of Gloss Type and Mode on Iranian EFL Learners' Reading Comprehension
citation: Karim Sadeghi & Negar Ahmadi. (2012). The Effect of Gloss Type and Mode on Iranian EFL Learners' Reading Comprehension. English Language Teaching, 5(12). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n12p100
title: Dual-channel processing account for why multimodal (extended audio) glosses aid reading comprehension
description: The article explains the extended audio gloss advantage through a multimedia-learning account: "providing learners with different modes of gloss presentation can assist the learners to process information through different channels allowing participants to better comprehend the text (Mayer, 2001)". On this view, adding a spoken rendering of the target word's meaning plus an L2 example sentence gives learners extra information about key words through an additional channel, supporting comprehension. The article cites Mayer and Moreno (1998) on the superiority of combining audio with text over text only.
requirements: Gloss presentation must combine at least two modes, here the voice of a speaker reading the target word's meaning plus one L2 example sentence
constraints: The account is the authors' interpretation citing Mayer (2001), not a mechanism tested in the study
target_learners: adolescent and young adult foreign-language learners (ages 17-21 in the study)
target_learning_goals: L2 reading comprehension
vocabulary meaning access while reading
examples: The extended audio gloss condition gave learners a speaker's voice reading the meaning of the target word plus one example sentence, and that group scored highest (M = 7.87)
key_sources: Karim Sadeghi & Negar Ahmadi. (2012). The Effect of Gloss Type and Mode on Iranian EFL Learners' Reading Comprehension. English Language Teaching, 5(12). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n12p100

article_title: Climbing up the Leaderboard: An Empirical Study of Applying Gamification Techniques to a Computer Programming Class
citation: Fotaris P, Mastoras T, Leinfellner R and Rosunally Y. (2016). Climbing Up the Leaderboard: An Empirical Study of Applying Gamification Techniques to a Computer Programming Class. The Electronic Journal of e-Learning Volume 14 Issue 2, pp94-110. www.ejel.org
title: Multi-dimensional gamified learning model combining instructor feedback, scored quizzes, and live coding
description: The article's learning model integrates three interlocking game-based components: Kahoot! formative-assessment cycles (micro-lecture, game, discussion), a collaborative WWTBAM revision seminar, and Codecademy's interactive Python exercises with points, badges, and leaderboards. The authors describe it as "a gamified, multi -dimensional, problem-based learning approach" applied to an entry-level Python course, grounded in Self-Determination Theory principles of relatedness, competence, and autonomy. It was designed to counter declining lecture attention spans by delivering "a fully interactive learning experience" similar to a quality game experience.
requirements: Instructor authoring of weekly game questions (540 Python MC questions for WWTBAM; three Kahoot! games per week)
A virtual learning environment (Blackboard) to host public leaderboards and distribute materials
Student devices or class desktops with browser access to the platforms
constraints: The authors note the limited length of multiple-choice questions and answers made authoring challenging
Some Codecademy lessons were not a good fit to the FSD syllabus and had unclear instructions and vague error messages
target_learners: higher education students in an entry-level Python programming course
target_learning_goals: Python programming concepts including loops, functions, object-oriented programming, GUI applications
problem solving, critical thinking, and collaboration skills
examples: Lectures were replaced by three 20-minute cycles of micro-lecture, Kahoot! game, and discussion; seminars used a 540-question WWTBAM implementation with lifelines; labs used 36 mapped Codecademy lessons with weekly challenges
key_sources: Fotaris P, Mastoras T, Leinfellner R and Rosunally Y. (2016). Climbing Up the Leaderboard: An Empirical Study of Applying Gamification Techniques to a Computer Programming Class. The Electronic Journal of e-Learning Volume 14 Issue 2, pp94-110. www.ejel.org. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1101229

article_title: Bridging the Evidence Gap in Developmental Education
citation: Collins, M. L. (2010). Bridging the Evidence Gap in Developmental Education. Journal of Developmental Education, 34(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?q=%22Bridging+the+Evidence+Gap+in+Developmental+Education%22
title: Because every research design has limitations, community college leaders and policymakers should consider multiple types of evidence rather than reifying a single hierarchy
description: The article argues that presenting evidence as discrete from robust to weak is less useful for identifying promising practices than weighing the strengths and limitations of each research type. It states that "it is imprudent to reify the quantitative or the practitioner-oriented researchers' characterization of the evidence without considering the important elements that their respective research methodologies omit." Leaders should draw on experimental, quasiexperimental, and descriptive evidence together when deciding which programs and strategies to implement.
requirements: Willingness of practitioners, researchers, and policymakers to interpret findings with explicit attention to what each methodology does and does not capture
constraints: The article cautions that even the most rigorous quantitative methods cannot control for hard-to-measure student characteristics such as determination, grit, and resilience
target_learners: community college leaders and state policymakers serving academically underprepared students
target_learning_goals: identifying effective developmental education programs, practices, and policies
examples: The article weighs descriptive best-practices research against regression-discontinuity and random assignment studies, identifying the false-positive and false-negative risks of each before recommending a continuous improvement approach
key_sources: Collins, M. L. (2010). Bridging the Evidence Gap in Developmental Education. Journal of Developmental Education, 34(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ942875

article_title: From Research to Practice: The Effect of Multi-Component Vocabulary Instruction on Increasing Vocabulary and Comprehension Performance in Social Studies
citation: Graham, L., Graham, A., & West, C. (2015). From Research to Practice: The Effect of Multi-Component Vocabulary Instruction on Increasing Vocabulary and Comprehension Performance in Social Studies. International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education, 8(1), 147-160. https://www.iejee.com
title: Six-week multi-component social studies vocabulary intervention package for fourth grade
description: A researcher-designed six-week curriculum for fourth-grade social studies in which treatment teachers spent at least 90 minutes per week of language arts time on vocabulary instruction, preferably in 30-minute segments three times per week. "The training  included the use of each of the following: explicit instruction; student study teams; active engagement in learning tasks; vocabulary maps; connections webs; semantic feature analysis." Teachers received curriculum notebooks, supplemental materials, and games such as Ready, Set, Go, Vocabulary Memory, and Jeopardy, providing repetition and use of words in multiple contexts. Implementation was monitored weekly by trained observers using a checklist with quality rated on a 0-2 scale.
requirements: Teacher training in the vocabulary instructional methods prior to implementation
A minimum of 90 minutes per week of instructional time, preferably 30 minutes three times per week
constraints: Teachers reported lack of time to complete the instructional strategies and concern that the vocabulary focus limited coverage of textbook content
target_learning_goals: retention of social studies word meanings in isolation and in context
comprehension of expository content-area text
examples: Treatment teachers followed researcher-created lesson plans; an example connections web is included in the article's appendix
key_sources: Graham, L., Graham, A., & West, C. (2015). From Research to Practice: The Effect of Multi-Component Vocabulary Instruction on Increasing Vocabulary and Comprehension Performance in Social Studies. International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education, 8(1), 147-160. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1078850

article_title: Reading in L2 (English) and L1 (Persian): An Investigation into Reverse Transfer of Reading Strategies
citation: Seyed Hassan Talebi. (2012). Reading in L2 (English) and L1 (Persian): An Investigation into Reveres Transfer of Reading Strategies. English Language Teaching, 5(3). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n3p217
title: Multicompetence and reverse (borrowing) transfer as a framework for L2 effects on L1
description: The article frames its study with Cook's multicompetence view, that the knowledge of two or more languages in one mind forms a system in which "the first language and the other language or languages are in the same mind" and must form a language super-system at some level. Within this frame, transfer is bidirectional: influence from L2 back to L1 is called borrowing transfer, reverse or backward transfer. The study applies this framework to reading strategies, testing whether strategy instruction in L2 raises L1 reading ability and strategy use.
requirements: Learners who already have an established L1 and are learning an L2
Instruments measuring reading and strategy use in both languages
constraints: The L1's phonetic and phonological features are not likely to be affected, since it is so established in the speaker, as the article cites from Arranz
target_learners: Bilingual or L2-learning adolescents and adults
target_learning_goals: Cross-linguistic transfer of reading strategies and reading ability
examples: The study tested reverse transfer by giving parallel English and Persian reading tests and strategy questionnaires before and after L2-only strategy instruction
key_sources: Seyed Hassan Talebi. (2012). Reading in L2 (English) and L1 (Persian): An Investigation into Reveres Transfer of Reading Strategies. English Language Teaching, 5(3). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n3p217

article_title: A Study of Multimedia Application-Based Vocabulary Acquisition
citation: Jing Shao. (2012). A Study of Multimedia Application-based Vocabulary Acquisition. English Language Teaching, 5(10). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n10p202
title: Four beneficial characteristics of multimedia for language learning: combination of media, interactivity, non-judgmental environment, and efficiency
description: The article organizes the benefits of multimedia for vocabulary learning under four headings. Combination of media holds that pictures, sounds, written texts and videos each reinforce the other, since "Most people seem to remember more efficiently what they have experienced rather than what they have just read". Interactivity puts learning elements under learners' control; the non-judgmental property lets errors stay private and can "low affective filters"; and efficiency frees time for learning rather than searching. The study uses this account to motivate its experimental application of multimedia software to vocabulary acquisition.
requirements: Multimedia software contents and navigation must be mastered before the efficiency benefit is realized
constraints: The account is presented as literature-based rationale, not tested in this study
target_learning_goals: foreign language vocabulary acquisition
examples: The experimental study applied the I Love English Vocabulary software, which the article says is used to assist word input, word retention and word use.
key_sources: Jing Shao. (2012). A Study of Multimedia Application-based Vocabulary Acquisition. English Language Teaching, 5(10). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n10p202

article_title: Painting with the Multiple Intelligences: Defining Student Success and Permanence in Art Class
citation: Şeyda Eraslan Taşpınar, Ali Kaya. (2016). Painting with the Multiple Intelligences: Defining Student Success and Permanence in Art Class. Journal of Education and Training Studies. https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v4i7.1684
title: Multiple Intelligence Theory (Gardner): eight mental dimensions guiding differentiated instruction
description: The article presents MIT as Gardner's framework holding that "individuals with different characteristics cannot learn in the same way" and that education should be shaped around defined individual differences. It "involves 8 mental dimensions defining individual differences": verbal-linguistic, logical-mathematical, visual-spatial, bodily-kinaesthetic, musical-rhythmic, social, intrapersonal, and naturalist intelligence. The study operationalises the theory by grouping students by intelligence profile and assigning intelligence-matched art activities.
requirements: Students' intelligence profiles must be identified (here via an MI inventory) so activities can be matched to intelligence groups
constraints: The article states using only some intelligence types in teaching may cause unfavourable effects for students with different intelligence properties
target_learning_goals: visual arts understanding and production (miniature picture topic)
examples: Students were categorised into intelligence groups from MI inventory results and given group-specific tasks such as writing stories, analysing symmetry, guided picture questions, role play, song writing, buzz groups, diary writing, and naming objects
key_sources: Şeyda Eraslan Taşpınar, Ali Kaya. (2016). Painting with the Multiple Intelligences: Defining Student Success and Permanence in Art Class. Journal of Education and Training Studies. https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v4i7.1684

article_title: Teaching Music as a University Elective Course through e-Learning
citation: Adileh, M. (2012). Teaching music as a university elective course through e-learning. Australian Journal of Music Education, 2012(1), 71-79. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ976542
title: Course website with multimedia-rich music learning materials (screen captures, assessment simulations, online tutorials)
description: The blended group used a website "developed like a small model of a learning management system" that students accessed with passwords to reach "systematically structured learning materials." Materials included online lecture notes and multimedia-rich components such as screen captures, assessment simulations, and online tutorials, supporting flexible pacing and repeated engagement with musical content.
requirements: Password-protected login and systematically structured learning materials
constraints: Used alongside 1.5-hour weekly FTF meetings, not as a standalone delivery method
target_learners: university students in an elective music course
target_learning_goals: music history, listening and appreciation, orchestral instruments, musical forms and notation
examples: Students could watch and rewatch videos, pause or rewind them, and perform instrument-usage simulations in a safe environment

article_title: The Effect of a Disability Camp Program on Attitudes towards the Inclusion of Children with Disabilities in a Summer Sport and Leisure Activity Camp
citation: Papaioannou, C., Evaggelinou, C., & Block, M. (2014). The effect of a disability camp program on attitudes towards the inclusion of children with disabilities in a summer sport and leisure activity camp. International Journal of Special Education, 29(1), 121-127.
title: Disability awareness programs in recreational settings should combine theoretical and practical activities including simulation, information, and interactive discussion
description: The article's DCP combined ten theoretical-practical activities including disability simulation sports, Paralympic Games information via lectures and videos, drawing activities, and end-of-day interactive discussions. The authors state the program's multifarious nature and the camp's enjoyable environment were key to its success. They recommend such programs be implemented in recreational and educational settings.
requirements: Programs need to be planned rather than happening spontaneously; content and duration appear to play a key role
constraints: Some activities like shooting a basketball from a wheelchair proved too difficult for children aged 11 years old; age of participants and choice of activities should be considered
target_learners: children without disabilities aged approximately 11 years in camp settings
target_learning_goals: positive attitudes toward inclusion of peers with disabilities
examples: The DCP involved ten activities over 20 consecutive days, each lasting 35 minutes, with children rotating through all activities in subgroups of approximately 20
key_sources: Papaioannou, C., Evaggelinou, C., & Block, M. (2014). The effect of a disability camp program on attitudes towards the inclusion of children with disabilities in a summer sport and leisure activity camp. International Journal of Special Education, 29(1), 121-127. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1033944

article_title: Effectiveness of Mutual Learning Approach in the Academic Achievement of B.Ed Students in Learning Optional II English
citation: Arulselvi, E. (2013). Effectiveness of Mutual Learning Approach in the Academic Achievement of B.Ed Students in Learning Optional II English. i-manager's Journal of English Language Teaching, 3(3), 25-31. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1078963
title: Mutual learning approach (learning by teaching) as an instructional method
description: Mutual learning is a small-group instructional technique in which students prepare and teach lessons or parts of lessons to classmates, choosing their own methods and didactic approaches rather than merely presenting. The article describes it as the method by Jean-Pol Martin, distinguishing it from tutoring because "the teacher has intensive control of, and gives support for, the learning process." In the study it was implemented with 25 B.Ed students in 5 teams of 5, contrasted with a traditionally taught control group.
requirements: Small-group structure with positive interdependence, individual accountability, designated roles with shared leadership, and directly taught communication skills, monitored by the group and instructor.
constraints: The article notes it should not be confused with student presentations or lectures, nor with tutoring.
target_learners: pupils and students in professional education
target_learning_goals: Subject content mastery
teamwork, planning abilities, reliability, presentation and moderation skills, self-confidence
examples: In the study, the experimental group of 25 learners worked in 5 teams of 5 members each, sharing information and ideas on topics selected from the Optional II English content.
key_sources: Arulselvi, E. (2013). Effectiveness of Mutual Learning Approach in the Academic Achievement of B.Ed Students in Learning Optional II English. i-manager's Journal of English Language Teaching, 3(3), 25-31. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1068866

article_title: Multimedia Modular Approach for Augmenting the Speaking Skill of the Student-Teachers
citation: Jose, G. R., & Dharma Raja, B. W. (2012). Multimedia Modular Approach for Augmenting the Speaking Skill of the Student-Teachers. i-manager's Journal of English Language Teaching, 2(4). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1075044
title: Multimedia module of 30 units for teaching speaking skill
description: The investigators prepared a multimedia module consisting of 30 units for teaching speaking skill to student-teachers. Each unit contained two audio and video clips of five to ten minutes each, with content accommodated to one hour per unit. The module covered phonology, minimal pairs, pronunciation, dialogue, intonation, stress and rhythm, accent, syllables, and description of people, places, events and objects. All content was fused with multimedia effects including audio, video, graphics, sound and animation.
requirements: Content and face validity was established through expert review by four experts from multimedia, software industry, psychology and English departments.
constraints: The module was designed specifically for B.Ed. student-teachers in the Indian context.
target_learning_goals: Speaking skill in English
Pronunciation and phonology
Dialogue and conversation
key_sources: Jose, G. R., & Dharma Raja, B. W. (2012). Multimedia Modular Approach for Augmenting the Speaking Skill of the Student-Teachers. i-manager's Journal of English Language Teaching, 2(4). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1070215

article_title: Multimedia Modular Approach for Augmenting the Speaking Skill of the Student-Teachers
citation: Jose, G. R., & Dharma Raja, B. W. (2012). Multimedia Modular Approach for Augmenting the Speaking Skill of the Student-Teachers. i-manager's Journal of English Language Teaching, 2(4). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1075044
title: Multimedia Modular Approach as a framework for language skill instruction
description: Multimedia Modular Approach is defined as a way or method of teaching a subject or language part with the help of a module, which is a division of a selected segment into small units in accordance with the strength of the portion to be taught, through different media including text, picture, animation, graphics, audio and video. It is described as a planned and organized combination for deriving maximum output in a particular communication situation, with potential for facilitating autonomous language learning where learners become self-achieving and assess their own progress.
requirements: Modules must be structured into small units matched to the strength of the content portion being taught.
constraints: The framework was developed and tested specifically in the context of English speaking-skill instruction for Indian B.Ed. student-teachers.
target_learning_goals: Speaking skill in English
Autonomous language learning
