article_title: Using Multi-Component Consultation to Increase the Integrity with Which Teachers Implement Behavioral Classroom Interventions: A Pilot Study
citation: Julie Sarno Owens, Erika K. Coles, Steven W. Evans, Lina K. Himawan, Erin Girio-Herrera, Alex S. Holdaway, Allison K. Zoromski, Terah Schamberg, and Ann Schulte. (2017). Using Multi-Component Consultation to Increase the Integrity with which Teachers Implement Behavioral Classroom Interventions: A Pilot Study. School Mental Health, 9, 218-234. https://doi.org/0.1007/s12310-017-9217-4
title: Multi-component consultation theory of change: simultaneously addressing teacher knowledge, skills, and beliefs to maximize intervention integrity
description: This framework holds that three malleable teacher characteristics — knowledge about best practices, skills to implement them, and beliefs about acceptability, feasibility, and one's own competence — act as facilitators or barriers to intervention integrity. Drawing on theories of adult learning and behavior change, it holds that "all three may need to be addressed to maximize the outcomes of consultation." The package therefore combines a knowledge component (fact sheets in each session), a skills component (observation, practice, and graphic performance feedback), and a beliefs component informed by motivational interviewing (values interviews, eliciting change talk, decisional balance, and Socratic questioning). The study tested whether this package outperforms best-practice consultation, particularly for teachers with barriers.
requirements: Consultation delivered by trained facilitators with integrity monitoring (facilitators achieved 92.93% average adherence across coded sessions)
constraints: The study was an underpowered pilot; support relies on interpretation of trends rather than statistical significance
The advantage was observed only among teachers with baseline knowledge, skill, or belief barriers
target_learners: elementary school teachers implementing behavioral classroom interventions
target_learning_goals: classroom management skills such as labeled praise and appropriate response to rule violations
implementation integrity of targeted interventions such as the daily report card
examples: Teachers in the multi-component condition received up to eight biweekly sessions including News You Can Use fact sheets, skills practice such as role playing and video model review, and beliefs work using values interviews and decisional balance
key_sources: Julie Sarno Owens, Erika K. Coles, Steven W. Evans, Lina K. Himawan, Erin Girio-Herrera, Alex S. Holdaway, Allison K. Zoromski, Terah Schamberg, and Ann Schulte. (2017). Using Multi-Component Consultation to Increase the Integrity with which Teachers Implement Behavioral Classroom Interventions: A Pilot Study. School Mental Health, 9, 218-234. https://doi.org/0.1007/s12310-017-9217-4

article_title: The Use of Music as a Way of Formation of Communicative Skills of Students in Teaching English Language
citation: R. M. Akhmadullina, A. R. Abdrafikova & N. V. Vanyukhina. (2016). The Use of Music as a Way of Formation of Communicative Skills of Students in Teaching English language. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(6), 1295-1302.
title: Indirect mechanism of music's effect on language learning via psycho-emotional and emotional state
description: The article's explanatory framework holds that music as an external factor affects the person "not directly but indirectly, through the internal factors", chiefly the psycho-physiological and emotional state of the student. Emotional state in turn modulates cognition: the methodological basis is the linguistic concept of emotions, in which "cognition raises emotions because it is emotiogenic and emotions cause cognition". Music also acts through analogies between music and speech, which share a rhythmic basis and arouse speech associations.
requirements: Teaching methods must take into account the psychophysiological and emotional state of students, as the discussion states for effective use of music
constraints: The article states it is too early to speak about direct effects of music on thinking processes; the claimed pathway is indirect
target_learners: junior university students, future teachers of English
target_learning_goals: foreign-language communicative skills in English
examples: The formation stage used selected instrumental works (e.g., Mozart, Beethoven, Tchaikovsky) chosen to form stable associations and influence emotional state
key_sources: R. M. Akhmadullina, A. R. Abdrafikova & N. V. Vanyukhina. (2016). The Use of Music as a Way of Formation of Communicative Skills of Students in Teaching English language. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(6), 1295-1302. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1114401

article_title: The Use of Music as a Way of Formation of Communicative Skills of Students in Teaching English Language
citation: R. M. Akhmadullina, A. R. Abdrafikova & N. V. Vanyukhina. (2016). The Use of Music as a Way of Formation of Communicative Skills of Students in Teaching English language. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(6), 1295-1302.
title: Use music to build a favourable psychological climate and sustain motivation in language classes
description: The article concludes that its identified methodological techniques of music and musical information "create favorable psychological climate, reduce the psychological tension, activate language activities, increase the emotional tone, support the motivation to study a foreign language". Music or songs listened to by the whole group simultaneously are said to promote team-building and fuller disclosure of each student's creative abilities. This principle frames why music belongs in lesson planning for pre-service language teachers.
requirements: Appropriate use of teaching methods in lesson planning, taking into account students' psychophysiological and emotional state
target_learners: university students, future teachers of English
target_learning_goals: motivation for foreign-language learning; communicative skills
examples: Instrumental music was used for mood creation, stress relief, emotional switching between activities, and adding national tints to communication situations
key_sources: R. M. Akhmadullina, A. R. Abdrafikova & N. V. Vanyukhina. (2016). The Use of Music as a Way of Formation of Communicative Skills of Students in Teaching English language. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(6), 1295-1302. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1114401

article_title: Towards a Practical Framework of the Remediation of Cognitive Skills at Primary Level
citation: Outi Kyrö-Ämmälä & Kaarina Määttä. (2011). Towards a Practical Framework of the Remediation of Cognitive Skills at Primary Level. World Journal of Education. https://doi.org/10.5430/wje.v1n1p28
title: Use multiple sense channels in teaching rather than relying on sight and hearing
description: The article states that "It is important, that the teacher utilizes different senses in teaching", because pupils' capacity to use information from different sense channels differs greatly and their working, learning and thinking styles vary. Learners may be visual, auditory, kinesthetic or tactile, and many use several channels, so the teacher must consciously employ different sense channels. The article adds that kinesthetic and tactile modalities remain central for most school-aged children through the primary level, a fact teachers usually ignore by leaning on sight and hearing.
requirements: The teacher must consciously take care to use different sense channels in teaching
constraints: Schools' facilities often offer little opportunity for versatile, sense-rich activity; classrooms and desks are treated as the prerequisite for learning
target_learners: primary-level pupils with differing sense-channel preferences
target_learning_goals: receiving and processing information through multiple senses
examples: The article describes a developmental sequence from whole-body (kinesthetic) learning in early childhood towards visual and, around age 11, auditory modality dominance
key_sources: Outi Kyrö-Ämmälä & Kaarina Määttä. (2011). Towards a Practical Framework of the Remediation of Cognitive Skills at Primary Level. World Journal of Education. https://doi.org/10.5430/wje.v1n1p28

article_title: The Effect of Multiple Intelligence Theory on Students' Academic Success in the Subject of Geometric Shapes in Elementary School
citation: Gülşah Batdal Karaduman & Halime Cihan. (2018). The Effect of Multiple Intelligence Theory on Students' Academic Success in the Subject of Geometric Shapes in Elementary School. International Journal of Higher Education, 7(2). https://doi.org/10.5430/ijhe.v7n2p227
title: Gardner's Multiple Intelligence Theory as a framework of nine areas of intelligence
description: The article presents Multiple Intelligence Theory, developed by Howard Gardner in the 1980s, as a constructivist approach holding that "human intelligence cannot be objectively measured by IQ tests in a traditional way" and that people have talents in different fields. Gardner divided intelligence into "areas with 9 different abilities": linguistic, logical-mathematical, spatial, bodily-kinesthetic, musical, interpersonal, intrapersonal, naturalist, and existential. The study operationalizes the theory by preparing curricula addressing these areas for a geometry unit.
requirements: Curricula must be prepared in accordance with the multiple intelligence areas for instruction to follow the theory
constraints: The article applies the theory to second-grade elementary mathematics on geometric objects
target_learning_goals: understanding geometric objects
mathematics achievement
examples: The experimental group's geometric objects unit was taught with curricula prepared according to the Multiple Intelligence Theory over 4 weeks
key_sources: Gülşah Batdal Karaduman & Halime Cihan. (2018). The Effect of Multiple Intelligence Theory on Students' Academic Success in the Subject of Geometric Shapes in Elementary School. International Journal of Higher Education, 7(2). https://doi.org/10.5430/ijhe.v7n2p227

article_title: Historic and Ethnic Music Found to Increase Geographic Understanding: A Quasi-Experimental Study
citation: Richardson, Ronald; Brouillette, Liane. (2013). Historic and Ethnic Music Found to Increase Geographic Understanding: A Quasi-Experimental Study. Journal for Learning through the Arts, 9(1). http://escholarship.org/uc/item/71g4x3cr
title: Music as a biologically grounded, cross-culturally powerful pedagogical tool
description: The article proposes that music's effectiveness in teaching cultural geography stems from its sensory directness and possible evolutionary roots. The authors note that "the mere presence of music in every known culture implies a genetic basis" and draw on Mithen's argument that pre-modern communication used holistic, pitch- and rhythm-based phrases, implying a common origin of language and music. If music is a formalized version of emotionally infused ancestral expression, this could explain its power to "cut through boredom and routine, communicating with primal directness, even in the face of cultural difference." The theory frames the study's engagement findings, though the authors flag it as speculative.
requirements: Further research to establish whether music is an adaptive function or a side effect of other evolved traits
constraints: The authors state "Further research is needed"; ethnomusicologists assume broad cultural differences in sound experience, so the universality premise is debated
target_learning_goals: cross-cultural understanding
engagement and interest in geography
historical empathy
examples: The authors contrast musical psychologists, who assume broad similarities in sound experience, with ethnomusicologists, who assume culture-bound differences
key_sources: Richardson, Ronald; Brouillette, Liane. (2013). Historic and Ethnic Music Found to Increase Geographic Understanding: A Quasi-Experimental Study. Journal for Learning through the Arts, 9(1). http://escholarship.org/uc/item/71g4x3cr

article_title: Problem Based Learning in Cooperative Situation (PBLCS) and Its Impact on Development of Personal Intelligence
citation: Ahmad Talib, Ismail Bin Kailani. (2014). Problem Based Learning in Cooperative Situation (PBLCS) and Its Impact on Development of Personal Intelligence. International Journal of Evaluation and Research in Education (IJERE), 3(4). http://iaesjournal.com/online/index.php/IJERE
title: Multiple intelligences theory: personal intelligences as developable through learning activities
description: The article draws on Gardner's multiple intelligences theory, which holds that "a person's intelligence can be developed through learning activities" and that intelligences are "changeable and dynamic". It focuses on the personal intelligences: interpersonal intelligence (social sensitivity, social vision, social communication) enabling students to understand others' moods, motives and intentions, and intrapersonal intelligence (identifying oneself, self-motivation, self-management) enabling self-knowledge and self-motivation. This framework supplies the study's two dependent variables.
requirements: Learning models that include elements or positive activities capable of developing multiple intelligences
constraints: Development "does not occur incidentally or immediately, but requires time and processes"
target_learning_goals: development of interpersonal and intrapersonal intelligence
examples: The interpersonal questionnaire was built on indicators of social sensitivity, social vision and social communication; the intrapersonal questionnaire on identifying himself, self-motivation and manage themselves
key_sources: Ahmad Talib, Ismail Bin Kailani. (2014). Problem Based Learning in Cooperative Situation (PBLCS) and Its Impact on Development of Personal Intelligence. International Journal of Evaluation and Research in Education (IJERE), 3(4). http://iaesjournal.com/online/index.php/IJERE

article_title: Multi-Component Communication Intervention for Children with Autism: A Randomized Controlled Trial
citation: Lauren H Hampton, Ann P Kaiser and Elizabeth A Fuller. (2020). Multi-component communication intervention for children with autism: A randomized controlled trial. Autism, 24(8), 2104–2116. https://doi.org/10.1177/1362361320934558
title: Multi-component communication intervention (DTT + JASP+EMT+SGD + caregiver training) for preverbal preschoolers with autism
description: A 36-session adaptive intervention delivered over 4 months combining three components: 'therapist-implemented DTT with the child to teach foundational skills', therapist-implemented JASP+EMT+SGD during play and routines, and caregiver training to implement JASP+EMT+SGD. Sessions occurred two clinic days and one home day per week (45–60 min), with three caregiver workshops. The intervention was adaptive: caregiver practice time increased with caregiver skill fluency and child DTT decreased as foundational skills were mastered. All families also received an iPad with Proloquo2Go and caregiver SGD programming training.
requirements: Children must be preverbal or at first-words stage (fewer than 20 different spontaneous words in a 20-min language sample) with a confirmed autism diagnosis
Master's-level therapists meeting fidelity criteria for all components; the same therapist implements all components for a family
constraints: Components were implemented at lower doses than previous studies of DTT and clinician-delivered JASP-EMT+SGD, which the authors state may have impacted effectiveness
target_learners: preschool children with autism (ages 3–5) who are preverbal or minimally verbal
target_learning_goals: joint attention
social communication
spoken language
foundational skills (imitation, receptive language, SGD use)
examples: In the trial, 68 children were randomized to intervention or community comparison; both groups received an SGD and caregiver SGD programming training
key_sources: Lauren H Hampton, Ann P Kaiser and Elizabeth A Fuller. (2020). Multi-component communication intervention for children with autism: A randomized controlled trial. Autism, 24(8), 2104–2116. https://doi.org/10.1177/1362361320934558

article_title: Longitudinal Impacts of the Children's Literacy Initiative Professional Development, Coaching, and Model Classroom Intervention on Early Literacy Achievement
citation: Parkinson, J., Meakin, J., & Salinger, T. (2015). Longitudinal Impacts of the Children's Literacy Initiative Professional Development, Coaching, and Model Classroom Intervention on Early Literacy Achievement. SREE Spring 2015 Conference. https://sree.org
title: Sustained, multi-year PD with classroom-embedded coaching can improve early-grade teachers' literacy instruction and, in kindergarten, student reading outcomes
description: The article's conclusion treats prolonged participation as the mechanism worth testing: "The impact of CLI on kindergarten word reading for two cohorts of students is promising evidence of the impact of prolonged participation in the CLI program." It further notes that "the significant impact of CLI on student achievement after only one year stands in contrast to a number of studies of professional development programs that have found no significant effects." The principle is that multi-year, coaching-embedded PD with model teachers can shift both practice and student outcomes, with effects appearing earliest in the earliest grades.
requirements: High-dosage, content-focused PD (98 hours in year 1 plus 49 in year 2 for colleague teachers) with classroom-embedded coaching and model teachers who mentor colleagues
constraints: The lack of effect in first grade despite high levels of implementation could indicate poor alignment of the coaching content with student learning objectives in that grade
target_learners: kindergarten through second grade teachers and their students in low-income, low-performing school districts
target_learning_goals: teacher literacy instructional practice, classroom environment, and early literacy achievement
examples: The i3 evaluation assigned 78 schools across four districts to treatment or control and found significant ELLCO practice gains and kindergarten PAR gains after two years of the program.
key_sources: Parkinson, J., Meakin, J., & Salinger, T. (2015). Longitudinal Impacts of the Children's Literacy Initiative Professional Development, Coaching, and Model Classroom Intervention on Early Literacy Achievement. SREE Spring 2015 Conference. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED562357

article_title: Family-Based Training Program Improves Brain Function, Cognition, and Behavior in Lower Socioeconomic Status Preschoolers
citation: Pakulak, E., Stevens, C., Bell, T. A., Fanning, J., Klein, S., Isbell, E., & Neville, H. (2013). Family-based training program improves brain function, cognition, and behavior in lower socioeconomic status preschoolers. SREE Fall 2013 Conference Abstract. https://www.sree.org
title: Target multiple pathways, including parents and the home environment, to narrow the SES school-readiness gap
description: The article concludes that programs targeting child attention through a family-based model involving both children and parents can change children's neurocognitive function and parents' caregiving behaviors within eight weeks. It recommends that "programs that target multiple pathways, including parents and the home environment, have the potential to narrow the large and growing gap in school readiness and academic achievement between higher and lower SES children."
requirements: Combine child-directed attention training with a parent-directed component addressing family stress regulation, discipline, responsiveness, and facilitation of child attention
constraints: Evidence comes from an eight-week program with lower SES Head Start families; the abstract presents potential rather than demonstrated long-term gap narrowing
target_learners: Lower SES preschool children and their families
target_learning_goals: School readiness and academic achievement via improved selective attention and caregiving behaviors
examples: PCMC-A paired children's small-group attention activities with parents' weekly classes, support calls, and home practice
key_sources: Pakulak, E., Stevens, C., Bell, T. A., Fanning, J., Klein, S., Isbell, E., & Neville, H. (2013). Family-based training program improves brain function, cognition, and behavior in lower socioeconomic status preschoolers. SREE Fall 2013 Conference Abstract. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED563293

article_title: Use of Multiple Representations in Developing Preservice Chemistry Teachers' Understanding of the Structure of Matter
citation: Yakmaci-Guzel, B., & Adadan, E. (2013). Use of multiple representations in developing preservice chemistry teachers' understanding of the structure of matter. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 8(1), 109-130. http://www.ijese.com/
title: Multiple-representational tasks combined with collaborative group work, whole-class discussion, and self-reflection for restructuring teachers' conceptions of matter
description: A lesson-level instructional pattern in which learners classify physical models (paper-clip arrangements), draw particulate representations of solids, liquids, gases, elements, compounds and mixtures, view dynamic animations, build play-dough models, and share and discuss representations. The article states that "multiple representational tasks, combined with collaborative group work, discussion, and self-reflection, provided preservice teachers an opportunity for generating more scientific representations of matter." The instruction lasted three class periods in two phases.
requirements: Tasks must span the macroscopic, submicroscopic, and symbolic representational levels
Whole-class discussion to reach consensus views about representations and definitions
constraints: The article notes the instruction gave no special attention to distinguishing homogeneous from heterogeneous mixtures, which it links to weaker gains on physical composition
target_learners: third-year students in a five-year teacher education program
target_learning_goals: understanding the structure of matter at three physical states
classifying elements, compounds, pure substances, and mixtures at different representational levels
examples: Groups classified seven zip-lock bags of coloured paper clips as mixtures or pure substances; participants drew particulate representations, viewed animations of solids, liquids, and gases, and built play-dough models of an element, a compound, and a mixture
key_sources: Yakmaci-Guzel, B., & Adadan, E. (2013). Use of multiple representations in developing preservice chemistry teachers' understanding of the structure of matter. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 8(1), 109-130. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1008597

article_title: The Impact of Musical Mnemonic on Vocabulary Recalling of Iranian Young Learners
citation: Bahrami, Z. N., Izadpanah, S. & Bijani, H. (2019). The Impact of Musical Mnemonic on Vocabulary Recalling of Iranian Young Learners. International Journal of Instruction, 12(1), 977-994. http://www.e-iji.net
title: Musical mnemonic word-list intervention: 14 validated vocabulary items sung to a familiar melody
description: A recorded musical mnemonic treatment in which a list of 14 unrelated vocabulary words from the coursebook Hey There 3A was harmonized to the familiar melody of "Let It Go" by Indina Menzel and recorded in a professional studio under skilled musicians' supervision. Word validity was checked by an expert panel of English teachers and musicians using Lawsh CVR (threshold above 0.42) and Waltz and Bausell CVI (acceptable index 0.79). The non-musical control heard the same words spoken at one word per second.
requirements: Words must be validated by an expert panel using Lawsh CVR and CVI before inclusion
The melody must be familiar to learners, since familiar melody "provides a link between melody and text"
Recording requires musicians familiar with correct English pronunciation of the words
constraints: The intervention was tested only with intermediate-level teenage EFL learners in an Iranian language institute using words from Hey There 3A
target_learners: teenage EFL learners (aged 14-19) at intermediate level
target_learning_goals: vocabulary remembering and recall
vocabulary comprehension of new words in new contexts
examples: The vocalist sang the 14-word list (goal, score, tackle, cheer, dressy, lazy, moody, scientific, genius, discount, borrow, beat, gloves, communicate) to the "Let It Go" melody for the experimental group
key_sources: Bahrami, Z. N., Izadpanah, S. & Bijani, H. (2019). The Impact of Musical Mnemonic on Vocabulary Recalling of Iranian Young Learners. International Journal of Instruction, 12(1), 977-994. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1201149

article_title: Multilevel Mixture Structural Equation Modeling with Propensity Score Weights for Quasi-Experimental Evaluation of Virtual Learning Environments
citation: Walter L. Leite, Zeyuan Jing, Huan Kuang, Dongho Kim & A. Corinne Huggins-Manley (2021). Multilevel Mixture Modeling with Propensity Score Weights for Quasi-Experimental Evaluation of Virtual Learning Environments. Structural Equation Modeling: A Multidisciplinary Journal, 28:6, 964-982. https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2021.1919895
title: Multilevel mixture modeling with propensity score weights operationalizing VLE usage as latent classes
description: This methodological framework treats VLE usage as a discrete latent variable: latent class analyses at student and classroom levels characterize usage patterns, generalized propensity scores with inverse probability weighting remove selection bias into classes, and Vermunt's three-step method accounts for classification uncertainty. The article states its objective is "to demonstrate a multilevel approach for quasi-experimental evaluation of VLEs which operationalizes treatment statuses as latent classes", extending Bray et al.'s single-level approach so that both students and classrooms are participants of usage groups.
requirements: Covariates in the propensity score model must be measured before VLE usage occurs or be time-invariant characteristics
Data on usage indicators from system logs and pre-usage covariates from student records are needed
constraints: The approach addresses settings where data on non-users may not be available and the construct validity of "VLE user" may not be well established
target_learners: secondary students using a VLE for algebra
target_learning_goals: Algebra I achievement as measured by a standardized end-of-course assessment
examples: Applied to Algebra Nation logs: four student classes and three classroom classes were identified, and ATEs and joint effects on the Algebra I EOC were estimated with planned contrasts of mean intercepts
key_sources: Walter L. Leite, Zeyuan Jing, Huan Kuang, Dongho Kim & A. Corinne Huggins-Manley (2021). Multilevel Mixture Modeling with Propensity Score Weights for Quasi-Experimental Evaluation of Virtual Learning Environments. Structural Equation Modeling: A Multidisciplinary Journal, 28:6, 964-982. https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2021.1919895

article_title: The Effects of Multiple Intelligences Instructional Strategy on the Environmental Awareness Knowledge and Environmental Attitude Levels of Elementary Students in Science Course
citation: Gökhan BAŞ. (2010). The Effects of Multiple Intelligences Instructional Strategy on the Environmental Awareness Knowledge and Environmental Attitude Levels of Elementary Students in Science Course. International Electronic Journal of Environmental Education, 1(1). http://www.iejeegreen.com
title: Gardner's theory of multiple intelligences as the framework for the instructional strategy
description: The article uses Gardner's theory, which "proposes a means to understanding many ways in which people are intelligent", holding that individuals can process information "in at least eight different ways": visual-spatial, bodily-kinaesthetic, musical-rhythmical, interpersonal, intrapersonal, logical-mathematical, verbal-linguistic, and naturalistic. It frames the theory as offering "eight ways of teaching and eight ways of learning", contrasting with traditional schooling directed only at verbal-linguistic and logical-mathematical intelligences.
requirements: Teachers must plan activities addressing the eight intelligences rather than only lecture-based verbal instruction
constraints: The article notes some teachers avoid MI because problems occur and traditional methods save time
target_learning_goals: environmental awareness knowledge
positive environmental attitudes
examples: The experiment group studied environmental topics through centres organized by intelligence type, then created projects integrating the eight intelligences
key_sources: Gökhan BAŞ. (2010). The Effects of Multiple Intelligences Instructional Strategy on the Environmental Awareness Knowledge and Environmental Attitude Levels of Elementary Students in Science Course. International Electronic Journal of Environmental Education, 1(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1055373

article_title: Effects of Multimedia on Knowledge, Understanding, Skills, Practice and Confidence in Environmental Sustainability: A Non-Equivalent Pre-Test-Post-Test, Quasi Experimental Design
citation: Ananta Kumar Jena, Satarupa Bhattacharjee, Pimily Langthasa. (2015). Effects of Multimedia on Knowledge, Understanding, Skills, Practice and Confidence in Environmental Sustainability: A Non-equivalent Pre-test-Post-test, Quasi Experimental Design. i-manager's Journal of Educational Technology, Vol. 12 No. 3, October-December 2015. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Effects+of+Multimedia+on+Knowledge%2C+Understanding%2C+Skills%2C+Practice+and+Confidence+in+Environmental+Sustainability%22
title: Multimedia in Environmental Sustainability Programme Feedback cum Questionnaire (Parts I and II)
description: A two-part instrument developed for the study to rate participants' knowledge, understanding, skills, practice and confidence before and after the multimedia programme. Part I is a feedback scale of "ten dichotomous (i.e. yes/no) type items" with "content validity ratio of part I of the questionnaire was .65 whereas the KR20  reliability was .74". Part II is a 25-item four-point Likert-type rating scale (Poor, Fair, Good, Excellent) scored Poor=0 to Excellent=1, with content validity ratio .66 and Cronbach's alpha .74. Items cover topics such as solid waste management, rain water harvesting, and sustainable transport.
requirements: Administered before and after the multimedia programme to obtain comparable pre and post total scores
constraints: Developed and validated within this single study's sample of secondary school students, local community members, and university students in Silchar, India
target_learning_goals: Knowledge, understanding, skills, practice, and confidence in environmental sustainability
examples: Used on 17 September 2014 at Assam University and on 16 September 2014 at Irongmara High School alongside a forty-minute MP4 CD on environmental awareness
key_sources: Ananta Kumar Jena, Satarupa Bhattacharjee, Pimily Langthasa. (2015). Effects of Multimedia on Knowledge, Understanding, Skills, Practice and Confidence in Environmental Sustainability: A Non-equivalent Pre-test-Post-test, Quasi Experimental Design. i-manager's Journal of Educational Technology, Vol. 12 No. 3, October-December 2015. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Effects+of+Multimedia+on+Knowledge%2C+Understanding%2C+Skills%2C+Practice+and+Confidence+in+Environmental+Sustainability%22

article_title: Investigating the Longitudinal Effects of a Core Mathematics Program on Evidence-Based Teaching Practices in Mathematics
citation: Doabler, C. T., Nelson, N. J., Kennedy, P. C., Stoolmiller, M., Fien, H., Clarke, B., Gearin, B., Smolkowski, K., & Baker, S. K. (2018). Investigating the longitudinal effects of a core mathematics program on evidence-based teaching practices in mathematics. Learning Disability Quarterly, 41(3), 144–158. https://doi.org/10.1177/0731948718756040
title: Provide teachers with sustained multi-year experience and professional development with explicit mathematics programs to sustain and enhance evidence-based practices
description: The article suggests additional years of experience with explicit mathematics programs may serve as an optimal mechanism to enhance teachers' use of evidence-based practices, and recommends increasing professional development opportunities to help sustain implementation. The article states "Additional years of experience with such programs may serve as an optimal mechanism to enhance teachers' use of evidence-based practices."
requirements: Teachers need ongoing professional development workshops distributed across the school year, such as the four 6-hour workshops aligned to ELM's quarterly teacher manuals
constraints: Cross-sectional effect sizes favoring second-year teachers were non-significant, and the effect for individual responses was quite small
target_learners: Kindergarten teachers implementing explicit mathematics programs
target_learning_goals: Sustained teacher implementation of explicit mathematics instruction
examples: ELM teachers participated in four 6-hour workshops distributed across the school year according to the program's quarterly teacher manuals
key_sources: Doabler, C. T., Nelson, N. J., Kennedy, P. C., Stoolmiller, M., Fien, H., Clarke, B., Gearin, B., Smolkowski, K., & Baker, S. K. (2018). Investigating the longitudinal effects of a core mathematics program on evidence-based teaching practices in mathematics. Learning Disability Quarterly, 41(3), 144–158. https://doi.org/10.1177/0731948718756040

article_title: Impact of Electronic Teaching Materials on Process of Education--Results of an Experiment
citation: Záhorec, J., Hašková, A., & Munk, M. (2010). Impact of Electronic Teaching Materials on Process of Education – Results of an Experiment. Informatics in Education, 9(2), 261–281. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ894821
title: Multimedia teaching materials must offer interactivity and hands-on student use to influence attitudes
description: The article concludes that the effect of electronic teaching materials on students' attitudes depends on the interactivity level and on hands-on activities: "not any way of the use of multimedia materials in teaching process has an automatical impact on students". Merely presenting multimedia demonstrations, as in the lower-interactivity CD group, was insufficient to elicit attitude change, while the group working directly with animations and simulations showed significant positive shifts.
requirements: Students must have the possibility to work with the materials and gain hands-on experience, either at school or at home
Materials need a high level of interactivity (e.g. flash animations and interactive simulations)
constraints: Presentation-only use of multimedia materials did not produce significant attitude changes in this experiment
target_learning_goals: Improving attitudes toward unpopular science subjects such as physics
examples: Used in experimental group A during regular physics lessons and seminars over a 3-month pedagogical experiment
key_sources: Záhorec, J., Hašková, A., & Munk, M. (2010). Impact of Electronic Teaching Materials on Process of Education – Results of an Experiment. Informatics in Education, 9(2), 261–281. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1064255

article_title: Learning Vocabulary in a Foreign Language: A Computer Software Based Model Attempt
citation: Yelbay Yılmaz, Y. (2015). Learning vocabulary in a foreign language: A computer software based model attempt. Journal of Language and Linguistic Studies, 11(2), 23-38. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1075414
title: Multi-channel encoding model for vocabulary learning
description: The article proposes that vocabulary is learned and retained more effectively when encoded through multiple memory pathways rather than a single channel. Drawing on the multi store model, dual coding, elaboration, and retrieval practice, the model holds that "in order to ensure better encoding, the same word could be represented in different forms and thus stor ed in different memory systems that would make recall and retrieval easier for the learner."
requirements: Learners must engage with words through multiple representations such as visuals, sound, and elaborative processing
constraints: The article states that how these concepts affect retention is a broad topic that cannot be discussed in detail within the study's scope
target_learning_goals: Encoding and retrieval of vocabulary items in long-term memory
examples: The Parole software operationalizes this model by allowing each word to be encoded via visuals, music, keyword mnemonics, and elaborative sentence writing
key_sources: Yelbay Yılmaz, Y. (2015). Learning vocabulary in a foreign language: A computer software based model attempt. Journal of Language and Linguistic Studies, 11(2), 23-38. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1105162

article_title: Effectiveness of Multipurpose Unit Early Classroom Intervention Program for 4-5-Year-Old Children
citation: Ozlem CELEBIOGLU MORKOC & Ebru AKTAN ACAR. (2014). Effectiveness of Multipurpose Unit Early Classroom Intervention Program for 4–5-Year-Old Children. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice. https://doi.org/10.12738/estp.2014.5.2065
title: Multipurpose Unit Early Classroom Intervention Program (MUECIP)
description: MUECIP is a center-based early intervention program developed by the researchers for 4–5-year-old (48–60 months) children whose development is at risk because of family socioeconomic conditions. It was built after examining programs such as Head Start, Incredible Years and Portage and models including "Orff's Persona Dolls and High/Scope Approaches". It was "conducted 4 days a week with 5 activities every day for 13 weeks", with weekly field trips, parent participation forms, home visits and one-hour individual family interviews.
requirements: Delivery required the researcher and informed undergraduate support students, a prepared classroom environment with routine graphics and boards, and family participation components
constraints: Evaluated only with 4–5-year-old children from lower socioeconomic families in Canakkale Province in a 13-week implementation
target_learners: 4–5-year-old children at developmental risk due to socioeconomic conditions
target_learning_goals: promoting all child developmental areas: cognitive, psychomotor, language, personal-social and self-care skills, and preparing children for nursery class
examples: In the study, MUECIP was applied to the 14-child experimental group at the ÇABA Multipurpose Early Childhood Classroom Unit between 22 November 2010 and 18 February 2011
key_sources: Ozlem CELEBIOGLU MORKOC & Ebru AKTAN ACAR. (2014). Effectiveness of Multipurpose Unit Early Classroom Intervention Program for 4–5-Year-Old Children. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice. https://doi.org/10.12738/estp.2014.5.2065

article_title: Evaluating the Flipped Classroom Model through the Multi-Complementary Approach
citation: Talan, T. & Batdi, V. (2020). Evaluating the Flipped Classroom Model through the Multi-Complementary Approach. Turkish Online Journal of Distance Education-TOJDE, 21(4). https://tojde.anadolu.edu.tr
title: Multi-complementary approach (MCA): a three-stage mixed-methods evaluation framework
description: The MCA is the article's own methodological framework for combining quantitative and qualitative evidence under a single roof, grounded in constructivist learning theory and the Gestalt holistic approach. It "consists of three basic stages, which allow access to pre-complementary, post-complementary and complementary information": a literature stage (meta-analysis plus meta-thematic analysis), an application stage (an experimental implementation plus participant interviews), and a synthesis stage combining both. The authors present MCA as distinct from standard mixed-methods approaches because single data sources are deemed insufficient and results are gathered "under a single roof".
requirements: Multiple data sources and analysis programs dealing with a common area of interest, with results combined across stages
constraints: The authors state the concept was preferred because existing mixed-method labels did not exactly correspond to the approach adopted in the present study
target_learning_goals: Evaluating the effectiveness of instructional models through combined quantitative and qualitative evidence
examples: The article applied MCA to FCM: 64 studies meta-analysed, 32 studies meta-thematically analysed, and an experiment with 64 teacher candidates, synthesised in the complementary information stage
key_sources: Talan, T. & Batdi, V. (2020). Evaluating the Flipped Classroom Model through the Multi-Complementary Approach. Turkish Online Journal of Distance Education-TOJDE, 21(4). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1269613

article_title: Assessing Implementation Fidelity: Challenges as Seen through the Lens of Two Experimental Studies
citation: Vig, R., Taylor, M. W., Star, J. R., & Chao, T. (2014). Assessing implementation fidelity: Challenges as seen through the lens of two experimental studies. SREE Spring 2014 Conference. https://www.sree.org/conferences/2014/annualmeeting/abstracts/view.asp
title: Use multiple measures of implementation fidelity to gain different perspectives on teacher adaptation, particularly during early stages of the research cycle
description: The Contrasting Cases project used three fidelity measures: video coding rubrics, a twice-yearly instructional practices survey, and a teacher log. The researchers conclude that the use of multiple measures provides different perspectives on teacher adaptation, which can be of considerable value during early stages in the research cycle when the intervention is still in the process of revision.
requirements: Develop and pilot fidelity instruments designed by research team members to improve validity
Collect videos of lessons and code them with binary yes/no rubrics about the presence of key features
constraints: The predictive value of different measures may not differ in determining student outcome measures, bringing the notion that more is better into question
When two teachers have the same fidelity score, similarities in their scores might obscure important differences in their classroom practice
target_learning_goals: maintaining high-level cognitive demand during curriculum implementation
examples: In the Contrasting Cases project, approximately 100 8th and 9th grade Algebra I teachers were randomly assigned to treatment or control, and implementation fidelity was assessed three ways: video coding rubrics, a twice-yearly instructional practices survey, and a teacher log
key_sources: Vig, R., Taylor, M. W., Star, J. R., & Chao, T. (2014). Assessing implementation fidelity: Challenges as seen through the lens of two experimental studies. SREE Spring 2014 Conference. https://www.sree.org/conferences/2014/annualmeeting/abstracts/view.asp

article_title: Integrating Argument-Based Science Inquiry with Modal Representations: Impact on Science Achievement, Argumentation, and Writing Skills
citation: Demirbag, M., & Gunel, M. (2014). Integrating Argument-Based Science Inquiry with Modal Representations: Impact on Science Achievement, Argumentation, and Writing Skills. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice, 14(1), 386-391. https://doi.org/10.12738/estp.2014.1.1632
title: Multi-modal representations as essential elements of meaningful science learning
description: The article frames multi-modal representations as "forms to demonstrate concepts or convey an understanding in the form of a picture, text, diagram, or mathematical expression" (e.g. text, mathematical formulas, graphs, and tables). Drawing on Generative Learning Theory, Dual Coding Learning Theory, and Generative Theory of Multimedia Learning, researchers argue that modal representations are "the essential elements for learning meaningful science and for building necessary science literacy skills." This study applies the framework by adding multi-modal instruction to argument-based inquiry.
requirements: Instruction that makes the roles and functions of different modes explicit to learners
constraints: The article notes prior studies largely did not focus on modal representations within argument-based settings, calling for further consideration
target_learning_goals: meaningful science learning
science literacy
examples: The treatment group experienced multi-staged multi-modal instruction covering roles and functions of modes, integration into written communication, and evaluation of written materials with modal representations.
key_sources: Demirbag, M., & Gunel, M. (2014). Integrating Argument-Based Science Inquiry with Modal Representations: Impact on Science Achievement, Argumentation, and Writing Skills. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice, 14(1), 386-391. https://doi.org/10.12738/estp.2014.1.1632

article_title: Bridging the Gaps: Multimodal Theme-Sets in the Global Composition Classroom
citation: Ruefman, D. (2015). Bridging the Gaps: Multimodal Theme-Sets in the Global Composition Classroom. The CATESOL Journal, 27(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1085663
title: Multimodal theme-sets: thematically linked supplemental texts reinforcing a core reading
description: A multimodal theme-set is "a collection of readings that are thematically linked to a common core text and may comprise anything from children's books and novellas to video clips and interactive games." Commonalities among the texts help students make connections that reinforce key concepts from the primary reading. The article illustrates the pattern with a logical-fallacies unit pairing a Goshgarian chapter with web texts and YouTube videos.
requirements: Supplemental resources must be thematically linked to the same topics discussed in the core reading
constraints: Student motivation is imperative; resources should appeal cross-culturally and reflect class demographics
target_learners: L2 international students in mainstream first-year composition
target_learning_goals: comprehension of core course concepts
applied rhetorical knowledge in writing
examples: A logical fallacy unit pairing the Goshgarian core chapter with Writing Commons and Purdue OWL web texts and a YouTube critical thinking playlist
key_sources: Ruefman, D. (2015). Bridging the Gaps: Multimodal Theme-Sets in the Global Composition Classroom. The CATESOL Journal, 27(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1111750

article_title: Detecting Intervention Effects Using a Multilevel Latent Transition Analysis with a Mixture IRT Model
citation: Sun-Joo Cho, Allan S. Cohen, and Brian Bottge. (2013). Detecting Intervention Effects Using a Multilevel Latent Transition Analysis with a Mixture IRT Model. Psychometrika. https://doi.org/10.1007/S11336-012-9314-0
title: Multilevel latent transition analysis with a mixture IRT measurement model (multilevel LTA–MixIRTM)
description: The multilevel LTA–MixIRTM extends latent transition analysis by incorporating a mixture IRT measurement model into a two-level LTA, so that "change can be accounted for as a transition from one latent class to another and as progress or lack thereof along a latent continuous variable (e.g., ability) within a latent class." It models students nested within teachers, with teacher-level latent classes characterized by different proportions of student-level latent classes, and regresses transition proportions on intervention status at the teacher level. The article presents it as the first model to simultaneously combine a continuous latent variable within a mixture, a latent Markov process for longitudinal data, and a multilevel data structure.
requirements: Anchor items are needed to ensure scale comparability among latent classes
Item parameter invariance across time points and group-level latent classes is assumed
constraints: The large number of transition patterns in LCM-based multilevel LTA makes parameter estimation difficult unless sample size is large
target_learners: adolescent middle-school students with math disabilities in special education settings
target_learning_goals: fraction computation and problem-solving skills
examples: Applied to a cluster-randomized study comparing Enhanced Anchored Instruction with business as usual in 31 middle schools
key_sources: Sun-Joo Cho, Allan S. Cohen, and Brian Bottge. (2013). Detecting Intervention Effects Using a Multilevel Latent Transition Analysis with a Mixture IRT Model. Psychometrika. https://doi.org/10.1007/S11336-012-9314-0

article_title: Word Knowledge and Comprehension Effects of an Academic Vocabulary Intervention for Middle School Students
citation: McKeown, M. G., Crosson, A. C., Moore, D. W., & Beck, I. L. (2018). Word Knowledge and Comprehension Effects of an Academic Vocabulary Intervention for Middle School Students. American Educational Research Journal. https://doi.org/10.3102/0002831217744181
title: Teach academic words through multiple authentic contexts and active processing rather than definitions alone
description: The article argues that vocabulary instruction likely to support comprehension is based on multiple encounters with words in varied contexts and active processing, a consensus the authors trace to reviews from the 1980s onward. RAVE instantiates this by presenting each word in a pair of authentic contexts from different domains, prompting students to integrate word meaning with context, and sequencing activities from simpler to more complex processing across seven-day lesson cycles.
requirements: Multiple encounters with words in varied contexts and active engagement with words
constraints: Evidence of transfer to new words and reading comprehension from morphology instruction is often small
target_learning_goals: academic vocabulary knowledge supporting reading comprehension
examples: RAVE lessons sequenced activities from choosing a context that fits a word to using words in writing, with a writing activity in Lesson 6 followed by students sharing what they had written.
key_sources: McKeown, M. G., Crosson, A. C., Moore, D. W., & Beck, I. L. (2018). Word Knowledge and Comprehension Effects of an Academic Vocabulary Intervention for Middle School Students. American Educational Research Journal. https://doi.org/10.3102/0002831217744181

article_title: Fostering Team Creativity in Higher Education Settings
citation: de Villiers Scheepers, M. J. & Maree, L. (2015). Fostering Team Creativity in Higher Education Settings. e-Journal of Business Education & Scholarship of Teaching, 9(1). http://www.ejbest.org
title: Assess skills development multiple times across stickiness stages to ensure effects endure
description: The article argues that investing in creativity development is of little use unless effects endure over time, so "skills development should be assessed multiple times over several stickiness stages, to ensure the effects endure over time". Measuring only immediately after a workshop may yield biased results if participants have highly positive feelings but no real skills transfer. Tracking over time enables learners and educators to examine the relevance of graduate attributes in the future world of work.
requirements: Multiple measurements at different time intervals, including a retrospective pre-rating and a delayed post-rating (e.g. three months)
constraints: Voluntary participation produced substantial sample attrition from initiation to integration stage
target_learning_goals: graduate attribute development
team creative skills
examples: The study measured skills at O1 (before), O2 (immediately after) and O3 (three months later, with retrospective and current ratings)
key_sources: de Villiers Scheepers, M. J. & Maree, L. (2015). Fostering Team Creativity in Higher Education Settings. e-Journal of Business Education & Scholarship of Teaching, 9(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1167371

article_title: "The Joy of Reading"--An Intervention Program to Increase Reading Motivation for Pupils with Learning Disabilities
citation: Tovli, E. (2014). "The Joy of Reading" - An Intervention Program to Increase Reading Motivation for Pupils with Learning Disabilities. Journal of Education and Training Studies, 2(4). http://dx.doi.org/10.11114/jets.v2i4.496
title: Multi-sensory, multi-intelligence reading activities matched to learning-disability profiles
description: The intervention matched activity design to specific difficulty profiles: short-term activities for attention difficulties, multi-sensory stimuli for perception difficulties, repetitive structured activities for processing difficulties, and systematic exposure to new words for language difficulties. Differentiated instruction challenged learners through individual capabilities, interests, and preferred learning styles, with literate products displayed to build personal competence and self-confidence.
requirements: Assessment of each pupil's difficulty profile
Display of pupil-produced literate products
Activities that avoid confronting pupils with their difficulties
constraints: Developed for pupils with learning disabilities whose IQ is normal and reading ability is below age norm
target_learning_goals: Reading motivation
Self-efficacy as a reader
Story schema development
examples: Discovery reading stopped mid-sentence for pupils to guess continuations using semantic and morphological knowledge

citation: Hernández-González Samuel, Gómez-Climent María Ángeles, Clemente-Soriano Albert, Alba Robles Jose Luis, Caurín-Alonso Carlos, Solbes Jordi (2026). Reduced cognitive empathy and differences in EEG activity in low-achieving adolescents. PLOS One 21(10): e0361520. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0361520
title: Use a multimethod approach combining self-report, behavioural, and neurophysiological indicators to characterise socioemotional functioning, interpreting the measures as complementary rather than convergent.
description: The article argues that combining self-report questionnaires, behavioural tests, and EEG recordings provides complementary perspectives on socioemotional functioning: a multimethod approach "may provide complementary information and reduce reliance on any single measure". Because the three indicators "assess partially distinct aspects of socioemotional functioning", differences in one measure (e.g. self-reported cognitive empathy) should not be read as confirmation of a deficit on another (e.g. facial emotion recognition accuracy). The authors apply this by reporting the self-report, behavioural, and electrophysiological results as "complementary observations rather than convergent evidence of a single socioemotional or neural deficit".
requirements: Self-report, behavioural, and electrophysiological indicators must be interpreted as assessing partially distinct aspects of socioemotional functioning, not as interchangeable measures of one construct.
constraints: EEG findings from limited electrode configurations are exploratory and cannot establish precise anatomical localisation or confirm behavioural deficits.
target_learners: Adolescents aged 14–17 in secondary school, including students in learning support or reinforcement programmes
target_learning_goals: Cognitive and affective empathy
Facial emotion recognition
Social and personal values development
examples: The study assessed 40 adolescents with the Basic Empathy Scale, a 56-image Karolinska Directed Emotional Faces recognition test, and EEG recordings during the task, then reported the three measure types as complementary observations.

citation: Stolze Franka, Lehm Manuel, Behme Daniel, Fuchs Erelle, Schwab Roland. (2026). Comparison of video-based and presentation-based self-directed instruction for learning basic neuroangiography. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-10418-0
title: Multimedia learning and cognitive load account for video-based procedural instruction benefits and costs
description: The article interprets its findings through Mayer's cognitive theory of multimedia learning and cognitive load theory: "combining visual demonstration with verbal explanation can support the integration of procedural information, particularly when learners have limited prior knowledge". Expert-narrated videos are said to reduce cognitive load by providing a coherent visual sequence with verbal explanation, helping novices build a spatial and procedural model of catheter navigation. Applying that newly built model during hands-on performance, however, consumes working-memory resources, which the authors use to explain the longer fluoroscopy times and the precision-before-fluency pattern in novices.
requirements: Applies to learners with limited prior knowledge; experienced learners' existing procedural schemes reduce the added value of the video format.
constraints: The account is the authors' interpretation of an exploratory study, not a tested mechanism in this article.
target_learners: Novice medical students and residents learning procedural skills
target_learning_goals: Procedural and spatial understanding of catheter navigation
examples: The authors explain that video-trained novices may develop precision before fluency, with automation reducing the time cost over repeated guided practice.

description: This pattern organizes a single-day learning event around multiple distinct clinical scenarios, each with defined tasks and learning objectives tied to basic science concepts. Students "assumed different roles within a healthcare team," worked in small groups (average 5 students per day), and rotated through scenarios including one with a live standardized patient, preceded by a traditional lecture and followed by structured debriefing.

Small team sizes to allow active role participation

clinical skills such as intubation and CPR

title: Role-separated multiagent LLM framework comprising Student, Patient, Evaluator, and Feedback agents for psychotherapy training simulation and rubric-based fidelity assessment
description: The article introduces a role-separated multiagent LLM framework in which four specialized agents serve distinct functions within one simulation workflow: a Student agent conducts the synthetic psychotherapy encounter, a Patient agent enacts structured profiles with case-consistent responses, an Evaluator agent scores the completed transcript against predefined rubric criteria, and a Feedback agent generates criterion-referenced narrative recommendations. title: Continuum of multidisciplinary, interdisciplinary, and transdisciplinary learning
description: The article distinguishes three modes of integrating disciplines, representing "a continuum from partial to full integration of disciplines." Multidisciplinary learning involves parallel analysis by several disciplines without true integration; interdisciplinary learning emphasizes integration and interaction between disciplines, with students synthesizing knowledge from multiple fields; transdisciplinary learning involves synthesizing new knowledge into a unified field through the learner's exploration of fragmented disciplinary knowledge. This taxonomy frames the study's interdisciplinary TBL session as distinct from merely parallel disciplinary teaching.
requirements: For interdisciplinary learning: integration and interaction between disciplines rather than parallel analysis
For transdisciplinary learning: learner exploration of fragmented disciplines to establish a new synthesis
constraints: The article notes most interdisciplinary courses are offered at advanced undergraduate or postgraduate levels, though it argues undergraduate participation is beneficial
target_learning_goals: Synthesizing knowledge from multiple disciplines
Developing novel perspectives on a topic
Crossing disciplinary boundaries
examples: The study's session on bronchial asthma asked teams to answer questions emphasizing the specific contributions of each discipline to pathophysiology, diagnosis, and management

Wearable smart glasses record first-person video, gaze, and audio from all team members; fixations are mapped to five areas of interest ("patient," "member," "device," "screen," "unknown") and eye-contact events are detected with YOLOv8-based face detection combined with gaze-vector estimation. title: Multidimensional academic readiness framework integrating Bandura's self-efficacy theory, Pintrich's self-regulated learning, and Tinto's academic integration theory
description: The article proposes a multidimensional academic readiness framework grounded in three theories: Bandura's self-efficacy theory, Pintrich's model of self-regulated learning, and Tinto's theory of academic integration. The framework holds that "academic referrals are not exclusively a result of institutional shortcomings but may reflect deeper disparities in academic readiness at the point of entry into professional training." It integrates prior academic background (SHS programme and core subject performance) with self-efficacy beliefs and self-regulated learning behaviours, extending existing theoretical discourse beyond post-enrolment determinants. The framework treats institutional support not as an independent forecaster but as a controlling variable, and positions academic risk identification as anticipatory rather than reactive.
requirements: The framework requires integration of objective pre-tertiary academic indicators (SHS programme, WASSCE grades) with validated measures of psychological preparedness constructs within a theoretically grounded model.
constraints: The article states that students with low academic readiness may still be at peril even with the best environmental supports, per Tinto's theory.

target_learning_goals: Academic performance (GPA) and reduction of academic referral risk in professional nursing education

title: Use multiple role-specific LLM agents with memory mapping rather than a single chatbot interface for guideline-based team simulation
description: The article recommends structuring LLM training simulations as several role-specific agents linked through shared memory instead of one direct chatbot. It states that "the use of multiple role-specific agents with memory mapping further reduced inconsistency and improved adherence to ACLS guidelines", and that this design "addresses common weaknesses of single agent chatbots and supports consistent, reproducible training in critical care scenarios." Structured role-specific prompts and closed-loop communication protocols binding outputs to guideline content
constraints: Potential biases stemming from the pre-defined AI role traits and prompt engineering may have influenced system performance
Agents may not fully capture non-verbal cues and emotional interactions in real resuscitation situations
target_learners: Emergency medicine trainees and physicians practicing resuscitation team leadership
target_learning_goals: Consistent, guideline-compliant team-member responses during simulated resuscitation
examples: The authors contrast their four-agent Claude 3.5 Sonnet system with prior ChatGPT-based single-agent approaches that skipped critical steps and gave inconsistent responses to identical inputs

article_title: Job competence gap of quantity surveying graduates of higher vocational colleges with a high dimensional measurement error model.
citation: Huangfu Dongmei, Chang Yun Fah. (2026). Job competence gap of quantity surveying graduates of higher vocational colleges with a high dimensional measurement error model. PLOS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0328617
title: MULFR model with R² as a competency gap measure for multidimensional self-report data
description: The multidimensional unreplicated linear functional relationship (MULFR) model compares two sets of p-dimensional variables—graduate competencies and industry expectations—both measured with error via questionnaires, yielding a single coefficient of determination. The article states "1−Rp2 measure the competency gap reflected on the fresh graduated quantity surveyors," with criteria adapted from Cohen classifying gaps as large, medium, small, or none. This study is presented as the first application of MULFR to competency gap analysis.
requirements: Both the response and independent variable sets are subject to measurement error, which the model's expanded assumptions accommodate
Multidimensional domains and indicators must be compared as a single model rather than pairwise
constraints: The purposive sampling method means the sample is not statistically representative of the entire national population of QS HVC graduates
Rp2 differences below 5% are regarded as inconsequential by the study's own criterion
target_learners: recent higher vocational college graduates in quantity surveying
target_learning_goals: professional competency development across knowledge, skills, personality, and ethics domains
examples: The model was applied to 324 valid questionnaire responses scored on a five-point Likert scale across 20 competency indicators in four domains

article_title: Executive function predicts academic and social skills in autistic kindergartners based on a multimodal approach.
citation: Choi, B., Lee, H., Kuhn, L., Kim, J., Hong, S.-J., Di Martino, A., Gozzi, A., Lombardo, M. V., Morrison, F. J., Lord, C., & Kim, S. H. (2026). Executive function predicts academic and social skills in autistic kindergartners based on a multimodal approach. Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, and Allied Disciplines. https://doi.org/10.1111/jcpp.70038
title: Assess executive function multimodally — combining computerized tasks, behavioral observation, and informant report — to capture its broader impact on developmental outcomes
description: The article argues that because different EF measurement approaches complement each other — computerized tasks provide precise data but may lack ecological validity, behavioral observations capture naturalistic performance, and informant measures add day-to-day perspective — no single assessment captures the entire scope of EF. The study itself used "three distinct, yet complementary, methods" and found different measures related to different outcomes. The authors conclude "the importance of a multimeasurement approach to EF assessment, as it provides a more comprehensive understanding of the broader impact of EF on key developmental outcomes in ASD."
requirements: Assessment must include at least computerized EF tasks, behavioral observation, and informant report to cover different EF contexts
constraints: The article notes observed correlations among measures were small to moderate and only a subset of children completed all three EF measures
target_learners: Cognitively able, verbal autistic kindergartners aged 4–6 years
target_learning_goals: Executive function skills supporting academic achievement and peer play/social skills
examples: The study measured EF with EF Touch, HTKS, and BRIEF-II at kindergarten entry and exit and found each measure predicted different outcomes

Executive function predicts academic and social skills in autistic kindergartners based on a multimodal approach. article_title: Stereotype Threat and a Multiple Identity Intervention Among First- and Second-Generation Students of Migrant Descent.
citation: Mocevic, H., and B. Gniewosz. 2025. "Stereotype Threat and a Multiple Identity Intervention Among First‐ and Second‐Generation Students of Migrant Descent." Journal of Community Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1002/jcop.70065
title: Multiple identity vs. single identity priming intervention (adapted Aspects of Identity Questionnaire vs. Collective Self-Esteem Scale)
description: A brief pre-test identity priming manipulation in which students either reflected on multiple aspects of the self via a 22-item adapted Aspects of Identity Questionnaire covering "personal", "relational", "social", and "collective" aspects rated on a 5-point Likert scale (about 5 min), or reflected on a single cultural identity via a six-item adapted Collective Self-Esteem Scale. A manipulation check showed a significant association between condition and identity self-descriptions, χ²(1) = 22.59, p < 0.001, with coding agreement Cohen's κ = 0.67.
requirements: Administered before a performance task so that identity salience is active during the test; effectiveness was checked with an open-ended "Who am I?" self-description
constraints: The authors state the brief questionnaire "might not have led to a sufficiently in‐depth reflection" and may not have contained the identity dimensions most relevant to participants
target_learners: Secondary school students in grades 9 and 10, including students of migrant descent
target_learning_goals: Maintaining academic test performance in evaluative, stereotype-relevant situations
examples: Students in the multiple identity condition rated the importance of 22 identity aspects; those in the single identity condition rated six collective self-esteem items about their cultural background.
key_sources: Mocevic, H., and B. Gniewosz. 2025. "Stereotype Threat and a Multiple Identity Intervention Among First‐ and Second‐Generation Students of Migrant Descent." Journal of Community Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1002/jcop.70065

article_title: Assessing shared decision-making: a case study of third-year medical student standardized patient encounters.
citation: Induru Vikranth, Deffendall Catherine, Theobald Ceceila, Green Jennifer, Ridinger Heather. (2025). Assessing shared decision-making: a case study of third-year medical student standardized patient encounters. International Journal of Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.5116/ijme.676f.d093
title: Use multisource feedback (self, standardized patient, faculty) when assessing communication skills
description: The study's central design recommendation: communication-skill assessment should not rely on self-assessment alone. The authors "demonstrated the limitations of self-perception of SDM and empathy skills, highlighting the importance of multisource feedback for assessing trainee communication skills." Because students and SPs diverged in opposite directions on the two subscales, each source contributes distinct information the others miss. The intervention delivered SP written feedback and expert faculty written feedback alongside self-assessment, followed by a group debrief to reflect on discrepancies.
requirements: At least one external assessor source (SP or faculty) in addition to learner self-assessment
A shared rubric so ratings are comparable across sources
constraints: SP feedback may not be an accurate substitute for faculty feedback; faculty rater stringency and assessor expectations may differ
target_learning_goals: accurate self-awareness of communication skills
improved SDM practice
examples: Students compared written SP feedback with self-assessment in a facilitator-led debrief; some were surprised the SP rated their communication lower than they perceived

article_title: Big data analytics platform enhances teaching abilities in normal university students through triple helix collaboration.
citation: Zhao Juan, Hu Zhongjun. (2025). Big data analytics platform enhances teaching abilities in normal university students through triple helix collaboration. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-27799-9
title: Multimodal data collection and preprocessing pipeline with computer vision, NLP, and entity matching
description: The platform ingests six data types (teaching videos, classroom interactions, teaching plans, internship feedback, learning analytics, reflective journals) with specified collection frequencies and storage formats (Table 1). Preprocessing includes automated behavioral coding of video, NLP of reflective journals, parsing of interaction logs, and probabilistic entity matching that creates unified teaching profiles. The article reports that video coding used "pre-trained computer vision algorithms (ResNet-50 based) for pedagogical action taxonomies, with manual validation by three trained coders achieving 92% inter-rater reliability (κ = 0.89)".
requirements: Standardized collection protocols ensuring interoperability across institutional boundaries within the Triple Helix network
constraints: Pipeline performance figures (92% inter-rater reliability, 87% NLP accuracy, 95% entity-matching precision) are reported for this platform's implementation context
target_learning_goals: Holistic profiling of teaching competencies from authentic practice data
examples: Reflective journals are processed through NLP pipelines using BERT-base-Chinese models for semantic theme extraction and sentiment analysis, achieving 87% accuracy on validation dataset
key_sources: Zhao Juan, Hu Zhongjun. (2025). Big data analytics platform enhances teaching abilities in normal university students through triple helix collaboration. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-27799-9

article_title: Evidence-Based Suturing Education for Midwives.
citation: Yeager Amanda Love CNM, DNP; Nypaver Cynthia CNM, PhD, WHNP‐BC. (2025). Evidence‐Based Suturing Education for Midwives. Journal of Midwifery & Women's Health. https://doi.org/10.1111/jmwh.70018
title: Multimodal suturing workshop design combining online preparation, expert demonstration, hands-on practice with feedback, and end-of-session competency evaluation
description: The article's literature review identifies a set of design characteristics for suturing education: "interprofessional learning, multimodal content delivery that incorporates technology, opportunities for repeated review, direct faculty feedback, and repeated hands‐on practice with return demonstrations." The redesigned workshop implements these: preparatory lectures and videos in Canvas, live demonstration streamed to iPads, individual foam-model practice with faculty guidance, and OSCE-verified competency at the end of the session.
requirements: Students must complete online preparatory materials and practice knot-tying before attending the in-person session, so faculty can focus on laceration repair techniques
constraints: Creating such a workshop entails significant financial investment in supplies, space, faculty time, and student costs; students may present with a wide range of background experience
target_learning_goals: perineal laceration repair skill
suturing confidence and competence
examples: The program devoted 4 hours of a 2-day on-campus intrapartum skills workshop to hands-on perineal laceration repair using sutures, instruments, and high-density sponges to simulate human tissue

article_title: Predictive Validity of Preadmission Assessment on Early Nursing Academic Readiness: Impact of COVID-19.
citation: Yoo H, Zhou X, Phillips B. (2025). Predictive validity of preadmission assessment on early nursing academic readiness: impact of COVID-19. Nurse Educ. https://doi.org/10.1097/NNE.0000000000001891
title: Use multiple cognitive content areas—Reading, Math, Science, and English—together rather than a single criterion in nursing admission decisions
description: The article recommends that nursing programs base admission decisions on standardized academic tests covering all major cognitive content areas rather than one measure, because each area carries predictive information about early program success. It states that areas "deemed as essential cognitive academic skills should be considered" and that "it is not sufficient to adopt one single criterion to predict students' success." The recommendation rests on the study's finding that all four TEAS content areas significantly predicted Fundamentals scores.
requirements: Programs need admission test data covering Reading, Math, Science, and English content areas, and an early-program outcome such as a Fundamentals-style assessment to validate the criteria against
constraints: The authors note the relationship found with a large-scale national dataset may not apply to different student subgroups such as different nursing programs or specific institutions
target_learners: Applicants to associate degree in nursing (ADN) and bachelor of science in nursing (BSN) programs
target_learning_goals: Predicting early academic success in nursing programs to improve student retention and inform evidence-based admission criteria
examples: The study analyzed adjusted TEAS content area scores and Fundamentals scores for more than 100 000 students using correlation and regression analyses to support evidence-based admission criteria

article_title: Flipped classroom-based blended learning in histology education: investigating the effectiveness of applying a new approach to improve medical students' learning.
citation: Pour Mitra Barzroodi, Azizi Seyyed Mohsen, Bayat Mohamad. (2025). Flipped classroom-based blended learning in histology education: investigating the effectiveness of applying a new approach to improve medical students’ learning. BMC Medical Education 25. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08065-y
title: Multimedia-principles-based electronic histology content (annotated slide images with text and audio, built in Articulate Storyline and PowerPoint, delivered via LMS and Telegram)
description: The intervention’s e-learning component was electronic histology content built by photographing histological slides with a trinocular microscope and adding explanatory "text and voice" to the images. The authors state that "Articulate Storyline software and PowerPoint were used to produce electronic content", which was uploaded to the Learning Management System and also shared with intervention students via the Telegram social network before each in-person session. The authors identify this content, designed based on multimedia principles, as the study’s most important strength.
requirements: High-quality slide photographs with added text and voice explanations, produced in Articulate Storyline and PowerPoint
Distribution infrastructure: a Learning Management System and the Telegram social network for sharing each session’s content
constraints: The authors caution that in some similar studies only static virtual slides were used, and that "the quality of electronic content in the flipped classroom plays a crucial role in enhancing student learning"
target_learners: Undergraduate medical students in a histology course
target_learning_goals: Histological structure recognition and understanding of histology course concepts
examples: Electronic content for each of the 16 sessions was shared with intervention-group students via Telegram (Fig. 2 shows screenshots), and all content was later given to control students for educational equity
