article_title: Improving Intensive Care Unit Nurses' Delirium Assessment Performance Through a Multimodal Educational Intervention.
citation: R.‐L. Chang, S.‐F. Siao, S.‐C. Ku, Y.‐C. Yeh, Y.‐C. Chang, and C. C.‐H. Chen (2025). Improving Intensive Care Unit Nurses' Delirium Assessment Performance Through a Multimodal Educational Intervention. Nursing in Critical Care 30(5): e70168. https://doi.org/10.1111/nicc.70168
title: Multimodal delirium assessment education combining didactic lectures, scenario-based case discussions, and one-to-one bedside mentoring with immediate corrective feedback
description: This quality improvement pattern delivered delirium assessment training in three components: "didactic lectures equipped nurses with evidence‐based knowledge", case discussions of challenging scenarios identified through pre-test error data, and "one‐on‐one bedside mentoring provided personalized, hands‐on instruction from an expert nurse" who observed assessments and gave immediate corrective feedback. Sessions were embedded in routine ward meetings and scheduled around individual shift rotations. It was well received, particularly among new nurses.
requirements: An expert nurse with specialized delirium training available to deliver lectures, lead case discussions, and conduct one-on-one bedside mentoring
Participation embedded in routine ward meetings to reach high participation rates
Scheduling of mentoring sessions according to individual shift rotations to ensure comprehensive coverage of all bedside nurses
constraints: This study was conducted at a single centre, which may restrict the generalizability of the findings to other healthcare settings
Adherence to the intervention could not be tracked, as informed consent was waived for individual bedside nurses
The possibility of a Hawthorne effect cannot be excluded, as nurses may have altered their behaviour because of the awareness of being observed
target_learners: Newly recruited or transferred ICU nurses
target_learning_goals: Accurate and reliable bedside delirium screening using the Intensive Care Delirium Screening Checklist (ICDSC)
examples: In December 2023, didactic lectures and case discussions were integrated into routine ward meetings, with two 30–60 min sections in each ICU, achieving participation rates of 80% or higher
During January and February 2024, each bedside nurse received two one-on-one mentoring sessions that included four instances of hands-on practice with the ICDSC assessment
key_sources: R.‐L. Chang, S.‐F. Siao, S.‐C. Ku, Y.‐C. Yeh, Y.‐C. Chang, and C. C.‐H. Chen (2025). Improving Intensive Care Unit Nurses' Delirium Assessment Performance Through a Multimodal Educational Intervention. Nursing in Critical Care 30(5): e70168. https://doi.org/10.1111/nicc.70168

article_title: Online assessment of medical students' communication competence in patient encounters: Validation of the VA-MeCo situational judgement test.
citation: Reiser S, Schacht L, Thomm E, Janssen L, Pittroff SID, Dörfler E, Schick K, Berberat PO, Gartmeier M, Bauer J. (2025). Online assessment of medical students' communication competence in patient encounters: Validation of the VA-MeCo situational judgement test. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0332957
title: Munich Model of Professional Conversation Competence: medical communication competence as a hierarchical, multidimensional construct with three correlated sub-dimensions
description: The Munich Model of Professional Conversation Competence is an empirically validated model of professional communication competence used to guide curriculum and assessment development in medical education. The article states it "conceptualises professional communication competence as a hierarchical, multidimensional construct where the top-level factor of general medical communication competence subsumes three correlated sub-dimensions": facilitating joint-problem solving, organising conversations proactively and transparently, and fostering a strong working relationship. The VA-MeCo's three scales were designed to represent this structure.
requirements: Assessment or curriculum instruments intended to represent the model must operationalise its three sub-dimensions distinctly, as the VA-MeCo does with its three scales.
constraints: The model's dimensional structure is empirically corroborated per the article, but the present study's high inter-factor correlations (r ≥ .8) show the sub-dimensions are closely related rather than independent.
target_learning_goals: medical communication competence in patient encounters
examples: The VA-MeCo test was designed so its three scales (advancing content, providing structure, building relationship) map onto the model's three sub-dimensions.
key_sources: Reiser S, Schacht L, Thomm E, Janssen L, Pittroff SID, Dörfler E, Schick K, Berberat PO, Gartmeier M, Bauer J. (2025). article_title: Enhancing medical students' diagnostic accuracy of infectious keratitis with AI-generated images.
citation: Xie Wenjia, Yuan Zhouhang, Si Yuxuan, Huang Zhengxing, Li Yingming, Wu Fei, Yao Yu-Feng. (2025). Enhancing medical students’ diagnostic accuracy of infectious keratitis with AI-generated images. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07592-y
title: Multi-condition diffusion model for generating infectious keratitis teaching images
description: The article develops an AI image generation model built on Stable Diffusion 1.5 for producing infectious keratitis teaching images. The authors state that "we adopt a multi-condition diffusion model, generating both text and images simultaneously as conditions for the diffusion model," adding a text-condition module and an image-condition module and fine-tuning the conditional models on Stable Diffusion 1.5 parameters. The model draws on a dataset of 115,408 slit-lamp photographs from 10,609 patients and generates controllable varieties of bacterial, fungal, and herpetic keratitis images as an educational resource.
requirements: All AI-generated images used in teaching were evaluated by three senior ophthalmologists to verify clinical accuracy, including disease classification and disease-specific visual characteristics
constraints: AI-generated images still require manual review and affirmation by teachers before use, and teacher guidance is necessary when students interpret the images to avoid potential misguidance
target_learners: fourth-year medical students in ophthalmology clerkship
target_learning_goals: diagnosing bacterial, fungal, and herpetic keratitis from slit-lamp images
examples: 50 AI-generated images of each keratitis type were used in the G2 group's 1-hour image reading session
key_sources: Xie Wenjia, Yuan Zhouhang, Si Yuxuan, Huang Zhengxing, Li Yingming, Wu Fei, Yao Yu-Feng. (2025). Enhancing medical students’ diagnostic accuracy of infectious keratitis with AI-generated images. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07592-y

article_title: Performance of single-agent and multi-agent language models in Spanish language medical competency exams.
citation: Altermatt Fernando R., Neyem Andres, Sumonte Nicolas, Mendoza Marcelo, Villagran Ignacio, Lacassie Hector J. (2025). Performance of single-agent and multi-agent language models in Spanish language medical competency exams. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07250-3
title: Multi-agent LLM frameworks as collaborative diagnostic environments mimicking interdisciplinary medical decision-making
description: The article describes multi-agent frameworks as configurations in which "multiple instances of GPT-4o working in concert" emulate a collaborative diagnostic environment. Strategies include simple voting among six independent agents, weighted voting with Borda count, MEDAGENTS assigning domain-specific roles such as cardiologist or pediatrician, and MDAGENTS adapting agent reasoning strategies to the diagnostic or therapeutic context. The authors frame these as mimicking real-world interdisciplinary medical decision-making, enhancing robustness and accuracy in error-prone scenarios.
requirements: Multiple coordinated LLM agent instances with defined voting or role mechanisms
constraints: Evaluated only on multiple-choice EUNACOM questions with GPT-4o as the base model without fine-tuning; higher computational cost than single-agent methods
target_learners: medical trainees and clinicians in Spanish-speaking healthcare and education contexts
target_learning_goals: diagnostic accuracy and medical decision-making support in Spanish-language contexts
examples: MDAGENTS assigned adaptive reasoning strategies per diagnostic context and achieved the study's highest mean accuracy of 89.97%

article_title: A novel multi-measure approach to study medical students' communication performance and predictors of their communication quality - a cross-sectional study.
citation: Zerbini Giulia, Schneider Pia, Reicherts Miriam, Roob Nina, Jung-Can Kathrin, Kunz Miriam, Reicherts Philipp. (2025). A novel multi-measure approach to study medical students’ communication performance and predictors of their communication quality - a cross-sectional study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07018-9
title: Assess medical communication training outcomes with a multi-measure approach combining blinded observer ratings with objective non-verbal and physiological measures
description: The article advocates assessing communication performance across multiple modalities and response systems rather than relying solely on global self- or observer reports, which "might overlook critical details, and are prone to certain biases such as social desirability (self-report) or halo effects (observer reports)". In the study this meant combining blinded expert (BGR) and standardized-patient (MISS-21) ratings with video-annotated back-channeling, turn-taking, verbal dominance, automated facial-expression analysis and skin conductance level. This multi-measure approach revealed non-verbal differences between semester groups and identified physiological arousal as a predictor of expert-rated quality.
requirements: A highly standardized simulated consultation setting with the same scenario, setting and standardized patient for all students
Blinded raters to avoid semester bias
Video recording equipment and annotation/coding software for non-verbal measures
constraints: Cross-sectional semester comparison cannot support causal conclusions about curriculum effects; the authors note longitudinal designs are better suited for causality
The selection of non-verbal variables is not conclusive and replication in larger samples is needed
target_learners: medical students in early vs. later stages of medical training
target_learning_goals: doctor-patient communication quality
non-verbal communication and active listening skills
examples: 43 medical students completed a standardized simulated tick-bite consultation with one standardized patient while a blinded expert rated BGR quality and non-verbal parameters were extracted from video and electrodermal recordings

article_title: Advancing healthcare practice and education via data sharing: demonstrating the utility of open data by training an artificial intelligence model to assess cardiopulmonary resuscitation skills.
citation: Constable, M. D., Zhang, F. X., Conner, T., Monk, D., Rajsic, J., Ford, C., Park, L. J., Platt, A., Porteous, D., Grierson, L., & Shum, H. P. H. (2025). Advancing healthcare practice and education via data sharing: demonstrating the utility of open data by training an artificial intelligence model to assess cardiopulmonary resuscitation skills. Advances in Health Sciences Education, 30(1), 15-35. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-024-10369-5
title: Multiview spatial-temporal graph convolutional network framework for Automatic Action Quality Assessment of CPR
description: An automatic assessment pipeline combining markerless pose estimation with a deep learning network for Automatic Action Quality Assessment. MediaPipe captures 3D joint positions from each camera viewpoint without physical markers; the human skeleton is represented as a graph (nodes as joints, edges as bones), and a five-layer Spatial Temporal Graph Convolutional Network processes each view, with learned features fused via a learnable parameter and a two-layer fully connected network predicting item scores. The article describes it as providing "an objective, automated evaluation of the participant's skill level" against the same criteria used in manual expert assessments.
requirements: Video recorded from multiple viewpoints with a common landmark for calibration; training on expert-rated item scores; more powerful hardware than a standard computer for pose estimation and network training.
constraints: The current framework relies solely on participant pose information and does not capture visual interaction between the participant and the dummy, which the authors link to higher error on compression depth and rate items.
target_learning_goals: automated assessment of CPR technique quality
postural safety and form in chest compressions
examples: Trained with Adam optimiser (initial learning rate 0.01, weight decay 0.1) minimising Mean Absolute Error; implemented in PyTorch 1.10.1 on one Nvidia GeForce GTX 2080 Ti GPU; code and deployment instructions released on the authors' GitHub page.

article_title: Identifying Culturally Relevant School Support Profiles and Links to Academic Functioning in Adolescents.
citation: Hernández, M. M., Kornienko, O., Figueroa, J. M., Coker, M., Paredes, K., Toth, C., Carrillo, J. P., Rogers, A. A., & Ha, T. (2024). Identifying Culturally Relevant School Support Profiles and Links to Academic Functioning in Adolescents. Journal of Youth and Adolescence. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10964-024-02098-0
title: Culturally relevant school support as a multidimensional construct of general teacher support, cultural competence promotion, and critical consciousness socialization
description: The article conceptualizes culturally relevant school support as multi-dimensional, comprising teacher support (helpfulness and availability of support from teachers), promotion of cultural competence (learning about ethnoracial group histories and traditions other than one's own), and critical consciousness socialization (learning about power, privilege, and systems of oppression). Drawing on culturally relevant pedagogy, it argues these dimensions are interdependent: "In the absence of critical or cultural support, general teacher support does not respond to the needs of youth to make sense of an increasingly diversifying and socially stratified society." Thus, "experiencing highly culturally relevant support requires high levels of critical consciousness, cultural (e.g., promoting multicultural skills), and general teacher support." The construct grounds the study's latent profile analysis of support constellations.
requirements: All three support dimensions must be present at high levels for support to be experienced as highly culturally relevant.
constraints: The article states general support alone does not respond to youth's needs to make sense of a diversifying, socially stratified society, and that without general support, critical or cultural support might not be perceived as authentic or caring.
target_learning_goals: Academic engagement
Academic aspirations and expectations
Cultural competence and critical reflection
examples: The study operationalized the construct with the Teacher and Classmate Support Scale and the School Climate for Diversity - Secondary scale's critical consciousness socialization and promotion of cultural competence subscales.
key_sources: Hernández, M. M., Kornienko, O., Figueroa, J. M., Coker, M., Paredes, K., Toth, C., Carrillo, J. P., Rogers, A. A., & Ha, T. (2024). Identifying Culturally Relevant School Support Profiles and Links to Academic Functioning in Adolescents. Journal of Youth and Adolescence. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10964-024-02098-0

article_title: Impact of a 3-year transformational change project in family violence clinical response: Qualitative evaluation of the depth and breadth of knowledge in hospital clinicians by training level.
citation: Troy K, Rushan C, Withiel TD, Felmingham KL, Fisher CA. (2025). Impact of a 3-year transformational change project in family violence clinical response: Qualitative evaluation of the depth and breadth of knowledge in hospital clinicians by training level. Women's Health, 21. https://doi.org/10.1177/17455057241305264
title: Sustained clinician behaviour change in complex healthcare practices requires multifaceted, system-wide intervention with ongoing supports, not one-off training
description: The article recommends that complex healthcare practices like family violence response need system-wide change rather than isolated training: 'a multifaceted intervention approach that incorporates local opinion leaders, educational outreach, audit and feedback loops and reminders, is likely to be most effective in maintaining organisational behaviour change'. The evaluated project paired policy development, a specialist team, tiered training and a champions community of practice, and the authors conclude ongoing supports are needed to sustain knowledge and practice change.
requirements: appropriate resourcing, multiple training types and opportunities and a comprehensive transformational change project plan
constraints: Issues with maintaining sustained improvement from one-off training episodes have been raised in prior research
target_learners: Hospital clinical staff across medical, nursing and allied health professions
target_learning_goals: Family violence identification, enquiry and disclosure response knowledge and skills
examples: The Royal Melbourne Hospital project established family violence policies and procedures, a specialist Family Safety Team, tiered short-duration modules and a clinical champions model with monthly supervision and quarterly network meetings
key_sources: Troy K, Rushan C, Withiel TD, Felmingham KL, Fisher CA. (2025). Impact of a 3-year transformational change project in family violence clinical response: Qualitative evaluation of the depth and breadth of knowledge in hospital clinicians by training level. Women's Health, 21. https://doi.org/10.1177/17455057241305264

article_title: Design and Development of an Integrated Virtual Reality (VR)-Based Training System for Difficult Airway Management.
citation: Jain Saurabh, Dripta Barua Chowdhury Bijoy, Mosier Jarrod M., Subbian Vignesh, Hughes Kate, Son Young-Jun. (2025). Design and Development of an Integrated Virtual Reality (VR)-Based Training System for Difficult Airway Management. IEEE Journal of Translational Engineering in Health and Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1109/JTEHM.2025.3529748
title: Multi-modal sensing framework with pressure-instrumented laryngoscope and biometric vest
description: The system's data-acquisition layer streams real-time performance and physiological data during simulation. The article states that "The backend data collection module captures and utilizes real-time sensory data from: (a) HTC Vive VR headset, (b) pressure sensing module, and (c) Hexoskin biometric vest", with five pressure sensors, an Arduino nano BLE, and battery embedded in the laryngoscope. Data stream at 10 Hz, capturing pressure profiles, tool position, heart rate variability and respiratory rate for offline analysis of technical and cognitive performance.
requirements: A data streaming frequency of 10 Hz to ensure smooth data collection and real-time analysis without lag
Pressure values streamed only when the laryngoscope tip approaches the collider near goal anatomical structures to reduce computational lag
target_learning_goals: objective measurement of procedural performance
study of decision-making and stress responses during airway management
examples: Pressure profiles along the laryngoscope blade inform virtual soft-tissue deformation in real time during intubation trials
key_sources: Jain Saurabh, Dripta Barua Chowdhury Bijoy, Mosier Jarrod M., Subbian Vignesh, Hughes Kate, Son Young-Jun. (2025). Design and Development of an Integrated Virtual Reality (VR)-Based Training System for Difficult Airway Management. IEEE Journal of Translational Engineering in Health and Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1109/JTEHM.2025.3529748

article_title: Study of the impact of introducing a multimedia learning tool in podiatric medical courses.
citation: Hoyt Garrik, Adegboyega Samuel, Constantouris Gus, Basu Paramita. (2024). Study of the impact of introducing a multimedia learning tool in podiatric medical courses. Journal of Foot and Ankle Research. https://doi.org/10.1002/jfa2.12018
title: Use multimedia learning resources to complement, not replace, traditional instruction and course content delivery
description: The article's conclusion states that "The data reported here do not support replacing traditional instructional and learning methods with multimedia‐based learning resources, but rather contributes to the mounting evidence backing the potential of these audiovisual web‐based tools in further enhancing the students' learning experience in traditional course content delivery." Multimedia tools work best when layered onto lectures, textbooks, and instructor materials — students in the survey also overwhelmingly credited class lectures and instructor-uploaded materials as helpful.
requirements: Traditional course elements (didactic instruction, textbooks, summative assessments) remain in place; the multimedia resource supplements them for review and reinforcement.
constraints: Evidence comes from a single-institution quasi-experiment with no randomization; exam-score differences were not statistically significant, so the principle rests partly on perception and correlation data.
target_learners: undergraduate medical and podiatric medical students
target_learning_goals: supporting learning of complex preclinical course content
improving retention and exam performance
examples: In the study, both cohorts received identical didactic instruction, textbooks, and assessments; only the treatment group additionally received Osmosis video playlists, quizzes, and flashcards.
key_sources: Hoyt Garrik, Adegboyega Samuel, Constantouris Gus, Basu Paramita. (2024). Study of the impact of introducing a multimedia learning tool in podiatric medical courses. Journal of Foot and Ankle Research. https://doi.org/10.1002/jfa2.12018

article_title: [Digitally based clinically oriented anatomy: the future of teaching].
citation: Maier Esther C., Ödemis Veysel, Bräuer Anja U. (2025). Digitally based clinically oriented anatomy: the future of teaching. Chirurgie. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00104-024-02211-w
title: Multimodal teaching approach as the current consensus for conveying the diverse content of anatomy
description: The review states that current consensus in anatomical education research holds that a multimodal approach is best suited to convey anatomy's diverse content. It combines dissection and prosection with digital and AR/VR tools so that different learner types find themselves represented, and establishes clinical relevance already in the preclinical phase. The review frames this as the organizing answer to reduced teaching hours and changed student expectations: "Konsensus in der anatomischen Lehrforschung ist aktuell, dass ein multimodaler Ansatz am besten geeignet ist, die vielfältigen Inhalte der Anatomie zu vermitteln".
requirements: Combines multiple learning modalities, including dissection or prosection alongside digital tools
Teaching methods should address different learner types and student learning preferences
constraints: Digital methods can complement but not replace classical methods such as dissection
target_learners: Medical students in preclinical anatomy education
target_learning_goals: Topographic-anatomical knowledge
Clinical relevance of anatomical structures
Professional development including manual skills and ethical experience
examples: The review describes dissection as the gold standard per teacher consensus, while digital and AR/VR tools serve as accompanying, preparatory and deepening methods
key_sources: Maier Esther C., Ödemis Veysel, Bräuer Anja U. (2025). Digitally based clinically oriented anatomy: the future of teaching. Chirurgie. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00104-024-02211-w

article_title: Opening Pandora's box - key facilitators of practice change in detecting and responding to childhood adversity - a practitioner perspective.
citation: Loveday Sarah, Chen Lingling, Constable Leanne N., Kabir Ashraful, White Natalie, Goldfeld Sharon, Sanci Lena, Hiscock Harriet. (2024). Opening Pandora's box - key facilitators of practice change in detecting and responding to childhood adversity - a practitioner perspective. BMC Pediatrics. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12887-024-04918-5
title: Multimodal practice-change intervention combining training, coaching, goal setting, social support and prompts mapped to behaviour change techniques
description: The intervention employed "a range of behavioural change techniques as defined by Michie et al." mapped onto different TDF domains, including goal setting, goal review, social support, social comparison, homework tasks, role play, instruction and prompts. Practitioners attended a one-day training session and then received regular coaching and support in a community of practice (lunchtime learning collaborative), with co-designed posters and postcards as prompts. Asking about adversity was adapted to clinical practice to not burden time-limited practitioners.
requirements: Regular coaching and support in a community of practice following initial training
Mapped referral pathways so practitioners have services to respond to
constraints: Single interventions such as education alone are rarely effective in achieving sustained practice change, per the article's background
target_learning_goals: directly asking about childhood adversity and responding to identified adversity
examples: Practitioners were given specific homework following learning collaboratives, i.e. to ask 1 family each day at least 1 direct question about adversity.

Opening Pandora's box - key facilitators of practice change in detecting and responding to childhood adversity - a practitioner perspective. article_title: Higher level domain specific skills in mathematics; The relationship between algebra, geometry, executive function skills and mathematics achievement.
citation: Spiller J, Clayton S, Cragg L, Johnson S, Simms V, Gilmore C. (2023). Higher level domain specific skills in mathematics; The relationship between algebra, geometry, executive function skills and mathematics achievement. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0291796
title: Multi-level framework of mathematics achievement: overall achievement arises from specific components drawing on basic processes, with domain-general skills acting directly and indirectly
description: The study applies the multi-level framework in which "overall achievement in mathematics, i.e. as measured by curriculum assessments or broad standardised tests, arises out of proficiency with specific components of mathematics" such as calculation skills, number fact knowledge and algebra, which in turn draw on basic mathematical processes. Domain-general executive function skills play a direct role in basic processes and specific components, and may also relate directly to overall achievement. This study extended the framework by adding algebra and geometry as specific components beyond the arithmetic focus of prior work.
requirements: Assessment of both specific mathematical components and broad context-rich achievement measures to reveal the multiple pathways
constraints: Relationships tested are correlational and cross-sectional, so causal direction between components and achievement cannot be established
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement
algebra
geometry
arithmetic
key_sources: Spiller J, Clayton S, Cragg L, Johnson S, Simms V, Gilmore C. (2023). Higher level domain specific skills in mathematics; The relationship between algebra, geometry, executive function skills and mathematics achievement. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0291796

article_title: Assessor discomfort and failure to fail in clinical performance assessments.
citation: Scarff Catherine E, Bearman Margaret, Chiavaroli Neville, Trumble Stephen. (2023). Assessor discomfort and failure to fail in clinical performance assessments. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04688-1
title: The MUM effect as a lens on the gap between assessors' private judgements and public assessment messages
description: The article uses the MUM effect — keeping "Mum about Undesirable Messages" — as an explanatory lens for failure to fail. It predicts a teller will be reluctant to deliver a message perceived as negative by the recipient, and will instead "delay giving the message", "distort (or sugarcoat) the message" or "avoid giving it altogether". In medical education this may result in failure to fail or grade inflation, undermining both summative and developmental purposes of workplace assessment.
requirements: Assessors must have private judgements that may diverge from the public judgement they deliver for the lens to apply
constraints: Reasons for keeping MUM may lie in concerns about outcomes for teller or recipient, or the prevailing norms of the setting; impact varies across assessment contexts (feedback conversation vs low- vs high-stakes documentation)
target_learning_goals: Accurate assessment judgements and feedback to underperforming trainees
examples: The survey operationalised MUM behaviours with a modified MUM effect scale measuring distortion (sugarcoating) and avoidance, plus author-added items
key_sources: Scarff Catherine E, Bearman Margaret, Chiavaroli Neville, Trumble Stephen. (2023). Assessor discomfort and failure to fail in clinical performance assessments. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04688-1

article_title: Are students performing the same in E-learning and In-person education? An introspective look at learning environments from an Iranian medical school standpoint.
citation: Mastour Haniye, Emadzadeh Ali, Hamidi Haji Abadi Omid, Niroumand Shabnam. (2023). Are students performing the same in E-learning and In-person education? An introspective look at learning environments from an Iranian medical school standpoint. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04159-7
title: MUMS Learning Object e-learning delivery system with multimedia formats and embedded assessment modules
description: The e-learning delivery system evaluated in this study organised content into Learning Objects, each ending with formative and summative assessment modules. Content appeared in interactive multimedia formats including "slide-based lectures, standalone training videos, embedded videos, webinar or live training playback, podcasts, dialogue simulations, animations, and interactive videos". Students received asynchronous content through the MUMS Learning Management System NAVID and attended synchronous sessions via Adobe Connect and Skyroom.
requirements: Learning Objects were designed and created in collaboration with instructional designers and electronic content developers under the supervision of an expert panel, including relevant faculty members
formative and summative assessment modules at the end of each Learning Object
target_learners: undergraduate medical students in the preclinical (physiopathology) phase
target_learning_goals: knowledge of preclinical medical courses (pharmacology, pathology, semiology)
examples: The same courses were taught in two successive semesters, first face-to-face with lectures and interactive presentations, then via the e-learning system, with knowledge test scores of 20 MCQs per lesson collected in both semesters.
key_sources: Mastour Haniye, Emadzadeh Ali, Hamidi Haji Abadi Omid, Niroumand Shabnam. (2023). Are students performing the same in E-learning and In-person education? An introspective look at learning environments from an Iranian medical school standpoint. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04159-7

article_title: Measuring the Effectiveness of a Multicomponent Program to Manage Academic Stress through a Resilience to Stress Index.
citation: Figueroa Carlos, Ayala Andrés, Trejo Luis A., Ramos Bertha, Briz Clara L., Noriega Isabella, Chávez Alejandro. (2023). Measuring the Effectiveness of a Multicomponent Program to Manage Academic Stress through a Resilience to Stress Index. Sensors. https://doi.org/10.3390/s23052650
title: Multicomponent academic-stress program: psychoeducation, mindfulness training, and biofeedback-assisted mindfulness across 16 sessions in 8 weeks
description: A structured intervention for university students consisting of "16 individual sessions during 8 weeks, divided into 3 phases: pre-test evaluation, multicomponent intervention program, and post-test evaluation". The program integrates three components: one asynchronous online psychoeducation session on academic stress (conceptualization, sources, symptoms, risk and protective factors, coping); ten daily online mindfulness sessions with body scan and breathing awareness meditations; and three in-person biofeedback-assisted mindfulness sessions in which participants meditate while watching an HRV-driven video. It was adapted from the Mindfulness Suite by the Biofeedback Federation of Europe, translated into Spanish.
requirements: Participants must be able to attend pre-test and post-test psychophysiological stress-profile sessions and the in-person biofeedback sessions using ProComp5 equipment recording HRV, BVP, breathing rate, and galvanic skin response.
constraints: Designed and piloted with high-performing scholarship students during the COVID pandemic; the authors state the sample may not be representative of all university students.
target_learners: Undergraduate university students, specifically high-achieving scholarship students (Leaders of Tomorrow)
target_learning_goals: Academic stress management and self-regulation of psychophysiological stress responses
examples: Sessions 13–15 place surface sensors and use an HRV biofeedback video that advances only when the participant increases HRV; mindfulness training spans weeks 3–4 with one session per day.
key_sources: Figueroa Carlos, Ayala Andrés, Trejo Luis A., Ramos Bertha, Briz Clara L., Noriega Isabella, Chávez Alejandro. (2023). Measuring the Effectiveness of a Multicomponent Program to Manage Academic Stress through a Resilience to Stress Index. Sensors. https://doi.org/10.3390/s23052650

article_title: Impact of high-fidelity simulation exposure of nursing students with their objective structured clinical examination: A quasi-experimental study.
citation: Guerrero, J. G., Rosales, N. S., & Castro, G. M. T. (2023). Impact of high‐fidelity simulation exposure of nursing students with their objective structured clinical examination: A quasi‐experimental study. Nursing Open, 10, 765–772. https://doi.org/10.1002/nop2.1343
title: Multi‐station OSCE design with dual raters, 4‐point rubrics and a piloted rating scale
description: The OSCE design used multiple stations combining nursing procedures and written interpretation: 'For the midterm, seven OSCE stations were set, five for nursing procedures and two for written interpretation, each with an equivalency of 10% of students' midterm grade'. The final used ten stations weighted at 20% of the grade. Rubrics used a 4‐point Likert‐type scale, two trained raters scored each station, and a pilot test preceded the examinations.
requirements: Trained raters and a piloted rating scale appropriate for assessing the students
Standardized patients and station equipment set up according to the blueprint
constraints: The procedural rubrics were adopted from course‐appropriate reference books but were not tested for reliability, which the authors list as a limitation
target_learning_goals: clinical competence in nursing procedures
communication and patient‐teaching skills under simulated clinical conditions
examples: Midterm OSCE: seven stations worth 10% of the midterm grade; final OSCE: ten stations worth 20% of the final grade
key_sources: Guerrero, J. G., Rosales, N. S., & Castro, G. M. T. (2023). Impact of high‐fidelity simulation exposure of nursing students with their objective structured clinical examination: A quasi‐experimental study. Nursing Open, 10, 765–772. https://doi.org/10.1002/nop2.1343

article_title: The Associations Between Sluggish Cognitive Tempo, Internalizing Symptoms, and Academic Performance in Children With Reading Disorder: A Longitudinal Cohort Study.
citation: Hossain Bushra, Bent Stephen, Parenteau China, Widjaja Felicia, Davis Matthew, Hendren Robert L. (2022). The Associations Between Sluggish Cognitive Tempo, Internalizing Symptoms, and Academic Performance in Children With Reading Disorder: A Longitudinal Cohort Study. Journal of Attention Disorders. https://doi.org/10.1177/10870547221085493
title: Use multiple raters including teachers when assessing SCT in school populations
description: Because SCT associations with anxiety and academic performance emerged only for teacher-reported measures in this cohort, the authors argue assessments should draw on multiple raters. They state that using multiple raters "offers different perspectives and provides information on how SCT manifests in different contexts." Teacher ratings may capture SCT-related difficulty in school-based cognitive tasks, while parent ratings reflect the home context; both contribute information.
requirements: Access to both teacher and parent raters, with teachers able to observe the student across sustained school-based cognitive tasks.
constraints: The article notes there is no nationally normative data for teacher-reported SCT.
target_learning_goals: accurate identification of SCT symptoms affecting academic performance and internalizing symptoms
examples: In this cohort, parent and teacher versions of the K-SCT were administered approximately every 3 months across 18 months, and only teacher-reported SCT showed significant associations with anxiety and academic performance.

The Associations Between Sluggish Cognitive Tempo, Internalizing Symptoms, and Academic Performance in Children With Reading Disorder: A Longitudinal Cohort Study. Journal of Attention Disorders. https://doi.org/10.1177/10870547221085493

article_title: The SIMULATE ureteroscopy training curriculum: educational value and transfer of skills.
citation: Aydın Abdullatif, Ahmed Kamran, Baig Umair, Raison Nicholas, Lantz Powers Andrea G., Macchione Nicola, Al-Jabir Ahmed, Abe Takashige, Khan Muhammad Shamim, Dasgupta Prokar, the SIMULATE Trial Contributors. (2021). The SIMULATE ureteroscopy training curriculum: educational value and transfer of skills. World Journal of Urology. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00345-021-03604-w
title: Multi-modality simulation curriculum combining didactic lectures, VR, bench models and cadavers
description: A curricular pattern in which different simulation modalities are sequenced to exploit each model's strengths: didactic lectures first, then VR simulator tasks, bench model cases, and diagnostic cases on fresh frozen cadavers if available. The article states "Different simulation modalities may be utilised in a curricular fashion to benefit from the strengths of each training model," and that models should be "utilised in combined curricula which address specific learning needs."
requirements: Available training models with the highest levels of evidence for the target procedure
Delphi-process curriculum development with input from experts and trainees
Standardised delivery across sites
constraints: Some modalities may be locally unavailable (cadavers restricted to UK participants; VR unavailable for Japanese trainees)
target_learners: Novice surgical trainees learning a core procedure
target_learning_goals: Procedural technical skills with transfer to the operating room
examples: The SIMULATE curriculum began with five didactic lecture topics, then URO-Mentor VR tasks, bench model cases, and diagnostic cases on fresh frozen cadavers

article_title: Focused educational intervention improves intern knowledge of perioperative patient blood management principles.
citation: Wyssusek K, Taylor K, Concha-Blamey S. (2021). Focused educational intervention improves intern knowledge of perioperative patient blood management principles. BMJ Open Quality. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjoq-2021-001390
title: 50-minute multidisciplinary expert-led perioperative PBM educational intervention delivered every 10 weeks
description: A 50-minute tutorial "collaboratively delivered... by a preoperative anaemia Clinical Nurse Consultant, blood transfusion Clinical Nurse Consultant, Haematology Physician and Anaesthetist", delivered every 10 weeks (five interventions total) to different intern groups. Content covered PBM definition, the NBA perioperative module, the three pillars, anaemia management, transfusion practice and hospital policies, with case studies, PowerPoint presentations, hard-copy handouts and emailed soft copies.
requirements: Same staff members facilitated each educational intervention; attendance tracked via QR code scanner
constraints: Delivered at a single site; generalisability is limited as the intervention was undertaken at one hospital
target_learning_goals: perioperative patient blood management principles
safe blood transfusion practice
examples: Multiple iron deficiency and anaemia case studies and a single surgical patient's perioperative journey case study were discussed

article_title: Dose-Response Relationship between High-Fidelity Simulation and Intensive Care Nursing Students' Learning Outcomes: An Italian Multimethod Study.
citation: Dante Angelo, La Cerra Carmen, Caponnetto Valeria, Masotta Vittorio, Marcotullio Alessia, Bertocchi Luca, Ferraiuolo Fabio, Petrucci Cristina, Lancia Loreto. (2022). Dose–Response Relationship between High-Fidelity Simulation and Intensive Care Nursing Students’ Learning Outcomes: An Italian Multimethod Study. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph19020617
title: Modified teaching model of multiple spaced exposures to high-fidelity simulation built on Kolb's experiential learning cycle
description: The article develops a modified version of a previously used teaching model in which each 2 h guided activity includes a briefing, a 20 min high-fidelity simulation, a first debriefing and a 30 min skill reinforcement session, followed by a second simulation of the same scenario and a final debriefing. Kolb's Experiential Learning Theory structures the phases, a "spaced learning" approach repeats a more complex scenario 15 days later, and scaffolding-inspired personalized faculty support runs through debriefing and reinforcement. The model was applied in an Italian graduate intensive care nursing course and evaluated with Kirkpatrick-level outcomes.
requirements: Graduate nurses enrolled in an intensive care program; very realistic scenarios, high student engagement, educators with deep clinical experience, and serious organizational efforts are stated as required for graduate-level simulation
A dedicated room for the three-step debriefing and video recording of sessions
constraints: Evaluated in a single Italian course with a small sample, explorative nature, and no control group, so the authors call for caution in generalizing to other educational settings
target_learners: Graduate nurses enrolled in intensive care specialization courses
target_learning_goals: Managing life-threatening conditions such as acute respiratory failure
Advanced technical and nontechnical critical care nursing skills
examples: After lectures on acute respiratory failure, students completed a 2 h guided activity with briefing (15 min), simulation (20 min), debriefing (15–20 min), skill reinforcement (30 min), a second simulation (20 min) and final debriefing, repeated 15 days later with arrhythmia added to the pneumonia scenario

Dose–Response Relationship between High-Fidelity Simulation and Intensive Care Nursing Students’ Learning Outcomes: An Italian Multimethod Study. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph19020617

article_title: Haptic exploration improves performance of a laparoscopic training task.
citation: Postema Roelf R., van Gastel Leonie A., Hardon Sem F., Bonjer H. Jaap, Horeman Tim. (2020). Haptic exploration improves performance of a laparoscopic training task. Surgical Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-020-07898-6
title: Multisensory convergence: visual and haptic inputs combine into a more robust mental representation of an object
description: The article's explanatory framework holds that visual and haptic inputs "combine or converge to form a mental representation of an object" that is more refined and robust than a representation formed by a single sense. Haptic information is defined as tactile input from skin receptors together with kinaesthetic input from receptors in muscles, tendons and joints. The authors use this account to explain why two minutes of manual exploration of a model before practice lowered the forces applied during a laparoscopic task on that model.
requirements: The article defines haptic information as the combination of tactile input through the skin receptors and kinaesthetic receptors in muscles, tendons and joints.
constraints: The authors state that more research is needed to clarify the exact neuropsychological explanation of the positive results.
target_learning_goals: safer tissue manipulation
formation of a robust mental representation of anatomical structures
examples: The study's touch group explored the geometry and different structures of the silicone ileocecal model by hand for two minutes before performing the needle-driving task.
key_sources: Postema Roelf R., van Gastel Leonie A., Hardon Sem F., Bonjer H. Jaap, Horeman Tim. (2020). Haptic exploration improves performance of a laparoscopic training task. Surgical Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-020-07898-6

article_title: The Indirect Role of Executive Functions on the Relationship between Cardiorespiratory Fitness and School Grades.
citation: YANGÜEZ MARC, BEDIOU BENOIT, HILLMAN CHARLES H., BAVELIER DAPHNE, CHANAL JULIEN. (2021). The Indirect Role of Executive Functions on the Relationship between Cardiorespiratory Fitness and School Grades. Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise. https://doi.org/10.1249/MSS.0000000000002630
title: Use a multitask latent variable approach when measuring executive functions in relation to academic outcomes
description: The article argues that measuring each executive function component with multiple tasks and latent variable procedures avoids task impurity and unreliability. It notes that prior studies treating executive functions as unitary constructs were limited by small task batteries, and that a multitask approach "addresses the issue of task impurity and unreliability through the use of latent variable procedures" while enabling a more representative model of distinct but interrelated constructs.
requirements: At least three separate tasks per executive function component, ideally reaction-time based for inhibition and cognitive flexibility
constraints: Requires sufficiently large samples for latent variable estimation; school-based data collection may preclude direct fitness measurement
target_learning_goals: accurate measurement of executive functions in education research
examples: The study used nine tasks, three per component, combining response speed and accuracy via inverse efficiency scores
key_sources: YANGÜEZ MARC, BEDIOU BENOIT, HILLMAN CHARLES H., BAVELIER DAPHNE, CHANAL JULIEN. (2021). The Indirect Role of Executive Functions on the Relationship between Cardiorespiratory Fitness and School Grades. Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise. https://doi.org/10.1249/MSS.0000000000002630

article_title: The national dental undergraduate clinical skills competition known as the Guanghua Cup: an innovative and effective program that promoted undergraduate dental education in China.
citation: Li Xiaolan, Shan Yanbo, Liu Yangjingwen, Lin Yingwen, Li Lin, Lin Zhengmei, Huang Shuheng, Hong Yun. (2021). The national dental undergraduate clinical skills competition known as the Guanghua Cup: an innovative and effective program that promoted undergraduate dental education in China. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-021-02841-2
title: Multi-station clinical skills competition pattern combining operative-skill stations, a knowledge quiz, expert refereeing, and digital scoring
description: The Guanghua Cup was organized as two sections with seven stations: six operative-skill stations (cavity preparation, scaling and suture, bandaging and suture, impressions and crown preparation, tooth carving, CPR and BP measurement) run simultaneously with teams rotating every 25 minutes, followed by a multiple-choice knowledge competition. Dental experts from participating schools designed the projects and scoring standards, and 2–6 referees per station scored each team with averaged scores. The article presents this as a reusable program design that let students "exhibit their clinical skills in a competitive environment and develop collegiality and teamwork".
requirements: Dental experts from participating schools design the competition projects and develop the scoring standards, announced in advance
Referee training before the competition so referees are familiar with rules, procedures, evaluation forms, and scoring standards
constraints: The article notes the competition was on a smaller scale than the China National Clinical Skills Competition for medical students and did not fully cover all oral dentistry-related knowledge and skills
target_learners: Fifth-year undergraduate dental students in their clinical practice stage
target_learning_goals: Clinical operative skills across seven dental disciplines
Professional theoretical knowledge of oral diseases
First aid ability
Collegiality and teamwork
examples: Teams of four students selected through school-level competitions rotated through six simultaneous 25-minute skill stations, then competed together in a buzzer-format knowledge quiz; awards went to the top four teams from each station
key_sources: Li Xiaolan, Shan Yanbo, Liu Yangjingwen, Lin Yingwen, Li Lin, Lin Zhengmei, Huang Shuheng, Hong Yun. (2021). The national dental undergraduate clinical skills competition known as the Guanghua Cup: an innovative and effective program that promoted undergraduate dental education in China. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-021-02841-2

article_title: A protocol to examine the learning effects of 'multisystem mapping' training combined with post-training sleep consolidation in beginning readers.
citation: Pegado F., Torres A.R., Weissheimer J., Ribeiro S. (2021). A protocol to examine the learning effects of 'multisystem mapping' training combined with post-training sleep consolidation in beginning readers. STAR Protocols. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.xpro.2021.100712
title: Multisystem mapping: a hypothetical mechanism of mirror discrimination learning for letters
description: The article proposes a hypothetical learning model in which mirror invariance for letters is slowly overcome at school through multisensory-motor mappings between the systems representing letters. Training activities are built "based on our 'multisystem mapping' hypothetical mechanism of mirror discrimination learning for letters", aiming to "maximize mappings between systems representing letters". Beyond the auditory, visual, and writing-gesture systems traditionally involved in school letter representations, the design adds tactile perception and 'perception for action' activities to expand mappings towards the somatosensory and dorsal systems respectively.
requirements: Training must pair multiple letter-representation systems (auditory, visual, writing gestures, tactile, dorsal) within the same sessions, using mirror-letter pairs in training groups.
constraints: The article labels the mechanism hypothetical; it is the model the intervention was designed from, not a directly tested mechanism in this protocol.
target_learning_goals: Mirror discrimination for letters and reading fluency
examples: Training sessions used air-writing, writing on paper, perceiving letters on hands, and a 'perception for action' game indicating letter parts with left and right hands.
key_sources: Pegado F., Torres A.R., Weissheimer J., Ribeiro S. (2021). A protocol to examine the learning effects of 'multisystem mapping' training combined with post-training sleep consolidation in beginning readers. STAR Protocols. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.xpro.2021.100712

article_title: Development and validation of a new Multidisciplinary Approach Competency Scale for Prevention of Child Abuse from Pregnancy (MUSCAT).
citation: Sakakida Chika, Tadaka Etsuko, Arimoto Azusa. (2021). Development and validation of a new Multidisciplinary Approach Competency Scale for Prevention of Child Abuse from Pregnancy (MUSCAT). PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0249623
title: MUSCAT two-factor competency framework: Collaborative Networking and Professional Commitment
description: The MUSCAT conceptualizes multidisciplinary competency for child abuse prevention from pregnancy as two correlated factors. Factor 1, "Collaborative Networking", covers "the mutual connections of relationships and collaboration between multiple professional groups"; Factor 2, "Professional Commitment", covers "the responsibilities and involvement during support and care, which reflected the importance of awareness as professionals". The article presents Professional Commitment, centered on keeping the child first, as a novel concept relative to existing collaboration scales.
requirements: Professionals with experience of interprofessional collaboration for child abuse prevention from pregnancy, since the scale is completed by self-evaluation against a reported case
constraints: Developed for self-evaluation of individual abilities; the article notes abilities may differ by job type and the cross-sectional design could not reveal causal relationships with collaboration outcomes
target_learners: Healthcare and welfare professionals (public health nurses, doctors, nurses, midwives, social workers, child welfare workers, kindergarten teachers)
target_learning_goals: Competency in multidisciplinary collaboration for early prevention of child abuse, from primary to tertiary prevention
examples: The final 10-item scale loads five items on each factor, with items such as coping with interprofessional conflict (Factor 1) and protecting the rights of the child (Factor 2)
key_sources: Sakakida Chika, Tadaka Etsuko, Arimoto Azusa. (2021). Development and validation of a new Multidisciplinary Approach Competency Scale for Prevention of Child Abuse from Pregnancy (MUSCAT). PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0249623

article_title: Development and validation of a new Multidisciplinary Approach Competency Scale for Prevention of Child Abuse from Pregnancy (MUSCAT).
citation: Sakakida Chika, Tadaka Etsuko, Arimoto Azusa. (2021). Development and validation of a new Multidisciplinary Approach Competency Scale for Prevention of Child Abuse from Pregnancy (MUSCAT). PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0249623
title: MUSCAT scale (Multidisciplinary Approach Competency Scale for Prevention of Child Abuse from Pregnancy)
description: A self-reflection questionnaire measuring professional competency in multidisciplinary approaches to preventing child abuse from pregnancy. Drafted as 30 items from a literature review, refined to 21 via expert interviews, and finalized at 10 items on two factors after item and factor analyses. Respondents rate each item on 4-point Likert-like scales for importance and applicability to a reported child abuse case. The article reports total-scale Cronbach's alpha of 0.903 and English and Japanese versions in supporting information.
requirements: Respondents report one child abuse case requiring support from pregnancy and multi-professional cooperation before completing the scale
constraints: Validated with a cross-sectional sample in Japan; the authors note a longitudinal design is needed to determine predictive validity
target_learners: Professionals across health centers, perinatal medical centers/hospitals, child consultation centers, midwife clinics, and kindergartens
target_learning_goals: Self-evaluation and development of multidisciplinary collaboration competency for child abuse prevention
examples: Used in the validation survey by 276 professionals who applied the provisional scale to a reported case
key_sources: Sakakida Chika, Tadaka Etsuko, Arimoto Azusa. (2021). Development and validation of a new Multidisciplinary Approach Competency Scale for Prevention of Child Abuse from Pregnancy (MUSCAT). PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0249623

article_title: Development and validation of a new Multidisciplinary Approach Competency Scale for Prevention of Child Abuse from Pregnancy (MUSCAT).
citation: Sakakida Chika, Tadaka Etsuko, Arimoto Azusa. (2021). Development and validation of a new Multidisciplinary Approach Competency Scale for Prevention of Child Abuse from Pregnancy (MUSCAT). PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0249623
title: Assess multidisciplinary competency for child abuse prevention with a scale spanning primary to tertiary prevention and the whole family
description: The article argues that competency measurement for multidisciplinary child abuse prevention should cover all prevention stages and the entire family. It states the MUSCAT "is a measure that can comprehensively evaluate healthcare professionals' competency in relation to providing a multidisciplinary approach, from primary to tertiary prevention", and that targeting high-risk caregivers requires "consideration of the entire family, including babies, children, and fathers". This scope distinguishes it from existing collaboration scales.
requirements: A competency scale grounded in the three prevention stages (primary, secondary, tertiary) and in competencies for collaboration starting from pregnancy
constraints: Existing multidisciplinary approach scales target children living at home, care recipients, and medical care personnel, and do not focus on preventing child abuse from pregnancy
target_learners: Professionals supporting high-risk caregivers from pregnancy through the puerperal and childcare periods
target_learning_goals: Evaluating and developing competency for multidisciplinary approaches across primary, secondary, and tertiary prevention of child abuse
examples: The MUSCAT items were drafted to apply to multiple professionals rather than specific professional groups and to be practically useful in community health settings
key_sources: Sakakida Chika, Tadaka Etsuko, Arimoto Azusa. (2021). Development and validation of a new Multidisciplinary Approach Competency Scale for Prevention of Child Abuse from Pregnancy (MUSCAT). PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0249623

article_title: The predictive value of high school grade point average to academic achievement and career satisfaction of dental graduates.
citation: Al-Asmar Ayah A., Oweis Yara, Ismail Noor H., Sabrah Alaa H. A., Abd-Raheam Islam M. (2021). The predictive value of high school grade point average to academic achievement and career satisfaction of dental graduates. BMC Oral Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12903-021-01662-5
title: Use multiple admission criteria beyond high school GPA because HS-GPA has limited predictive value
description: The article recommends that dental schools not rely on high school GPA alone for admission, because its significant correlation with graduating GPA is weak: "correlations below 0.40 have limited predictive value, even if statistically significant." The authors argue this "necessitates using multiple criteria to better characterize the academic and psychomotor skills required for success in dental schools," since HS-GPA left more performance variance unexplained than explained.
requirements: Access to additional selection measures capturing noncognitive elements, psychomotor skills, and personal characteristics alongside HS-GPA.
constraints: The article states the finding is from a retrospective single-institution cohort and that correlations below 0.40 have limited predictive value.
target_learning_goals: Selecting students likely to succeed academically in dental education
examples: The University of Jordan admits dental students using HS-GPA as the sole selection tool; 63% of the 736-student cohort had HS-GPA ≥ 95.5%.
key_sources: Al-Asmar Ayah A., Oweis Yara, Ismail Noor H., Sabrah Alaa H. A., Abd-Raheam Islam M. (2021). The predictive value of high school grade point average to academic achievement and career satisfaction of dental graduates. BMC Oral Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12903-021-01662-5

article_title: Effectiveness of an Emotional Intelligence Intervention and Its Impact on Academic Performance in Spanish Pre-Adolescent Elementary Students: Results from the EDI Program.
citation: Cantero María-José, Bañuls Raquel, Viguer Paz. (2020). Effectiveness of an Emotional Intelligence Intervention and Its Impact on Academic Performance in Spanish Pre-Adolescent Elementary Students: Results from the EDI Program. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph17207621
title: Deliver EI interventions across multiple school years, with particular attention to 6th grade
description: The article's results show first-year EI gains remained stable but only continued growing with a second intervention year, while the non-intervention group's EI declined during 6th grade. The authors conclude "this study provides clear evidence of the need to apply programs to enhance EI during several academic school years" and stress the importance of intervening especially in 6th grade to aid the transition to adolescence.
requirements: A sustained program structure spanning at least two academic years with repeated sessions
constraints: The academic-performance benefit remained stable only during the intervention period; the article calls for new studies on the stability of the change
target_learners: pre-adolescent elementary students, especially those in 6th grade
target_learning_goals: emotional intelligence development and academic performance support
examples: The EDI program was implemented over two academic years, with EI gains compounding across years while comparison-group EI declined in the second year

Effectiveness of an Emotional Intelligence Intervention and Its Impact on Academic Performance in Spanish Pre-Adolescent Elementary Students: Results from the EDI Program. article_title: Toward interprofessional team training for surgeons and anesthesiologists using virtual reality.
citation: Chheang Vuthea, Fischer Virve, Buggenhagen Holger, Huber Tobias, Huettl Florentine, Kneist Werner, Preim Bernhard, Saalfeld Patrick, Hansen Christian. (2020). Toward interprofessional team training for surgeons and anesthesiologists using virtual reality. International Journal of Computer Assisted Radiology and Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11548-020-02276-y
title: Multi-user VR prototype integrating LLEAP anesthesia simulation with laparoscopic surgery simulation
description: A client–server VR system in which "an anesthesia simulation software and laparoscopic simulation software are combined within a multi-user virtual reality (VR) environment." Built in Unity with HTC Vive head-mounted displays, Simball joystick laparoscopic instruments, and foot pedals; LLEAP (Laerdal) with the SimMan 3G profile supplies vital signs, whose screen is captured and rendered on a virtual respirator. Medication adjustments drive automated virtual mouse and keyboard inputs into LLEAP, and vital-sign changes follow simple linear-interpolation models for narcosis, bleeding, and muscle relaxant offset.
requirements: Three VR-ready computers connected to a local wireless network in a client–server configuration
LLEAP anesthesia simulation software and the previously developed laparoscopic simulation component
constraints: The authors note devices are still expensive and development is time-consuming, and that some anesthesiologist tasks could be utilized in a simple 2D display
target_learning_goals: intraoperative communication between anesthesiologists and surgeons during laparoscopic procedures
examples: Scenario 1 triggers a clip slipping off during a phone-call distraction, dropping ABP and raising pulse until the vessel is re-clipped
Scenario 2 shows organ pressing animation and rising TOF until the anesthesiologist injects a refreshment dose of muscle relaxant

article_title: Interactive Clinical Avatar Use in Pharmacist Preregistration Training: Design and Review.
citation: Jessica Thompson, Simon White, Stephen Chapman. (2020). Interactive Clinical Avatar Use in Pharmacist Preregistration Training: Design and Review. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/17146
title: Multistep design-and-review process establishing content and face validity of avatar simulations
description: A reusable design pattern in which simulations move through case design from literature, syllabus, and practitioner discussion; script design reviewed against constructive alignment principles with a pharmacist consultant for each case; and avatar design balancing realism against the uncanny valley. "Creating the interactive clinical avatar simulations involved multiple reviews and subsequent amendments to ensure content and face validity of the cases." Internal review by the research and digital development teams and registered pharmacists preceded trainee review of the EHC case, with ethical approval obtained.
requirements: Review by registered pharmacists to establish content and face validity of all cases
A decision tree script with an ideal pathway against which decisions are categorized
constraints: The article notes only one round of recruitment occurred as saturation of themes was reached
target_learning_goals: valid development of simulation-based clinical training cases
examples: Avatars were "designed to express humanistic characteristics through simple body language, movements, and prerecorded voice replies" to avoid the uncanny valley, such as the EHC avatar blushing when requesting the morning after pill
key_sources: Jessica Thompson, Simon White, Stephen Chapman. (2020). Interactive Clinical Avatar Use in Pharmacist Preregistration Training: Design and Review. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/17146

article_title: Application of multidirectional stitching technology in a laparoscopic suturing instructional program: a randomized controlled trial.
citation: Yu Zhao, Qiong Chen, Jia-Ning Hu, Qi Shen, Lu Xia, Lin-Zhi Yan, Yi Wang, Xiu-Jie Zhu, Wen-Ju Li, Yue Hu, Qiong Zhang. (2020). Application of multidirectional stitching technology in a laparoscopic suturing instructional program: a randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-020-02146-w
title: Multidirectional stitching technology and circular suture training module
description: A training module in which learners practice laparoscopic needle delivery using varied needle-holding directions — positive, reverse, oblique (left, right), and swivel ("loosely clipping") — on a circular sponge pad with four incisions in different directions. Each incision is marked with "a small dot with a diameter of 0.5 cm on both sides of the incision" placed 0.75 cm from the incision centre, guiding needle entry and exit points. The module contrasts with traditional instruction on a 3D silicone model pad where the suture angle is fixed at 90 degrees to the needle.
requirements: A laparoscopic trainer box with camera and video display, two lockable needle holders, and a No. 1, 26 mm, 1/2 c round-bodied needle with 30 cm thread
An experienced instructor guiding four hands-on courses
constraints: Evaluated only against traditional teaching, in a small single-centre sample of junior residents
target_learning_goals: manual laparoscopic suturing and knot-tying proficiency
examples: The experimental group trained on the circular sponge module while the control group used a 3D silicone model pad, both for four forty-minute courses
key_sources: Yu Zhao, Qiong Chen, Jia-Ning Hu, Qi Shen, Lu Xia, Lin-Zhi Yan, Yi Wang, Xiu-Jie Zhu, Wen-Ju Li, Yue Hu, Qiong Zhang. (2020). BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-020-02146-w

article_title: Opening the black box of selection.
citation: Sanne Schreurs, Kitty Cleutjens, Carlos F. Collares, Jennifer Cleland, Mirjam G. A. oude Egbrink. (2019). Opening the black box of selection. Advances in Health Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-019-09925-1
title: MUMS multi-tool, outcome-based medical school selection procedure (V-SJT and WAT)
description: The Maastricht University selection procedure is a two-round, three-tool procedure based on a blueprint of derived competencies from the CanMEDS framework. The article states "The selection procedure consists of two rounds containing three tools (hence, multi-tool)": an online portfolio pre-screening, then a selection day with a video-based situational judgment test (90 min, 11 items) and a written aptitude test (75 min, 8 items). Scores are z-transformed, averaged per tool, and ranked for admission decisions. The V-SJT focuses on interpersonal competencies; the WAT covers a broader array.
requirements: A selection committee of subject matter experts who translate CanMEDS competencies into measurable entry-level derived competencies and create items with answer keys
constraints: Validity evidence in this study covers only the second round; evidence should be gathered for the procedure as a whole
The issue of how constructs and tools should be weighted remains an open question in the general selection literature
target_learners: Applicants to the Bachelor of Medicine at Maastricht University
target_learning_goals: Selecting candidates on predetermined (inter)personal and cognitive competencies
examples: In 2016, 547 candidates completed the second round consisting of the V-SJT and WAT
key_sources: Sanne Schreurs, Kitty Cleutjens, Carlos F. Collares, Jennifer Cleland, Mirjam G. A. oude Egbrink. (2019). Opening the black box of selection. Advances in Health Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-019-09925-1

article_title: Utilization of high-fidelity simulation to address challenges with the basic science immunology education of preclinical medical students.
citation: Cavuoto Petrizzo Marie, Barilla-LaBarca Maria-Louise, Lim Youn Seon, Jongco Artemio M., Cassara Michael, Anglim James, Stern Joel N.H. (2019). Utilization of high-fidelity simulation to address challenges with the basic science immunology education of preclinical medical students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1786-5
title: Simulation structured through the phases of an integrated multi-theory adult learning model (base knowledge, dissonance, refinement, organization, feedback, consolidation)
description: The article organizes the simulation's learning mechanism using the 2013 AMEE Guide multi-theory model of adult learning, which the authors cite as combining conventional learning theories. Learning is structured on base knowledge from readings and didactic sessions; the "dissonance phase of this model [7] is entered when students engage in the simulation experience"; debriefing carries the refinement, organization and feedback phases, and consolidation occurs as learners reflect on the big picture. The authors position their joint-faculty debrief as compatible with this model.
requirements: Base knowledge established before the simulation via readings, didactic sessions, and problem/case-based learning
Content-expert debrief facilitators support students during refinement, organization and feedback phases
target_learning_goals: Integration of basic science immunology with clinical reasoning for immunodeficiency diseases
examples: The PIDD simulation debriefs, led by paired science and clinical faculty using a Socratic approach, were designed to let students reflect on, organize and articulate new immunologic explanations.
key_sources: Cavuoto Petrizzo Marie, Barilla-LaBarca Maria-Louise, Lim Youn Seon, Jongco Artemio M., Cassara Michael, Anglim James, Stern Joel N.H. (2019). Utilization of high-fidelity simulation to address challenges with the basic science immunology education of preclinical medical students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1786-5

article_title: Delayed Disaster Impacts on Academic Performance of Primary School Children.
citation: Gibbs, L., Nursey, J., Cook, J., Ireton, G., Alkemade, N., Roberts, M., Gallagher, H. C., Bryant, R., Block, K., Molyneaux, R., & Forbes, D. (2019). Delayed Disaster Impacts on Academic Performance of Primary School Children. Child Development. https://doi.org/10.1111/cdev.13200
title: Provide positive multilevel school strategies and targeted postdisaster support to mitigate delayed academic impacts
description: The article recommends that schools and education systems plan comprehensive postdisaster support extending beyond the first years after an event, because delayed academic impacts may otherwise be overlooked. It states that "there are opportunities to mitigate negative impacts on child academic achievements through positive multilevel school strategies," combining sensitive teacher support, targeted academic support, and extracurricular engagement.
requirements: School staff and systems must recognize that delayed impacts can arise from the disaster experience years later, since over time parents and schools may not recognize delayed impacts
constraints: The supporting evidence for specific mitigation factors is described as indicated but not yet proven; the article calls for research identifying the content and dose of effective school-level interventions
target_learners: Primary school children in disaster-affected communities
target_learning_goals: Maintaining expected academic progression in reading and numeracy after disaster exposure
examples: The study analyzed NAPLAN progression from Year 3 to Year 5 across low, moderate, and high affectedness regions up to 4 years after the Black Saturday bushfires, adjusting for demographics collected the year before the fires
key_sources: Gibbs, L., Nursey, J., Cook, J., Ireton, G., Alkemade, N., Roberts, M., Gallagher, H. C., Bryant, R., Block, K., Molyneaux, R., & Forbes, D. (2019). Delayed Disaster Impacts on Academic Performance of Primary School Children. Child Development. https://doi.org/10.1111/cdev.13200

article_title: Cluster Randomized Trial to Facilitate Breast Cancer Early Diagnosis in a Rural District of Rwanda.
citation: Pace LE, Dusengimana JMV, Shulman LN, Schleimer LE, Shyirambere C, Rusangwa C, Muvugabigwi G, Park PH, Huang C, Bigirimana JB, Hategekimana V, Rugema V, Umwizerwa A, Keating NL, Mpunga T. (2019). Cluster Randomized Trial to Facilitate Breast Cancer Early Diagnosis in a Rural District of Rwanda. Journal of Global Oncology. https://doi.org/10.1200/JGO.19.00209
title: Multilevel breast health training intervention for community health workers, health center nurses, and hospital clinicians in rural Rwanda
description: The intervention trained three levels of Rwanda's health system simultaneously. Community health workers learned breast cancer symptoms and messaging that community members should visit their health center for any breast symptom. Nurses "were taught about signs and symptoms of benign breast disease and cancer and how to perform a CBE" and received "simple clinical algorithms for managing breast symptoms", plus ongoing mentorship from a hospital-based nurse-midwife. Hospital clinicians were trained in diagnostic breast ultrasound and ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy, and weekly breast clinics were launched.
requirements: Training must reach all nurses at intervention health centers and all community health workers serving their catchment sectors
Ongoing mentorship and support from a hospital-based nurse-midwife trained in breast health
Hospital-level diagnostic capacity, including clinicians trained in ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy and onsite pathology services
constraints: The authors state their experience "may not be generalizable to other districts in Rwanda" because Burera patients already had shorter delays before the intervention
Programs must ensure access to timely, affordable, and high-quality treatment of all patients diagnosed with cancer
target_learners: hospital clinicians in a rural district health system
target_learning_goals: recognize symptoms of benign and malignant breast disease
perform clinical breast examination
triage and refer patients with concerning breast findings
perform diagnostic breast ultrasound and ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy
examples: Twelve of 18 eligible health centers were randomly assigned to receive training in two phases (7 in April to May 2015, 5 in November to December 2015), with 6 health centers serving as controls throughout
key_sources: Pace LE, Dusengimana JMV, Shulman LN, Schleimer LE, Shyirambere C, Rusangwa C, Muvugabigwi G, Park PH, Huang C, Bigirimana JB, Hategekimana V, Rugema V, Umwizerwa A, Keating NL, Mpunga T.
