article_title: Detecting Mistakes in CPR Training with Multimodal Data and Neural Networks.
citation: Di Mitri Daniele, Schneider Jan, Specht Marcus, Drachsler Hendrik. (2019). Detecting Mistakes in CPR Training with Multimodal Data and Neural Networks. Sensors (Basel, Switzerland). https://doi.org/10.3390/s19143099
title: Multimodal Tutor for CPR — a multi-sensor intelligent tutoring system combining Kinect, Myo armband and ResusciAnne manikin data
description: The Multimodal Tutor for CPR is "a multi-sensor, intelligent tutoring system to train CPR using the ResusciAnne manikins", built as "a specific implementation of the Multimodal Tutoring System, consisting of a Kinect camera and a Myo armband". It gathers 60 Kinect attributes from 15 body joints, 18 Myo attributes, and SimPad baseline indicators, and its mistake-detection system was validated with LSTM classifiers on data from 11 experts. The authors demonstrate that "multimodal data can be used as the base to drive machine reasoning and adaptation during learning" for automatic and retrospective feedback.
requirements: Requires the experimental setup to remain unchanged, since moving the Kinect or adding or removing a sensor yields a different feature set
Requires labelled performance-indicator annotations used as classification targets
constraints: The prototype was deemed unsuitable for complete beginners and was tested with participants who had previous training knowledge
Setup changes make generalising across settings more difficult
target_learners: Medical and dentistry students training in CPR
target_learning_goals: Correct chest compression rate, depth and release
Locked arms and correct body weight use during compressions
examples: Used with 11 medical students performing two two-minute compression sessions each in the Uniklinik Aachen simulation centre
key_sources: Di Mitri Daniele, Schneider Jan, Specht Marcus, Drachsler Hendrik. (2019). Detecting Mistakes in CPR Training with Multimodal Data and Neural Networks. Sensors (Basel, Switzerland). https://doi.org/10.3390/s19143099

article_title: Effectiveness of spiritual care training to enhance spiritual health and spiritual care competency among oncology nurses.
citation: Hu Yanli, Jiao Miaorui, Li Fan. (2019). Effectiveness of spiritual care training to enhance spiritual health and spiritual care competency among oncology nurses. BMC Palliative Care. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12904-019-0489-3
title: Mutual growth with patients as the organizing concept of spiritual care training
description: The protocol was designed "based on the concept of mutual growth with patients": enhancing nurses' own spiritual health is the point of entry for building their spiritual care competency, on the premise that nurses with spiritual health better recognize and respond to patients' spiritual needs. The authors describe team members forming "a cooperative learning team that enjoyed mutual growth," and argue that helping patients find meaning also strengthens nurses' own meaning-making, making the process "mutually influencing and mutually reinforcing."
requirements: Group settings in which nurses can share feelings and review their own spiritual needs with trusted colleagues over time
constraints: The authors frame the mutual-reinforcement pathway as a direction for future research to evaluate rather than a tested mechanism
target_learners: Clinical nurses, especially senior nurses who teach other nurses and nursing students
target_learning_goals: Nurses' spiritual self-awareness and spiritual growth
Ability to provide spiritual care to patients
examples: Group pledge and sharing of feelings sessions gave nurses an opportunity to review their own spiritual needs during the 12-month programme

article_title: A multifactorial approach of nutritional, intellectual, brain development, cardiovascular risk, socio-economic, demographic and educational variables affecting the scholastic achievement in Chilean students: An eight- year follow-up study.
citation: Ivanovic Daniza M. et al. (2019). A multifactorial approach of nutritional, intellectual, brain development, cardiovascular risk, socio-economic, demographic and educational variables affecting the scholastic achievement in Chilean students: An eight- year follow-up study. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0212279
title: Use multifactorial early assessment of child, family and school factors to identify risk groups with suboptimal learning
description: The article argues that scholastic achievement is a multifactorial phenomenon resulting from the interaction of child, family and educational-system factors, and that children with cognitive, behavioural and educational problems must be detected at an early age. It states the findings "allow the identification of risk groups with suboptimal learning, in order to implement all necessary measures to improve their outcomes starting from an early age". The relevant factors include intellectual ability, school achievement level, parental schooling, head circumference and sex.
requirements: Assessment must combine child (nutritional, intellectual, brain development), family and educational-system variables rather than any single factor
constraints: The results show statistical association and do not represent a direct cause and effect relationship, as the article states
target_learners: school-age children in elementary and high school
target_learning_goals: scholastic achievement in language and mathematics
examples: A representative stratified sample of 33 schools and 1,353 students in the Metropolitan Region of Chile was assessed in 2010 and followed up in 2015 and 2018

article_title: Teaching obstetric ultrasound at Mulago Hospital - Kampala, Uganda.
citation: Ahmadzia Homa, Cigna Sarah, Namagembe Imelda, Macri Charles, Galerneau France, Magriples Urania. (2018). Teaching obstetric ultrasound at Mulago Hospital - Kampala, Uganda. African Health Sciences. https://doi.org/10.4314/ahs.v18i1.21
title: Two-hour didactic-plus-hands-on obstetric ultrasound teaching intervention
description: A short instructional course combining didactic education with hands-on demonstration, totaling "approximately two hours". Topics included "fundamentals of performing an ultrasound and optimizing an image, fetal presentation, placental position, amniotic fluid index, fetal biometry and biophysical profile". Hands-on skills were taught in small groups of two to three participants at a time using patient volunteers with ongoing second-trimester pregnancies, delivered by a single trainer, with a post-test administered immediately afterward.
requirements: A trainer with senior-level experience in basic obstetric ultrasound
Patient volunteers with ongoing pregnancies for the hands-on demonstration portion
A pre- and post-test survey to assess knowledge change
constraints: The overall training period was very short, as the authors state
target_learning_goals: Basic obstetric ultrasound skills: fetal lie and presentation, placental position, amniotic fluid volume assessment, fetal biometry and biophysical profile
examples: Delivered at Mulago Hospital, Kampala, to 40 volunteer participants between mid-November and mid-December 2010

article_title: Developing and evaluating clinical leadership interventions for frontline healthcare providers: a review of the literature.
citation: Mianda Solange, Voce Anna. (2018). Developing and evaluating clinical leadership interventions for frontline healthcare providers: a review of the literature. BMC Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-018-3561-4
title: Deliver in-service clinical leadership training as multiple time-spaced contact sessions rather than intensive once-off training
description: The review finds that most interventions used multiple contact sessions of varying duration, from days to months, and concludes that "Multiple time-spaced contact sessions appear to be the most suitable approach to delivering in-service training programmes". Spaced sessions give participants time and space to engage, reflect on content, and apply knowledge and skills in the workplace. Intensive once-off sessions are shown to negatively affect participants' motivation.
requirements: A reasonable timeframe tailored to participants' needs
constraints: Interventions that were too intensive and demanding affected motivation and ability to attend all sessions; short timelines did not allow assessing impact on participants, service users or service delivery
target_learners: practicing frontline healthcare providers in in-service training
target_learning_goals: sustained development of clinical leadership competencies
examples: Reviewed interventions ranged from 2-day workshops to 12-month programmes with monthly sessions; one intervention offered one 2-h session monthly for 9 months
key_sources: Mianda Solange, Voce Anna. (2018). Developing and evaluating clinical leadership interventions for frontline healthcare providers: a review of the literature. BMC Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-018-3561-4

article_title: Learning through multiple lenses: analysis of self, peer, near-peer and faculty assessment of a clinical history taking task in Australia.
citation: Fitzgerald K, Vaughan B. (2018). Learning through multiple lenses: analysis of self, peer, nearpeer, and faculty assessments of a clinical history-taking task in Australia. J Educ Eval Health Prof. https://doi.org/10.3352/jeehp.2018.15.22
title: Multiple-source assessment as a means of developing evaluative judgement and calibrating self-assessment
description: The article frames peer, NP, and self assessment as complementary feedback sources under the theory of evaluative judgement, defined as "the ability to critically assess a performance in relation to a predefined but not necessarily explicit standard." Because single-source feedback "may not always capture all aspects of learners' performance," feedback from multiple sources may help develop assessment and feedback literacy and calibrate students' self-assessment against faculty standards.
requirements: Learners need support in developing assessment and feedback literacy
calibration is facilitated through feedback from multiple sources
constraints: Peer and NP marks' contribution to grades remains contested by students in this study
target_learners: health professional students in clinical skills courses
target_learning_goals: evaluative judgement
self-assessment calibration
assessment and feedback literacy
examples: Self and peer marks correlating moderately with faculty marks was interpreted as a shared understanding of the assessment standard
key_sources: Fitzgerald K, Vaughan B. (2018). Learning through multiple lenses: analysis of self, peer, nearpeer, and faculty assessments of a clinical history-taking task in Australia. J Educ Eval Health Prof. https://doi.org/10.3352/jeehp.2018.15.22

article_title: Disseminating START: training clinical psychologists and admiral nurses as trainers in a psychosocial intervention for carers of people with dementia's depressive and anxiety symptoms.
citation: Lord Kathryn, Rapaport Penny, Cooper Claudia, Livingston Gill. (2017). Disseminating START: training clinical psychologists and admiral nurses as trainers in a psychosocial intervention for carers of people with dementia's depressive and anxiety symptoms. BMJ Open 7(8): e017759. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2017-017759
title: Disseminate evidence-based interventions through multifaceted interactive train-the-trainer workshops with implementation planning, not passive information transfer
description: The article's dissemination approach was "based on evidence that effective interventions to disseminate research findings into practice are usually multifaceted, comprising interactive teaching with feedback on practice and making plans to implement interventions". Its 3-hour workshops combined evidence review, supervision vignette exercises and local action planning, and attendees left with next steps and named support needs.
requirements: Attendees read the START manual in advance and committed to the evaluation as a condition of free training
The trainer has experience of developing and trialling the intervention and provides all training materials for local adaptation
constraints: Passive dissemination of information may be ineffective even when people agree with the material
Attendee feedback indicated the 3-hour format was not sufficient, with requests for longer training
target_learning_goals: delivering and supervising the START intervention
implementing an evidence-based intervention in local services
examples: Workshops followed the table 1 structure: evidence overview, large- and small-group exercises on training and supervision dilemmas using clinical vignettes, and local implementation action planning
All manuals and training materials were made freely available on a website, and the research team offered ongoing tailored advice and reminders
key_sources: Lord Kathryn, Rapaport Penny, Cooper Claudia, Livingston Gill. (2017). Disseminating START: training clinical psychologists and admiral nurses as trainers in a psychosocial intervention for carers of people with dementia's depressive and anxiety symptoms. BMJ Open 7(8): e017759. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2017-017759

article_title: A Vision and Change Reform of Introductory Biology Shifts Faculty Perceptions and Use of Active Learning.
citation: Auerbach Anna Jo and Schussler Elisabeth. (2017). A Vision and Change Reform of Introductory Biology Shifts Faculty Perceptions and Use of Active Learning. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.16-08-0258
title: Sustain curricular reform through a multi-year community of practice with regular meetings, shared observation data, and collaborative decision-making
description: The article recommends embedding pedagogical change in a programmatic, multi-year reform community rather than one-time workshops. Faculty met monthly to discuss the reform, review literature, share resources, and make implementation decisions, and received anonymous feedback on their own and the program's active-learning use each semester. As the authors state, "it is recommended that institutions fostering reform should host regular meetings with the instructors where they are asked to discuss and make decisions about implementation of their courses."
requirements: Regular group meetings where instructors discuss and decide course implementation
Sharing of instructors' own and program-level active-learning observation data as feedback
Sufficient time (the reform ran 3 years) for instructors to integrate new ideas
constraints: The authors caution that time and a supportive group "may not be enough to shift instructional practices for all instructor groups," citing a 3-year professional development program where most faculty still used lecture-based pedagogy
The study was not designed to investigate causal mechanisms of change
target_learners: University faculty teaching large-enrollment introductory STEM courses
target_learning_goals: Increased use of student-centered active-learning pedagogies
Alignment of instructor perceptions with actual instructional practice
examples: Faculty met about once a month for at least 1 hour to review literature on backward design and student-centered learning and to set program goals such as increasing group AL
At the end of each semester, instructors received their own anonymized AL data and the compiled program data
key_sources: Auerbach Anna Jo and Schussler Elisabeth. (2017). A Vision and Change Reform of Introductory Biology Shifts Faculty Perceptions and Use of Active Learning. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.16-08-0258

article_title: Training on domestic violence and child safeguarding in general practice: a mixed method evaluation of a pilot intervention.
citation: Lewis Natalia V., Larkins Cath, Stanley Nicky, Szilassy Eszter, Turner William, Drinkwater Jessica, Feder Gene S. (2017). Training on domestic violence and child safeguarding in general practice: a mixed method evaluation of a pilot intervention. BMC Family Practice 18:33. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12875-017-0603-7
title: Co-deliver safeguarding training with local multi-agency trainers from health and children's social services
description: A design principle from the pilot: training that links DVA and child safeguarding is delivered by a pair of trainers, one from health care and one from local children's social work, so participants hear frontline perspectives from both systems. Participants valued this strongly: 'I think it's absolutely fantastic having professionals who are dealing with this day and day out' (TGP06), and the social services input was described as 'that extra thing' beyond existing IRIS training. The principle rests on the acceptability findings rather than measured outcome differences.
requirements: Access to local frontline professionals from both health and children's social services willing to co-train
constraints: The article values co-delivery qualitatively; it does not test co-delivery as a manipulated variable, so outcome superiority is not established
target_learners: general practice teams including GPs, nurses and allied primary care staff
target_learning_goals: understanding children's social services roles and referral processes
inter-agency collaboration in safeguarding
examples: Each observed session paired a health professional (e.g., named GP for safeguarding, MARAC liaison nurse) with a social worker (e.g., Early Help co-ordinator, children's social care senior practitioner)
key_sources: Lewis Natalia V., Larkins Cath, Stanley Nicky, Szilassy Eszter, Turner William, Drinkwater Jessica, Feder Gene S. (2017). Training on domestic violence and child safeguarding in general practice: a mixed method evaluation of a pilot intervention. BMC Family Practice 18:33. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12875-017-0603-7

article_title: Impact of multi-professional, scenario-based training on postpartum hemorrhage in Tanzania: a quasi-experimental, pre- vs. post-intervention study.
citation: Egenberg, S., Masenga, G., Bru, L. E., Eggebø, T. M., Mushi, C., Massay, D., & Øian, P. (2017). Impact of multi-professional, scenario-based training on postpartum hemorrhage in Tanzania: a quasi-experimental, pre- vs. post-intervention study. BMC Pregnancy and Childbirth. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12884-017-1478-2
title: Multi-professional scenario-based emergency training combining realistic repeated scenarios, vicarious observation, and team debriefing
description: A one-day, on-site training pattern in which small multi-professional teams (nurses, midwives, doctors, medical attendants) work through realistic clinical scenarios on a low-fidelity birthing simulator. The article states that "realistic PPH-scenarios were repeated in training, vicarious observation provided an objective learning experience, and reflective learning was encouraged through debriefings within the team". Each scenario is followed by debriefing, repeated, then roles swap so observers become participants, giving four scenarios per group per day, grounded in Kolb's experiential learning theory.
requirements: A local faculty of facilitators and scenario operators trained in debriefing
Low-fidelity simulator equipment and learning materials matched to local guidelines
Scenarios that reflect typical ward staffing, equipment, and medicines
constraints: The authors note low doctor attendance (50% and 29% in the two sessions), limiting doctors' opportunity to learn and practice teamwork
The study design could not determine causality, only association with transfusion rates
target_learners: All cadres of maternity staff in a hospital department (nurses, midwives, doctors, medical attendants)
target_learning_goals: Prevent, identify and treat postpartum hemorrhage
Communicate adequately, call for help, and lead within a team during obstetric emergencies
examples: At KCMC, 70 staff were trained in October 2013 and 67 in November 2014, in teams of 8–10, using the MamaNatalie simulator and translated Helping Mothers Survive: Bleeding after birth materials
key_sources: Egenberg, S., Masenga, G., Bru, L. E., Eggebø, T. M., Mushi, C., Massay, D., & Øian, P. (2017). Impact of multi-professional, scenario-based training on postpartum hemorrhage in Tanzania: a quasi-experimental, pre- vs. post-intervention study. BMC Pregnancy and Childbirth. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12884-017-1478-2

article_title: Multilevel Assessment of Middle School Students' Interest in the Health Sciences: Development and Validation of a New Measurement Tool.
citation: Romine William L., Miller Michele E., Knese Shawn A., Folk William R. (2016). Multilevel Assessment of Middle School Students' Interest in the Health Sciences: Development and Validation of a New Measurement Tool. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.15-02-0034
title: Multilevel assessment applied to affective constructs
description: Multilevel assessment, introduced by Ruiz-Primo and colleagues, negotiates location bias by "measuring students at a variety of locations with respect to the curriculum of instruction": assessments close to the curriculum trade generalizability for sensitivity, while distal assessments sacrifice sensitivity for generalizability. This article is the first to apply the framework to an affective construct, interest, by positioning three subscales (science, healthcare, vision care) at different distances from a 2-wk intervention. The authors extend the cognition–observation–interpretation triangle to an "affection–observation–interpretation" (AOI) triangle for affective conceptual change.
requirements: Subscales must be positioned at explicitly defined distances from the instructional context, with Rasch scales equated to a common metric before comparing sensitivity
constraints: Overaligned assessments risk inflated effect sizes and non-generalizable findings; the study found sensitivity did not differ between the proximal and distal subscales, suggesting students' own interpretation of curricular distance may differ from the researcher's labels
target_learning_goals: measuring change in personal interest in science and health careers
examples: The AIMS positioned Interest in Vision Care close, Interest in Healthcare proximal, and Interest in Science distal to a 2-wk eye and vision unit
key_sources: Romine William L., Miller Michele E., Knese Shawn A., Folk William R. (2016). Multilevel Assessment of Middle School Students' Interest in the Health Sciences: Development and Validation of a New Measurement Tool. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.15-02-0034

article_title: Improving confidence and competence of healthcare professionals in end-of-life care: an evaluation of the 'Transforming End of Life Care' course at an acute hospital trust.
citation: Selman L, Robinson V, Klass L, Khan S, George R, Shepherd K, Burman R, Koffman J. (2016). Improving confidence and competence of healthcare professionals in end-of-life care: an evaluation of the 'Transforming End of Life Care' course at an acute hospital trust. BMJ Support Palliat Care. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjspcare-2015-000879
title: End-of-life care training should combine multiple interactive teaching methods and be multiprofessional by design
description: The article attributes the course's perceived success to its combination of lectures, case-based group work, interactive workshops and Q&A, and to being multiprofessional by design, which the authors believe is "central to its success in increasing staff confidence and knowledge". This aligns with cited evidence that combined approaches and interactive workshops can produce moderately large changes in professional practice. The principle targets non-specialist providers caring for dying patients.
requirements: Taught by a multiprofessional palliative care team (nurses, consultants, social workers, chaplain)
Content responsive to participants' needs
constraints: Evidence for this attribution is the authors' interpretation and cited external reviews, not a direct comparison in this evaluation
target_learners: Non-specialist palliative care providers in hospitals and community settings
target_learning_goals: Confidence, knowledge and communication skills in end-of-life care
examples: The 2-day TEoLC course used lectures, group work on case studies and clinical scenarios, interactive workshops and question and answer sessions
key_sources: Selman L, Robinson V, Klass L, Khan S, George R, Shepherd K, Burman R, Koffman J. (2016). Improving confidence and competence of healthcare professionals in end-of-life care: an evaluation of the 'Transforming End of Life Care' course at an acute hospital trust. BMJ Support Palliat Care. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjspcare-2015-000879

article_title: A tertiary approach to improving equity in health: quantitative analysis of the Māori and Pacific Admission Scheme (MAPAS) process, 2008-2012.
citation: Curtis Elana, Wikaire Erena, Jiang Yannan, McMillan Louise, Loto Rob, Airini, Reid Papaarangi. (2015). A tertiary approach to improving equity in health: quantitative analysis of the Māori and Pacific Admission Scheme (MAPAS) process, 2008–2012. International Journal for Equity in Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12939-015-0133-7
title: Use multiple cognitive and non-cognitive selection tools with alternative entry pathways in equity-targeted tertiary admissions
description: The article recommends that tertiary admissions for indigenous and ethnic minority applicants combine cognitive tools (secondary results, tests) with non-cognitive tools (MMI stations assessing career aspirations, academic preparation, family support) and provide bridging/foundation pathways. It argues that "the MMI, applied within an equity and indigenous cultural context, can provide important information that supports a more holistic assessment" of applicant potential. The recommendation rests on the finding that only 13% of the cohort were assessed ready for direct Bachelor entry, making alternative pathways necessary.
requirements: a comprehensive tertiary admissions process using multiple tools for selection (cognitive and non-cognitive)
provision of alternative entry pathways such as bridging/foundation programmes
constraints: The MAPAS process requires significant staff contribution, faculty and government equity-funding for successful delivery
the approach may clash with institutional guaranteed-entry criteria driven by funding caps
target_learners: indigenous and ethnic minority tertiary applicants
Māori and Pacific health professional programme applicants
target_learning_goals: widening participation in health professional study
identifying the best starting point for academic success
examples: MAPAS recommends CertHSc bridging study for applicants not ready for direct Bachelor entry; the CertHSc programme is restricted to approximately 70 students
key_sources: Curtis Elana, Wikaire Erena, Jiang Yannan, McMillan Louise, Loto Rob, Airini, Reid Papaarangi. (2015). A tertiary approach to improving equity in health: quantitative analysis of the Māori and Pacific Admission Scheme (MAPAS) process, 2008–2012. International Journal for Equity in Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12939-015-0133-7

article_title: Training Sri Lankan public health midwives on intimate partner violence: a pre- and post-intervention study.
citation: Jayatilleke Achini Chinthika, Yoshikawa Kayoko, Yasuoka Junko, Poudel Krishna C, Fernando Nilani, Jayatilleke Achala Upendra, Jimba Masamine. (2015). Training Sri Lankan public health midwives on intimate partner violence: a pre- and post-intervention study. BMC Public Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-015-1674-9
title: Train community health providers on IPV over multiple days with role-playing, case reports, and culturally sensitive guidance
description: The article argues IPV training for community health providers should be long enough for skills practice and adapted to local cultural norms. It attributes the program's success partly to "the length of the training (four days), and the time allocated to role-playing and case reports", since previous programs ran less than two days, and to a culturally sensitive approach in which PHMs were advised to respect cultural values and act cautiously about separation. It cites research that opportunities to practice skills and receive feedback can significantly improve DV training outcomes.
requirements: Trainers skilled in role-playing and case discussion; understanding of local cultural norms around IPV; time and resources for multi-day delivery
constraints: The authors state generalization of their results is limited; they present the three success factors as possible explanations ("might"), not tested manipulations
target_learners: Community health providers in developing-country settings, such as public health midwives
target_learning_goals: Practical skills in identifying and assisting IPV sufferers
Culturally sensitive intervention and referral practices
examples: The Kandy program asked PHMs to respect cultural norms, ensure privacy, keep information confidential, and network with local women's groups and social services for referral
key_sources: Jayatilleke Achini Chinthika, Yoshikawa Kayoko, Yasuoka Junko, Poudel Krishna C, Fernando Nilani, Jayatilleke Achala Upendra, Jimba Masamine. (2015). Training Sri Lankan public health midwives on intimate partner violence: a pre- and post-intervention study. BMC Public Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-015-1674-9

article_title: The effect of active learning methodologies on the teaching of pharmaceutical care in a Brazilian pharmacy faculty.
citation: Mesquita Alessandra R., Souza Werlissandra M., Boaventura Thays C., Barros Izadora M. C., Antoniolli Angelo R., Silva Wellington B., Lyra Júnior Divaldo P. (2015). The Effect of Active Learning Methodologies on the Teaching of Pharmaceutical Care in a Brazilian Pharmacy Faculty. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0123141
title: A learner-centered pharmaceutical care course combining dialogic expository teaching, role play, simulated patient, case studies, and virtual patient
description: This 16-week mandatory course for fifth-year pharmacy students pairs pharmaceutical care content with a deliberately varied set of active learning strategies: dialogic classroom expository lessons in which knowledge is constructed through exchange, questions and discussion; role play with students alternating patient and pharmacist roles; a trained postgraduate simulated patient presenting a standardized scenario; case-study discussions; and virtual patient clinical cases running from patient assessment through care plan documentation. An expert focus group first identified the competencies needed for pharmaceutical care practice and developed activities to foster them. The course was piloted in 2013 and revised from student feedback before the 2014 study.
requirements: an expert focus group to identify the competencies necessary for the practice of pharmaceutical care and to develop specific learning activities and teaching methods that would foster these competencies
constraints: the article notes the course's little contact with real patients, so a set of active learning techniques were used that can decrease the gap between training and actual patient experience
target_learning_goals: pharmaceutical care competencies: assessing patients' drug-related needs, identifying and solving drug-related problems, care plan development, communication and counseling
examples: role-playing exercises in which the patient role is played by another pharmacy student with 5–10 minutes to review each role; a postgraduate pharmacy student trained to play a patient presenting a standardized scenario
key_sources: Mesquita Alessandra R., Souza Werlissandra M., Boaventura Thays C., Barros Izadora M. C., Antoniolli Angelo R., Silva Wellington B., Lyra Júnior Divaldo P. (2015). The Effect of Active Learning Methodologies on the Teaching of Pharmaceutical Care in a Brazilian Pharmacy Faculty. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0123141

article_title: Optimization of competency in obstetrical emergencies: a role for simulation training.
citation: Monod Cécile, Voekt Cora A., Gisin Martina, Gisin Stefan, Hoesli Irene M. (2013). Optimization of competency in obstetrical emergencies: a role for simulation training. Archives of Gynecology and Obstetrics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00404-013-3111-6
title: One-day multi-professional obstetrical emergency simulation course with role-retention, small mixed groups, standardized patients and video-supported debriefing
description: A reusable course design in which mixed teams of midwives and junior and senior obstetricians train six emergency scenarios (shoulder dystocia, postpartal haemorrhage, instrumental delivery, pre-eclampsia/eclampsia, maternal Basic Life Support, neonatal resuscitation) on simple and high-fidelity mannequins. Participants "trained in small groups and retained their normal function" under multi-professional tutor teams, with "scripted role players... as standardized patients at all the training stations". After each scenario a debriefing gave immediate feedback, with video extracts shown where applicable.
requirements: Multi-professional tutor-teams of experienced obstetricians, anaesthesiologists and neonatologists with special education in leading simulation courses
Small groups of maximum six participants mixing two midwives, two junior and two senior obstetricians
Presentation of clinical algorithms and crisis resource management essentials before training
constraints: Videotaping was done only with participant consent at three of six stations and records erased after the course
The course was voluntary and its financial costs may have attracted specially interested participants
target_learning_goals: management of obstetrical emergencies
team communication
knowledge of clinical algorithms
self-confidence in emergencies
examples: Six courses ran between November 2010 and March 2012 at the Swiss Center for Medical Simulation (SimBa), Basel, with 168 participants from public and private Swiss hospitals
key_sources: Monod Cécile, Voekt Cora A., Gisin Martina, Gisin Stefan, Hoesli Irene M. (2013). Optimization of competency in obstetrical emergencies: a role for simulation training. Archives of Gynecology and Obstetrics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00404-013-3111-6
